The black @-@ tailed jackrabbit is the most widely distributed jackrabbit ( Lepus species ) in North America . Native black @-@

tailed jackrabbits occur from the southern United States and northern Mexico through most of the western United States and Canada . They are the most abundant jackrabbit in the United States . Adult weight ranges from 2.6 to 7.7 pounds . The @-@ tailed jackrabbit is dark brown on the upper side and white on the underside . The long bushy ears are black . The front feet and lower sides are black tipped with white . The black tail is rather long with a black tip .

## Description

Black-tailed jackrabbits are the largest species of jackrabbit in North America. They can be identified by the black tips on their ears. These rabbits are dark brown on their upper side and white on their underside. They are larger than hares and have longer ears and darker fur.

## Habitat

The black-tailed jackrabbit is a non-migratory species of rabbit that lives in both open and rocky areas of deserts and prairies, as well as in agricultural fields.

## Reproduction

Breeding occurs year round, but the peak is in the spring and summer months. Black-tailed jackrabbits live in groups of up to 12 individuals.

## Predators

Black-tailed jackrabbits are prey to many birds of prey, including hawks, owls, and falcons. Coyotes, mountain lions, and bobcats also prey on black-tailed jackrabbits.

## Conservation

Black-tailed jackrabbits are not threatened.

Anekāntavāda played a pivotal role in the growth as well as the survival of Jainism in ancient India , especially against onsla

ught of the so-called Vedic Hinduism.
Anekāntavāda is the basic philosophy of Jainism and it is different from the similar sounding term nāstika (meaning atheist). The Jainas believe in a Supreme Being (Saundarya).
Anekāntavāda is the principle of the Jaina philosophy. It means "the doctrine of the relativity of truth".
(1) The doctrine that truth has relative value.
(2) The doctrine that truth may be viewed from different standpoints, according to the capacity, the time, the circumstances, the viewpoint of the perceiver.
(3) The doctrine that truth may be viewed from different viewpoints.
(4) The doctrine that truth may be viewed from different angles.
(5) The doctrine that no one viewpoint can claim that it has the absolute truth.
(6) The doctrine that there is no one viewpoint that can claim to be the absolute and ultimate.
Anekāntavāda is the central concept of Jainism. It is the key to understand the religion.
Relativism, pluralism, religious tolerance, liberalism, secularism, pluralism, holism, subjectivism, multiculturalism, Gandhian ahimsa, vegetarianism, and bhakti are all basics of the philosophy of anekāntavāda.
One of the most important aspects of anekāntavāda is its connection with non-violent conflict resolution (Ahimsa).
Anekāntavāda is the basis of ethics and morals.
It is the basis of the world view of the Jainas.
Anekāntavāda is the basis of science and skepticism.
It is also the foundation for the development of philosophy and logic.
The Jainas believe in the doctrine of Anekāntavāda. Jainism is the only religion in the world that has the doctrine of Anekāntavāda as its basis.
In the Jaina religion, Anekāntavāda is the supreme principle.
The famous Arthashastra of Kautilya, the political science treatise of the ancient Indian King Chandragupta, also contains the principle of Anekāntavāda.
The Arthashastra was written in the 4th century BC. It is the oldest surviving treatise of political science.
In ancient and medieval India, Anekāntavāda was used in the area of politics, governance, economics, trade, law and administration.
The potential of Anekāntavāda was understood by ancient Indians. That is why they used it in various fields of human activity.
In the 19th century, Anekāntavāda was used by Mahatma Gandhi and his followers to develop his philosophy of non-violence (Ahimsa) and liberate the Indian people from British rule.
The Indian Constitution, the supreme document of India, was ratified in December 1949. The Constitution is based on the principle of Anekāntavāda.

Oscar Hornung left Eton College in 1914 , intending to enter King 's College , Cambridge later that year . When Britain entered

the First World War , he was one of the few pupils to volunteer for the British Army right away. The course was regarded as an important part of the education of all pupils at Eton, and most of them would have followed it.
Manning the trenches was a bloody, unpleasant, and often futile business, but it was crucial to the Allies winning the war. It was a major focus of Hornung's writing, which he began in 1917, and which he continued to write after the war until his death in 1972. His experience of the trenches in the Great War, and his experience of life in Britain after the war, were central to his writing.
The work of a conscientious objector such as Hornung was difficult to accept. The public were reluctant to believe that pacifism was anything but a sham. The poet Siegfried Sassoon wrote that, 'no one, I think, has ever been shot for refusing to fight', although he was probably thinking of the only five men to be executed for refusing to fight in the First World War. The Eton College Magazine complained that Hornung would not be allowed to take a degree, but he did so in 1921, after a long period of controversy and an unsuccessful legal case.
Hornung's refusal to serve in the war meant that he was subject to a lengthy period of ostracism from society, and his writing about the war was groundbreaking. He was one of the first writers to describe the war from a pacifist position, and to describe the realities of trench warfare. His writings were brutally honest. He described war as 'organised murder', and he criticised the soldiers and officers who were prepared to fight in the war for 'glory'.
Hornung's work was well received. His memoir, Making Friends, was first published in 1931 and became a bestseller. It was praised by authors such as Graham Greene and William Faulkner, and reviewers described it as 'the most remarkable war book of the year'.
Hornung's work was also admired by other war writers. Anthony Powell called him 'the greatest English war writer', and Philip Larkin considered him to be the greatest war poet.
Siegfried Sassoon was another officer who refused to fight in the First World War. His poem 'Counter-Attack' shows the difficulties faced by those who refused to fight in the war.

This war, like every war, was a bloody and brutal business. How do you think the experience of war affected the generation who fought in it, and how was this reflected in their writing?
The 'peace' that followed the Great War was far from peaceful. Many of the men and women who had fought in the war were deeply traumatised by their experiences, and they struggled to readjust to civilian life. How do you think the experience of war affected the society in which these men and women lived?
How do you think people in the West were affected by the war after it had ended? What accounts do you know about the effect it had on the lives of people in the West?
Being a conscientious objector in the First World War was a difficult and lonely experience. How do you think the experience of being a conscientious objector has changed in the West?
Having lived through the First World War, Hornung was able to write about the war with real insight. Do you think his experience of the war made him a good writer?

On April 18, 1949, Montreal defenceman Doug Harvey took a puck to the face during a game at the Montreal Forum against the Chicago Black Hawks.  Harvey was rushed to hospital where he received 17 stitches to close the wound.  Harvey spent the next two days in the hospital, and was given a blood transfusion, as medical experts thought he would die from internal bleeding.  Harvey's mother, Jeanette Harvey, was asked by doctors if they could perform more tests on her son, which she refused.  Mrs. Harvey later said that she knew her son would survive, and that the transfusion was likely unnecessary.  Harvey was released from hospital on April 22, and returned to the Montreal Canadiens the following day.

The location chosen for the operation was between the headland of Gaba Tepe and the Fisherman 's Hut , three miles ( 4 @.@ 8 km

) east of Lone Pine, a place so remote that it was not even on the map of the region. The place had not yet been properly named. Later, it became known as Anzac Cove , but at that stage it was simply regarded as a place to land troops. The Turks would be waiting for an invasion that never came.
 The Australian and New Zealand forces were to land on the morning of 25 April 1915, under the command of General William Birdwood. In total, there were 24,000 Australian and New Zealand troops on the beachhead, supported by the 8,000 British troops who came ashore at the same time.
At 4.30 am, the first troops landed on the beach. They were the first of eight waves of troops that would be landed in the hours after sunrise. It was a brave landing, but they did not know the enemy was behind the cliffs, waiting to fire down on them. The first shots landed on the cliffs above and behind them, sending them scrambling for cover. In the end, 264 Australians and 290 British servicemen were killed, and another 1,000 wounded.

The fieldfare ( Turdus pilaris ) is a member of the thrush family Turdidae . It breeds in woodland and scrub in northern Europe

and western and central Asia .
The fieldfare is mainly resident in the British Isles , but northern birds are migratory, wintering south.
The fieldfare was formerly known as the rustic thrush, a name no longer in use.
The fieldfare is 18 cm ( 7 in ) long and weighs 35 g ( 1.2 oz ). The adult has a dark grey back and wings and a pale grey belly; the tail and head are dark with a white eyebrow. The sexes are similar, but the juvenile has a browner head.
Like many thrushes, the fieldfare is a bulky bird with a broad head and a short tail. The bill, legs and feet are black.
The adult fieldfare's call is a rough, mechanical tchew , but it also gives a deep, energetic chur chur chur, churr chur chur and a three-note whistle.
The fieldfare breeds in open coniferous and mixed woodland in northern Europe and winters in more southerly woodland.
The range of the fieldfare is expanding to the north in Europe as the coniferous forests of the north spread.
Its normal food is berries, particularly the fruit of rowan and hawthorn, and it also eats seeds, insects and worms.
The breeding season is from late April to early August, but the fieldfare may nest from mid-April to mid-July. The nest is a shallow cup made of grasses, moss and leaves, lined with hair and feathers.
The clutch is usually 4-5 eggs, which are incubated by both parents for 12-13 days. The young have a glossy black bill and brown eyes, and are able to fly about 10 days after hatching.
The fieldfare is near-threatened in England and Wales . It is a common bird in the north and east, but uncommon in the west and south.
The species is increasing in the UK, but this is partly due to the encroachment of coniferous forests.
The fieldfare is hunted by raptors and its numbers fluctuate as a result of changes in the availability of suitable food. Its numbers have also declined since the 1970s, although the reasons for this are unclear.
The fieldfare is not considered threatened by man.

* A painting has many colors, each with its own hue.
* A building has many rooms, each with its own door.
* A person has multiple personalities.

Thus, Jains believe that "truth is not a fixed entity, but flexible, changeable and relative."

According to Jains, syādvāda (inferentialism) is the way to determine the truth.

Syādvāda is a philosophical epistemology that allows Jains to accept the truths claimed by other systems without contradicting their own beliefs. More precisely, syādvāda teaches that truth is always limited, and that all truths are partial and relative. This means that the truths of one's own belief system cannot be used to refute the truth of another's belief system. Instead, they should be accepted as partial and relative truths.

The format of television sitcoms has been a complex one since the inception of the genre. The series can be viewed as either a cont _orporate_ or st _ructural_ unit. The structural unit is the scene or episode in which a particular plot point is resolved (Gist 1994: 8). In the former, the series is viewed as a whole, and the structural unit is the episode. In the latter, the series is viewed as a series of separate scenes which can be watched independently of each other, and the structural unit is the scene.
There are two main types of structure which can be identified in the sitcom. First, there are sitcoms which are structured as an ongoing serial narrative. In these series, each episode is built around a key situational set-up and a climax, which is resolved in the course of the episode. Second, there are sitcoms which are structured as a series of related episodes which share the same setting or common characters. In these series, resolution of plot points is achieved through the development of the characters rather than through the narrative. This chapter will focus on the former type of structure, which is the more common type of sitcom structure.
One of the key elements of the sitcom is the _set-up_ – a situation which introduces the key characters and the main problem which arises in the course of the episode. The set-up _and_ the solution to the problem, in other words the climax of the episode, are key moments in the sitcom structure. Thus, the key action of the episode is contained in the set-up and the climax and the rest of the scene is usually taken up with the _conflict_ – the problem which arises between the characters in the course of the episode.
The set-up is traditionally carried out by one of the main characters, thus setting in motion the problem which forms the basis for the rest of the episode. In the course of the episode, the characters attempt to resolve the problem, ultimately reaching a _climax_ – a key moment of resolution in the course of the scene. The resolution involves some new information being revealed about the characters, for example, the other characters' reactions to the problem or a new development in the problem itself. The characters then attempt to deal with the new information in such a way that it further complicates the problem and in the process, creates a further opportunity for the characters to attempt to resolve the problem. The process of the characters attempting to resolve the problem is then repeated until the climax of the episode is reached.
The sitcom is a closed form in that, unlike the narrative film, there is no possibility of a happy ending. In the narrative film, the resolution to the problem arises with the ending, although sometimes this is a tragic ending in which the characters fail to resolve the problem. Thus, in the narrative film, it is possible to have a happy ending which results in the characters overcoming the problem. In the sitcom, however, the resolution to the problem is not a result of the ending but rather a result of the continuous action of the episode. Thus, the resolution of the problem arises not at the end of the episode, but throughout the episode.
The resolution of the problem is a result of the characters' new understanding of the situation which has been compounded by their attempts to resolve the problem. As a result of the characters' actions, the situation has changed, and the characters now have a different understanding of the problem. This new understanding leads to their ability to successfully resolve the problem. The resolution of the problem, however, is not a result of the characters' individual efforts, but rather a result of their collective efforts. This is because the resolution of the problem is not the result of the characters' individual understanding of the problem, but rather the result of their collective understanding of the problem stemming from their collective attempts to resolve the problem. This, in turn, results in the characters' new understanding of the problem and their collective resolution of the problem.

This process is carried on over the course of the episode and results in the resolution of the problem. It is in this process of the characters' attempts to resolve the problem that the comedy of the sitcom lies.

It is the common view that the dodo was a flightless bird . In fact, it was (9,10) seen to fly by witnesses , and it is unlikely that the bird was flightless , since it was able to fly the 200 m to the water in order to swim to and from the island . It is more likely that the dodo was incapable of sustained flight .
The dodo was almost certainly the result of a hybridization between an ancestral species of pigeon , and the noddy . This is supported by the evidence of the skeleton (11-14) , and by the discovery of the remains of a pigeon-like bird in the same deposits . This hybridization occurred on Mauritius .
The dodo's last population was isolated on Réunion , and the island's faunal history suggests that it was isolated from the rest of the Mascarene Islands at least 2 Ma .
The dodo was probably a solitary, or at least a very shy , species , and it may have been nocturnal .
 It is generally thought that the dodo was a fruit-eater . In fact, the only definite evidence for its diet is from the stomach contents of one specimen , which contained 30% fruit , but it is possible that the dodo's diet was less frugivorous .
The dodo's feathers were used to distinguish it from the Mauritius grey pigeon , and it is possible that the dodo's feathers were used to make tails for the European sailors who arrived on the island in the 16th century .
 The dodo was so easily killed by the sailors that it was not long before the population of the island was reduced to a mere handful . The last two specimens were a male and a female , and their skins were prepared by the sailors and kept on board a ship .
The first written account of the dodo was by a sailor on the Dutch ship "Le Geelvinck", which called at Mauritius in 1601 or 1602 .
The dodo was one of the first birds to be described scientifically , in 1605-6, by Joris Coenraets , a Dutch sailor who was in Mauritius in 1601 .
The last specimen was killed by sailors from the Dutch East India Company in 1662 .

## Plot

On December 31, 1988, the weather takes an unexpected turn for the worse, with heavy rain and snowfall. As a result, New Year's Eve celebrations are cancelled. In the evening, the police department receives a report of a missing person. A man claiming to be the brother of the missing person calls the station, claiming to have seen the missing person. The missing person turns out to be a police officer, and the caller is later revealed to be none other than Chiaki Itoh, a police officer, who has been missing for ten years.

The following day, on January 1, 1989, the police station receives a report that the man claiming to be Chiaki's brother has been spotted. The call is received by Professor Hiroshi Konishi, a professor at the university where the police department is located, who has been working on a project known as "BSI", which involves using the "Memories of the Past" to investigate crimes. Memories of the Past (also known as Dark Memory, or DM) is a fictional technology that allows users to see memories from the past. When the police were first informed of the missing person, they were able to see where Chiaki was and had been. The BSI project was initially established to investigate the murder of a woman in the university. The professor thought that it was possible to use Memories of the Past as a crime-solving tool.

The police are able to track down Chiaki's brother, but he is shot and killed by an unknown assailant. The police are left with only a recording of the voice of the man claiming to be Chiaki's brother. They use the voice recording to track down the man, who turns out to be a police officer named Kyoji Itoh, Chiaki's older brother. Kyoji tells the police that he is the real Chiaki, having been impersonated by his younger brother. The police are left with two possibilities: either Chiaki is still missing, or Kyoji is the missing person. The police are able to find the real Chiaki's residence, where they find a body. The body is identified as Chiaki, who had been dead for ten years.

The United Nations Military Assistance Program (UNMAP) was originally a subcommittee of the United Nations, called the Special Committee for the Military Assistance Program (SCMAP).
The program was born in the aftermath of the Second World War and was designed to help member nations become self-sufficient.
The U.S. was the largest contributor.
In 1978, however, the UNMAP became an independent organization.
The UNMAP budget soared, as did its number of employees.
The program was no longer a "special committee" but a full-blown organization.
As the organization grew, it began to control the world's economy, not merely by providing military assistance, but by developing businesses in the countries it was helping.
The United Nations Military Assistance Program was now an independent organization, separate from the UN.
The UNMAP's responsibilities expanded to include the creation of businesses, as well as military assistance.
The UNMAP's largest business venture was a large-scale oil refinery in the South China Sea that was built in the early 2000s.
The UNMAP's business operations in Asia were so vast that they employed over two million people.
In 2012, the UNMAP's annual budget was estimated to be over $1 trillion.
In 2006, the UNMAP began to expand into the Middle East.
The UNMAP's largest projects were oil refineries in Saudi Arabia and Iran and in 2012, it began work on a new oil refinery in Iraq.
The UNMAP also developed a large-scale oil refinery in Afghanistan and began construction on a new refinery in Pakistan.
The UNMAP's largest energy project was a nuclear power plant in North Korea.
In 2013, the United Nations Military Assistance Program was dissolved and replaced by the United Nation's Security Council.
The Council, however, was unable to control the UNMAP's operations.
The U.N.'s budget was cut in half by the UN's decision to dissolve the UNMAP in 2013.
The UNMAP has continued to grow, as has its influence.

## Plot

The plot is based around the premise that the protagonist Hamlet, and his mother Gertrude, are both having an affair with Claudius, the new king of Denmark. Hamlet's father, the previous king, died not long before the play opens, and Hamlet suspects foul play. A ghost appears to him and tells him that the ghost is his father, who was murdered by Claudius. The ghost claims that Claudius is the new king because he murdered the previous king, Hamlet's father, and, to add to the plot, the ghost is also Hamlet's mother's lover. Hamlet decides to put on an act, and pretend to be insane, in order to find out the truth.

## Critical reception

Reviewing the musical at the Donmar Warehouse, Charles Spencer of The Guardian wrote: "This production is directed by Peter Hall with the unstinting flair and imagination that have marked out his career as probably the most ingenious director of the last half-century." He added: "The show is so bizarre that you can hardly believe that it works. But work it does, and it works very well indeed. Oldham's first public theatre was the Theatre Royal, which was built in 1832 by the Oldham Amateur Dramatic Society, who had formed the previous year. From 1841 the Oldham Operatic Society leased the theatre from the town council. It was destroyed by fire in 1853.

The Lyceum Theatre, Oldham, in 1894
In 1894 the Oldham Operatic Society leased the Theatre Royal for a period of five years and it was renamed the Lyceum Theatre. The society took over the lease and the building was renamed the Lyceum in 1901. In 1906 the Lyceum was purchased by the Oldham Co-operative Society and they sold it in 1926 to the Oldham Corporation Trades and Labour Council.
The Lyceum Theatre of 1927[edit]
The Lyceum Theatre of 1927
The theatre was demolished in 1927 and a new theatre was built in its place. The theatre was designed by Thomas Henry Worthington and built by T. H. Worthington and Son. The theatre opened on 26 June 1927 with a performance of the play The Clairvoyant. It had a seating capacity of 1,250 and was owned by the Oldham Corporation Trades and Labour Council. The theatre hosted several exhibitions, including the Oldham Arts and Crafts Exhibition in 1929 and the Oldham Industrial Exhibition in 1935. The theatre closed in 1948 when it was gutted by fire and reopened in 1952 as the Lyceum Cinema and Bingo Hall.[1]
The Lyceum Theatre of 1986[edit]
In 1986 the theatre was purchased by the Oldham Theatre Trust, renamed the Lyceum Theatre and restored as a theatre. It had a seating capacity of 950. The theatre was closed in 1998 due to financial difficulties.
The Lyceum Ballroom[edit]
In 1951 the Lyceum Cinema and Bingo Hall opened behind the theatre, and in 1952 it was renamed the Lyceum Ballroom. It was used for dancing and it contained a theatre which seated 1,200. The ballroom was also used for concerts. In 1970 the ballroom was renamed the Lyceum Ballroom and Music Bar. The ballroom closed in 1991.

# **THE PERFECT MATCH**
 _The season 1961 – 62 was City's most successful ever. They finished third in the old Division Two, reached the fourth round of the FA Cup for the first time and also reached the semi-finals of the League Cup. The reason, the reason for all this success was quite simple. In the middle of the season, City acquired a goal machine, a player who could do everything well. He was a player of astonishing technique, who could pass, dribble, run, take a corner, shoot and head. He could even score goals from the halfway line. He was Dave Laing, City's new striker._ _1_
The name Dave Laing first appeared in City's squad in 1958, when he was bought from Newcastle United for £12,000. He was a tall, handsome, strikingly good-looking young fellow, who was immediately installed as the club's new captain. He had been born in Newcastle and began his professional career with the club in 1955. He was 20 years old when he signed for City, and had made his Football League debut for Newcastle when he was just 17. He had been capped for England at Under 23 level.
Laing was almost certainly City's best ever player. He scored a remarkable 266 goals in 428 appearances for the club, and his record of 36 goals in 48 games during the 1961 – 62 season remains a club record. He was also City's first £100,000 player. The price was a lot of money in those days, but City were desperate to retain Laing's services and eventually agreed to pay the Newcastle club the huge fee.
Laing was born on 12 May 1936 and died on 27 January 2006, aged 69. After leaving City, he went on to play for Tottenham Hotspur, where he won the FA Cup in 1967, and then for Huddersfield Town, where he played until 1970.

Warren was born on Pitcairn Island on 28 June 1959 , the second child of Jacob Ralph " Chippie " Warren ( 1920 – 2007 ) and Mav

is Warren ( 1929 – 2007 ). After an unconventional childhood in which the family was evicted from their home on Pittcairn and lived for a time on the island of Norfolk , Warren attended a boarding school in the United Kingdom , where he was a talented athlete. He studied English literature at the School of Oriental and African Studies , London University , before travelling the world as a journalist. He met his future wife, Beverley Clarke , while studying in London and they married in September 1986 , having three children. He lived in Fiji and New Zealand before settling in Australia in 1994. Warren was a short story writer and poet who published four books of poetry, including his debut collection, A Field Guide to the Wetlands , in 1997. In subsequent years, Warren's prose books were published in Australia, Britain and the United States. His works included two acclaimed novels, The Thief's Journey ( 2002 ) and The Year of the Fist ( 2008 ), and a collection of essays, This Paper Water ( 2003 ). His poetry collections were published in 1999 as Thirst and in 2004 as He Drown She Drown , under the title of the former in Britain. His last book, The Blind Giant and Other Drawings , was published in 2007.
Warren had been diagnosed with cancer in 2004: he died on 21 February 2009 in Sydney , Australia , aged 49.

Wheeler and the brigade arrived in Italy on 20 November , and proceeded through the Italian Riviera to reach Caporetto , where

12th Brigade was relieved from front line duties in the valley of the Isonzo. The brigade was then sent to the Piave river, where it was to be employed in a number of minor actions against the Austrian forces.
The first of these, the Battle of the Solstice , occurred on 24 June 1918. During the battle, the brigade was heavily engaged, and its commander, Brigadier-General A. Jones, was killed. Wheeler's battalion, 1/1st Northumberland Fusiliers, was heavily engaged during the day, but managed to make a series of successful counter-attacks during the night. For his part in this, Wheeler was awarded the Military Cross.
The brigade was then sent to France in August 1918, and Wheeler was on leave in the United Kingdom at the time of Armistice.
After the war, Wheeler remained in the army, serving in India and Burma in the 1920s. He then commanded the 19th Battalion, the Royal Fusiliers, in India and Palestine, and then the 21st Battalion, Royal Fusiliers, during the next decade. He was given command of the 2nd Battalion, the Royal Fusiliers in 1936, and was promoted to major-general in 1938, the year after he was appointed Brigadier-General of the 24th Infantry Brigade.
Wheeler had a distinguished career in the Second World War, serving in France in 1940, and then in the Middle East, where he commanded the 1st Infantry Division between 1942 and 1943. He then served as Commander-in-Chief of the Burma Army from 1943 to 1944, and was responsible for the re-organisation of the Burmese Army and its re-entry into the Second World War. After the war, Wheeler was appointed Governor of the Falkland Islands in 1946, and was promoted to lieutenant-general in 1947. He retired from the army in 1948.
After leaving the army, Wheeler was appointed Governor of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines in 1948, and in 1952 Governor of Sierra Leone. He was made a Knight Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1952, and was promoted to Knight Grand Cross in 1960.
He died on 17 July 1969 at the age of 84.

The burning in 1789 of Christian Murphy , for coining , received practically no attention from the newspapers ( perhaps owing t

o the fact that the crime was perpetrated in the night time ). But in 1790, with the advent of the nascent opposition press, the story of the execution was widely covered and the anti-government newspapers seized on it as a means of attacking the administration. The case was, in fact, a miscarriage of justice. Murphy was subjected to a one-sided trial before the Privy Council and his coining was the result of a "mistake" on the part of his apprentice. The newspapers, however, ignored these facts and denounced him as a villain and a murderer.
I shall now relate to you an execrable murder, which has been lately committed in this city, and which has attracted the attention of every person.
On Wednesday the 2nd instant, the body of a young man was found lying in the street, near the place where he worked at the trade of a coiner . On examination by the attendants of the city, it was found that the deceased had a large wound on the left side of his temple, and that the blood had flowed copiously from the wound. The deceased was a young man, about nineteen or twenty years of age, of a very mild and gentle disposition; and was the apprentice of a Mr. Christian Murphy , a respectable coiner in the city. Soon after the discovery of the body, the deceased's master came to the city; and a few hours after, the evidence of the deceased being in a state of intoxication, it was concluded, by the city, that he had committed suicide.
This supposition was confirmed by the master of the deceased, who stated, that on the evening of the day previous to the discovery of the body, his apprentice came to him with his apron full of liquid silver, which was instantly detected as being spurious, and which the deceased declared he had coined but a few minutes before. This fact would seem to be perfectly conclusive; but when the apprentice was examined, he stated, that his master had instructed him how to make the spurious coinage, and that the poor young man had only been practising a trade which he had been taught by his master.
The case was then laid before the Privy Council, and on the 16th of March, it was unanimously agreed, that the deceased had murdered his master with malice aforethought, and that he was to be hanged on the 23rd of the same month.
This has been the conclusion of the whole business; and the public have been greatly surprised at the suspected impropriety of the conduct of the Privy Council.
Boston, April 15, 1790.
 A very melancholy and distressing case of murder has been lately brought under the cognizance of the Lords of the Privy Council . It was, on Thursday, the 17th instant, reported to the Lords of the Council, that a summons had been issued on the 15th instant, to the Sheriff of the county of Fife, for the apprehension of a certain Christian Murphy , who was charged with the murder of a person named John Wilson , coiner in the city of Edinburgh.
The Sheriff of Fife, on the receipt of the summons, caused the appellant to be brought before him, and the accusation against him was that he had murdered the said John Wilson , on the 13th instant, by stabbing him on the right side of the neck, and that the deceased died on the day following the murder, in consequence of the wound.
This was the state of the case upon which the appellant was committed to the castle of Edinburgh, to remain there until the day appointed for his trial at the bar of the Privy Council, viz., the 23rd instant.
On the day assigned for his trial, the appellant came before the Lords of the Council, to show cause why he should not be sentenced for the murder of John Wilson . The Lord Advocate, a person of honour and integrity, and well known to the generality of this country, being present on the occasion, laid the case fully before the Lords of the Council, and rendered a report of the facts which had come to his knowledge. The case was then committed to the consideration of the Lords of the Council, who were left to judge of the guilt or innocence of the accused person, on the evidence which had been laid before them.

When Tintin in the Congo was first released by the series ' Scandinavian publishers in 1975 , they objected to page 56 , where

20 000 Africans are shown being herded into the interior of the Belgian Congo by a white overseer .
In an attempt to defuse the outcry , the publishers argued that the 'upper lip' of the figure in the foreground was actually that of a black man , and that the white man's arm was in fact that of an African .
They also declared that the figure in the background who was leaning on a rifle , was in fact a black man .
This was not the only dispute that Tintin in the Congo provoked . The French publishers had had a major share in the movie rights to the adventures of Tintin , and from the beginning the movie producers had been wary of the idea of making a movie of the Congo story .
But they were persuaded to do so by the French Minister of Culture and the then Minister of State for the Arts , Jacquetot , who had a personal interest in the Congo story .
When the movie was finally made , it was a violent and brutal story .
The murder of the Belgian police commissioner at the beginning of the adventure , the killing of the man and the rape of his wife , the murder of the African boy at the hands of the Arab trafficker , the murder of the Arab by the villagers , the shooting of the villagers by the child soldiers and the killing of the trafficker by the rape victim , were all scenes that the movie producers felt would not be acceptable to the French authorities .
They therefore asked Professor Georges Marteau , a specialist in African culture , to 'edit' the movie and remove the offending scenes .
Professor Marteau agreed to do this , and stripped the film of five of the scenes .
However , the producers , concerned that some of the scenes might still be deemed too violent for French audiences , showed a reduced version of the film to the French Minister of State for the Arts , who had no objection to the film in its entirety .
The movie producers were delighted .
But when the film was subsequently released in the United States , it was a completely different story . The US distributors , who had been granted permission to release the movie in their own country , added the missing scenes back into the film .
The film was a box-office success , but it caused a major scandal in France , which led to an investigation into the movie by the French censorship board .
The scandal was so great that the French government decided to revoke all the movie rights that they held in Tintin .
The Belgian government was equally outraged by the movie , and the Belgian Minister of Culture demanded that the film be banned in his country .
In the light of these events , the Belgian publishers felt that they had to take a stand .
In 1975 , they reissued their Tintin books , and removed the three pages of the Congo story . The new editions , with the pages removed , were printed in 1975 .
The publishers were not at all pleased with this situation , and it was not until 1986 , when the book was reissued for the fifth time , that the story was once again reinstated .
But the damage had been done .
The book could no longer be seen as an edifying episode .

In Finkelstein 's doctoral thesis , he examined the claims made in Joan Peters 's From Time Immemorial , a best @-@ selling boo

@-@ k that tried to prove that most of the Arabs who reside in Israel are descendants of Jews who resettled there in the Middle Ages. Peters's book was published in 1984, and its central thesis was that there existed no Palestinians before the British Empire took control of Palestine.
Finkelstein's thesis was entitled: "Intoxication with Zion: A Study of Joan Peters's From Time Immemorial " [1988]. In this thesis, Finkelstein accused Peters of misrepresentation of the available evidence, and of falsifying data. He accused her of taking a "selective and self-serving approach to the evidence", in an attempt to prove her thesis.
The book was published by Merit Press in 1989.
The debate over the book's central thesis continued for many years.
In 1996, Finkelstein was appointed to the faculty of De Paul University's School of Communications, where he taught courses on the politics of the Middle East.
In 2000, he served as an adviser to the Palestinian delegation at Camp David.
In 2003, Finkelstein published Beyond Chutzpah: On the Misuse of Anti-Semitism and the Abuse of History . In this book, he argued that the Israeli-Palestinian conflict was not fueled by anti-Semitism, but rather by the interests of the Israeli state. The book became a New York Times bestseller  and was ranked by Publishers Weekly as one of the "top 25 best-selling books of 2005" .
In 2007, Finkelstein published The Holocaust Industry .
Finkelstein has been a frequent critic of the Israeli government, the Israeli lobby, and American foreign policy. In 2008, he was quoted as saying that Israel's treatment of the Palestinians was "the worst human rights violation in the world today".
In 2009, Finkelstein accused Israel of having a policy of "ethnic cleansing", in an article in The Nation .
In 2011, Finkelstein was accused by the Brandeis Center for Human Rights under Law of being anti-Semitic, after he called for the boycott of Israeli academic institutions.
Finkelstein has also been a strong critic of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), and has called for a US government investigation into its lobbying activities.
Finkelstein has been a vocal opponent of the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, which calls for a boycott of Israeli goods and services.
In 2008, Finkelstein was fired from DePaul University after he made comments about Israel that were deemed to be anti-Semitic by the university's administration.
In 2011, Finkelstein was banned from entering Israel after he was accused of making anti-Semitic statements.

In January 1844 , North Carolina Representative James Iver McKay , the chairman of the Committee on Ways and Means , solicited

the citizens of his district to supply information about the state's debt and assets. McKay, who would later serve as a U.S. congressman, governor, and president of the National Bank of North Carolina, wanted to know whether the convention should meet in Raleigh or in one of the other counties in the district. He also wanted to know whether the state should continue to operate under a two-year budget cycle, as was the case with most of the states, or should implement a single-year budget cycle.
In response to McKay's request, Wake County citizens sent him a list of questions about the state's finances. One of the most important questions, in their view, was whether the state should go into debt to fund a railroad system. They noted that although the state had recently issued bonds to fund internal improvements, the state's debt was still relatively low in relation to its assets. They argued that the state could easily afford to issue bonds for the railroads, which they argued would benefit counties outside Wake by stimulating commerce and travel. This view was, in fact, the prevailing opinion among the state's lawmakers.
During a debate about the state debt in the late 1840s, the _North Carolina Standard_ , a Democratic newspaper published in Wilmington, wrote that the state's debt was not excessive and that the railroads would make the debt more manageable. "North Carolina is one of the most prosperous and wealthy States on the continent," the paper argued. "She is growing in wealth and population, and has a well-filled treasury; and the only question that remains to be solved is, is she now, and will she hereafter, be able to pay the interest and the principal of her public debt, and can she make the roads, and other great enterprises that are necessary to her welfare? and if the answer to the questions be in the affirmative, then it is only a question of expediency, whether she now or hereafter shall have public roads, and other great enterprises."
To the paper's way of thinking, the state could afford to borrow money to build railroads. "It is nearly the same as if the State had large resources in the shape of large loans, that can be carried on with a small interest," the paper argued. "She has the railroads, and locomotives, and cars; and the interest and the repairs are comparatively nothing; and those who are not satisfied with this conclusive argument may have a great many more."
The _Standard_ was right, in this instance, about the state's ability to repay its debt. In 1849, the state's total debt amounted to only about 2.5 percent of its assets. The paper was also right about the benefits that railroads would bring to the state. As the state's railroad network expanded, the state's economy did as well. The growth in railroad traffic, in turn, led to increased revenues for the state. Between 1849 and 1855, for example, the state's railroad-related revenues increased from $4,156 to $20,351.
The state's railroad development, however, did not come without controversy. Many of the state's lawmakers believed that the state's railroad system was too expensive and that the money spent on the railroads should have been spent on other public improvements. During a debate about the issue in 1851, James L. Powell complained that the state was spending millions of dollars on the railroads while other public improvements were going unfunded. "How is this, my friends?" Powell asked. "We have lots of other public improvements to make that are much more important than railroads, and which ought to be made."
Powell's concerns were well founded. The state was spending a lot of money on the railroads, and the state was not getting the returns that it deserved from those investments. The state's railroads, as it turned out, were underfunded, and the state's railroad system was not as efficient as it could have been. The state's railroads, for example, were not equipped with the latest technology, and the state's railroad network was not connected.

The exploration of Jupiter has been conducted via close observations by automated spacecraft . It began with the arrival of Pio

lets Cassini at Jupiter in 1995. The first and most successful of Jupiter's moons to be explored was Io. It was discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610 and was visited by the Galileo spacecraft in 1999 and 2000. Jupiter's second known moon, Europa, was discovered in 1610 by Galileo. In 2003, the probe, Galileo, found evidence of a subsurface ocean of water on Europa and the possibility of life . The third and fourth moons to be discovered were not discovered until 1610 by Galileo. Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, with a diameter greater than that of the planet Mercury. Callisto , the fourth of Jupiter's moons, is only slightly smaller than Ganymede. The next discovery came in the form of five inner moons, which were discovered in 1999 by the Cassini spacecraft. The last known moon to be discovered was discovered in 2002 by the Cassini spacecraft.
 The exploration of Jupiter was one of the main goals of the Jupiter Icy Moons Orbiter (JIMO) and Jupiter Europa Orbiter (JEO) missions in the 2010s, but was cancelled in 2010 as funding was removed. 

## History

### Voyager 1 and Voyager 2

Main article: Jupiter flyby

In 1979, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 flew by Jupiter and sent back images of its atmosphere. The Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11 spacecraft also flew by Jupiter over the course of their exploration of the solar system.

### Galileo

Main article: Galileo orbiter

Galileo launched in 1989 and studied Jupiter for eight years, before crashing into the planet in 2003.

### Cassini

Main article: Cassini–Huygens

Cassini-Huygens transferred into Jupiter's orbit in 2000 and remained there for a year.

### Juno

Main article: Juno (spacecraft)

Juno launched in 2011 and arrived in orbit around Jupiter in 2016, where it is currently studying the planet.

### Europa Clipper

Main article: Europa Clipper

Europa Clipper launched in 2024 on a mission to study Jupiter's moon Europa.

### Others

Other missions that explored Jupiter include:

* Galileo Probe, which was released from Galileo spacecraft on 7 December 1999 and impacted Jupiter on 21 September 2003
* Jupiter Icy Moons Orbiter, a mission that would have been launched in 2018 and arrived in the Jovian system in 2020 to study the moons of Jupiter.
* Jupiter Europa Orbiter, a mission that would have been launched in 2018 and arrived in the Jovian system in 2020 to study the moons of Jupiter.
* Jupiter Ganymede Orbiter, a mission that would have been launched in 2018 and arrived in the Jovian system in 2020 to study the moons of Jupiter.
* Jupiter Science Orbiter, a mission that would have been launched in 2017 and arrived in the Jovian system in 2022 to study the moons of Jupiter.
* Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, a mission that would have been launched in 2022 and arrived in the Jovian system in 2029 to study the moons of Jupiter.

The surface composition of Ceres is broadly similar to that of C @-@ type asteroids . Some differences do exist . The ubiquitou

es carbonaceous chondrites are exceptional in containing organic matter, and Ceres is a carbonaceous asteroid . A carbonaceous C-type asteroid B is the most similar to Ceres in terms of its composition. Consistent with this, there are a number of similarities. Both are fairly spherical in shape, are relatively dark in color (Bp > 0.5) and have similar albedos (A = 0.06-.08),  but their spectra are different . The spectra of both B and Ceres are dominated by a strong 0.8 μm absorption feature, and both have a high albedo in the near-infrared. In addition, Ceres is a relatively low-density object, with an estimated density of 2.2 g cm−3 , while B is even lower at 1.9 g cm−3 . Ceres is also less differentiated than other asteroids of comparable size. The surface of Ceres is covered by a relatively thin layer of dust (~100 m thick) on top of which are deposits of hydrated minerals .
Ceres is the only member of the C-type asteroid family Ceres after the discovery of the dwarf planet in 1801 and is the largest object in the asteroid belt . The surface of Ceres is covered by an 100 m-thick layer of dust, with a large equatorial belt, which is flanked by less-bright "dark spots". At the center of the dark region is a 90 km-wide bright spot (diameter 90 km, albedo 0.15) that was first observed in 1801 and has puzzled astronomers ever since. The bright spot has a somewhat elliptical shape and rotates with a period of 9.6 h. A second, much smaller (5 km), bright spot, was imaged in 2004 by the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) .
Dust particles on the surface of Ceres have been detected by ground-based telescopes, and the OSIRIS-REx spacecraft will collect samples for return to Earth.
The ceramic-like mineral pyroxene is found on the asteroid (1) Ceres and is used by the OSIRIS-REx spacecraft for thermal control.

The asteroid belt is located between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. It is the region where most asteroids and other small Solar System bodies are found.

After ending his work at Verulamium , Wheeler turned his attention to the late Iron Age hill @-@ fort of Maidan Castle near to

Abergele in Wales. The first phase of excavations  were undertaken by the Maiden Castle  Excavation Fund  in 1896–7,  and Wheeler undertook a second phase in 1898–9. The results of these digs were published in 1899,  and a third and final phase was undertaken in 1910. The location of the hill fort is about half a mile inland from the north coast of Wales in the shadow of the cliffs of the Great Orme. The fort had a defensive ditch which was 12 feet wide,  and has been dated to the late Iron Age.

Wheeler's excavations at Maiden Castle were followed by further works at the site in the 1920s and 1930s by Glyn Edwards. When Wheeler returned to the site in 1910, he found the hill fort was occupied by a farmer and his livestock. Wheeler found the presence of cattle in the area to be an impediment to his work, but he was able to persuade the farmer to allow him to keep his cattle in a neighbouring field.

Oldham ( i/ˈoʊldəm/) is a large town in Greater Manchester, England,[1] with a population of 103,530 in 2011.[2] It lies amongst the Pennines, 5.3 miles (8.5 km) east of Rochdale, and 6.9 miles (11.1 km) north-northwest of the city of Manchester. Historically in Lancashire, Oldham is surrounded by the towns of Chadderton, Royton, Lees and Failsworth, as well as the villages of Delph, Sladeford and Dukinfield. In the 18th century, Oldham was a small rural township in the ancient parish of Chadderton in the large township of Oldham in the Salford Hundred.[3]
Oldham's early history is that of a number of separate settlements around the old market place, including the townships of Chadderton and Saddleworth. In 1894, the township of Oldham was incorporated as a municipal borough, with the townships of Chadderton and Saddleworth. In 1910, the Municipal Borough of Oldham was formed, with an area of 10,369 acres (4,199 ha) and a population of 108,303.[4] In 1932, the Municipal Borough of Oldham was extended to take in the urban districts of Chadderton and Saddleworth, forming the County Borough of Oldham. In 1974, under the Local Government Act 1972, the county borough was abolished and its former area was transferred to Greater Manchester.
Oldham has a temperate climate, with cool summers and mild winters. The town has a long and varied history, and was first recorded in the Domesday Book as being in the hundred of Salford. Oldham's early history is that of a number of separate settlements around the old market place, including the townships of Chadderton and Saddleworth, which was historically part of the West Riding of Yorkshire. In 1894, the township of Oldham was incorporated as a municipal borough, with the townships of Chadderton and Saddleworth. In 1910, the Municipal Borough of Oldham was formed, with an area of 10,369 acres (4,199 ha) and a population of 108,303.[4] In 1932, the Municipal Borough of Oldham was extended to take in the urban districts of Chadderton and Saddleworth, forming the County Borough of Oldham. In 1974, under the Local Government Act 1972, the county borough was abolished and its former area was transferred to Greater Manchester.
Oldham is the birthplace of the co-operative movement and was the first to install electric lighting outside London. The town's economy relied heavily on the cotton industry, but the industry declined due to increased mechanisation and stiff competition from the Low Countries and India. Oldham's economy has moved away from manufacturing to a service base and is home to companies and organisations in the private and public sectors. Oldham is one of the world's largest producers of textiles and clothing, and the UK's largest centre for textile-related businesses. The town's coat of arms was granted in 1961, depicting a cotton boll and a pair of compasses.

The original design was based on a pulsed laser pointer with a battery and an electronic circuit that temporarily increased the current to the laser diode so that a brighter and more intense flash could be achieved.

##
The first mention of the Wiśniowiecki family dates back to 1340, when the Wiśniowiecki coat of arms appeared in the chronicles of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, in the coat of arms of the Sapieha family. The coat of arms represents two crossed oak branches. It is not known why this particular coat of arms was chosen by the Sapiehas; however, the coat of arms of the Wiśniowiecki family bears a striking resemblance to the coat of arms of the Sapiehas.
Another theory suggests that the Wiśniowiecki coat of arms was introduced in the second half of the fourteenth century by the Wiśniowiecki clan that originated in the area of Wiśniowiec, near Lviv (Lwów), on the territories of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth . This theory is based on the coat of arms of the Wiśniowiecki clan, which represents a trefoil, a symbol of the heraldry of the Wiśniowieckis.
The first mention of Wiśniowiecki, as a surname, can be found in the chronicles dating back to 1413. The Wiśniowiecki clan was composed of several branches (groups): Wiśniowiecki–Mohylany (Wisniowiecki–Mościski), Wiśniowiecki–Berezowice (Wisniowiecki–Bereżowice), Wiśniowiecki–Kamieniórki (Wisniowiecki–Kamieńiołki), Wiśniowiecki–Konopki (Wisniowiecki–Konopki), Wiśniowiecki–Wierzbica (Wisniowiecki–Wierzbica), Wiśniowiecki–Dolina (Wisniowiecki–Dolina), Wiśniowiecki–Kolonia (Wisniowiecki–Kolonia), Wiśniowiecki–Łańcuchy (Wisniowiecki–Łańcuchy), Wiśniowiecki–Łopienka (Wisniowiecki–Łopienka), Wiśniowiecki–Małopolska (Wisniowiecki–Małopolska), Wiśniowiecki–Michałów (Wisniowiecki–Michałów), Wiśniowiecki–Nowa Wieś (Wisniowiecki–Nowa Wieś), Wiśniowiecki–Misztal (Wisniowiecki–Misztal), Wiśniowiecki–Olesnikowce (Wisniowiecki–Olesnikowce), Wiśniowiecki–Pustelnia (Wisniowiecki–Pustelnia), Wiśniowiecki–Ruda (Wisniowiecki–Ruda).

From the Rocky Mountains of Montana and Wyoming , three streams rise to form the headwaters of the Missouri River . The longest

of these three is the Bighorn , which flows out of the Great Plains to join the Missouri near Fort Benton, Montana. It was this stream, the Bighorn, that led the Lewis and Clark expedition to the edge of the Rockies and the westward expansion of the United States .
The Bighorn River was a key to the American West. It provided the easiest path through the mountains and into the heart of the great plains. Over the years, American history has been written along the banks of this river. In 1800, the Bighorn was the route of the Lewis and Clark expedition. Later, the Bighorn became the lifeline for homesteaders and ranchers, and the route of explorers and hunters flying in and out of the west.
In the 1960s, the Bighorn River became the proving ground for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. If the Bighorn could be controlled, then any river in America could be controlled. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built a dam on the Bighorn and flooded the canyon. The river was no longer a living stream, but a reservoir, a manmade lake. The Bighorn became a dam.
And the Bighorn's water was taken.
The water that was stored behind the dam flowed into irrigation canals, where it was used to grow wheat, alfalfa, and sugar beets. The water was used to irrigate cattle ranches, to make beer, and to grow grass. There was plenty of water—enough water for everyone. But the Bighorn River was a dam, not a river.
Who can remember the great, blue water of the Bighorn River ? Who can remember the brown water of the dammed Bighorn ?
Who can remember a river ?

The main mode of play in the Guitar Hero games is Career Mode , where the player and in @-@ game band travel between various fi

xtures, battling their way to the top of the music world.
The player chooses a band name and then a lead guitarist, bassist, drummer and vocalist (the fifth character, a roadie, is chosen automatically). The player then travels between various venues, battling against other bands to gain fans, and working towards unlocking new songs and venues to play.
A typical show begins with an audience excited to see the band perform, with the crowd's energy building as the band plays songs. When the energy level is high enough, the audience will cheer at the end of a song. The player receives the crowd's energy by playing the correct notes during the song, and can use that energy to unleash various power-ups including, for example, "Overdrive," which temporarily increases the note duration to easier levels. If the audience is not given enough energy, they will begin to become disinterested, and if the player continues not to give the audience energy, the audience will leave, and the player must keep playing until the audience returns.
The player can choose to play an instrument as they play, allowing them to control the lead guitarist, bassist, drummer or vocalist.
Songs are unlocked as the player progresses through the game, and the player can choose which songs they want to play in each set. In addition, the player can unlock new songs by playing the song on all the difficulties, and then playing the song on the next higher difficulty.
The show ends with a song selection screen, and the player is allowed to choose which venue to play at next.
There are four difficulty levels, with the easiest level being "Beginner," the second being "Expert," and the hardest being "Guitar Hero."
The player also has the option of playing a Quickplay set for some quick action, or playing Challenge Mode , where the player must perform a certain number of songs (depending on the difficulty) in a row without missing any.
Special Venues and Modes are also available, such as "VS" (where players compete against each other to see who can get the most fans), "Battle" (where the player competes against the computer to play as many songs as possible), "Duo" (where a second player can join in), and "Free Play" (where the player can play any song with any difficulty they wish, including those that have not been unlocked yet).
The player can also play a Jam Session , where they are given a random song and a random instrument, and must play the song on that instrument.
The player is given a rating at the end of each song according to how they performed, from "Fantastic" (the best) to "Poor" (the worst). The player's rating is also displayed on the screen while the song is playing, so the player knows if they are doing well or not.
The player also earns fans by playing songs, and can use those fans to unlock new songs, play as a different instrument, or choose a different venue. The player also earns fans by performing well in challenges and in special venues.
Players can also allow their friends to join in their game by sending out an invite, or by joining in on another player's game.

Roads leading out of Mogadishu connect the city to other localities in Somalia as well as to neighbouring countries . The capit

als of the small Somali states of Puntland and Somaliland are connected by road to Mogadishu .
As the capital of Somalia , Mogadishu is also the seat of the federal government and of the Somali parliament . It is also the financial capital of Somalia , home to the central bank , the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Commerce. Mogadishu is also an important diplomatic hub, with 62 embassies and consulates being represented in the city.
Mogadishu is divided into six districts: Hodan , Waberi , Hamarwet , Yaqshim , Kahda and Shibis.
The city is home to the University of Mogadishu .
The current location of the city was first settled in the 1st century, near the mouth of the River Shebelle . It is believed to have been an important port on the Indian Ocean , since the 1st century. The city was referred to by the ancient Greeks as "Abraxas". Ancient Greek writers also called it "Barbara", a name which has been used in the Somali language as a female given name until the 20th century. The city was known by Romans as "Lucistus" or "Lucistania". According to the 15th-century chronicler Ahmed ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi ("Ghazi"), the city was founded by a legendary Somali king named "Bara Darod".
The city was conquered and occupied by the Abyssinians in the 8th century and the city became part of Abyssinia , under the name "Dabar". In 1425, the city was taken by Sultan Yusuf I of the Adal Sultanate and it became part of the Adal Sultanate. The Oromo people governed the city from the 17th to the 19th century. The Italians invaded the city in 1925, and it was incorporated into the Italian colony of Somalia in 1927.
During the Italian rule, Mogadishu became a major port and a business centre. The city's population grew significantly. After independence in 1960, Mogadishu became the capital of the new Somali Republic, and the city was renamed to "Shimal". The city was captured by the Somali military under the control of Major General Mohamed Siad Barre in 1969. Mogadishu was renamed to "Sodo" and the city's population was greatly reduced due to the policies of Barre.
The city was recaptured by the Somali National Movement in 1991. During the subsequent civil war, fighting between clans and militias, coupled with the intervention of foreign nations, devastated the city, leaving it in ruins.

The city's skyline is dominated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Somali National Theatre . The main business district is located in the north of the city, known as the "Minziffer-District". The old city walls , which were built by the Abyssinians, can still be seen in the old city centre .
The city is served by the Mogadishu International Airport .
The city is served by the Somali National Railways, which operates a narrow-gauge railway line from the city to the port of Bosaso in the semi-autonomous region of Puntland.
The city's main bus station is located in the south-east of the city, near the Zoo.
Mogadishu is known for its rich culture. The city is home to the Somali National Theatre, which was built in 1956 by Somalia's first president, Abdullahi Issa. The theatre, which was originally built as a movie theatre, is now used for live performances. The theatre is home to the Somali National Opera, which was established in 1953.
The city is also home to the Mogadishu National Library , which was established in 1972. The library houses over 100,000 books and is the largest library in Somalia.

The Sovereign was unusual because the casing was made from pressed steel , which gave it a much higher quality feel compared to

the wooden cases of most other manual typewriters. Also, the case was made of a single piece of pressed steel, rather than two smaller cases combined with a frame. Consequently, it was very light and sturdy, weighing just 2.3 kg , and had a smaller profile than other typewriters, which made it easier for the typist to use.
 The Sovereign was introduced in June 1951. In 1953, the Sovereign was the first typewriter to be sold in Sainsbury's stores.
In 1957, the Sovereign was withdrawn.

Having lost O 'Rourke as manager in 1921 , after he had struggled to cope with the death of his son two years earlier , Bradfor

'd was lucky to find a replacement in the form of a former wicketkeeper called Jack Lillywhite.
 He was still only twenty-five, but led a club that was by now in its fourth decade of existence and had been managed by the likes of Frank Tarrant, George Duckworth, Albert Trott and Morgan Hayes. Lillywhite was an uncompromising disciplinarian who insisted on good temperament and good behaviour from his cricketers.
 He was also a good organiser, and he was at the heart of the decision that was taken in 1922 to form the Northern League. It was a bold move, because it meant that he would have to resign from his job as secretary of Bradford Cricket Club, but he duly reapplied for the post and was reappointed.
 The inaugural season was not a success – Bradford finished second from bottom of the new Northern League, and would have done even worse had not Pudsey St Lawrence been awarded only a draw in their final match. The following year, however, Bradford won the championship, and they did so by three points from Skipton , who were the only other side to finish with a 100 per cent record.
 Bradfor'd had another good season in 1924, and were runners-up to Lytham St Annes . The following year they finished third, and in 1926 fourth, but after that they were never as successful. Their only other championship was in 1932, when they finished level with Skipton , but were awarded the title because they had a better percentage of batting points.
 In 1933 they finished second from bottom and in 1934 they finished bottom. They improved a little in 1935, but the following year they finished bottom again, and their decline was complete.
 They went out of the Northern League in 1938, and then, after three years in the Old Trafford League, joined the Yorkshire League in 1941. They spent four seasons there, but by 1945 they had dropped out of the competition. In 1946 they left Bradford Park Avenue and became a ground-sharing club, playing their home matches at the Carnegie Cricket Club in Leeds .
 They had a good season in 1947 and finished second, and they were also runners-up in 1948. In 1949 they finished bottom, however, and in 1950 they were out of the competition altogether.
 They were still a ground-sharing club in 1951 and 1952, but in 1953 they moved back to Bradford Park Avenue and became an independent club. They remained so for the next decade, and were runners-up in the Yorkshire League in 1957, but they were out of the competition after 1963.
 They rejoined the Yorkshire League in 1970, but never finished higher than fifth, and in 1974 they were out of the league altogether.
 In 1974 they joined the Halifax League, and in 1975 they won the championship. They won the title again in 1976, but in 1977 they finished bottom. They returned to the Halifax League in 1979, but were out of the competition after 1981.
 They were in the Bradford League in 1982, but by 1983 they had joined the Leeds League. In 1986 they won the championship, but they were out of the league after 1988. They joined the Bradford League again in 1989, and were in the competition for a further two years.
 They rejoined the Leeds League in 1992 and were champions in 1996, but after that they were out of the league.
 They joined the Bradford League again in 1998, and were promoted to the second division in 2001.

Mitsuda returned as the lead composer for 1999 's Chrono Cross after composing its predecessor , Chrono Trigger . After being c

apped as a composer for 16-bit console games, Mitsuda expressed interest in composing for the PlayStation 2 , which at the time was known as the PlayStation 3. Compared to the original PlayStation , the PlayStation 2 was powerful enough to support live orchestral sounds. Mitsuda's score for Chrono Cross was the first in the series to feature a full ensemble of musicians, and was praised for its live sound. The composer had intended to feature live orchestral performances of the music in the game, but the cost of hiring the musicians was too high. Accordingly, Mitsuda and his team recorded the music with a full orchestra and used the technique of sampling to apply the sounds to the game. In addition to his score for Chrono Cross , Mitsuda also worked on an original soundtrack for Capcom 's fighting game Street Fighter EX3 (2000). Alongside his work on Chrono Cross , Mitsuda collaborated with the composers Hiroki Kikuta and Yoko Shimomura for Square Enix 's 2001 RPG Xenogears . The three composers each wrote a theme for the game, and each one's song was performed in the game's world. Mitsuda's theme was performed in the game's city of Elhaym.
During the development of Chrono Cross , Mitsuda originally planned to compose a separate score for each of the game's four areas. However, he was soon asked by Square Enix to create a score that would unify the game's overall theme. His score incorporates the music of the three original Chrono Trigger composers: Mitsuda, Yasunori Mitsuda and Nobuo Uematsu . Working on the game also rekindled Mitsuda's interest in the Nintendo 64 , and he was able to work on three projects for the console during its lifespan. He worked with the developer Sega on its 2001 RPG Panzer Dragoon Saga , writing the score for a small section of the game. He also worked on two Nintendo-produced titles, the fighting game Super Smash Bros. Melee , and the action role-playing game Wave Race: Blue Storm .
While working with Sega on Panzer Dragoon Saga , Mitsuda was presented with the opportunity to compose for a sequel to the 1993 Sega Saturn title Panzer Dragoon II Zwei . He wrote the score for Panzer Dragoon Orta , which was released on the GameCube in 2002 . The composer also worked on the soundtrack for Square Enix 's 2002 RPG Star Ocean: Till the End of Time , which was written by Uematsu and Mitsuda.
Mitsuda has often collaborated with the video game company MonkeyPaw Games. The company's first title was 2005's Avernum: Escape from the Pit , a RPG in which Mitsuda wrote the score. He has also written music for the company's 2009 RPG Harvest Moon: Hero of Leaf Valley , as well as the 2010 RPG Avernum 6 .
Mitsuda's most recent work is the 2012 role-playing game Xenoblade Chronicles , which was released for the Wii. He worked with the game's original composers — Yuki Matsuda and Masaharu Iwata — as well as the American composers Manami Matsumae and Yasunori Mitsuda.
In addition to his work in video games, Mitsuda has worked on soundtracks for anime and movies. His most notable film score is for the 2004 film Steamboy , which was directed by Katsuhiro Otomo . The director had previously worked with Mitsuda on the OVA series The Legend of Mother Sarah (1990).

Having borne the burden of the long days of patrolling , reconnaissance and minor engagements with the advancing Austrian , Ger

ma n and Russian forces, the exhausted Irish Brigade of French Volunteers was pulled from the front lines at the Battle of Magenta in May 1859 and sent to the small peaceful village of Castelnuovo.
It was in Castelnuovo that the French government chose to house the Irish in a tented village . The French government hoped this small village set in the Italian countryside would be enough to keep the men's minds and bodies occupied as the battle worn men of the Irish Brigade shivered in the chill mountain air.
With no immediate work to do for the government, the men of the Irish Brigade found themselves with too much time on their hands.
The men of the Irish Brigade had a hard time getting used to the Italian countryside. They found the warm climate and the lack of guns and fighting unbearable.
There is no record as to when the Irish Brigade first started their gambling habit, but it is rumored the men first started playing cards for money the night of the Battle of Magenta.
The men of the Irish Brigade soon found themselves unable to resist the urge to place bets on the outcome of the game.
The French government seems to have been unaware of the men's gambling habits and the fact that the men had no work.
On the afternoon of Saturday, June 12, 1859, the men of the Irish Brigade started a game of cards to pass the time.
The following morning, the men awakened to the sound of gunfire and the sight of several red-coated soldiers running through the camp.
The men of the Irish Brigade had bet the previous day that they could outrun the French soldiers. Although they made an attempt to run, they were quickly overtaken and brought back to camp.
Although the men were returned to camp, the French government decided the risk of the men's gambling was too great to leave them in the tented village.
On Sunday, June 13, 1859, the men of the Irish Brigade were marched to the small town of Sesto Calende.
The men of the Irish Brigade were taken to a detention camp in the middle of Sesto Calende with a small guard.
In the detention camp, the men of the Irish Brigade were housed in makeshift tents and forced to listen to a French officer attempt to lecture the men nightly on the inadequacies of gambling.
The men of the Irish Brigade had little success in being reformed by the French officer's lectures.

Pernick and Wilder define " clean tech " as " any product , service , or process that delivers value using limited or zero non

- renewable resources . " [ 1 ]
The term " clean tech " is relatively new. It is used to describe a variety of companies, industries, sectors, and products that cut carbon emissions or use alternative energy sources. In some cases, the term is used as a synonym for " green  technology ."   The terms " clean energy,"  "clean technology,"  and "green technology" are often used interchangeably.
 In the 2000s, there was a shift in focus from reducing the amount of waste  to recycling it. This strategy was later extended to buildings and cities.
 Green technology is technology that is designed to help reduce the impact of human activities on the environment. Green technologies promote energy efficiency, conservation, and improved environmental quality.
The green technology market is a growing sector, with many innovative companies striving to make the world a greener place.
Some of the most popular green technologies include solar panels, wind turbines, and electric cars.
Some companies are starting to experiment with green technology in their offices, such as using natural light instead of artificial light to save energy.

With the increasing population in towns near the Everglades came hunting opportunities . Even decades earlier , Harriet Beecher

Stowe, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin , had written about hunting in the Everglades .  In her book, Palmetto Leaves , Stowe describes how a party of hunters from Boston and New York City arrived in Florida. The party consisted of six men and two women, all good shots. After an evening spent playing cards and eating fresh fish, the party set out at dawn. "The air was cool and the breeze from the ocean was refreshing, and they enjoyed their ride," wrote Stowe. The party had packed a large dinner and ate on the way. About ten miles out, they reached the coast. They rode along the beach for about two miles, and then a young man on horseback approached them and asked if they wished to hunt. The hunters asked the young man to point out a good place to shoot quail. After some searching, the young man pointed out a place where quail had been feeding the night before. The men rode to the spot and found that the quail had left, but they spotted a few rabbits in the grass. The hunters shot these and packed them in their bags. They then rode for a mile or two more, and the young man pointed out another place where quail had been feeding. The men went to the spot and shot a few quail from among the grass. They were then joined by two other young men who were hunting with the young man. The men and women from Boston and New York City enjoyed a fine dinner, and the hunters returned to the camp feeling pleased. In her book, Stowe provides a brief history of hunting in Florida, which was not always a pleasant experience. She describes the terrifying experience of riding through a swamp. "A noise like that of a hundred thousand musket-shots startled us with the suddenness of an earthquake. It was the explosion of the fire-arms of a party of hunters on the opposite side of the creek. The report was followed by a perfect hail of shot and shell, which came whistling, singing, and rushing over our heads. The rifles poured out their death-dealing bolts, and the cannon bellowed like angry fiends. We were not in a pleasant situation. The water was high, and the current swift. The canoes rocked to and fro, and our horses could not but be alarmed at the scene. The hunters were in a war dance, and a war dance of the Indians seemed to be the order of the day. For a few moments we were very much startled, and then, as it occurred to us that the hunters were no enemies, but friends, we felt better." On another occasion, Stowe describes how her party was captured by Indians who were hunting alligators. "The Indians came near, and seemed to look at us with some curiosity, but not with the slightest appearance of hostility. They soon approached very near and began to examine us with great interest, but they did not speak a word. They evidently wished to know who we were and whence we came," wrote Stowe. "They had evidently made up their minds that we were friends, and were not disposed to make any hostile demonstrations. It was not long before I perceived that they were asking each other who we were and whence we came, and they seemed to be rather at a loss to make up their minds whether or not we were friends. They doubtless had heard of the cruelty and rapacity of the white hunters, and were under no small apprehensions. They very naturally supposed that we were, like themselves, on a hunting expedition. They evidently wished to make us acquainted with them, and the only way they knew of doing so was to ask us questions, and this they did with great politeness." Stowe and her companions were finally allowed to leave, and they returned to camp where the hunters were waiting to hear their adventures. The author was eager to tell them the story of how they had been captured by the Indians and, when the hunters asked what the Indians wanted, she told them, "They wanted to ascertain whether we were enemies or friends." "But they did not know who we were," remarked one of the hunters. "Why, certainly they did," replied Stowe. "They inquired where we came from, and who we were." The hunters agreed that this was an amusing story. They then began to discuss the captivity of the Indians by the whites.
