  " Raging Bender " is the 38th episode of Futurama . It aired on March 21, 1999 and was written by Eric Horsted and Steve Koter.
It is the last episode of Futurama to air on Fox. It is the second (and final) episode to feature Nudar, the first being " A Fishful of Dollars ".
In this episode, Fry gets a job working as a pizza delivery boy for Pizza Planet, while Bender and the Professor create a robot duplicate of Fry for use as a test subject in the Planet Express Research and Development Department. Meanwhile, Nudar begins working at a Pizza Planet as a delivery driver, and begins to develop a crush on Fry.
Fry's delivery job is turning out to be more difficult than he had anticipated, but he soon meets Nudar, a cute young alien who is also working as a delivery driver. The two become friends and start to date, although Nudar has a crush on Fry. As they are out on a delivery, Nudar tells Fry that she is really a princess from a distant planet who has come to Earth to find a husband. Fry is a bit surprised, but Nudar insists that she loves him and that her father will approve of their marriage. Fry takes Nudar to the Planet Express building, where they are given a tour of the facility by Hermes and the Professor. When they reach the Research and Development Department, Nudar becomes frightened by the many horrifying creations, and Fry tries to comfort her.
Fry and Nudar are then taken to the Professor's office, where they meet Bender, who is working on a new project. He has created a robot duplicate of Fry, which has been programmed to function as an identical version of Fry, including such things as his voice and mannerisms. Fry is shocked to see that his duplicate is an exact replica of himself, but Bender says it will be useful for testing the new PEPC device. Fry is taken aback by his duplicate's behavior, but he leaves the lab to prepare to leave for work. Fry is surprised to see that Nudar has followed him. At Pizza Planet, Fry and Nudar find that the delivery is being handled by a pizza robot, a machine that can produce pizzas at a high rate. Nudar is excited by it, but is shocked to discover that Fry is not delivering the pizza, but is sitting in a corner, watching the robot.
After the delivery, Fry and Nudar return to the Planet Express building, where they go into the Research and Development Department. Bender, who is working on the project, is surprised to see that Fry is fine with the duplicate, but he explains that he is tired of being treated like a robot, so he plans to use the duplicate as an excuse to get away from his duties for awhile. Fry, who is still unsure about the duplicate, is happy to oblige him.
In the meantime, Fry and Nudar are preparing to go to his apartment, but Nudar is bothered by the duplicate. She is worried that Fry will become jealous of his duplicate, but Fry says that he will not. Nudar heads to the bathroom to change into her date outfit, but is surprised to see that the duplicate has followed her. She tells the duplicate that she is afraid that Fry will become jealous of him, but the duplicate says that he is not bothered by Fry's presence. Nudar is confused by the duplicate's attitude, and she leaves to get ready for their date.
Fry and Nudar are preparing to leave for their date when the Professor comes into the room and tells them that he has something to show them. He takes them to his office, where Bender is working on the PEPC device. The Professor explains that the machine will allow him to zap anything with a pulse out of existence. Nudar is shocked to hear this, but the Professor says that he will only use it on things that are annoying, such as Bender. Bender, who is annoyed by the Professor's attitude, leaves for the lab.
Fry and Nudar go out on their date, and they go to a movie. During the film, Fry is shocked to see that the duplicate is sitting next to Nudar.

This article is about the archaeologist Arthur Evans. For the philologist, see Arthur Evans (philologist). For other uses, see Arthur Evans (disambiguation).

Arthur John Evans

He was born at Plas Gwyn in Llantwit Major , Glamorgan , Wales , the son of a Church of England clergyman, the Rev. Charles Evans. He was educated at Clifton College and King's College, Cambridge.

In 1869 Evans was appointed as Assistant Keeper of the Egyptian and Assyrian Antiquities in the British Museum, having earlier been appointed as Assistant in the same department in 1866. In 1870 he was appointed Keeper of the same department. In 1874 he became Keeper of the Coins and Medals, being in 1877 appointed Keeper of the Greek and Roman Antiquities. From 1898 he was Keeper of the Department of Prehistoric and Oriental Antiquities.

Evans was elected as a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1883.

Evans's career as an archaeologist was marked by a series of excavations at Mycenaean sites in Greece, beginning in 1874. In 1894 Evans wrote The Mycenaean age: a survey of Aegean civilization in its golden age, by Arthur Evans, which is a key to his publications and excavations.

In 1897 he began to excavate Knossos in Crete, and in 1900 the British Museum agreed to his excavation of the site. The area that he excavated was called "Palace" and was believed to be the palace of Knossos. In 1903, Evans announced that the palace dated to about 1,700 BC, and that it was the centre of a pre-Greek civilisation. He named this civilisation "Minoan", named after the mythical King Minos. The excavations continued until 1930 and the Palace of Knossos is still being excavated today.

Evans was the first to come up with the term "Minoan", and to date the Minoan civilisation as older than the Egyptian civilisation. He also suggested that it was the Minoans who had built the pyramids in Egypt. This idea was widely popularised in the 20th century, and is still often repeated.

In 1905 Evans was elected a fellow of the British Academy. In 1911 he became president of the Society of Antiquaries of London.

Evans died at his home in Swansea , Wales , on 5 May 1941.

## Work with the Society of Antiquaries of London

During his career, Evans was involved in many projects with the Society of Antiquaries of London , including organising the first excavations of the early Roman city of Silchester (Calleva Atrebatum). He served as President of the Society of Antiquaries of London from 1911 to 1913.

## Legacy

The archaeologist and museum curator, John Latham, was among those who promoted Arthur Evans's theories about Minoan civilisation, but was subsequently critical of Evans's politics and his treatment of the British Museum's collection of Mycenaean and Minoan artefacts.

## Works

* The Mycenaean Age: A Survey of Aegean Civilization in Its Golden Age (1901).
* The Palace of Minos (1921).
* Ritual of the Minotaur: The Minoan Frescoes in the Restored Palace of Knossos (1925).
* The Palace of Minos (1930).
* Palace of Minos (1933).

In 1912 , when Olivier was five , his father secured a permanent appointment as assistant priest at St Saviour 's , Pimlico . H

élène Olivier , his wife, was a keen amateur photographer and she took many photographs of her family . These were the first photographs that Olivier looked at when he began researching the album in the 1970s , and they were of great help to him in identifying all the people in the album. Olivier , who had been born in France , had left England in 1913 when his father was deemed unsuitable to be a priest in the English church and returned to France with his mother. At the age of eight he went to a French boarding school in Neuilly , where he remained for the next eight years .
The headmaster of Olivier's boarding school had a passion for photography and he also took numerous photographs during the course of the young Olivier's time there. These photographs gave Olivier his first real experience of being photographed and although he was not overly keen on having his photograph taken he was conscious of the fact that he was being photographed and that photographs were being taken of him.
The album was purchased at a jumble sale in 1972 by Olivier's friend Richard McAinsh . It is not known why Olivier was not present at the sale . Olivier had been invited to a party held by McAinsh 's friend and it was while he was there that he was approached by the vendor and asked if he would take the album . Olivier was not keen to do so but he agreed to take the album on the understanding that he would return it to McAinsh if he did not like it.
As soon as he returned to England Olivier began to look through the photographs in the album. The photographs that he had seen as a child and the photographs that he had seen as a young boy at the boarding school were very different from the photographs that he was now looking at. For the first time he was taken aback by the "fleshiness" of the faces in the photographs. He was also surprised to discover how many of the people in the photographs were naked.
As he continued to look through the album it became clear to him that this was a collection of photographs taken by one person. The photographs were all in the same style and the same style of camera was used throughout. The camera was a large wooden box with a lens on the top and a tripod on the bottom. The photographer had also taken the photographs in the same way. All the photographs were taken from a high vantage point with the subjects looking up at the camera. The photographer had also taken pictures of the same group of people in the same pose in the same place at the same time.

 The South Beltline Freeway is a 2.4 mile spur from I @-@ 10 to M @-@ 37 ( Broadmoor Avenue ) with two interchanges: I @-@ 40 and I @-@ 96. The South Beltline Freeway is the southernmost portion of the Birmingham Beltline.
 The $4.7 million project included the construction of four 1,000-foot long bridges, 9.5 miles of concrete, 82,000 cubic yards of fill, 1.25 million pounds of steel, 14,000 cubic yards of asphalt, 1.5 miles of drainage pipes, 11.5 miles of wire, 10,000 yards of rock, 4,500 yards of gravel, 1.25 million board feet of lumber, and 5,000 tons of sand and gravel.
 The Beltline Freeway was conceived as a means of relieving traffic congestion in the central business district and as a means of promoting economic development in the city and surrounding suburbs. The South Beltline Freeway was the first section of the Beltline Freeway to be completed.
 The 1968 opening date for the Birmingham Beltline was extended to 1970 by the addition of four spurs. The 17-mile Birmingham Beltline was completed in 1973.
After the South Beltline Freeway was completed, work began on the underpass at I @-@ 40 . The underpass tunnel was completed in 1960 and opened to traffic on November 29.

 The $1.1 million Birmingham Beltline Freeway overpass was completed in 1962 and was dedicated on December 1. The 1,000-foot long bridge was completed in 14 months, 17 days, and 12 hours.

During the first four years of Henry 's reign Gerard was one of the king 's chief advisors , along with Robert of Meulan , Coun

selor to King Henry II of England. In 1154 he was appointed to the Council of Regency to rule in Henry 's stead during his minority. It was through Gerard that Henry 's youngest brother, John, was brought to the court of his elder brother.

Gerard counselled Henry II to institute a new court system in England. He was a strong advocate of the Forest Charter of 1154 (which gave foresters the right to serve on juries) and the Suger Charter of 1155 (which gave landowners the right to hold a court of their own). He also fought to preserve the rights of the Church, and was appointed by Stephen of Blois as the first Bishop of Lincoln in 1152.

In 1155 Gerard was invited by Frederick Barbarossa to the Diet of Besançon and by Pope Hadrian IV to the Council of Vézelay. Gerard was appointed to the second Council of London in 1156, and was effectively in charge of the kingdom of England from that point on.

## Second Council

Gerard was the only member of the regency council who was opposed to the coronation of Henry as King of England in 1154. Following the coronation, he was on good terms with Henry II, who was then in his teens. Gerard's role at the second council of London of 1156 came at the request of the English and Norman magnates who were assembled there. The absence of the king, who had returned to Normandy to claim his duchy, had left the English magnates divided, with Stephen de Blois (the brother of Henry and a powerful figure in his own right) and Robert of Gloucester on one side and the earls of Chester and Leicester, the bishops of London and Lincoln, and the earls of Mortain and Norfolk, on the other. The magnates, however, demanded that Gerard be their spokesman at the council.

Gerard was put in charge of the council, and was charged with bringing the king back to England and into power. Gerard was appointed to the regency council in his stead, which caused some conflict with Stephen de Blois. Stephen was distrustful of Gerard, and he saw the appointment as an attempt to take power away from the king. The council was not disbanded, and Stephen de Blois was later appointed its leader. Stephen's overtures to the king in 1157 led to a rapprochement between Stephen and Gerard.

## Death

Gerard died in 1158, and was buried in Lincoln Cathedral.

## Legacy

The dedication to Gerard's memory "to that most Worthy Man Gerald, Bishop of Lincoln, and Henry's beloved counsellor" appears in the first stanza of the famous Twelfth-century liturgical hymn, Vexilla Regis prodeunt.

The Burlington, Vermont, not-for-profit organization was founded in 1912, with the bankrupted American Red Cross as a model. The organization was first involved in responding to fires in the city. In the 1930s, the group began to expand its international involvement. Today the organization devotes most of its resources to disaster relief and global health programs, and nearly all of its funding comes from private donations. A study in 2009 found the organization to be the second largest private health-care provider next to the United States Department of Defense.
The organization began its international expansion in 1965, when it started sending medical teams to Vietnam, and later, Bangladesh. In 1985, the organization began expanding its global presence, in part to provide medical assistance to people affected by the U.S.-supported Contra war in Nicaragua. The group's involvement in Central America led to a lawsuit in 1988, when a Nicaraguan family alleged that the organization had helped the U.S. government in spying on Nicaraguan refugees.

In 2010, the organization began serving the Haiti earthquake victims. own brand of humor among the traditional action, adventure, and superheroics. During the course of the storyline, Ennis had created the character of the Jackal, the Punisher's chief nemesis. The Jackal had been a former Special Forces operative, who had been responsible for the Punisher's wife and infant daughter's death. Ennis then wrote a ten-issue storyline in Punisher War Journal #21–30 (titled "The Platoon") that focused on the Jackal.

Garth Ennis had originally planned for Microchip to be a frenemy to Punisher. However, when he was given the chance to write The Punisher limited series, he decided to make Microchip the second-in-command and left the Jackal, who was the intended antagonist, as a supporting character.

The first hospital to treat burns opened in 1843 in London , England and the development of modern burn care began in the late

19 th century in North America. In the early 20 th century, the development of sterile surgery, anesthetic techniques and antiseptic wound care in the operating room led to the establishment of burn units in hospitals. A new era in burn care was ushered in when the United States military began using TLC (Tender Loving Care) in the burn units of military hospitals during the Second World War.
In the late 1950s, the University of Michigan started a burn care program. This program proved to be so effective that it was expanded to include children, and in 1962, the first pediatric burn unit in the United States was established ____________________________________________________________________________________________________________
Burns tend to be more serious in children than adults, and children have a lower risk for surviving severe burns.
The key to a child’s survival is to start early, before the burn is even recognized.  The patient should be taken to a hospital or doctor immediately.  If this is not possible, the important things to remember are to control the pain and to keep the burn clean.  Avoid touching the burn to prevent infection and keep the burn cool and covered with clean, dry bandages until the patient can be brought to a hospital.
Hot water, cold water, cloths, ointments, and rubbing alcohol should not be used on burns. They may damage the skin and make it more difficult to heal.
Children who have burns should be watched carefully and given pain medication as needed.  They should be encouraged to drink plenty of fluids.  The house should be kept clean and free of drafts to help prevent infection.  Visitors should be limited.  If the burn is not severe, the child may be allowed to go home.  If the burn is severe or the child has other serious injuries, the child may be admitted to the hospital.
The child may need to wear special clothing while in the hospital.  The burn may be treated with ointments, bandages, antibiotics, and antibiotics.  The child may have to be hospitalized for several weeks.  The burns should be cleaned frequently and the bandages changed every few days.  The treatment for a severe burn is not always successful.  A child with severe burns may have permanent scars.
___________________________________________________________________________________________________________
Burns can have both immediate and long-term effects on a child’s health.  The immediate effects may include shock and dehydration.  Physical therapy is often needed to help the child learn how to use his hands and arms again.  Long-term effects may include infections, depression, and emotional problems.  It’s important for the child and his family to get counseling to help them deal with the emotional after-effects of the injury.
__________________________________________________________________________________________________________
Burn injuries can be prevented by using caution around hot objects, such as stoves and irons.  When boiling water is used for cooking, it should be used with a lid on the pan and stored out of reach of children.  Children should be taught to keep things that are hot away from their faces, hands, and bodies.  Children should be taught to call for help if they are burned.

A final decision on a major operation would not be made until after the Tet Offensive.
 The Fishhook region of South Vietnam was in the westernmost part of Quang Ngai Province, about 15 miles north of the coastal city of Quang Ngai, and about 25 miles west of the city of Quang Tin. Near the center of the region, the area was bounded on the north and east by the Ben Hai River and on the west by the northern border of the Iron Triangle. A large portion of the Ben Hai River was in the Fishhook region, and a number of the larger tributaries of the Ben Hai River flowed into the Fishhook area.

The JGS estimated the strength of VC units in the Fishhook region on 18 May 1968 as 1,500.
As in other regions of South Vietnam, the VC had infiltrated through the Ben Hai River from North Vietnam into the Fishhook region to establish bases and to conduct infiltration and resupply operations from there into the Iron Triangle and other areas south of the Ben Hai River.
 After the North Vietnamese attack on Khe Sanh on 21 January 1968, General Abrams and U.S. advisers in South Vietnam requested that the 1st Infantry Division be reassigned to the III Corps area so that the division could be used to cover the Iron Triangle. General Abrams also requested that the 196th Light Infantry Brigade be reassigned to the II Corps area, so that it could be used to provide security for the installation of a large U.S. advisory team in the Fishhook region.
 In February 1968 the U.S. embassy in Saigon informed the Department of State that the 25th Infantry Division had been detached from the U.S. forces in the northern area. The 25th Infantry Division was a mechanized division with the capability of moving rapidly and conducting operations over a wide area. The division had 17,390 Americans and was divided into three subordinate elements. The 1st Brigade consisted of two infantry battalions and two artillery battalions; the 3rd Brigade consisted of two infantry battalions and one artillery battalion; and the 4th Brigade consisted of a mechanized infantry battalion, three artillery battalions, and a tank battalion.

Anderson is known for films set in the San Fernando Valley with realistically flawed and desperate characters . Among the theme

elements employed by Anderson are heightened sounds, camera angles and editing, exaggerated hair and makeup, and issues of class and race. Anderson hints at a comic view of the world and characters, but the films often reflect a sad, serious viewpoint.
In the late seventies to early eighties, Anderson's style was seen as a new, untapped vein of filmmaking. His films were often overlooked as being too similar or identical to his earlier films, a critical cliche of the film industry. Anderson has stated in interviews that he doesn't try to make his films different from each other, but rather tries to make them the best they can be.
Many of Anderson's films are set in the San Fernando Valley of Los Angeles, California. In the early 2000s, Anderson moved to the area. The Valley is often used as a setting for films and television shows, as it is home to many actors and celebrities. Anderson's films include various locations in the Valley, such as the Los Angeles River, the San Fernando Valley mall, and various neighborhoods, including Van Nuys, North Hollywood, and Encino.

In the dark the Fusiliers moved off , but amid dense fog they found it difficult to maintain their bearings and were not in pos

i tion to take advantage of any tactical opportunity. By 5.45 a.m. they had reached the southern edge of the wood and, as the fog lifted, they became involved in a fire fight with infantry and machine-guns. By 7.15 a.m., the situation was becoming critical, and the order was given to withdraw.
The casualties were heavy, and many were killed or captured. The 9th Battalion, however, captured many Germans and salvaged a number of machine-guns and ammunition. It is believed that this action was one of the first times the Germans used flame-throwers.
In a counter-attack, led by the Commanding Officer, Lieutenant-Colonel J. J. A. Swarbrick, a number of prisoners and a number of enemy guns were taken. The Commanding Officer was killed and the Commanding Officer, Major M. E. B. Crabtree, was wounded.
On the 26th, the 9th Battalion, less one Company, went into the line to the right of Mudugie, where it was attached to the 11th Brigade. It was decided to attack the German position in the rear. On the evening of the 26th, 'A' and 'B' Companies attacked and captured the position. 'A' Company advanced 400 yards and captured the enemy positions on the northern side of the railway line, north of the main road. 'B' Company advanced 200 yards, and captured the enemy position on the eastern side of the railway line.
At 11.30 p.m. the Battalion was relieved by the 7th Middlesex, and on the 28th moved to Bertry.
During the period from August 15th to August 31st, inclusive, the 9th Battalion had suffered a total of 348 casualties.
In the late evening of October 31st, the Battalion moved to Coxyde, where it was rested. On November 6th, the Battalion moved to the line at the junction of the 11th Brigade and the 34th Brigade.
On November 24th, 1918, the Battalion had been in the line for a period of 205 days.
On November 27th, it was relieved by the 10th Brigade and moved to Fleurbaix. On the following day, it moved to Bailleul.
The following day, the Battalion moved to St. Omer, where it was billeted and remained until the 5th January, 1919.
On the 5th January, the Battalion moved to St. Pol, and on the following day, was inspected by Major-General H. E. M. F. Pratt, C.M.G., D.S.O. The Brigade Commander, Brigadier-General J. G. S. MacDermott, D.S.O., arrived at 11.00 a.m., and at 12.30 p.m. the Battalion marched to the parade ground.
At 3.00 p.m., the Brigadier inspected the Regimental Detachment and the Medical Detachment, when he complimented the Commandant, Captain J. M. B. Hodson, D.S.O., on the way he had carried out the duties of Commandant, and also on the special work he had done as Commandant of the newly formed Regimental Detachment.
The Brigadier then inspected the Battalion, and later went on to inspect the other Battalions of the Brigade.
At the conclusion of the inspection, the Battalion returned to the billets.
On the 11th January, the Battalion moved to Wimille and on the following day to Pont-du-Sault and on the 13th to Bonnières and on the 14th to Cuinchy.
The following day, the Battalion marched to Merville, and on the 16th, the Battalion, less two Companies, moved to Lille. On the 19th, the Battalion moved to Armentières, and on the 20th, the Battalion moved to La Vacquerie.
On the 26th, the Battalion moved to St. Omer.

By 1850 , volunteer military organizations were widespread throughout America , but t hey were often hampered by poor training and obsolete equipment . The volunteer military was reorganized in 1855 , and after the outbreak of t he Civil War , t he volunteer force was revived and expanded . By the end of the Civil War , the volunteer force of the U.S. Army was 6,000 strong .
Military volunteers were also essential to the Union victory in the Civil War . T he volunteer force was disbanded by the federal government in 1862 , but the volunteer spirit continued to be fostered in public schools and in the Boy Scouts . In 1880 , the Boy's Brigade was formed , and it quickly gained popularity in the United States .

The kakapo was originally described by English ornithologist George Robert Gray in 1845 . The name " kakapo " is the English tr

imerism of the Maori word kākāpō, meaning "night parrot". It was Gray who first proposed the autonym for the species, which is derived from the Maori word for night, kākā. 

The species is sometimes called the owl parrot, the parrot owl, the owl parrot, or the night parrot; it is also known as the "stubfoot" or "woodhen" owl, because of its resemblance to a ground owl.

## Description

The kakapo is a large, flightless, green-feathered parrot, about the size of a turkey, with a heavy, leather-like, greyish-green body and a yellowish-brown head. The face is pale with a greyish-brown crown. The eyes are dark brown, and there is a dark brown, feathered cheek patch. The beak is reddish-brown, and the feet are all green, including their dark, greyish-green, claws.

The sexes are similar in size and coloration. Males are larger and heavier than females. The male is typically 65 to 76 cm (26 to 30 in) long, with a weight of 3 to 3.7 kg (6.6 to 8.2 lb), while the female is typically 60 to 70 cm (24 to 28 in) long, with a weight of 2.1 to 2.9 kg (4.6 to 6.4 lb).

The kakapo's feathers are darker and more rigid than those of most parrots, as the kakapo is in the subfamily Strigopoidea, which also includes the extinct New Zealand kakapo in the genus Strigops. The kakapo's feathers are also relatively short, and the birds often appear to be bald.

## Distribution and habitat

Kakapos live in New Zealand's south-western islands, in the Fiordland, Stewart Island, and the Chatham Islands. They are the only parrot native to New Zealand, and they are flightless because there are no land predators on the islands.

Kakapo in Codfish Island, New Zealand (also known as Whenua Hou).

The kakapo is restricted to areas of relatively high rainfall, with four distinct populations in the south-west of the South Island of New Zealand, including Fiordland, Stewart Island, and the Chatham Islands. Kakapo have been reintroduced to Codfish Island and Maud Island, and survive in small numbers in the Urupukapuka Island of the Chatham Islands. 

The largest population of kakapo is found on the offshore Codfish Island, where the population is estimated to be 130. The largest population of the species in the Fiordland region is 20 birds. The island of Stewart Island has 96 birds, and the Chatham Islands have a very small population of 3 birds.

Kakapo live in forests of rimu, beech, kahikatea, and matai trees, and in montane scrublands. They prefer areas higher than 600 m (2,000 ft) above sea level, and although they are not found in the sub-alpine zone, they have been known to feed in the alpine meadows. They are also found in dense, scrubby forests.

In 1995, the IUCN estimated that there were fewer than 100 mature kakapo left in the wild, and that this population was declining rapidly. The species was subsequently classified as critically endangered. After the last mature female died in 2007, the population was estimated to be 50 birds. A further increase in population was announced in 2014.

## Behaviour

### Diet

Kakapo are herbivores and eat leafy trees, ferns, seeds, berries, and a wide variety of other plant matter, including moss, lichen, and fungi. They also occasionally eat small invertebrates, including insects and earthworms.

They are fully nocturnal and feed after dark, and shelter in hollows during the day. If disturbed during the day, they will place themselves on the ground, making themselves look like a log on the forest floor.

In 1899 , Wheeler joined Bradford Grammar School shortly before his ninth birthday , where he proceeded straight to the second

3rd year . He then joined the staff of the Halifax and Huddersfield Railway in 1909, as an office boy, and was promoted to a junior clerk in 1911. In 1912, he transferred to the London and North Eastern Railway , as a junior clerk.
Wheeler was the first person to take the unofficial title of " Ploughman Poet " when he composed his first verse in 1912. It was his wife, Freda, who chose the title. He was often a guest at Yorkshire poetry and music evenings where he often read his own verse. He also wrote several songs. He was president of the Bradford Constitutional Club in the 1930s, and was a local organiser for the National Union of General Workers .
On 16 May 1915, Wheeler enlisted in the Sherwood Foresters , and in October 1915, he was posted to France as a private. He was promoted to lance-corporal in 1916, and to sergeant in 1917. On 1 July 1916, he was wounded and gassed in one of the battles of the Somme . In 1917 he was transferred to a railway transport unit. He was demobilised on 21 January 1919.
In 1920, Wheeler became an assistant stationmaster in Lynton, and then assistant stationmaster in Crowborough, Sussex . In 1922, he was appointed assistant stationmaster at Leeds , then assistant stationmaster at Great Horton , Bradford in 1923. He was promoted to stationmaster at Harrogate in 1926, and in 1930 was promoted to stationmaster at Hull .
Wheeler was a member of a number of literary and social clubs, including the Hull Philosophical Society .
Wheeler's verse is often seen as a protest against the First World War . It is also often seen as a protest against industrialisation , and the urbanisation of the countryside.
Wheeler's first volume of verse, Here's a Health to the Plough , was published in 1923, and was followed by Poems of War and Peace (1924), Last Summer (1925) and The Singing Ploughman (1926).
Wheeler's version of " The Three Jolly Pigeons " was published in The Singing Ploughman .

In May 1944 , it was announced that broadcast performers must organize themselves into a union , and that this union would be t

he American Federation of Radio Artists (AFRA), a new union within the AFL–CIO. The new union's goal was to protect the interests of those performing in radio dramas and other non-musical broadcast programs. AFRA was t he first union to represent broadcasters. It was also the first union to represent a substantial number of women—among them were actresses Lucille Ball and June Allyson.
 In 1952, Crosby sued the new union to have the judge declare that union members are not employees of their employers. In a surprising decision, the judge agreed with Crosby. "Those who work for radio or television stations are not working for the station," the judge declared, "but rather they are working for the public." The decision changed the legal status of broadcasters from "employees" (and thus covered by the National Labor Relations Act) to "independent contractors" (and not covered by the Act). The decision also strengthened AFRA's position.
 Many broadcasters felt Crosby had received preferential treatment. They argued that there was no difference between those who worked for radio and television and those who worked for movies or the theater. In 1953, the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) reversed the decision.
 Before the reversal, various broadcast unions had formed. In 1951, the American Guild of Variety Artists (AGVA) was formed and claimed to represent all those in broadcasting. In 1953, the Screen Actors Guild (SAG) attempted to organize the entertainment industry, including television and radio. Eventually, SAG and AGVA merged to form AGVA-SAG. In 1955, AFRA joined SAG to form the AFL–CIO Radio and Television Music Artists Guild (AFRA-SAG).
 In 1958, the NLRB ruled that broadcasters were employees and thus eligible for collective bargaining. The NLRB ruling, as well as the Crosby ruling, led to the formation of the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (AFTRA). The new union combined the resources of AFRA and AGVA-SAG.
 In 1959, SAG and AFRA-SAG merged to form the major union covering performers in film, television, and radio—the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA).
 In 1973, the Screen Actors Guild (SAG) and the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (AFTRA) merged into one union. However, in 1995, the union split into two separate unions.
 In 1999, the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (AFTRA) and the American Federation of Musicians (AFM) merged to form the American Federation of Musicians and the Actors' Equity Association (AFM–AEA), which today represents all performers in film, television, and radio, as well as musicians who perform in film and television.

As the Cold War grew hotter after 1947 , Innis grew increasingly hostile to the United States . He warned repeatedly that Canad

ians must "be very careful that we don't get dragged into a military alliance with the United States ." The growing American presence in Europe , he added, was "a very serious threat to the independence of Canada ."
Even as the Cold War intensified, Innis did not give up his hope of seeing the United States and the Soviet Union cooperate to end the Korean War. "The two great powers have to cooperate in the interest of world peace ." But, Innis insisted, "the United States is the greatest danger to peace."
Innis's outspoken criticism of America drew only limited support from his colleagues. In 1950 , the EFC passed a resolution calling for peace talks between the United States and China , and for a withdrawal of Canadian troops from the Korean War. Innis's vision of a peaceful world, however, was not shared by the vast majority of Canadians.
Another issue that divided Innis from his colleagues was his insistence that the West should not intervene militarily in the conflict between Israel and Egypt . In 1952 , after Israel declared a state of emergency, Innis warned that the West should not encourage Israel to wage war. "If we do," he said, "we will make ourselves partners in the guilt of the crime which the world is going to make a capital crime in the future."
Innis was also deeply disturbed by the actions of Canadian governments, which he saw as drifting steadily to the right. In 1957 , he warned that the Conservative government was "drifting to the right" and "taking the country with it." A year later, he criticized the Liberal government for its "slavish adherence to the cold war line." He lamented that "the present Trudeau government is as far to the right as any government in Canada since the Second World War ."
Innis was equally critical of the American government. "The United States is not the beacon of light it once was," he wrote. "Instead, it is the home of military dictatorship in the form of the Military-Industrial Complex." Innis's increasingly radical views on domestic and foreign policy were in sharp contrast to those of his colleagues in the EFC.
On a personal level, the relationship between Innis and the EFC became increasingly strained. Even as Innis's views became more radical, EFC leaders sought to marginalize his voice. They tried to control access to Innis by cutting off a direct telephone line to his farmhouse , and by denying him the right to send letters to members of the Council. Innis complained that his views were no longer being "heard in the organization as a whole." He resigned from the EFC in 1958 , and died three years later .
Innis's views on foreign policy would have been in step with those of the left-leaning New Democratic Party. In 1961 , the NDP expressed its opposition to the planned deployment of nuclear missiles in Canada. The party also supported disarmament, and warned that Canada's Security and Defence Agreements with the United States were "unconstitutional" and "a threat to Canadian sovereignty ."
Today, the NDP has become a major political force in Canada. The party won 103 seats in the 2011 election, and formed the Official Opposition . In its 2011 platform, the NDP promised to "urgently implement" the recommendations of the 2010 Parliamentary Committee on the Review of Canada's Mission in Afghanistan . The NDP vowed to promote "peace and diplomacy" as the basis of Canadian foreign policy.
The NDP's views on Afghanistan have been criticized by some as "naïve" and "unrealistic." In 2010 , the former head of Canadian military intelligence described the NDP's position on Afghanistan as "disingenuous" and "uninformed." #  The Archaeology of Ritual and Magic
Introduction
The book that follows is an attempt to provide a synthetic archaeological view of the development of Western religious tradition from its emergence in the prehistoric period to its final form in the early medieval period. The book's approach is archaeological in the sense that it is concerned with the ways in which the development of religious practice, ritual behaviour and beliefs can be understood through their material remains. This material is the product of human activity and thus reveals the ways in which human beings change from the prehistoric period to the present.
The study of ritual and magic in prehistory and the early Medieval period is a relatively new area of study. It is the first attempt in the archaeology of ritual and magic to provide a comprehensive synthesis of the material evidence from the prehistoric and early medieval periods. In the past, much archaeological work has focused on the development of the early Christian church, and on the use of magic in the early medieval period. In the last twenty years there has been renewed interest in the role of ritual and magic in prehistoric societies, with a focus on the nature of ritual, social interactions and the role of magic in the development of religious beliefs. However, much of this work has been specific in its approach, focusing on particular aspects of ritual and magic. This has resulted in piecemeal and fragmented research. This book provides a more holistic archaeological approach to the study of ritual and magic, attempting to assess the larger picture of social change that is revealed through the examination of the archaeological evidence.
In the past, there has been a tendency for archaeologists to focus on the role of ritual and magic in isolated sites, such as the monuments and ritual spaces of prehistoric societies, or the material culture of those who practised magic in the early medieval period. The archaeology of ritual and magic has been seen as the study of particular aspects of the past. This has resulted in a disparate and scattered approach to the subject. This book aims to provide a more coherent and holistic approach to the archaeology of ritual and magic by examining the evidence for ritual and magic from a variety of perspectives. The evidence from a range of sites, including both prehistoric and early medieval, is examined in order to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the role of ritual and magic in social change.
The book is divided into three parts. The first part provides an overview of the development of ritual and magic in prehistoric and early medieval societies. The second part provides a detailed examination of the archaeological evidence for ritual and magic from a variety of sites. The final part provides an assessment of the ways in which ritual and magic have been studied in the past, and the future directions that archaeology can take in the field.
The book provides an analysis of the ways in which ritual and magic have been studied in the past, and provides a platform from which to explore the ways in which archaeology can develop the field of ritual and magic study in the future. US 67 connects the Texas metropolitan areas of Texarkana, Waco, College Station, and Houston with several smaller cities as well as the communities of Llano Estacado, Mountain Home, and White Sands National Monument. The highway runs through rural areas but also passes through the Texas cities of Waxahachie, Hillsboro, Hillsboro, Stephenville, Weatherford, Burkburnett, Wichita Falls, and Lamesa. At the time, the highway ran through the Texas cities of Denison, Denton, Dallas, Fort Worth, and San Angelo.

The US 67/US 77 concurrency between Oglesby and Gainesville, Texas, was removed in 1992, with US 67 extended northward to the Oklahoma state line. In 2003, due to the removal of the US 67/US 77 concurrency, the U.S. Highway System eliminated the US 77 designation in Texas.

In 2012, the US 67 designation was removed from its concurrency with US 287 in San Angelo. The U.S. Highway System removed the US 67 designation in its entirety on September 10, 2012. The Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) assumed the state responsibility for US 67 a day later on September 11, 2012.

On September 23, 1925, the highway was extended northward to the Oklahoma state line. On March 27, 1926, the highway was extended to Erath County, and then extended northward to Denton on April 29, 1926. On May 18, 1926, the highway was extended northward to the Oklahoma state line, replacing SH 54. On October 1, 1927, SH 20 was extended northward to Oklahoma, replacing SH 163, SH 165, and SH 193.

The conscription law of World War I provided for noncombatant service for members of a religious organization whose members wer

en't eligible for exemption from military service. _Provided_ , that is, that the religious organization had applied for special permission to be exempted from military service. And _provided_ , too, that the individual in question was willing to serve in the organization's noncombatant service.
The Salvation Army had applied for and been granted special permission to be exempt from military service. The Army's noncombatant service was a form of service that was known as "friendly enemies." And the Salvation Army was willing to accept the service of friendly enemies.
Those who were willing to serve in the Salvation Army's friendly enemy service had to agree to abide by two provisions:
1. They had to be willing to work in the friendly enemy service for a period of twelve months.
2. They had to be willing to take an oath that they would not take up arms, nor fight against the United States in any way, shape, or form.
For the first time in its history, the Salvation Army began to accept applications from friendly enemies.
About a week after the United States entered the war, a man named William McCarthy came to the Salvation Army's office in New York City. He was a thirty-three-year-old, seventy-five-pound, five-foot-five-inch-tall Irish American who was unemployed. His wife and three children were living in Ireland.
When the Salvation Army worker asked him if he was willing to serve in friendly enemy service, Mr. McCarthy replied, "Absolutely. I'll do anything I can to help the Allies."
The Salvation Army worker then told Mr. McCarthy, "All right. If you want to help the Allies, you'll have to take two oaths. First, you'll have to agree to work in the friendly enemy service for a period of twelve months. Second, you'll have to swear that you won't take up arms, nor fight against the United States in any way, shape, or form."
"I'll take those two oaths," Mr. McCarthy said.
"Good," the Salvation Army worker replied. "You'll have to take the oaths in the presence of a notary public."
Then the Salvation Army worker said, "William, I want you to take the oaths right here in this office as soon as possible."
"I'll come back tomorrow," Mr. McCarthy said.
"I don't want you to come back tomorrow," the Salvation Army worker said. "I want you to come back now."
Mr. McCarthy shook his head. "You're asking me to come back within the next few minutes. That's impossible."
"I'm sorry," the Salvation Army worker said. "It's impossible for us to help you if you don't take the oaths right away."
"I can't take them right away," Mr. McCarthy said. "I've got to go back to my apartment and find a notary public."
"You don't have to find a notary public," the Salvation Army worker said. "I'll be glad to take your oaths. I'm a notary public. You can take the oaths right here in this office."
"That's very kind of you," Mr. McCarthy said. "But I've got to go back to my apartment and get my wife to sign a permission slip."
"You don't have to go back to your apartment to get your wife to sign a permission slip," the Salvation Army worker said. "Your wife is here in this office now. I'll call her in."

It has been a long @-@ held assumption that the majority of stars occur in gravitationally bound , multiple @-@ star systems .

This assumption was based on the fact that observed multiple star systems are typically found in dense star-forming regions and thus are likely to be young and have not had enough time to significantly disperse through gravitational interactions.  However, multiple @-@ star systems are also frequently observed in regions of low star-formation rate,  and it has recently been found that young single star-forming regions are more likely to contain multiple @-@ systems than are older regions.  These results have led to the hypothesis that many stars form in multiple systems, but that these systems disperse on short timescales, implying that the gravitational field of a star system must be efficient in dispersing young stars.  Here we resolve this conflict by pointing out that it is the ages of individual stars within a multiple system that is important in determining the fraction of systems that remain bound.  We demonstrate that for the average star forming region, the typical lifetime of a young (within 5 Myr) multiple system is only a few Myr (<3 Myr).  This is well within the typical lifetime a single star remains in a bound multiple system (5-10 Myr).  Therefore, the duration of the period of multiple star formation in a given region is independent of the dynamical dispersal time of young binaries.

2008-02-10 00:00:00 PDT Washington -- Anonymous, a loose federation of computer activists, has announced a series of coordinated actions against several U.S. corporations for their support of the Iraq war.
In an email to CNET News, Anonymous stated that coordinated activities were planned for February 10, in many major cities, in response to the war.
The email stated that protesters were to target Starbucks, Borders, Staples and The Gap, which are all members of the Business Industry Political Action Committee, which supports Republican candidates.
The email stated, "We believe that these companies are directly complicit in the deaths of every soldier, sailor, airman and marine. We will be targeting them, and many more, for disruption and boycotts until they pull their funding from the Bush administration and the Iraq war."
The companies did not immediately respond to requests for comments.
The email was sent by "Anonymous," a loose federation of activists that has been credited with bringing down the Church of Scientology's Web site in December.
Anonymous has also been credited with being the group behind "Operation Payback" which attacked the computer systems of the Motion Picture Association of America.
CNET News' Robert McMillan contributed to this report.
Source: CNET News

The favoured name for this species among naturalists has changed over the years , with " landrail " and variants of " corncrake

" being used by many authors. The name " Australian corncrake " is still commonly used and is more specific than " landrail ", which is a family name that includes the Australian species. The other two landrail species found in Australia ( _G. _flavirostris and _G. _septentrionalis ) also have common names that are sometimes used for the Australian species, but they are of little help. The genus name, _Grallina ,_ was chosen by John Gould in 1841 after the Greek _grallos_ , meaning "crane". Gould's intention was to link together the Australian and New Zealand species, but his use of the Greek form was probably influenced by the notion that the two groups of birds were ancient in origin. This form was used by many authors until the late 19th century, although Gould also used the name _Pentheria_ , based on a name used by Vieillot in 1817.
 The third and final member of the landrail family is the Western Ground Parrot ( _Pezophaps solitaria_ ). Its original name was the Torresian Ground Parrot ( _Pezophaps torquatus_ ), but this was changed to _P. solitaria_ in 1991. It is rare enough, and has been studied and written about sufficiently, for its own chapter.
 The Australian landrail is found only in the north east of Australia. Its range extends from Cape York Peninsula in Queensland to the central coast of New South Wales and the south coast of the Northern Territory (and possibly also from Northern Territory to the Kimberley region of Western Australia). The species is found only in Australia, although it may have been introduced to New Guinea. The range of the landrail is divided into three subspecies, the nominate subspecies ( _G. _m. _m._ ) and _G. _m. _mahonyi_ and _G. _m. _boweri_ (Rothschild, 1907). It is sometimes claimed that there is also a fourth subspecies, _G. _m. _lindsayi,_ but this is generally considered to be a synonym of _G. _m. _mahonyi_.
The Australian landrail has a preference for low-lying sandy heathland, but also occurs in other habitat types. It is strongly associated with mallee and other small trees, short grass and herbs. It is usually found in a dry habitat, but it may be found in a variety of habitats that are seasonally or occasionally flooded. It occurs in coastal areas, but only inland from the sea. It is found around rivers, creeks, lakes, flooded grasslands and flooded mallee and heathland. It seems to prefer a fairly open habitat, although it sometimes occurs in dense scrub. It is found as far inland as water supplies, but is not usually found in grasslands that have little or no groundwater. The species is sedentary, but may undertake some seasonal movement in response to food availability.
The species is usually found at altitudes of less than 400 m. It rarely occurs above 100 m, but is occasionally found around 400 m. The range of the species is from 2,940 km2 to 3,600 km2. It is found in a number of protected areas and is not seriously threatened.

and Shewanow ( 2003 ) and Holschuh ( 2004 ).
Function of spacing in oral and signed communication.
Spacing in spoken communication is of great interest to the speech-language pathologist who is working with children who are deaf or hard of hearing. In this chapter I discuss the spacing of speech in normal-hearing children and adults who are deaf, as well as in children who are deaf and use American Sign Language (ASL).
Normally hearing children and adults who are deaf have been found to widely space sentences (Clinton et al., 2003; Holschuh, 2004). Clinton et al. (2003) also found that children and adults who are deaf are less likely to use sentence spacing than normally hearing children. However, children who are deaf who use ASL use pauses, glottal stops, and other speech prosodic markers to indicate grammatical boundaries. These prosodic markers are used both in ASL and in English (Shewanow & Keller, 2002).
In addition, we know that children who are deaf who have cochlear implants also use prosodic markers to indicate grammatical boundaries. These prosodic markers are used both in ASL and in English (Holschuh, 2004).
Therefore, the spacing of speech in this population varies depending on the language being used. The prosodic markers are used to demonstrate a grammatical boundary, as in ASL, and the use of glottal stops and pauses is used to demonstrate a grammatical boundary, as in English. The tawny nurse shark ( _Ginglymostoma cirratum_ ) is not quite as colourful as the name might suggest. Its pattern of dots and dashes is not as neat as that of its nurse shark cousin, but it makes up for this with a more placid disposition. It does not travel in large schools and is more often found alone or in small groups of two or three individuals.
The tawny nurse shark is found in tropical and subtropical waters throughout the Indian and Pacific Oceans, from South Africa to Hawaii and beyond. It is a highly migratory species and can often be found in coastal waters near coral reefs, as well as the pelagic zone.
The tawny nurse shark is a relatively large shark, with a maximum length of 2.5 m (8 ft). It is a slim shark, with a long, narrow snout, small eyes and powerful jaws. Its most distinguishable feature is its long, skinny, sickle-shaped tail, which has a dark brown or black skin around the tip, and the rest of its body is a light grey colour. The top of its body is often covered in small, dark spots, resembling a leopard's fur.
The tawny nurse shark lives on the bottom of the sea floor, but it is common to see them near the surface at night. Tawny nurse sharks are slow swimmers and are often seen pacing back and forth near the bottom, rather than swimming. They are solitary and non-aggressive sharks, but they are not timid and can become quite curious around divers. They will often allow themselves to be touched and can often be seen resting on the bottom, apparently getting a good night's sleep.
The tawny nurse shark is an opportunistic feeder. It will eat almost anything it can fit in its small mouth, including fish, bony fish, squid, crabs and shrimps. They also enjoy eating algae and other sea vegetables.
The tawny nurse shark is a slow-moving shark and does not reach sexual maturity until it is 12 years old and 1.5 m (5 ft) long. Its reproduction cycle is unique in that it does not follow the seasonal pattern of many other shark species. The sharks mate throughout the year. They give birth to their young after a pregnancy period of 10 months. The young are born with a length of 45 cm (18 in) and they reach maturity after about 8 years.
Tawny nurse sharks are not considered to be a threatened species, although there is some concern over the decline of their numbers due to incidental catching in fishing nets.
One of the more interesting aspects of the tawny nurse shark is that it is able to detach its lower jaw. This is a survival mechanism so that if one jaw is caught in a net, the shark can still breathe as it swims. The lower jaw is also able to detach if the shark is attacked by a predator, which is why it is often referred to as the "gummy shark".
Divers often refer to tawny nurse sharks as "walking sharks" because they often walk along the bottom of the seafloor, often at dusk.
The tawny nurse shark is also known as the "spotted gummy shark", the "spotted sand shark", the "spotted stingray shark" and the "spotted wobbegong".
When the tawny nurse shark feels threatened, it will often swim away from the danger. If this is not possible, it will curl its body into a tight ball, with its head tucked under its pectoral fin, and will use its tail to try to protect itself.
Tawny nurse sharks are commonly found for sale at fish markets and are also often consumed by humans for food. Their meat and fins are considered a delicacy in some countries. Their liver is also used as a source of vitamin A.

The West Hendford Cricket Ground was a first class cricket ground located in Yeovil , Somerset . The land for the ground was first leased in 1855, and the ground was first used in 1856. The ground was an important venue for cricket fixtures in the south west of England. The ground ceased to operate as a cricket ground in 1940 when the land was requisitioned by the Government for use in the Second World War. The land was then returned to its former owner, the Duke of Beaufort, and it is now a housing development.
The ground was located on the northern edge of Yeovil. It was located around the junction of Church Street, West Hendford and South Street. The main ground was approximately 1 acre in size and was bounded by a fence on three sides. The main entrance was located on Church Street. The ground was three-sided and measured 100 yards by 65 yards. The ground had two short straight sides and one long straight side. The two short sides were 80 yards and 90 yards in length respectively. As a result of the short sides, the ground was regarded as one of the most bowler-friendly in England. The ground had a pavilion that was constructed in 1891. The pavilion was brick built and was located to the north-east corner of the ground. It was 30 ft (9.1 m) by 30 ft (9.1 m) and had a slate roof. A number of temporary stands were located at the southern end of the ground. These stands seated 1500 spectators. The ground was owned by the Town Hall, and was leased to the Yeovil Cricket Club.

Climate in Nova Scotia is influenced by two factors, the North Atlantic Current, and the Gulf Stream, which wash warm waters along the eastern Canadian and American coastlines from the Gulf of Mexico. Nova Scotia is also affected by weather systems that develop in the interior of North America and move eastward, especially in the winter.
The annual mean temperature of Nova Scotia varies from a low of 2°C (36°F) in the cooler regions of the north, such as Cape Breton Island, to 11°C (52°F) in the southwest. The mean annual precipitation varies across the province from 1,400 mm (55 in) on the north shore of Cape Breton Island to 125 mm (5 in) on the Cabot Trail in western Cape Breton. During the winter and early spring, coastal areas are affected by sea fog and the coastal climate is moderated by the warm waters of the Gulf Stream.
The temperature of Nova Scotia's ocean waters is affected by the Gulf Stream. In the summer, ocean temperatures reach 15°C (59°F) in the south and 12°C (54°F) off the Nova Scotia coast. The temperature of the upper 700 m (2,300 ft) of the ocean is about 5°C (41°F) warmer than the temperature of the atmosphere. This warmer water causes winds to rise faster in the winter and, as a result, makes the land cooler and drier.
The oceanic and atmospheric circulation of the Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Current affect the climate of Nova Scotia, causing warmer winters in the southeast, and cooler and wetter winters in the north.
The climate of Nova Scotia is moderate. The warmth of the Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Current creates a climate that is milder than that of interior North America. The cold Labrador Current and the cold air from the interior also affect the climate. The combination of these weather systems creates a climate that is cool to cold in the winter and warm and humid in the summer.
Low temperatures in Nova Scotia occur in the winter and early spring, between November and April. The average daily minimum temperature in January is –1°C (30°F) on the south shore of Nova Scotia, and –12°C (10°F) in Yarmouth. Winters are usually cloudy and snowy. The average annual snowfall in Nova Scotia is 158 cm (62 in)  The snow usually falls in the form of brief, heavy snowfalls. Nova Scotia's coldest month is January, when the temperature falls below freezing for 14 to 15 days of the month.
The lowest temperature ever recorded in Nova Scotia was –43°C (–45°F), on February 1, 1969, in Poley Mountain, near Amherst.
Nova Scotia's summer temperatures are influenced by the moderating effect of the ocean. The average daily maximum temperature in July is 22°C (72°F) on the south shore of Nova Scotia, and 18°C (64°F) in Yarmouth. The average high temperature in the summer is 25°C (77°F).
During the summer, the sun shines for 16 to 17 hours per day. The summer season is short, but very warm and humid. The months of July, August, and September are usually the warmest.
In summer, high temperatures are sometimes associated with tropical storms that develop in the Gulf of Mexico or the Caribbean Sea. These storms, known as hurricanes or tropical storms, can produce heavy rainfall and, in some cases, flooding. The last severe tropical storm to affect Nova Scotia was Hurricane Juan, which made landfall near Halifax on September 29, 2003.
The warmest temperature ever recorded in Nova Scotia was 37°C (99°F), on August 14, 1966, on the coast of Nova Scotia.

Plunketts Creek is a 20.7-mile-long (33.3 km) tributary of the Susquehanna River in Lycoming and Sullivan counties, in Pennsylvania, United States. Plunketts Creek was formerly called Lycoming Creek, and was renamed in 1827 by an act of the Pennsylvania General Assembly in honor of Thomas Plunket, a leading local citizen. The United States Geological Survey (USGS) has designated a gauging station on Plunketts Creek, named Plunketts Creek near South Abington Township, which has been monitoring the water level of the stream since 1940.
As of 1920, the name Plunketts Creek was also applied to an abandoned former railroad line that ran from the town of Factoryville to the town of Dushore, with a spur line connecting the village of Tunkhannock to the line.
The stream rises 1,300 feet (396 m) above sea level on the southeast slope of the eastern Alleghenies in Sullivan County, and flows generally westward through Lycoming County into the Susquehanna River. The Susquehanna River flows northeast, and finally into the Chesapeake Bay.
The Plunketts Creek Trail, a 9.0-mile (14.5 km) hiking and biking trail, runs along the south bank of the creek in Lycoming County. The trail begins near the village of Factoryville and runs to the borough of Dushore in the township of South Abington.
The stream passes through the villages of Factoryville and Dushore, the boroughs of Forks Township, Factoryville, and Dushore, and the townships of Forks Township, South Abington Township, and Tunkhannock Township.
As of 2007, the borough of Forks Township was planning to replace the bridge that carries Plunketts Creek Road over the stream with a new bridge, but the project was delayed.
The former Plunketts Creek Museum, a museum of local history, was located along the Plunketts Creek Trail near Orson Station in South Abington Township. It was closed in 2002, and its contents were relocated to the Susquehanna Heritage Museum in Montgomery, Pennsylvania.
The bridge crossing Plunketts Creek was originally built in 1851 and last rebuilt in 1938.

Black-tailed jackrabbits are found in North America from Alaska east to central Florida and south to Texas and northern Mexico. They are the most widely distributed of all the desert hare species. Jackrabbits prefer open, rocky terrain and avoid dense forests.
Jackrabbits are solitary animals with territories ten to twenty square miles in area. They will, however, gather in large numbers on wintering grounds and around water sources.
The jackrabbit's burrow is usually a slight depression in the ground with a single opening that is used only for emergency escape. The jackrabbit sleeps in its burrow during the day and comes out at night to feed.
Jackrabbits are classified as Leporids and are related to hares, rabbits, and pikas. Jackrabbits are unique in that they can run up to 40 miles per hour.
Jackrabbits are herbivores . They eat a wide variety of forbs, grasses, and occasionally shrubs. Their digestive system is adapted to allow them to eat plants that are inedible to most other animals.
Reproduction in jackrabbits is seasonal and occurs twice each year. A gestation period of 30 to 40 days results in a litter of one to eight kits. The kits are born with pink skin that becomes brown as they mature. By the time they reach sexual maturity, their black-tipped ears have grown to a length of 5 to 6 inches. Jackrabbits are basically solitary animals, except when females gather to give birth in spring or fall.
Jackrabbits are hunted by many predators, including coyotes, bobcats, hawks, and owls.

Grand River Avenue started as the path of an early wagon trail in the Michigan Territory , carrying settlers from Detroit inlan

d. The territory's first governor, Stevens T. Mason , referred to the path as "Michigan's Throat," a winding route that was the only way to get through the northern prairie to the land of the Huron and Potawatomi Indians. Near the junction of the Grand and Clinton rivers, a small trading post was built in 1832, and the community soon took the name Grand Rapids . The soon-to-be-named Grand River Avenue was the only direct road to the area.
During the 1830s the road was graded, and at the end of the decade a new route was cut that followed the Grand River. This road became the first public highway in the state of Michigan .
In 1868, the Grand River Avenue was designated as a state trunk line, with the state paying for road improvements.
Although the road is no longer heavily traveled, it still serves as a major thoroughfare in West Michigan and is part of the Lake Michigan Circle Tour.
# 1
The Grand River Avenue, Grand Rapids to Grand Haven
The Grand River Avenue is 163 miles long, all in West Michigan. It begins at the eastern end of the five-lane highway that carries traffic into the heart of downtown Grand Rapids from the north. There is a split in the road on the east end of the city—the Grand River Avenue follows the river to the north, and the Grandville Avenue goes to the south. This is the northern trail of the original wagon path.
The road then turns west and follows the river, passing the city park, the Grand River Dam, and the dam's hydroelectric plant as it reaches the Grand River exit from Interstate 96. The highway then skirts the west edge of the city, running parallel to the Grand River.
The road continues west as it passes through the town of Rockford, then enters the city of Grand Haven . It is now called the 22nd Street Bridge and crosses the Grand River, then the bridge becomes the 22nd Avenue Bridge over the Grand Haven Channel .
This is the western end of the Grand River Avenue.
# 2
The Grand River Avenue, Grand Haven to Grandville
The road begins on the west end of the 22nd Avenue Bridge over the Grand Haven Channel. It is now called the 22nd Street Bridge . It crosses the channel, then the bridge becomes the 22nd Avenue Bridge over the Grand River.
The road continues west as it passes through the city of Grand Haven and crosses the Grand River, then it turns north and reaches the city of Grandville. It continues north as it crosses the Rogue River, then enters the city.
The road continues north through Grandville, passing under Interstate 96, then it crosses another river, the Rumsey Creek, and joins the Grandville Avenue. This is the eastern end of the Grand River Avenue.
# 3
The Grand River Avenue, Grandville to Walker
The road begins on the north end of the Grandville Avenue, where the two roads join, and follows the Grand River. It passes under Interstate 96 one last time, crosses the Grand River again, then heads north.
The road continues north, passing through the towns of Comstock Park and Cutlerville. It crosses several local rivers and streams, then reaches the city of Walker , where it turns west and crosses the Grand River.
The road continues west as it passes through the city and reaches the western end of the Grand River Avenue.
# 4
The Grand River Avenue, Walker to Waukazoo
The road begins on the west end of the Grand River Avenue, following the road as it crosses the Grand River. It continues west as it passes through the city and reaches the city limits.
The road continues west as it passes through the city of Walker, then crosses the Rogue River and enters the city of Muskegon . It passes through the city and crosses the White River , then continues west as it reaches the city limits again.
The road continues as it passes through the city of Muskegon, then enters the town of Twin Lake . It passes through the town and meets the Grand River again, then crosses the river once more.
The road continues west as it passes through the city of Muskegon again and crosses the Pere Marquette River . It enters the town of Muskegon Heights and reaches the city limits, then crosses the Grand River once more and turns north.

Breese was launched on 11 May 1918 out of Newport News , Virginia . She was sponsored by Gilbert McIlvaine , daughter of Breese

's captain. She was commissioned on 20 May 1918 , with Lieutenant Commander Frank J. Hough in command.
Breese completed her shakedown training in the Chesapeake Bay and sailed for Europe on 13 June 1918 , arriving at Brest , France , on 16 July 1918. She joined the United States Naval Detachment in France (USNDE) on 22 July 1918 for service in support of the Allied cause. Breese operated in the English Channel and along the French coast, transporting soldiers, equipment and supplies to the front.
On 29 September 1918, Breese was ordered to England to join the British Grand Fleet. She arrived in Scapa Flow on 2 October 1918, and subsequently patrolled the Bay of Biscay for two weeks. She returned to Brest on 27 October 1918 to resume her transport assignment in the English Channel.
Between 1 and 12 November 1918, Breese transported troops and equipment from the United States to Cherbourg, France. On 13 November 1918, Breese returned to Brest, and sailed for the United States on 16 December 1918. She arrived at Norfolk , Virginia on 29 December 1918.
Breese was decommissioned at the Norfolk Navy Yard on 28 December 1918, and remained in reserve until 10 November 1920.
Returning to active duty in the USN early in 1921, Breese was assigned to the Naval Coast Defense Reserve. Based at Newport , Rhode Island, she guarded the approaches to Newport Harbor until 1923. She was then moved to Boston , Massachusetts , where she operated out of the Boston Navy Yard until she was decommissioned at that yard on 20 June 1923.
Breese was recommissioned on 24 February 1926, and assigned to the Naval Auxiliary Reserve. She operated along the New England coast and in Chesapeake Bay until decommissioned again at the Philadelphia Navy Yard on 13 August 1926. Breese was sold to the Bethlehem Shipbuilding Corporation on 2 July 1927.

The shores of Corpus Christi ( or Body of Christ ) Bay are thought to have been inhabited by the Karankawa Indians before the E

ight Elders ( a religious group) of the Spanish missions of Texas came to the area in 1751. The Karankawa were a nomadic sea-faring tribe, from the Texas coast to the mouth of the Mississippi River. Their name means " The People " in their native tongue and is the same as the name of the native tribe of the Lousiana bayou country.
 The Spanish devastated the Karankawa and the Eight Elders of the religious order started the missions to " Christianize " the Indians. The Karankawa Indians did not give up their old nomadic ways and were constantly in conflict with the Spanish. The Spanish nicknamed the Karankawa "The Cuero Indians" "The Hairy Ones" because they were not the peaceful Indians they thought they were.
 The Spanish efforts to " Christianize " the Indians were not as successful as they wished. They were only partially successful in converting the Karankawa.
 Eight years later the Spanish soldiers returned to the mission to find that the Karankawa had killed the priests and the Spanish soldiers and had returned to their old ways.

They are unusual among parrots in that they are flightless , unable to fly as a result of having a small keeled sternum , which is intended to keep the wings stiff and rigid. They have a small, weak flight muscle and an elongated clavicle , which makes it difficult for them to fly. They are the only living members of the family Strigopidae.
The kakapo is endemic to New Zealand and has been found on the main island of New Zealand , the Chatham Islands and outlying islands. They are the only New Zealand bird to have been listed as critically endangered since 1992, and the only species where all known individuals are owned by the New Zealand Department of Conservation .

May 1963
Canyon Country
More than a thousand miles of the wildest canyons in North America are about to be dammed and flooded to generate hydroelectric power. The Colorado River is surging through its last 350 miles of natural channels, but the battle to keep this great river free has just begun.
The Colorado River is the greatest popular monument in the American West. It runs 1,400 miles from the Rockies to the Gulf of California. Nearly 25 million people live in its drainage basin as the waters spread out into the arid deserts of Arizona, California, Utah and Nevada. Its tributaries—the Green, San Juan, Gila, San Pedro, Little Colorado and Virgin—widen its basin to 140,000 square miles, an area larger than Tennessee, or the states of Pennsylvania and Delaware combined.
For 550 miles the lower Colorado is one of the most beautiful rivers in the world. It flows through the Grand Canyon, one of the seven wonders of the world, with its red-rock walls 18 miles high. The first documented mention of Qedar is from a stele ( c . 737 BCE ) of Tiglath @-@ Pileser III , a king of the Neo @-@ Assyri

ans.  The stele mentions that Qedar was defeated in battle by Tiglath @-@ Pileser III and that the king of Qedar was taken prisoner. From this time on, the land of Qedar was an Assyrian possession.
 The Assyrians ( Neo @-@ Assyrians ) continued to remain in control of Qedar until the fall of the Neo @-@ Assyrian Empire. After the fall of Assyria, Qedar became a part of the Chaldean Empire under King Nabonidus.
 Nabonidus also built the city of Babylon and made it the capital of the Chaldean Empire. After the death of Nabonidus in 539 BCE, the Chaldean Empire was divided between his son Belshazzar and the Medes and Persians.
 Eventually, the Medes and Persians took control of all the lands of the Chaldean Empire. At this time, the Medes and Persians were under the control of Cyrus the Great.
 Qedar was considered a city-state and was under the control of the Medes and Persians. In 330 BCE, Alexander the Great died and the Medes and Persians became part of the Seleucid Empire under Seleucus I . In 305 BCE, Seleucus I divided his empire into four parts and gave the largest part to Seleucus II , also called Seleucus II Callinicus. Seleucus II became king of the Seleucid Empire and ruled until 225 BCE.
 During the reign of Seleucus II Callinicus, the greatest threat to the Seleucid Empire was the Parthian Empire. At this time, the Parthians were under the control of Arses . In 216 BCE, Arses died and Seleucus II Callinicus took advantage of the situation and went to war with the Parthians.
 In 212 BCE, Seleucus II Callinicus and the Seleucid Empire were defeated by the Parthians. Seleucus II Callinicus was taken prisoner and sent to the Parthian capital of Pasargadae.
 In 211 BCE, Seleucus II Callinicus died in captivity. The Seleucid Empire was split between the Parthians and the Ptolemies . The Parthians took control of the Seleucid Empire and placed on the throne their own king, Antiochus III the Great .
 At this time, the kingdom of Qedar was under the control of the Parthians and was given to the king of the Parthians, Antiochus III the Great.
 Qedar was a city-state and was under the control of the Parthians. However, in 163 BCE, the Parthians were under the control of the Scythians , and the kingdom of Qedar was given to the king of the Scythians, Mithridates I .
 Mithridates I remained in control of the kingdom of Qedar until 120 BCE, when his son, Mithridates II , became king of the Scythians and took control of Qedar. In 120 BCE, Mithridates II was defeated by the Parthians. In 109 BCE, Mithridates II was killed.
 In 107 BCE, the Parthians and the Scythians made peace and the kingdom of Qedar was returned to the Parthians.
 The kingdom of Qedar remained under the control of the Parthians until 63 BCE, when it was given to the Romans.
In 63 BCE, the Roman general Pompey entered the Parthian Empire and took control of the kingdom of Qedar.

 In 54 BCE, the Parthians and the Romans made peace and the kingdom of Qedar was returned to the Romans.
 In 37 BCE, the kingdom of Qedar was taken by the Romans and became part of the Roman Province of Syria.
