he Normans in 1096, this time accompanied by the emperor's son, Isaac. John's penchant for disguise was once again revealed when he attempted to enter the land of the Normans without being recognized, disguised as a Frankish knight. 26 He was unsuccessful in his attempt to surprise the Normans, and they captured him and imprisoned him in prison in the city of Nicaea.27 John III Vatatzes was able to negotiate his release, and John returned to Constantinople where he was made droungarios of the imperial guard.
In 1101, while his father was campaigning in Asia Minor, John was sent to Cilicia as a provincial governor. Here he met and married Irene, daughter of Constantine Lambadaran, a patrician and a military leader who held the post of strategos autokrator and katepano of Cilicia. John's father, Emperor John II, was impressed by John's military prowess and thus made John a sebastokrator and domestikos of the East.28 John also received the title of katepano of Cilicia.
In 1107, John was appointed again as the strategos of the Theme of Cappadocia, which he held until 1116. He was later appointed as the Domestic of the Schools, which he held from 1116 to 1118. In 1118, John was appointed the Domestic of the East, a post from which he retired in 1122. 29
John is known to have been a man of considerable wealth, possibly due to his marriage to Irene Lambadaran, an heiress, who inherited a large fortune from her father. John also received a number of grants of land from his father, Emperor John II, many of which were in Asia Minor, in particular in the area of the city of Smyrna.
John III Vatatzes also had two brothers, Alexios and Isaac, who both held important posts in the imperial government.
Alexios, a son of Emperor Alexios I, was a sebastokrator and served as the katepano of Makedonia during the reign of his brother, John III Vatatzes. He later served as the Domestic of the Schools under his brother, John III Vatatzes, and later again as the katepano of Makedonia under John's son, Isaac II.
Isaac, another son of Emperor Alexios I, was a sebastokrator and served as the strategos of Cilicia during the reign of his brother, John III Vatatzes. He later served as the Domestic of the Schools under his brother, John III Vatatzes, and later again as the katepano of Cilicia under John's son, Isaac II.
John III Vatatzes married Irene Lambadaran, daughter of Constantine Lambadaran. She was the heiress to the estates owned by her father, who had been a patrician and a prominent military leader. Irene Lambadaran was the daughter of Constantine Lambadaran, who is thought to have been a patrician, and the granddaughter of the general, Theodoros Lambadaran. It is possible that Constantine was related to the Lambadaran family, which is known to have been a prominent family in Cilicia during the eleventh century.
The marriage of John and Irene seems to have been arranged by Isaac Komnenos, who was Irene's brother.
John III Vatatzes and Irene Lambadaran had two children:
Their first child, Constantine, was born in 1118 and died in 1119.
Their second child, Isaac II, was born in 1119 and died in 1159.
John III Vatatzes died on February 16, 1138, presumably from natural causes.
 John III Vatatzes, the son of Emperor John II Komnenos and Anna Dalassene, was born in the year 1087. He was the eldest of the emperor's three sons. John II Komnenos attempted to rule the empire as a military dictator, and in 1096, his first son, Isaac, was forced to flee to the court of the emir of Aleppo, where he was imprisoned for several years. John II Komnenos was unable to see his son, and Isaac did not return to Constantinople until 1100.

Some algorithms become simpler when used on DAGs instead of general graphs , based on the principle of topological ordering . F

The first spacecraft to explore Jupiter was Pioneer 10 , which flew past the planet in December 1973 , followed by Pioneer 11 t

hree months later. The data of greatest interest to us is the first flyby of the Galileo spacecraft in 1995.
While the Galileo spacecraft was orbiting Jupiter's largest moon, Ganymede, it gave us the first direct look at the planet. This was a major surprise—it was much larger than we had expected.
The Galileo spacecraft flew by another and much smaller moon, Europa, in 1997. It was during this encounter that we learned that Europa has a global ocean under a thick shell of ice, not unlike the Antarctic continent.
The Cassini spacecraft flew by Jupiter in 2000, obtaining data that allowed us to map the magnetic field lines around Jupiter. We also obtained the first detailed high-resolution images of Jupiter's polar regions.
This book is the story of Jupiter—the planet and its moons.
The Jupiter we see today is a planet about 1.9 times as massive as the Earth and slightly more than one tenth the volume of the Sun. Jupiter has a diameter of 11.2 times that of the Earth, a mass of 318 Earth masses, and a surface gravity of 24 times that of the Earth.
Jupiter orbits the Sun once every 11.86 years. The mean distance of Jupiter from the Sun is 778 million km (483 million miles).
Jupiter's four largest moons (Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto) are sometimes referred to as the Galilean moons because they were the first to be discovered by Galileo Galilei. It is thought that these moons are fragments of a giant planet that collided with Jupiter in the early history of the solar system.
Jupiter has 63 known satellites. Thirty-one of these satellites are named after mythological figures associated with the planet Jupiter. The other 32 moons are designated as numerical progression.
Jupiter's atmospheric coverage is about half that of the Earth—20 percent. Jupiter's troposphere, the layer of atmosphere directly above the cloud tops, is a turbulent region. The turbulence arises from the fact that Jupiter's atmosphere rotates at a different rate from the planet itself. For every 10 hours that the Earth rotates once on its axis, Jupiter rotates once on its axis in 9 hours 55 minutes.
The clouds in Jupiter's troposphere are arranged in bands of different colors, the most prominent of which are the _ammonia_ bands and the _methane_ bands. These bands are named for the chemicals that cause them to appear in different colors. They are visible in the visible light range, but with a slight red tint, because of light absorption.
Jupiter is mainly hydrogen and helium, with traces of methane, ammonia, and water. This mixture is very different from the Earth's atmosphere, which is mainly nitrogen and oxygen with some carbon dioxide, methane, and traces of ammonia and water.
Jupiter is the only planet whose magnetic field is not aligned with the rotational axis of the planet. This is because the planet's metallic core is a liquid and rotates more quickly than the atmosphere above it, which is composed only of gases.
Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the third largest planet in the solar system. However, the fourth planet from the Sun is not Uranus but Neptune, which is just less massive than Uranus.
Jupiter and the other outer planets must have formed early in the history of the solar system, before the inner planets had formed.
The only reason why Jupiter is visible to us is because it passes in front of the Sun from Earth's point of view. Jupiter has only 0.00004 percent of the Sun's light, but when it passes in front of the Sun it blocks 96 percent of the Sun's light.
Jupiter has been visited by five spacecraft. The first of these was Pioneer 10 , which flew past Jupiter on 4 December 1973. Pioneer 11 followed three months later on 1 October 1979. Galileo was launched in 1989 and reached Jupiter in 1995. Cassini flew through the Jupiter system in 2000 and Io Express flew by the volcanic moon Io in 2003.

During the winter of 1915-16 they were employed for coast defence in England, but in June 1916 were embarked for the Near East. In the same month they arrived at Alexandria; and, after a few weeks' training, they were employed in the defence of the Suez Canal. As soon as the 51st and 52nd Divisions arrived in the theatre of war, it was no longer possible to retain them for the defence of the Canal; and on 24 July 1916 they were disbanded, and their personnel was incorporated in the 53rd (Welsh) Division, which was then being formed in the United Kingdom.
 The duties of the 51st and 52nd Divisions in the defence of the Canal had been the responsibility of the 5th (Naval) Division and the 8th (Indian) Division, which had been despatched from India. The Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 reduced the importance of the House of Lords in the passage of legislation. In 1976, the Constitutional Reform Act transferred a number of powers from the House of Lords to the House of Commons.
Historically, the bills passed by the Commons and Lords, along with the Sovereign's assent, formed the basis of an Act of Parliament. The bill could originate in the Commons or Lords, but most originated in the Commons as a result of MPs being elected by the electorate. However, the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 reduced the power of the Lords over the Commons, and in 1976, the Constitutional Reform Act transferred a number of powers from the Lords to the Commons.
The Parliament Acts are two acts of the Parliament of the United Kingdom that changed the rules for the approval of legislation by the Parliament of the United Kingdom. The first, the Parliament Act 1911, which received the assent of the Crown on 17 December 1911, reduced the power of the House of Lords to veto legislation passed by the House of Commons, while the second, the Parliament Act 1949, which received the assent of the Crown on 17 July 1949, established the principle that the Lords should not be able to delay Bills from receiving Royal Assent for more than two years.

The Temple of Eshmun ( Arabic : معبد أشمون ) is an ancient place of worship dedicated to Eshmun , the Phoenician god of healing

, in the Beqaa Valley , Lebanon .
The temple is part of the Beqaa Valley Archaeological Park , which includes the nearby Baalbek .
The temple was built in the 1st century BC, at the end of the Hellenistic period, on the site of a sanctuary dedicated to Eshmun already located there, and which was destroyed in 64 BC. His worship has been practiced during the Roman era (Ist century AD)
The temple was badly damaged during the Lebanese civil war, but was restored in 1999.

The 1968 presidential election was held on November 5, 1968. Murali was born in a village named Karumathampatti in Coimbatore district, Tamil Nadu. He studied in primary and secondary schools in his village. He moved to Chennai and did a diploma in computer hardware and networking. He then worked as a network and system administrator in a Chennai based company. He has also worked as an assistant director for a few films. He then decided to pursue acting and moved to Mumbai, where he trained himself as an actor. He has also worked as a dubbing artist for films.
In 2002, Murali started his acting career in Tamil cinema with the film Parthale Paravasam directed by Shaji Kailas. He then got noticed for his performance in the 2004 film Pandavar Bhoomi, directed by Selva, which won him the Filmfare Best Supporting Actor Award. After working in films like Vidiyum Varaiyum, Kurumbu, and Naadodigal, he got his breakthrough with the successful films Chellamae (2004) and Aayutha Ezhuthu (2004). He then got noticed for his performances in the films Kattradhu Thamizh (2007) and Pasanga (2009). He is noted for his performance as a father in the film Aadukalam (2011) which won him the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor.
Murali has also acted in over 250 television serials.
He married a doctor by profession named Jayashree in 2009.
Murali's son Vijay Murali, who also worked as an assistant director in movies, made his acting debut in the film Enakkal Thol Vilayattu (2016).

The 1984–85 season was Motherwell Football Club's 82nd season in existence, and their second consecutive season in the top-flight of Scottish football. Along with Celtic, Rangers and Aberdeen, they contested the Premier Division, the top division of the time. The club ended the season as runners-up, although they did win the Scottish Cup.
Following the defeat of Rangers in the Scottish Cup Final, Motherwell were only one point behind Celtic, having played two games (one of which was a Premier Division game) more.
Sadly though, Motherwell's great cup run of 1984–85 was to come to an end as they were defeated 3–1 by Celtic in the final.
At the start of the following season, Motherwell lost only one match in their first six making them joint leaders of the Scottish Premier Division with Aberdeen.
On 29 December 1984, Motherwell beat Celtic 2–1 at Celtic Park to move to the top of the Scottish Premier Division table, the first time in 12 years that they had taken top spot.
Motherwell were in the running for the Scottish Premier League title until the last few days of the season, when an injury to their star player, midfielder Dave Bowman, left them without a reliable goal scorer. They finished the season runners-up to Aberdeen.
To add to their disappointments at the end of the season, Motherwell were defeated 1–0 in the final of the Scottish Cup by Aberdeen.
Motherwell's reserve team finished second in the Central Division of the Scottish Reserve League.
Motherwell's youth team finished 3rd in the Midland Regional Youth League.

Around 1600, the names of the constellations were used to name the stars in the corresponding regions of the sky. The German aphorist Michael Maestlin (1550-1631) was the first to write down the names of the constellations in the modern form. 1637 The names of the constellations were officially adopted in the first astronomical textbook of Johannes Kepler, entitled "De Stella Nova Triangulorum" ( "On the New Star in Triangulum ") and published in Prague. 1687 was the first time that the constellations were depicted in the form in which they are known today.
As the constellations were originally created as guides for seafarers, the name of the stars in the constellations was not based on the Greek myths, but on the description of the objects of the night sky (e.g. "The Charioteer" = the bright star of the North Star). The stars that are now in the constellations were also often named after the constellations in which they are located, so the star Algibi , which is now in the constellation of Hydra and Canis Major , was also called Alpha Hydri at that time.
In the course of the centuries, the names of the constellations changed several times. The constellations of the Greco-Roman astronomy were usually depicted as figures in the form of a person who could be identified with an ancient god. The Babylonian constellations were also based on the general perception of the constellations as a whole, but they were more abstract in their depiction. Reconstructions of the Babylonian constellations gave the constellations of the Greco-Roman astronomy their human form.
The constellations are divided into zodiac constellations and non-zodiac constellations . In the zodiac , the Sun, Moon and planets rise and set. The non-zodiac constellations are more distant from the ecliptic (ecliptic), which is why they are less interesting to human observers. Some of the non-zodiac constellations are quite well known, such as the Andromeda , the Auriga , the Cetus , the Camelopardalis , the Cepheus , the Corvus , the Draco , the Equuleus , the Grus , the Hydra , the Leo , the Lynx , the Ophiuchus , the Pisces , the Piscis Austrinus , the Sagittarius , the Scutum , the Sextans , the Taurus , the Ursa Major , the Ursa Minor and the Virgo . The Ursa Major is also in the Northern Hemisphere but is not a zodiac constellation.
The fact that the constellations were not originally built to represent a god or a mythological figure, but to serve as a navigation guide, is also shown by the fact that some of the constellations are a bit strange in their depiction. The constellation Ursa Major consists of two parts, the "Big Dipper" and the "Little Dipper", which serve as a guide to the North Star. The constellation Andromeda , on the other hand, is largely defined by the stars of the Milky Way galaxy, which is not related to the mythological story. Nevertheless, the constellations of the Greco-Roman astronomy were often depicted in the form of humans.
At the beginning of the 20th century, the constellations were also divided into southern and northern constellations. However, since the Southern Hemisphere also has its zodiac constellations, there is no longer any exact distinction.

Tennyson adopts aspects of the Ulysses character and narrative from many sources ; his treatment of Ulysses is the first modern

version of a literary character from The Odyssey. While the poem does not adhere to the original story (Dublin is not Ithaca ; the Trojan War is mentioned only in passing), it does contain various elements of the original.

Tennyson uses the Homeric scansion in the original and translates it into his own rhyme-scheme. He also uses the Homeric "epic simile" in the "sailing home" passage: "as when night-flying swallows Homeward, some in flock, and some, half-scattered, Still fluttering, drop into the fields and cover The sown furrows, and the standing upland grain, And all the orchard tops with white mice strewn."

The "Ulysses" passage, the central portion of the poem, was written in the summer of 1833, and Tennyson wrote it at height of his career, when he had received three of his four Laureateships. This passage is the most quoted of Tennyson's poems.

The poem was first published in the year of Tennyson's marriage to Emily Sellwood in 1850, in the collection Poems by Two Brothers. The poem was first published in book form in Poems, Chiefly Lyrical in 1830. The 1850 volume was published by E. L. Carey & A. Hart.

The poem was set to music by the 19th-century composer Sir Arthur Sullivan.

## Form

Tennyson's poem is titled Ulysses, after the eponymous hero of Homer's epic poem, and is in the form of a dramatic monologue. The poem is written in thirty-two quatrains, with the rhyme scheme ababcc. Each stanza is a distinct scene, with a narrative arc beginning in medias res, with an action already in progress.

### Structure

Tennyson's poem is divided into three parts:

Part I: "The Voyage" (lines 1–43)
Part II: "The Cradle Song" (lines 44–102)
Part III: "The Old Men" (lines 103–120)

### Style

Tennyson's diction is natural and conversational with frequent colloquialisms, as befits the epic monologue of a character in the middle ages.

## Characters

The poem's main character is Odysseus, King of Ithaca, who, in the poem, is called Ulysses. Although the poem is written in the form of a dramatic monologue, it is not a dramatic monologue; the poem is in the voice of the character and not of the author.

## Synopsis

The poem opens with Ulysses reflecting on his age and the length of his life. He feels that he is too old to attempt any more great ideas or undertakings.

In the second section, Ulysses tells of the last time he returned home after a long trip. He was a young man then, and his wife, Penelope, had not yet given birth to their son, Telemachus. He had come home to his palace, victorious, and was received by his family and the entire city of Ithaca. Despite this, Ulysses still longs for new adventure, and wishes he could return to the sea.

Lines 80–89Ulysses has a moment of self-doubt

In the third section, Ulysses invokes the image of his friend, the blind bard Demodocus, who sings of the adventures of Odysseus and his fellow heroes, gaining him glory and fame. Ulysses is frightened by his own mortality and wishes he could "sing" himself, that is, to tell of his former greatness. He calls for his men to come out of the palace to hear his song, but they are afraid of him, thinking he is mad.

## Plot

The film begins with a group of people playing cards. The host of the game, Ram Kumar, is cheating in the game. He is the youngest of four brothers – the other three being Arun Verma (Mahendra Sandhu), Chandrashekhar Verma (Rajesh Khanna) and the eldest, Balraj Verma (Jeetendra), who is a very powerful and influential man. Ram is slightly ashamed of his brothers' growing reputations as gangsters, and although he is a part of the gang, he refuses to kill anyone.

Ram is soon introduced to a beautiful young woman named Anita Sharma (Sridevi), who has come to see her brother's body, which Ram has been instructed to take to the police station. After Anita's brother is killed, Ram brings her to his house, and soon realizes that Anita is the owner of a hotel, which is frequented by criminals.

Over time, Ram and Anita fall in love with each other, and Ram vows to make her his wife. However, in order to do so, he tells Anita that he wants to marry her only after he has become a police officer. But Anita is very upset with Ram, and tells him that she is not interested in marrying him unless he gets married to her at once. She also tells him that she does not want to marry him. However, Ram insists on marrying her, and tells her that if she does not agree to marry him, he will kill himself. Later, Anita tells Ram that she will marry him if he promises to keep her away from the gang.

With most work finished on the dam itself ( the powerhouse remained uncompleted ) , a formal dedication ceremony was arranged f

or the reservoir, which took place on 13 September 1898. The dam structure was opened to inspection, the control house was officially opened and the sluice gates were opened to release water from the reservoir into the river. The reservoir was initially filled from the river by gravity feed, but it is known that the water supply was supplemented by pumping water from the river canal at Cowbridge along the old tramway to the reservoir. The reservoir was officially opened by the Marquess of Bute.
On 31 August 1911, the reservoir was officially renamed Llanddewi Rhydderch. The name 'Llanddewi Rhydderch' is a Welsh language name for the village of Llanrhydderch ( pronounced 'Llanddewi Rhydderch ' ) which is on the north bank of the river. The name is said to have been chosen by the then owners of the reservoir, the Trustees of the Cardiff Corporation Waterworks, because the village of Llanrhydderch was the nearest settlement to the reservoir.
 In 1930, a series of flash floods hit the upper Rhondda Valley, due to heavy rainfall and flooding which caused the failure of two major dams. The Llyn-y-Fan dam failed first, and then the Llyn-y-Dalsen dam failed, causing further flooding. The Llyn-y-Fan dam had been built in 1880 by the Llwydcoed Colliery Company, but had been abandoned for many years. After the failure of the dam, the river was diverted into the Llyn-y-Fan reservoir, while repairs were made to the dam. On 16 March 1930, the Llyn-y-Dalsen dam failed, causing flooding which killed 11 people. The dam was rebuilt and then abandoned. The Llyn-y-Dalsen dam was finally demolished in 1975.
 By 1990, the reservoir was no longer used as a water supply for the main water supply system. The sluices and turbines were no longer needed as the water supply was taken from a new reservoir at Llyn Fan Fawr. However, the dam remained in use for the treatment of waste water and also as a flood protection reservoir.
In 1997, the reservoir was sold to the village of Llantrisant for use as a recreational reservoir. The Marquess of Bute sold the reservoir to Llantrisant Council for £50,000, to be used as a small area of recreational waters. Plans are in place to refurbish the reservoir, allowing it to be used for angling, water sports and a walking trail. The reservoir is looked after by the Cardiff and Vale of Glamorgan Waterfront Trust.
The water quality status of the reservoir is unknown.

Harold Innis 's study of the effects of interconnected lakes and rivers on Canadian development and European empire sparked his

interest in the concept of "interchange."  But as Innis shows in his analysis of the early nineteenth-century canoe routes, the fur trade established a vast interconnected network of ports and travel routes before any of the other empires of the period. Innis notes in this regard that "the fur trade was long before the time of steamships the most important factor in making Canada an interchange of the world." The fur trade was the conduit for a vast network of trade with the western interior of North America and the entirety of the Pacific Rim, from India to China to Japan and back again. Traders, clerks, intermediaries, and leatherworkers were all part of the fur trade's great procession.
There was also a second dimension to the fur trade, one that was less obvious at the time but that is now much more apparent. This second dimension was the "exchange" of cultural values, knowledge, and goods. The fur trade was an exchange of goods, and it was also a conduit for the exchange of ideas, and of knowledge. The exchange of ideas and knowledge was not a new phenomenon. The exchange of ideas and knowledge was a part of earlier trading networks, such as the Silk Road. However, the fur trade developed and expanded at a remarkable rate. The exchange of ideas and knowledge was also a part of the fur trade at an uneven rate. Some of the cultural values and knowledge that were exchanged were exchanged in a very unequal manner. The ideas, knowledge, and culture of the First Nations, the Métis, and the Canadian settlers were exchanged with the dominant British culture and European culture to a much larger extent than the reverse was true. Typhoon Imbudo , known in the Philippines as Typhoon Harurot , was a powerful typhoon that struck the Philippines and southern

China in September 1959.
Typhoon Imbudo of 1959 was the strongest typhoon to have struck Luzon since Typhoon Haiphong in 1951 (the tropical cyclone that caused the worst typhoon-related flooding in the Philippines ).  The typhoon brought winds of 260 km/h (160 mph) and caused 620 deaths, mainly on Luzon. All of the casualties occurred on Luzon.
Imbudo was the sixth typhoon of the 1959 Pacific typhoon season. It was also the seventh tropical storm of the 1959 Pacific typhoon season.
Imbudo formed from a tropical disturbance on September 9, about 375 km (235 mi) east-southeast of Manila, Philippines. The disturbance moved westward, and by the next day, it had developed into a tropical depression, and was named Imbudo by the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC). On September 11, the storm intensified into Tropical Storm 06W. On the same day, the storm's movement slowed as it turned west-northwestward, and the storm's convection moved to the storm's north. The JTWC upgraded the storm to typhoon status on September 12, and the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) assigned the name Imbudo to the storm. Over the next few days, the typhoon meandered around the central Philippine Sea, and on September 14, Imbudo briefly attained typhoon status once again. On September 15, Imbudo began to move westward, and on September 16, it turned northwestward, skirting the northern portion of Luzon. On September 17, the typhoon attained its peak intensity of 260 km/h (160 mph) and became extratropical over southern China on September 18.

Kenyan world record holders Ndiku Mutua and Bernard Lagat each held the 1500 m record through most of the 1980s. Hispanic American and Olympic 1500 m champion Alberto Salazar held the 1500 m world record for a record 15 years.
As of the start of 2016, the 1500 m world record holder was Ethiopian Hagos Gebrhiwet, who ran 3:26.81 in the 2015 Berlin Diamond League. The 2016 Olympic champion, as well as the 2012 and 2014 world indoor champion, was Matthew Centrowitz of the United States, who ran 3:50.46.
British athlete Hannah England ran 4:12.54 for 1500 m in 2007.

Theatres such as the Opéra in Paris and the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, were the social and cultural centres of the cities in which they were located, and the public had come to expect a certain level of spectacle in their entertainment. In a world in which social, political and economic upheavals were the order of the day, and where the opera house was a place for the people to revel in the fantasy of the human voice and the glorious music that accompanied it, the public were keen to see their favourite composers and their operas stage-managed with the greatest possible skill.

als, Duluth , Minnesota , on 24 May 1941, the son of Abraham Zimmerman ( also known as Abe Zimmerman ), a Ukrainian Jewish immigrant who moved to the USA in 1923, and his wife Beatrice Stone ( née Stone ) , who was born in the USA.
 Dylan's father had been a sign-writer by profession, but, following the birth of his son, took a job as a plumber, then a carpenter and finally a salesman. He had little interest in music, but did listen to it on the radio.
 Dylan's mother was a high school teacher at the Denfeld High School in Duluth. She had an active, politically minded social circle and was a firm believer in the tenets of the Socialist Party. She was a member of the local branch of the National Education Association ( NEA ) , and became active in various other social groups concerned with social issues.
 In 1946 the family moved to Hibbing, a city of about 25,000 residents, 160 km north of Duluth, where Dylan's father had found work as a travelling salesman. Dylan's mother was a supporter of the local chapter of the Civil Rights Congress and was a member of the Hibbing chapter of the Civil Rights Congress. She was also active in the Hibbing chapter of the United Packinghouse Workers of America ( UPWA ) and the Hibbing branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People ( NAACP ). She was also involved in the local chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union ( ACLU ). The Zimmermans lived in a three-bedroom, 70-square-metre ( 750 sq ft ) house in Hibbing, and, by 1953, had added an extension.  It was not until 1949 that Dylan became aware of the significance of the place of his birth. He was born in St Mary's Hospital and, although he was not baptised, Beatrice Zimmerman registered his birth as a Jew.
 Abraham Zimmerman died of a heart attack on 16 September 1961, when Dylan was 20 years old.

The streets of Buenos Aires overflowed with huge piles of flowers . Within a day of Perón 's death , all flower shops in Buenos

Aires had sold out. There were hundreds of mourners outside the house, and a full military funeral was ordered for Perón.  The funeral cortège was the most impressive ever seen in Buenos Aires. The coffin, draped in a flag, was followed by a 1,000-man honour guard from the Escuela de Suboficiales, who took up their positions at the corners of the 1,000-yard route from the official residence to the cemetery.  The funeral procession, which included virtually every important Argentine politician, was a true example of Latin American spectacle. As the coffin was borne down the Calle Corrientes, the street was lined with 20,000 Argentines, most of whom had rushed out to catch a glimpse of the general's final journey.
The funeral was attended by seven presidents and several crowned heads from Central and South America, who flew into Buenos Aires to pay their respects to the general. These included the presidents of Uruguay, Paraguay, Chile, Bolivia, Brazil, Cuba, Panama, Venezuela and Peru. The town was recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086 as "Odhelmes" (or "Odhelmesete"), in the manor of Rochdale, and was a settlement of 10 households. Oldham was part of the ancient parish of Rochdale, and in 1866 it was included in the Rochdale Poor Law Union.

Oldham became a municipal borough in 1894, and by 1933 it had absorbed four of its neighbouring towns: Chadderton, Greenacres, Royton, and Saddleworth—the last being a separate ancient parish. Some primary frameworks are the race and ethnicity of an individual or group. For example, Asian Americans are assumed to be all the same, and they are often depicted as meek and passive. Individuals and groups can be defined as oppressed or oppressor groups in a society. Oppressed groups are groups who are discriminated against in a society and experience negative conditions. In 1986 and 1987 , Dylan toured with Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers , sharing vocals with Petty on several songs each night .

The two became close friends and Petty would later produce Dylan's 1997 album Time Out of Mind .
Dylan's next studio album, Oh Mercy , was released in 1989, and he received a Grammy Award nomination for the song " Political World ".  The album's sound was a radical departure from the backing of the last few albums, and Dylan's voice was backed by a harder-edged, rock-oriented sound. The album also included contributions from many of the same musicians who had played on Time Out of Mind . Dylan's next album, Under the Red Sky , was released in 1990, and included a cover of the O'Jays ' "Love Train".
 In 2010, Dylan and Petty toured together with the Heartbreakers as the Traveling Wilburys in honor of the 20th anniversary of the original Traveling Wilburys albums.
Dylan was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama at the 2012 National Medal of Arts and National Humanities Medal ceremonies.
In 2016, Dylan released The Cutting Edge 1965–1966: The Bootleg Series Vol. 12, a box set of unreleased songs from the 1965–1966 period.  The set received a Grammy Award nomination for Best Historical Album.
In 2018, Dylan appeared as a guest vocalist on multiple songs on Willie Nelson's album Ride Me Back Home.  The next year, Dylan released his thirty-eighth studio album, Rough and Rowdy Ways , his first album of original material in eight years.  The album received widespread critical acclaim.  Dylan's next studio album, More Blood, More Tracks: The Bootleg Series Vol. 14, a compilation of outtakes from his 1975 album Blood on the Tracks , was released in 2020.
In 1960, Dylan met Joan Baez at the 1959 Newport Folk Festival , where he was performing with Paul Butterfield 's blues band.  She was twenty years old, he was twenty-three.  They began what was known as "the first big love affair of the folk scene", as described by one of her biographers.  Baez helped introduce Dylan to the folk music scene.  She included two of his early songs, "With God on Our Side" and "North Country Blues", on her 1961 debut album, Joan Baez .  They began touring together, and Dylan accompanied her on a tour of Europe in the summer of 1962.
Dylan's first marriage was to his high school sweetheart, Sue Webster , on November 4, 1965.  They had four children and divorced in 1977.
In 1986, Dylan married Carolyn Dennis , a backup singer in his touring band.  They had three children together and were divorced in 1992.
In 1992, Dylan married Carolyn Dennis again, following her divorce from her first husband.  They had a daughter.  Their marriage ended in divorce in 1999.

He was the youngest of four children. He was educated at home, as were his siblings, and later studied English at the University of London. He worked as an editor at the publishing house Macmillan until 1930, when he began to write full-time. He was a member of the Inklings, a literary discussion group that included J.R.R. Tolkien and C.S. Lewis. In 1940, he married Princess Elisabeth of Yugoslavia, daughter of the King of Yugoslavia. They had two sons before divorcing in 1948.

The growing unrest in Portugal culminated on April 25 , 1974 , when the Carnation Revolution , a peaceful leftist military coup

, overthrew the regime. The revolution was anticipated, but not planned, by the United States. The U.S. government had decided on a policy of "national interests" in Portugal , as in so many countries in the developing world. In the early 1970s the U.S. used its power to support the dictatorships in Portugal and other European countries. But the Carnation Revolution was the first political wave in the developing world that really worried the U.S. government. The revolutionary government needed to fight against external and internal enemies. The United States was, therefore, the first outside country to be recognized as a friend.
The Chilean Revolution, which started in 1970, and the Nicaraguan Revolution, which started in 1978, were the other two great political waves that shook the developing world in the 1970s. Both revolutions were also deeply unsettling to the United States, which found itself unable to contain them. However, in the case of Chile, the United States supported a military junta against the first democratically elected president, Salvador Allende. In the case of Nicaragua, the United States organized a counterrevolution against the Sandinistas with the aid of the contras.
The United States was, therefore, the main enemy of the revolutionary governments in Portugal and Nicaragua. The two countries were the first to be involved in a confrontation between the United States and revolutionary governments from the developing world. Nevertheless, in both cases the United States did not attack these countries. Instead, it supported internal opposition movements that tried to overthrow the revolutionary governments.
The United States initially thought that it could control the situation in Portugal. It recognized the revolutionary government, but the U.S. ambassador played an important role in the formation of the first government. The U.S. government gave its support to the right-wing parties in the first Portuguese elections so that they would not form a government. The United States also supported conservative forces in Nicaragua. In the end, the internally generated opposition movements did not succeed in overthrowing the Portuguese and Nicaraguan governments. The United States was, therefore, disappointed by the outcomes of these two revolutions.
The Cold War was over, but the United States had difficulties in determining its role in the developing world. In the 1980s, the United States felt that, in general, external support was not necessary for the survival of revolutionary governments. In Nicaragua, the U.S. government was preoccupied by the humanitarian crisis and tried to find a peaceful solution to the conflict. The United States had, therefore, a more positive attitude toward revolutionary governments.
However, in the 1990s, the United States became more worried about the survival of the revolutionary governments. The United States had to determine its role with respect to revolutionary governments in El Salvador , Haiti , and Guatemala . In these countries, the United States was divided in its attitude toward revolutionary governments, which were still viewed as enemies. This book discusses the role of the United States in these revolutionary countries and the reasons for the division in the U.S. attitude toward the revolutionary governments.
The United States supported the Salvadoran government in its war against the guerrillas because the Salvadorans were democratically elected. In Haiti , the United States supported the reelection of the Duvalier government and tried to destabilize the government after the coup d'etat on February 7, 1986. In Guatemala , the United States supported the right-wing military government against the insurgents. In all these countries, the U.S. government supported governments that were considered to be democratic.
The United States was divided in its attitude toward revolutionary governments because it could not determine its role in the developing world. The U.S. government was not willing to give up its hegemony in the developing world. However, the Cold War was over, and the United States had to find new allies in the developing world.
The United States was not able to find new allies in the developing world. It had, therefore, to develop new strategies for the survival of the revolutionary governments. The United States wanted to maintain its hegemony in the world, but it had to accept the end of the Cold War. The United States could not control the developing world anymore.

The competition was composed of three stages:

Smith , in 1923 , noted that "one god is described as 'the wife of' another, and this is repeated in several different texts." Hornung goes on to say that "this is a case of the goddess being identified with the god." The ancient Egyptian term for identification was _šnȝ_ , which appears in the titles of many Egyptian deities and the names of many temples. It is also the root of the word _šnȝ_ , "gold," which appears in the titles of several deities, including Min. #  _Hathor_
Hathor was one of the earliest of Egyptian deities , appearing in Predynastic art as a cow. She was the daughter of the primeval goddess Nut (the sky) and the sun god, Geb. The Kemetic word _htr_ means "house." Hathor was originally known as _Hwt-Hrw_ , meaning "The House of Horus." She had a temple at Dendera, located in the Fayum region. The temple was built to resemble a mansion and was called _Hwt-Ssut_ , "The House of the Sycamore."
Hathor was the patron deity of the city of Memphis. She was also the patron deity of the city of Thinis. In the 2nd Dynasty she became a patron deity of the 2nd Dynasty pharaoh Djoser. Under the pharaohs of the Old Kingdom, Hathor was the patron deity of the 4th Dynasty pharaoh Akhenaten (Amenhotep IV). Her worship was suppressed for a time under the 18th Dynasty pharaohs, only to flourish again under the 19th Dynasty pharaohs.
Hathor was the wife of the sun god Ra, the mother of Horus, and the mother of Seth. Hathor was a representation of the goddess Neith. Hathor was also identified with the goddess Maat.
Hathor was a cow goddess. She was also a goddess of music and dance, and a goddess of joy and love. Another name for Hathor was _Mehet-Weret_ , "Great Flood," a reference to her association with the flooding of the Nile.
Hathor was sometimes depicted as a cow-headed woman, sometimes as a human woman wearing a sun disk, and sometimes as a woman wearing a cow's head.

The second stage of construction in the 17th and 18th centuries , when the tower was under the charge of the Vatican librarian

and the custodian of the Secret Archives, marks one of the turning points in the Tower's history. It was at this point that the cardinals shifted from a defensive policy to one of offence: the construction of the Vatican Palace, the building of the library, the adoption of the Enlightenment, and the publication of the Index of Prohibited Books all help to explain why the Tower became a fortress of safety and a repository of knowledge and enlightenment rather than a prison.
**The Papal Tower, as it was called, was built within the city walls under the direction of Pope Urban VIII in 1626–27. It was completed by Pope Alexander VIII in 1689. The name was changed to the _Torre delle Armi_ (the Armoury Tower) in the 18th century. The tower is 135 metres high (443 feet) and has sixteen floors.
**The Pope's library was built on the first floor of the tower during the reign of Pope Pius V (1572–1576). It was designed by Antonio Sangallo (1538–1603), the nephew of the architect Baldassare Peruzzi (1481–1536), who had also designed the library.
**Pope Pius V had the library built on a site that had been the site of the Etruscan _acqueduct_ , the _acqua Claudia_ , and the first Christian catacombs. He chose the site because it was near the papal residence and the Vatican Palace.
**The library was a fortress of knowledge and enlightenment in the 16th century. It was called the _Bibliotheca Apostolica Vaticana_ (the Vatican Apostolic Library) in 1604. (The name was changed to the _Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana_ in 1887.)
**The Library holds the _Codex Vaticanus B_ , which was written in the 4th century. It is a collection of 750 papyrus leaves and is one of the oldest and most important books in the world. The Vatican Apostolic Library also holds the _Codex Vaticanus_ , _Codex Sinaiticus_ , and _Codex Alexandrinus_ , which are the oldest and most important books in the world.

The ARVN operation soon settled down to become a search and destroy mission , with South Vietnamese troops combing the countrys

ide in search of the Viet Cong. This approach was largely successful, although there were several small and very bloody clashes between the ARVN and NVA. The Viet Cong were falling back in the face of superior American forces and there was no sign of an imminent attack on Saigon. The American presence in the country was gradually diminished. In January 1964 the USAF had 1,500 aircraft based in the country, by the end of the year the number had shrunk to 800. On 13 April 1965 President Lyndon Baines Johnson ordered the first major US combat operation in Vietnam, with the landing of US Marines at Da Nang. In 1965, the Americans were directly involved in the fighting for the first time.
The Marines were followed by the first US Army combat units, and a new US military headquarters was established at Long Binh, five kilometres outside Saigon. This base, the largest US base in South Vietnam, eventually included eight airfields, four helicopter landing pads, a hospital, a telecommunications centre, and a 21,000-bed hospital.
The soldiers at Long Binh were the first in a line of American combat units to serve in Vietnam. They were followed by the 196th Light Infantry Brigade (Separate), the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile), the 1st Infantry Division and the 173rd Airborne Brigade. There was fierce opposition to the war in the US, and by 1970 the number of regular army units committed to Vietnam had risen to 500,000.
The Americans were well equipped, with sophisticated equipment and weapons, but they were not well trained for jungle warfare. They relied heavily on air power and helicopters, but these proved to be vulnerable and unreliable. The Americans were confined to the major cities. They made little impact on the remote areas of the country, where the Viet Cong and NVA were able to roam freely. The war was fought on their terms, and the Americans were forced to adapt. The numbers of casualties on both sides increased. The Americans were losing the war, and the situation was deteriorating rapidly.
The Americans were supported by the South Vietnamese military, including the Army of the Republic of Vietnam (ARVN), the Navy of the Republic of Vietnam, the South Vietnamese Air Force (VNAF), the South Vietnamese Marines and the paramilitary forces known as the People's Self-Defence Forces. The ARVN was formed in 1955 by the US and the French colonial authorities, but most of its officers had been trained in France, rather than in South Vietnam. The ARVN was initially composed of the former colonial army and the newly formed national army. It was placed under the command of the Joint General Staff, with the French high commissioner as its commander-in-chief. The Joint General Staff was a large organisation with a central headquarters in Saigon and provincial headquarters in the major cities of the country.
The ARVN was divided into six army corps, with a seventh corps being formed in 1964. The corps were supported by 11 independent regiments. The first three corps were located in the northern half of the country, and the other three were situated in the southern half of South Vietnam. The seventh corps was formed in 1964 as part of the expansion of the South Vietnamese army after the commitment of American forces. The corps were supported by Provincial Forces and the Rural Forces, which were made up of the militia and the local territorial forces. These were separate units, and the ARVN was not an integrated army. There were many problems with the ARVN, including a lack of equipment, poor training, poor morale and low troop numbers. By 1967 the ARVN was estimated to have 192,000 men, but this was far short of the total required to police the country.

It was later expanded to include four fighter groups and five fighter squadrons. The VNAF was supported by the Airborne Division and the Airborne Command. At the beginning of the First World War , Black Prince was one of the four armoured cruisers serving in the 1st Cruiser Squadro

n. The 1st Cruiser Squadron was to be the main striking force of the British Mediterranean Fleet in the event of war, and its four armoured cruisers were to hunt down and destroy enemy commerce raiders. Its most famous action was the 1916 engagement with _Möwe_ , the German commerce raider that had sunk 13 fishing vessels and two sailing ships in the North Sea.
Black Prince was in the Mediterranean when the war began in August 1914, and as such, had the opportunity to take part in the pursuit of Goeben and Breslau, the German cruisers that had sailed from the Mediterranean to escape British blockade. The armoured cruiser HMS _Firefly_ was sunk by these two ships, and Black Prince, under the command of Captain (later Admiral) William Goodenough, was ordered to search for and destroy the two German cruisers. After a brief interlude in Malta, Goodenough resumed his search for Goeben and Breslau.
However, the initial search proved fruitless, and Goodenough was ordered to search for the German light cruiser SMS _Emden_ , which had been raiding shipping in the Indian Ocean. On 9 November 1914 _Emden_ encountered and sank the Russian light cruiser Rurik. Goodenough was then ordered to search for _Emden_ , and on 28 November he found and engaged her. _Emden_ was badly damaged and was forced to beach herself in the Cocos Islands. The remaining crew of 147 was taken prisoner by the Australian Navy, and the gunboat HMAS _Sydney_ was sent to destroy _Emden_ by exploding a magazine. _Emden_ was scuttled by her crew to prevent her falling into Australian hands.
Goodenough was awarded the Distinguished Service Order for his actions during this campaign.
Captain Goodenough was then appointed to command the 2nd Cruiser Squadron, and took part in the Battle of Dogger Bank in January 1915. During this action, he demonstrated a decisive and aggressive attitude, and the _Daily Mail_ noted that his ships 'had shown themselves to be not only the finest but the most aggressive and dashing in the fleet'.
On 25 January 1915 Black Prince was torpedoed by the German light cruiser SMS _Stralsund_ while returning to Rosyth from an operations off the Dutch coast. The cruiser was temporarily repaired and returned to active service.
Black Prince was ordered to join the Grand Fleet in Scapa Flow, and remained with the fleet throughout the war. She was part of the fleet during the Battle of Jutland in May 1916, and was flagship of Rear-Admiral (later Admiral Sir John) de Robeck when he commanded the battlecruiser _Queen Mary_ , the battlecruiser _Indefatigable_ and the battlecruiser _Invincible_ during the Battle of Dogger Bank.
After the war, Black Prince was refitted at Devonport, and was sent to the Mediterranean as a member of the Royal Navy's 'Black Sea Squadron'. Black Prince was ordered to Constantinople to help the Allies to bring about the end of the Ottoman Empire, and remained in the Black Sea until the end of the war.
Black Prince was then ordered to Brest, France, where she served as a storage hulk, and was eventually sold for scrap in 1921.

The World Chess Championship 1993 was a match contested between World Champion Garry Kasparov and challenger Nigel Short. It was Kasparov's third title defence. The match took place from 10 to 21 October 1993 in the Kremlin Palace in Moscow, Russia. Kasparov defended his title with a 12½–7½ victory. The match was notable for the "Karpov Rule", whereby Short was given the option to use the computer program Crafty to aid his analysis if Kasparov did so.
The World Chess Championship 1995 was a match contested between world champion Garry Kasparov and challenger Viswanathan Anand. It was Kasparov's fourth title defence, and took place from 24 September to 13 October 1995 in New York City and on a floating television studio at sea. Kasparov won the title with a score of 10½–7½.
The World Chess Championship 1996 was a match contested between World Chess Champion Garry Kasparov and challenger Vladimir Kramnik. It was Kasparov's fifth title defence, and took place from 11 to 30 June 1996 in New York City. The match was notable for being the first time that the World Chess Championship was played to a tie-break. Kramnik won the match 8½–7½ to become the first challenger to defeat Kasparov.
The World Chess Championship 1997 was a match contested between World Chess Champion Garry Kasparov and challenger Anatoly Karpov. It was Kasparov's sixth title defence, and took place from 10 to 28 October 1997 in New York City and at the World Trade Center in New York City.

The canteen of the 1st Battalion still had its own unofficial name. It had been called the 'Hungry Hundred' because the soldiers had to wait up to an hour to be served. The cooks could not cope with rationing (corpsmen and medical orderlies worked in the canteen as well as cooks) and the canteen could not supply enough food for the hungry soldiers.
Major Alister MacDonald was in charge of the Hungry Hundred, and the soldiers knew him as 'Black Mac'. He was a tall, athletic man with curly black hair and a moustache. He had a reputation for being tough and fair, and the men liked him.
The soldiers had been waiting for hours to be served. They had been told only that there would be a long wait for food and that they must not leave the canteen. But as time went on and they grew more and more hungry, the men began to leave. They went to the mess tents and ate all they could find, but now they had to return to the canteen. They knew they could not go to sleep until they had eaten.
A little later, MacDonald was handed a note by the orderly sergeant. It was a message from Birdwood's headquarters. MacDonald read it and handed it to the sergeant.
There was a moment's silence. Then, the men began to cheer.
MacDonald could not believe what he had just heard. He was sure no one had got to the men ahead of him. He had been expecting to be called to Birdwood's headquarters the next day, so he had not even had time to pick up a message from Birdwood's office. MacDonald knew that he was in serious trouble.
As he walked back to the canteen, he was followed by a group of soldiers who were still cheering. He glanced at them as he passed but, not knowing most of the names, he could not see who was with him.
The soldiers were relieved to see that the Hungry Hundred was open again. They began to eat, and then they sat down to wait for an explanation from MacDonald.
MacDonald called them all to the front of the canteen. He told them to sit down. He did not know what to say.
 MacDonald decided to go to Birdwood's headquarters to explain what had happened.
When he arrived Birdwood was not there. He left a note for Birdwood, explaining what had happened.
MacDonald was then sent to a conference with his brigadier, Brigadier-General Harold Walker.
MacDonald knew he must explain what had happened. At first, Walker's tone was polite, but soon he became angry.
MacDonald explained that the men had had a long wait to be served. They were hungry, so they left the canteen to get something to eat. It was only then that he had received a message from Birdwood's headquarters.
Walker did not believe him.
MacDonald felt humiliated. He was a professional soldier. How could he be accused of letting the soldiers down?
MacDonald was sent to the 2nd Brigade.
The next day, MacDonald was woken early to be taken to the 2nd Brigade headquarters. He was accused of being a coward, but he knew he was not a coward. He was promoted to major and sent to the 1st Brigade headquarters as adjutant.
Some of the soldiers were angry about what MacDonald had done, but most of them respected him. They knew he had done it to protect them.

He said that he had read the message to the soldiers and handed it to the orderly sergeant. He was not aware of any other message from Birdwood.

Fulton was promoted to major and transferred to another battalion.

The basic anthropomorphic form varies . Child gods are depicted nude , as are some adult gods when their procreative powers are

being emphasised. They may also be shown with a human face, but with animal ears, a tail, or a forepart of the body resembling a lion, a bird, a bull, a serpent, or another animal. When not depicted as human, some gods are shown with human upper bodies and bird lower bodies, or with human upper bodies and a human head on the body of a bull or other animal.
A large number of deities are shown with a _gada_ , a round object resembling a pestle or an axe, in the left hand or in the crook of the right arm; this is a symbol of power and is thought to represent the creation of the world. Some gods are also shown with a _vajra_ , a thunderbolt, in the right hand.
Gods are often shown with elaborate headdresses in the shape of a crown, a _mukuta_ , or a _trivikrama_ , which resemble a lotus flower. This is the crown of the god Vishnu, who is the most important of the Hindu gods.
The gods may be shown with a large phallus in their left hand; this is the _linga_ , the symbol of the male generative power. A female deity may be shown with a _yoni_ , the symbol of the female generative power, in the same way.
The gods are usually shown with an _upavita_ , a sacred thread, around the neck, or with a _jata_ , a topknot of hair, on the top of the head.
Gods may be shown with a _tika_ on the forehead, a mark of auspiciousness, or with a _tilaka_ , a dot of sandal paste, on the forehead.
Some gods are shown with a _danda_ , a staff, in the left hand; this is the symbol of Siva, one of the most important Hindu gods.

Degenerate stars have contracted into a compact mass , resulting in a rapid rate of rotation . However they have relatively low

surface gravities . This is because the matter that would make up the surface gravity is now compressed into a smaller volume .
The star is supported by its own gravity while the escape velocity from the surface exceeds the speed of the rotation at the equator . The star is therefore a rapidly rotating, gravitationally-supported, degenerate star .
This is the situation for a star in a binary system . The binary orbit is periodically disturbed by the presence of the other star . This causes the periastron distance to be reduced . The binary orbit is therefore forced into a smaller orbit . The star is then supported by its own gravity while the escape velocity from the surface exceeds the speed of the rotation at the equator . The star is therefore a rapidly rotating, gravitationally-supported, degenerate star .

A number of ancient texts mention the Eshmun Temple and its location . The Phoenician inscriptions on the sarcophagus of Eshmun

confirm the identification of the site with the "Sanctuary of Eshmun" mentioned in the Amarna letters.
The temple of Eshmun is first mentioned in the Amarna letters of Tushratta, king of Mitanni, who wrote to the Egyptian Pharaoh Amenhotep III. The texts were written around 1375 BC and were found in Tell el-Amarna.
In letters 108 and 109, Tushratta mentions the temple of Eshmun and its location.
The site of Eshmun is also mentioned in the Testament of Melchizedek as a place which contains a synagogue. Eshmun is also mentioned in 1 Maccabees 11:55.
The pagan temple of Eshmun was still in use in the 2nd century AD. It is mentioned by the geographer Ptolemy as sanctuarium Semeum (Arabic: سانتوس الإشمون, Sāntus al Ishmūn). The geographer Pliny the Elder also mentions the temple.
Pliny's 37th book, chapter 4, mentions that Eshmun had a temple in Canaan, which the people of Tyre regarded as a sacred place because it had been made holy by the oracle of the deity.
In the 3rd century, the Christian author Eusebius of Caesarea (325 AD) describes the temple of Eshmun as a pagan temple on a mountain, which was still in use in his time.
In 536 AD, the Persian shah Khosrau I conquered Tyre and soon afterwards destroyed the temple.

and recorded them as broken ‘Sunga’ or ‘Kusana’ (2nd century BCE – 2nd century CE) pottery .  The 19 th century French explorer  Bartholomew (1807-1885) , while passing through Arikamedu on the 25 th of December 1857 , did not mention that he had seen any Buddhist remains .
The first detailed archaeological excavation of Arikamedu was undertaken in 1948 by the French Archaeological Mission led by C. Coppens. The first mention of Arikamedu as a Roman site was made by R. E.M. Wheeler in the 1950s, based on the excavations carried out by Coppens.  After that Arikamedu was excavated twice by the French Archaeological Mission in 1974 and 1978; the latter excavation was conducted under the supervision of the Director General of Archaeological Survey of India (ASI). The excavations were carried out by the French Archaeological Mission from the period 1974 to 1979 and the ASI from 1979 to 1986, based on the modus operandi of classical excavation and lithic analysis.
Arikamedu is a well-known historical site, which has been mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythrean Sea, a Greek travelogue written during the 1st century CE.  This work describes the Periplus of the Erythrean Sea, the coastal route from the Red Sea to India, that the ancient Greeks would have taken. It mentions three main ports along the coast of India: Barygaza (today’s Broach), Arikamedu and the capital of the Pandya kings,  Korkai (today’s Korkai). Ptolemy’s Geography (140 CE) and the 11th century Arab historian Masudi (d. 1058) also mention Arikamedu. The Periplus refers to Arikamedu as a port city on the Coromandel Coast, which was a prominent port for trade and commercial activity in the 2nd century BCE. The archaeological evidence of the site bears out the port city status of Arikamedu.
The Arikamedu site shows traces of a settlement that dates between the pre-Christian era and the 14 th century CE. The site has an extensive pottery assemblage dated from the 1 st century BCE to the 14 th century CE, which shows a wide variety of cultural influences. Arikamedu is one of the few sites in India that bear archaeological evidence of trade relations with the Roman Empire. The site has a rich assemblage of Roman coins, which is dated between the 2 nd century BCE and the 14 th century CE. The shipwreck of a Roman ship has been discovered at the site, with a cargo containing 6000 amphorae (pottery jars), dating from the 1 st century BCE.  The ship is the only evidence of the Roman presence on the Coromandel Coast until the discovery of the Arikamedu site.

The old school was demolished in 1959, when the present buildings were erected. The school was re-organised for the teaching of boys aged 11 to 18 from 1977. As a result of the building programme, the school was re-organised in 2009 to be a single-sex school for boys only, with an intake of 120 pupils aged 11–16. Elections were held on 27 November 1915 . The result was a victory for the Constitutionalists , who obtained 160 seats in the Congress of the Union. A group of Conservative deputies, led by Francisco León de la Barra , refused to recognise the results and held a meeting in the National Palace, where they declared themselves the legitimate Congress of the Union. This body was supported by the other Conservative deputies.
The Constitutionalists responded by occupying the National Palace to prevent the Conservatives from entering. The next day the Constitutionalist Congress held its first session in the Palace of Fine Arts .
The president of the Constitutionalist Congress was Francisco Sánchez , while the president of the Conservative Congress was Víctoriano Huerta .
The conflict was resolved when Huerta was selected as the new president of Mexico on 11 December 1915 . This move was not supported by the Constitutionalists , who view Huerta as a usurper.
 The Zapatistas , led by Emiliano Zapata , continued to defend their cause in the south of the country, and launched a series of attacks against Huerta's government. The Zapatistas were eventually defeated in 1920 .
Huerta's government was overthrown by the government of Venustiano Carranza , who assumed the presidency of Mexico on 19 February 1917.
The principles of the treaty of Aguascalientes were maintained by Carranza's government, which also continued the war against Huerta's forces in the south. The war was concluded in 1920 , when the remaining Zapatista forces were defeated at the Battle of Tampate .

The cleavage site may also be located in the middle of the coding region.

Wales have competed at every Rugby World Cup and have qualified for all but one, the 1999 tournament. Wales withdrew from the Five Nations championship in 2007 to join the newly formed Six Nations, but rejoined in 2009. Since 2021, they have been competing for the Six Nations trophy with England, France, Ireland, Italy and Scotland.

By 1907 , new university buildings completely surrounded the observatory ; dust from the construction clogged meteorological in

let tubes and obscured the viewing room. In 1912 , the observatory was relocated to the summit of Davis Hill on the south edge of the campus.
The observatory was dedicated on September 13, 1849 . A number of prominent astronomers served as directors of the observatory, including John Herschel (1849–1850) and George Bond (1850–1896), as well as other notable scientists, such as Thomas Edison (1876), Henry Draper (1882–1886), Edward Charles Pickering (1887–1919), and Harlow Shapley (1921–1953). The first female director of the observatory was Annie Jump Cannon (1932–1957).
The observatory is the location of the 24-inch (610 mm) refracting telescope, built in 1847 by the French firm of Alvan Clark, used by Edison for his research on the spectrum of the sun. The observatory also houses a 40-inch (1,000 mm) reflecting telescope built by the British firm of Alvan Clark and Sons, and stands next to a 26-inch (660 mm) reflecting telescope built by the company in 1885.
In 1955 , the observatory was renamed after the Harvard astronomer David A. O. Murray (1854–1932), who served as director from 1903 until 1931, and was featured in numerous astronomical discoveries, including the first detection of the spiral structure of the Milky Way.

The work of Marshall McLuhan is the most important in the field of communication. His pioneering work in the field of communication theory and his popular books, especially The Gutenberg Galaxy, The Mechanical Bride, and Understanding Media, are all seminal texts in the field. It is difficult to think of a text on communication without thinking of McLuhan.
Born in Edmonton, Alberta, in 1911, McLuhan was educated at the University of Manitoba and Oxford University. He taught at the University of Toronto for nearly forty years, where he founded the Centre for Culture and Technology. He was named to the Order of Canada in 1967. He died in 1980.
McLuhan studied at the University of Manitoba and at St. Louis University, where he received his B.A. in 1932. He attended the University of Cambridge, where he wrote his M.A. thesis on the poet George Herbert. After receiving his degree in 1934, he returned to the University of Manitoba to teach English. He spent two years teaching at the University of Wisconsin before being called to Oxford by Harold J. Laski to teach at St. Anne's College. While at Oxford, McLuhan wrote a dissertation on the poet Edmund Spenser. He received his Ph.D. from the University of Cambridge in 1940.
He returned to St. Anne's College after completing his doctorate and taught there until 1943 when he moved to the University of Toronto to become the first chairman of the English Department. He remained there until his retirement in 1979, and he established the Centre for Culture and Technology in 1951. He was appointed to the Order of Canada in 1967 and received the Governor General's Award in 1968. He died on December 31, 1980, in Toronto.
In The Gutenberg Galaxy, McLuhan argued that the printing press had a profound impact on Western culture. He argued that the printing press changed the way we think and the way we communicate. In Understanding Media, he argued that media have a profound impact on our lives. He also argued that media have a profound impact on our culture.

Stansfield has represented England at Under-18 and Under-19 levels.
In October 2001 Stansfield was called up to a training camp with the England under-21 squad.
On 12 February 2003 Stansfield was called up to the England under-21 squad for the first time. He made his debut as a second-half substitute in a 3–0 win against Italy under-21 on March 26, 2003 , and went on to make six appearances for the team.

Stansfield was called up to the England squad on September 16, 2007 , ahead of the 2007 FIFA World Cup qualifiers against Greece and Russia.
On 1 October 2007 Stansfield won his first senior international cap as a second-half substitute in England's 2–0 Euro 2008 qualifying win against Russia.

Kanti ( 1108 ) , known for her wit and humour , was one of the earliest female poets of the Kannada language and a contemporary

of the 12 th century poet Ranna ( 1134 ). She is also the author of the first Kannada devotional work, a poem to Durga. Kanti is also known for her controversial lifelong relationship with a king of the Hoysala Dynasty.
Kanti was born into a Brahmin family in the village of Kukke in the present-day Udupi district of Karnataka. Her mother died when she was young. Kanti was married to a Brahmin scholar called Brahmananda. Her husband was an ardent devotee of the goddess Durga and had consecrated an image of her. Kanti worshipped the goddess as well. Her husband died when she was young. She lived with her father-in-law and brother-in-law after this. Her brother-in-law was a scholar of the Vedas and the Puranas and a guru of Kanti. According to Karnataka State Gazetteers , Kanti was about 18 years old when she married King Veeraballala I ( 1121-1152 ) of the Hoysala Dynasty.
Kanti was a devotee of the goddess Durga and wrote a poem in her praise in the early 12 th century. She is known to have received a royal salary for her writing. Her poem in praise of Durga is called Durgasaptasati . The poem consists of 700 verses and is based on the Sanskrit text called Devi Mahatmya , composed in the 5 th century AD. Kanti also wrote a poem in praise of the god Vishnu. The poem is called Vishnusaptasati .
Kanti took part in a number of wars. She is said to have fought alongside her husband Veeraballala I in the Battle of Talakad , in which he defeated the Chalukyan ruler Taila III.
Kanti died in the village of Kukke in the early 12 th century. She is revered as a poet and saint of the Kannada language.

Danny Everette is in his fourth year as the full time strength and conditioning coach at East Carolina University.
A native of Caldwell, N.C., Everette graduated from UNC-Chapel Hill with a Bachelor of Arts in History in 1995, while earning a Master of Arts in History in 1998. Everette earned his Master of Science in Sport and Exercise Psychology from East Carolina University in 2006.
Everette has worked in the strength and conditioning field for the past 12 years. He has been with the Pirates since 2005.
Prior to his employment at ECU, Everette worked at the University of North Carolina from 2003-05 and served as the assistant strength and conditioning coach for the football and men's basketball teams.
Under Everette's direction, the ECU football team has been highly successful in the classroom. The Pirates have led the American Athletic Conference in the team GPA each of the last three years, while also leading the South Division in 2009 and 2010. Additionally, the football team led the AAC in the Graduate Success Rate for three consecutive years (2008-10).
Everette has worked with ECU football players that have been named to the All-AAC Academic Team, including 2008 and 2009 first team honoree defensive lineman Cliff Avril and 2009 third team honoree wide receiver Dwayne Harris.
Prior to working at UNC, Everette spent three years at the University of Connecticut. He served as the director of athletics strength and conditioning from 2000-02 and as the associate director from 1997-99.
During his tenure, the men's basketball team qualified for the NCAA Tournament in 2000 and 2002. Additionally, the men's basketball team was a runner-up in the NIT in 2002.
The football team was a 2001 Big East Conference champion and also finished second in the Big East in 1998 and 1999.
Everette started his career in 1997 at the University of Virginia, where he served as the director of sports performance and the strength and conditioning coach for the football team.
Everette is married to the former Kerry Parker of Charlotte, N.C. The couple has two boys, Danny Everette II and Hunter.
Matt Dodge is in his first season as a graduate assistant strength and conditioning coach at East Carolina University.
A native of Meridian, Miss., Dodge graduated from the University of Mississippi in 2010 with a Bachelor of Science in Kinesiology and a minor in Sports Administration.
While at Ole Miss, Dodge was a volunteer assistant strength and conditioning coach for the football team from 2009-10.
Dodge is pursuing his Master of Science in Sport and Exercise Psychology at ECU.

Geopyxis carbonaria is a species of fungus in the genus Geopyxis , family Pyronemataceae . First described to science in 1805 ,

it is found in North America and Europe .
Growing in coniferous forests , it occurs primarily on the bark of living conifer trees. The fungus is distinguished from other Geopyxis species by its cream-colored to yellow-brown, gelatinous fruit bodies that are coral-like in structure. These fruit bodies are roughly spherical and measure 1 to 2 cm (0.39 to 0.79 in) in diameter. The fungus is considered inedible .
Geopyxis carbonaria is on the list of European Union priority species, which means it is considered imperiled in Europe. In the United States, the fungus is reported from several states, and is considered endangered in North Carolina .
Geopyxis carbonaria was first scientifically described in 1805 by Christiaan Hendrik Persoon . The fungus was originally placed in the genus Karstenia by Persoon, who named it Karstenia carbonaria, but this species name has been used for a number of other fungi since 1900. The fungus was transferred to the genus Geopyxis in 1995, along with Karstenia carbonaria stat. pers. and Geopyxis lindae . Geopyxis carbonaria is the type species of the genus, and the genus name is derived from the Greek geo ("earth") and pyxis ("box"). The specific epithet means "carbonaceous" in reference to the color of the fruit bodies.
Growing on the bark of conifer trees, Geopyxis carbonaria appears as a coral-like, gelatinous structure .The fruit bodies are roughly spherical, range in size from 1 to 2 cm (0.39 to 0.79 in) in diameter (0.5 to 1 cm (0.20 to 0.39 in) in North America), and are colored white to creamy yellow to creamy brown. In Europe, the fruit bodies are usually yellow to brown, while in North America they are usually yellow to yellow-brown. The gelatinous structure is hollow. These fruit bodies have a short stalk that is bent upward. The fruit bodies are covered with a blackish sheath that is more developed in North America.
The fungus is saprobic , occurring on the bark of living trees, and has been found growing on Fraser fir, white pine, and Douglas fir. It is considered inedible .

In North America, the species has been reported from Alaska , Colorado , Maine , New Brunswick , New Hampshire , New York , Ohio , Oregon , Quebec , Vermont , and Washington .

On September 12, 2013, an area of low pressure developed in the southwestern Gulf of Mexico. This system was initially considered to be a tropical depression on September 12, and was upgraded to Tropical Storm Ingrid on September 13. On September 13, the storm was upgraded to a Category 1 hurricane. On September 14, the storm was upgraded to a Category 2 hurricane.

Ingrid then passed over the Yucatán Peninsula and emerged into the warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico, where it rapidly intensified into a Category 4 hurricane. Ingrid made landfall on the coast of Veracruz, Mexico as a Category 2 hurricane on September 16. While over land, the storm weakened back to a tropical storm. Ingrid weakened to a tropical depression on September 17, and dissipated on September 18.

## Preparations

View from the International Space Station (ISS) of Ingrid on September 16, 2013

In advance of Ingrid's arrival in the Gulf of Mexico, the Port of Veracruz was closed due to the storm and the Mexican government issued hurricane watches and warnings for the state of Veracruz and the Gulf of Mexico. In Mexico, the states of Nuevo León, Coahuila, Tamaulipas and San Luis Potosí were also put under hurricane watches and warnings. Several states in Mexico, including Chiapas, Oaxaca and Guerrero, were also put under tropical storm warnings. On September 16, civil defense officials in Veracruz ordered the evacuation of approximately 50,000 people.

The United States National Hurricane Center issued a hurricane watch for the coast of Mexico from Boca Brava to Rio Panuco. Later, the watch was extended to the coast of the Mexican state of Tamaulipas and the United States Gulf Coast from the mouth of the Rio Grande River to Morgan City, Louisiana.

## Impact

### Mexico

Ingrid made landfall early Saturday morning, September 14, 2013, near Corpus Christi, Texas as a category 1 hurricane, just offshore from the city.

Ingrid made landfall in southern Veracruz at 01:15 UTC on September 16, 2013, about 50 miles (80 km) southwest of Tampico as a Category 2 hurricane. The storm then moved northwestward through the country until dissipating on September 18, 2013.

Ingrid produced 22 inches of rain in 48 hours in Acapulco, Guerrero.

Tropical Storm Ingrid resulted in the death of 12 people and caused $92 million (2013 USD) in damages.
