The Importance of Being Earnest in French is called L'importance d'être Ernest ; in German, Der Wicht des Earnest ; in Spanish, El Aprecio de Ser Ernest ; in Italian, Valore D'essere Ernesto ; in Russian, Вздорность быть Эрнестом ; in Polish, Wortho być Ernesto ; in Hebrew, החושך להיות ארנסטו ; in Finnish, Merkityksen olevan Ärne ; and in Hungarian, A jelentőség Ernszt .
Given the popularity of the play, it has been adapted into many other forms. As with many of Wilde's other works, including the 1891 novel The Picture of Dorian Gray , The Importance of Being Earnest is in the public domain in its country of origin and in other countries where copyright term is the author's life plus 70 years or less.
The play has been filmed several times, and was adapted as a 1964 musical by Frank Loesser with book and lyrics by the same. A 1982 Broadway musical by the same name features music by Andrew Lloyd Webber and lyrics and book by Alan Ayckbourn and Wilde. It starred Judi Dench and Colin Firth and was directed by Simon Callow .
The Importance of Being Earnest plays on the Victorian love of puns and plays on words. The title is an example of the homophonic pun commonly found in Wilde's most popular plays. The name "Ernest" is used as a pun: it is pronounced differently in different dialects. In Ruritania, "Ernest" is pronounced /'ɜːnəst/ , but in England it is pronounced /ˈɜːrnəst/ . In the play, Algernon's butler, Lane, is also referred to as "Ernest".
The play's characters all have names that are puns on the homophonic pun, including Gwendolen ("Gwendolyn" in the US), Cecily, Lane, Lady Bracknell, and Miss Prism.
The play is set in London in the late Victorian period. The exact date is not given, though it is a time of year when English people spend time in the countryside, so the action presumably takes place in the spring or summer.
The play opens with an argument between Jack and Algernon over the latter's insistence they have met before. Algernon claims they have met in the gardens of a country house in the countryside, but Jack dismisses this, objecting that Algernon is lying.
Their argument is interrupted by the arrival of a maid, Lane, who shows a letter to Algernon. The letter is from Jack, who asks Algernon to come to his aunt Augusta's house immediately. Algernon decides to go, but Jack asks him to bring a cigarette, for he is bored and wishes to smoke.
The scene changes and Algernon has arrived at Jack's aunt's house. Jack is also there, along with his two sisters, Gwendolen and Cecily. Algernon and Jack introduce themselves to Jack's aunt, Lady Bracknell. Algernon suggests they play a game of billiards, and Lady Bracknell agrees. As the game progresses, Lady Bracknell notices that Cecily is in the room. Cecily asks Algernon to come and examine a painting that she has made, and he obliges. When Algernon leaves the room, Jack tells Lady Bracknell that Algernon is not related to her, and that they are in fact brother and sister. Lady Bracknell is shocked, and asks for proof. Jack produces his own handwriting on a piece of paper, proving that he is Algernon's brother, and that they are in fact brother and sister.

Algernon reveals that he met Jack in the country, and that they were friends. Lady Bracknell is satisfied, but Jack tells her that Algernon is not his real name, but that he is using it because his real name is Ernest. The exact date of " Ode to a Nightingale " , as well as " Ode on Indolence " , " Ode on Melancholy " , and " Ode on a Grecian U

sher " , is not certain. In the " Letter to Mr. Wharton " , which was published in 1713, the author speaks of " Ode on Melancholy " as " of long standing, being written when I was at school." (p. 122. )  This letter is dated at " Oxford, Sept. 27th, 1700."  If therefore the four Odes were written at the same time, the date must be referred to the autumn of 1700. But the chronology of this period is so uncertain, and the question of priority is so involved, that it is needless to attempt to fix the precise date. Whether " Ode to a Nightingale " was written before or after " Ode on a Grecian Usher " is a question which may be answered in either of the following ways. It may be taken from the circumstance, that in the latter poem the poet mentions a book which he had ordered to be sent him from the Bodleian Library, and which, he says, he had been obliged to order again, because he had not received it in time for the purpose for which it was wanted; and it may be inferred that the Ode was written in the summer, and the book sent in the autumn. But this is a purely conjectural inference, and it is certain that the question is not settled by it. And it may be taken from the fact that in " Ode to a Nightingale " the poet has not yet attained the manner which he describes in " Ode on Melancholy " as the result of the experience of ten years of toil. He is now composing his first poems; his style is still irregular, and his diction is often careless and uncouth. The facts therefore which determine the date of " Ode to a Nightingale " are, first, that it was written in 1700, and, secondly, that it was written before " Ode on Melancholy." If therefore we may venture to give an estimate of time, it must be about the middle or latter part of the year 1700.
 The Ode has been often compared with the celebrated passage in Ovid, where he describes the death of Procris. I have not been able to find the passage referred to, but the subject appears to be the same; the death of a loved and faithful mistress, the remembrance of which is heightened by the song of a nightingale.
 The allusion to the nightingale is perhaps not inappropriate to the subject, and it is at least a pleasing image. The same note of sadness is sounded in the closing line of the Ode, where the notes of the bird are compared to " the echoes," which, though they are not, like the song of the nightingale, of the living creature, are scarcely less so in their origin.

Critical reception of the album was positive. At Metacritic, which assigns a normalized rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream critics, the album received an average score of 72, based on 18 reviews. At AnyDecentMusic?, which gives ratings from 1 to 10, based on a calculation done by their algorithmic consensus, it received a score of 8.0.

In a positive review for AllMusic, Andy Kellman called it "daring and captivating" and the musicianship "impeccable". He gave it four out of five stars. In a less positive review for Entertainment Weekly, Marc Snetiker called it a "stunning album", but a "sonic mess".

1968 Apollo 8 : The Apollo 8 mission was the first manned mission to the Moon, launched on Dec. 21, 1968. The mission was part of the U.S. Apollo program, which was the third human spaceflight program undertaken by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). The three Apollo missions that landed men on the Moon all involved the lunar module, which was a separate spacecraft. The module was launched to the Moon along with the command and service module (CSM), which carried the crew to lunar orbit. The command module (CM) then returned all three men safely to Earth.
Apollo 8 was launched atop a Saturn V rocket from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, on December 21, 1968. The mission was the first manned spacecraft to leave Earth orbit, and the first to visit another celestial body. The goal of the mission was to perform a "space endurance" mission: to leave Earth orbit, travel to the Moon, and return, all while keeping a manned spacecraft in orbit for the first time. Apollo 8 was also the first crewed mission to encounter another celestial body: the Moon.
Apollo 8 was the third mission with the goal of landing humans on the Moon, and the first to successfully achieve this goal. The mission's goal was to perform a "space endurance" mission: to leave Earth orbit, travel to the Moon, and return, all while keeping a manned spacecraft in orbit for the first time. Apollo 8 was also the first crewed mission to encounter another celestial body: the Moon.
The mission's crew consisted of Commander Frank Borman, Command Module Pilot James Lovell, and Lunar Module Pilot William Anders. The crew conducted 10 lunar orbits and transmitted over 100 images of the lunar surface to Earth. While on the way to the Moon, the crew performed a Christmas Eve television broadcast from lunar orbit, in which they read from the Book of Genesis. This broadcast is popularly known as the "Christmas Eve Sermon". Upon the mission's return to Earth, the crew safely splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on December 27, 1968.

Youth on the Prow , and Pleasure at the Helm met with a mixed reception on exhibition , and while critics generally praised Ett

linger's skill with the brush, others were less impressed by the subject matter.
 Notwithstanding Mr . Ettlinger's rich talent , I think he , nevertheless , could not have chosen a very happy subject for his first painting .
How could Mr . Ettlinger , who is a very clever artist , and an excellent draughtsman not have seen that his subject was not only unsuitable in itself , but that the treatment he gave it was calculated to excite a feeling of disgust in the minds of the spectators ?
 I do not know whether the young man in the picture , who is pictured as a very fine fellow , is the artist's son , but if he is , I hope he will not be led by the example of his parents to ruin his health , and if he is not , he had better beware of picturing his father in the character of a very fine fellow , for the sake of gaining the approbation of foolish people .
 It is not only unsuitable , but it is unnatural , to represent a young man , in the full flush of health and vigour , employed in the not over agreeable occupation of extinguishing candles in a room where so many young ladies are enjoying themselves .
 The young man in the picture might , with equal propriety , have been pictured as a sad disconsolate wretch , with his head in his hands , instead of being represented as a jovial , hearty fellow , who is evidently " quite satisfied " with his situation .
 I can conceive , that the artist may have been influenced by the opinion , that it is rather a novelty , to paint a subject of this kind , but it is not very novel , and it is only necessary to look at the picture to see that it is a very immoral one .
 I do not know whether the artist intended to paint the picture in as light a manner as it appears , but if he did , it is a pity that he did not take more pains in the execution of it .
 I should like to know what the artist has to say for his picture ?
 The picture , which is attributed to Mr . Ettlinger , represents a young man in the act of extinguishing candles in a room where a party of young ladies were enjoying themselves .
 This picture has attracted considerable attention , and has met with a mixed reception .
 While the artists generally admire the skill displayed in the picture , there are others who express their disapprobation of the subject .
 We have no doubt , however , that the artist will be amply repaid for his trouble , and we hope that his future efforts may be more successful than his first .

 All the virtues of painting are on the canvass presented to our view in Pleasure at the Helm and Youth on the Prow , and the faults of the artist are the only defects which can be pointed out.
 The picture is an introduction to the artist's future labours, and the public ought to be very grateful to him for his first effort, as it is a good specimen of the kind of work which he is about to produce.
 The subjects are both appropriate, and the artist has treated them with all the skill and delicacy which he possesses.

Antimony is a chemical element with symbol Sb ( from Latin : stibium ) and atomic number 51 . A lustrous gray metalloid , it is

found naturally in the sulfide mineral stibnite ( Sb 2 S 3 ) which also contains 1 to 2 % antimony . It has no color , no smell , and a density of 6.79 g/cm 3 . Antimony is a brittle solid that can be made into a variety of alloy s by combining it with other metals .
In nature , antimony typically exists as the sulfide Sb 2 S 3 (stibnite) . It is also found as the oxide Sb 2 O 5 , and as the halides SbCl 3 , SbBr 3 , and SbI 3 .
Antimony is a silvery-white, brittle, crystalline solid with a relatively high specific gravity at 6.67 (20 °C/100°C). It has poor mechanical properties, other than its strength and hardness. It has no smell and a low melting point (446.7 °C).
The density of antimony is about 6.67 grams per cubic centimeter (g/cm³), which is more than lead (11.34 g/cm³) but less than that of gold (19.3 g/cm³). It is a relatively hard metal, with a vickers hardness of 5.5–6.0 MPa. Its melting point is 630 °C (1,154 °F) and its boiling point is 1,670 °C (3,038 °F).
The most common minerals of antimony include stibnite (Sb 2 S 3 ), tetrahedrite (Cu 3 SbS 3 ), and boulangerite (Cu 9 Sb 2 S 11 ). The metal is extracted from its sulfide, which is the most important commercial ore mineral.
Because antimony is a semimetal , it is possible to use it as a semiconductor and to create p-type and n-type semiconductors .
The antimony compounds that have been used for centuries as fire retardants and in other applications include antimony trichloride , antimony sulfide , and antimony oxide .
Antimony is used in combination with lead to make alloys that are hard and stable at high temperatures.

It is used in alloys such as typewriter mechanisms, fusible alloy , solder , bearings, and soft solders. It is put into alloys that are used to make batteries, fireworks, and explosives.
In alloys, antimony combines with lead to form eutectic alloys with a low melting point. The most common type of eutectic alloy is type metal , which is used to make the typewriter carriage and the typewriter print head. The alloy is 5–10% antimony by weight.

This property is used to make antimony alloys that are used to make semiconductors. Antimony semiconductors are made by doping antimony with arsenic and phosphorus to create p-type and n-type semiconductors.

 While the armor scheme was not detailed in the original plans , it is known that the upper deck was protected by 1.25 in ( 32 mm ) of steel . The side armor plates were 1.5 in ( 38 mm ) in thickness . The conning tower had 10.63 in ( 270 mm ) of armor .

 Vasco da Gama was laid down on 15 October 1881 at the William Doxford & Sons shipyard in Sunderland . She was launched on 11 March 1883 , and commissioned on 7 May 1885.
 Vasco da Gama was a member of the Royal Navy's Royal Sovereign class , but was a larger ship than her contemporaries. She was built to a design by Nathaniel Barnaby originally intended for the Chilean Navy , but cancelled when Chile was victorious over Peru in the War of the Pacific . It is possible that her design was influenced by the Japanese battleship Azuma , which was launched and commissioned in 1879.
 Vasco da Gama's career was uneventful. She was deployed to the Mediterranean twice and participated in training and fleet exercises , but spent most of her time in Home waters . She was modernized in 1893, and refitted again in 1899. She was sold to be broken up in 1905.

The St. Petersburg Times was an American newspaper published in Florida since 1884. It was Florida's oldest continually operated business and the state's first newspaper with statewide circulation. It was initially known as The Evening Times, and later as the St. Petersburg Evening Independent. In 1981, after the publicly traded company became part of Knight-Ridder, the newspaper was renamed The St. Petersburg Times. It was owned by the E. W. Scripps Company from 1994 to 2011, when it was purchased by the Times Publishing Company, which was founded by the Poynter Institute for Media Studies and chaired by Nelson Poynter.

The St. Petersburg Times

## History

### Early years

The Evening Times debuted in 1884 as a five-column weekly newspaper with a circulation of 750, founded by Alfred W. Green and his brother-in-law, William J. McClure. Green had previously worked as a typesetter in St. Petersburg and acquired the local newspaper, the St. Petersburg Gazette, in 1882. In 1886, Green and his brother-in-law, McClure, bought out the Gazette and merged it with their new paper, which was renamed the Evening Times. In 1889, Green sold his shares in the newspaper to McClure.

In 1895, McClure and his brother, W. B., sold the paper to James M. Taylor, a local businessman. Taylor changed the paper's name to the St. Petersburg Times in 1896. Two years later, Taylor sold the paper to J. Frank Sinclair.

With the advent of the Spanish–American War in 1898, the Times began to focus more on national news, and soon afterward, the paper began replacing its page of local news with a page of national news, becoming the first newspaper to do so in the state. In 1907, Sinclair sold the paper to Joseph McCarty.

In 1917, McCarty sold the Times to Morris B. Kaplan and Henry F. Ring, who were joined by Ring's son-in-law, Frank C. McElroy, the next year. The Times became a morning newspaper in 1925, and became a daily newspaper the following year. In 1936, McElroy was joined by his brother-in-law, George W. Scripps, in control of the paper. In 1952, the paper was acquired by Scripps' son, Edward W. Scripps, and became owned by Scripps Enterprises.

In 1964, the Times merged with the Tampa Times, which had been founded in 1888. In 1981, Scripps sold the Times to Knight-Ridder, which changed the paper's name to the St. Petersburg-Tampa Times in 1983.

### The Poynter Institute

The newspaper was owned by the E. W. Scripps Company from 1994 to 2011. In 1994, E.W. Scripps Company sold the paper to the Poynter Institute for Media Studies, a nonprofit organization that was founded in 1975 by Nelson Poynter, former chairman of Scripps. Poynter had been a reporter, editor and publisher of the Scripps papers and had acquired the St. Petersburg Evening Independent in 1969. The newspaper's name was changed to the St. Petersburg Times in 1999, with the E.W. Scripps Company retaining control of the Times' website, TBO.com.

In 2005, the Times and its website were one of the first in the United States to use a masthead-less design. On February 13, 2007, the Times became the first newspaper in the United States to make its content available through the Apple iPhone. In 2008, the Times launched the Times Connect app for the Apple iPad.

In 2011, the Times and Tampa Bay Online were sold to the Times Publishing Company, a newly established company founded by the Poynter Institute

The First Ostend Raid ( part of Operation ZO ) was the first of two attacks by the Royal Navy on the German @-@ held port of Os

rden ( Ostend ) under the command of the 12th Destroyer Flotilla, which took place between 23 and 26 September 1917.  The first raid consisted of a battlecruiser force under the command of Rear-Admiral Hugh Evan-Thomas, which was intended to divert German attention from the main raid.
The second raid took place four days later.  This time the ships were protected by an allied fleet from the newly-created German naval air force.
The first raid resulted in the sinking of the German submarine U-41, the inconclusive Battle of the Heligoland Bight, and the destruction of the German cruisers Emden ( which sank at her moorings ) and Koln, and the German destroyer G38.  The British battlecruiser Lion was also damaged, though not sunk.  The second raid resulted in the sinking of the German destroyer G16, which was scuttled by its crew after it was rammed and set on fire by the light cruiser HMS Southampton.  The German cruisers Dresden and Koln were both badly damaged but managed to make it to port.

Government decided to "preserve the telescope for the use of the scientific world"  . The observatory was closed to the public in 1854 .
The observatory had been fitted with an instrument called a traverse , a mechanical device used to measure the pointing of a telescope . Whenever the telescope was pointed at a celestial object , a clockwork mechanism would re-align the telescope to its original position . This was done to prevent the telescope from drifting and to preserve its accuracy .
The observatory had a clock that was designed and made by Thomas Earnshaw and was used to record the times when observations were made . The clock was attached to the telescope's telescope table and would ring every minute .
It is likely that the clock will have been powered by a weight-driven mechanism  , a common feature of clocks at the time .
The telescope was used by the Royal Society until 1858 . After the observatory closed , the telescope and instruments were stored in the Tower of London .
The telescope was used for research by scientific institutions after the observatory closed . In 1862 it went to the United States , where it was used at the Harvard College Observatory . In 1864 it was given by the Royal Society to the United States Navy for use in the West Indies .
The telescope was returned to the Royal Society in 1869 and was housed at the Society's Burlington House premises . In 1896 the telescope was moved to the Science Museum and was set up in the museum's Hall of Machines .
The telescope is on loan to the Science Museum. It is housed in the Telegraph Museum in Porthcurno, Cornwall .

Erected as a permanent memorial to the men of Oldham who were killed in the First World War , Oldham 's war memorial consists o

a stone obelisk set on a granite plinth. 

## History

The memorial was unveiled on 15 December 1922 by the Right Honourable Horatio Herbert Kitchener, 1st Earl Kitchener.

The monument was extended in 1939 to include the names of the 24 men of Oldham who were killed in the Second World War.

## Design

The monument, designed by Manchester architects, J. R. Rigby & Sons, stands on the site of the county gaol on the corner of St Mary's Gate and Union Street in Oldham town centre. It is made of granite and stands 36 ft 6 in high.

### Inscription

The monument bears the inscription: 

In honour of the men of Oldham who made the supreme sacrifice in the Great War 1914–1918 

### Men commemorated

The memorial commemorates the 619 men of Oldham who were killed in the First World War.

### Extension to the Second World War

In 1939, the memorial was extended to include the names of the 24 men of Oldham who were killed in the Second World War.

## Condition

The memorial is listed Grade II on the National Heritage List for England.

The helmet appears to have been deliberately folded up and deposited in an artificial stone structure . It is thought to have b

affled archaeologists for decades.
What is seen is the face of a human skull fixed to a surprisingly small and fragile helmet. It is made of a lightweight metallic material.
It is a remarkable find that has been described as a game-changer.
The skull is that of a woman and there are indications that she was heavily pregnant. It's a sad reminder that even in the most advanced civilisations, violence and warfare were far from unknown.
The skull is believed to have been placed there deliberately. When it was first found archaeologists thought the helmet had been placed on the woman's head and then she had been decapitated.
What was then dismissed as a trophy has now been redescribed.
The image of the skull has been shown to scientists at the University of Bradford, UK, who have confirmed it was not placed on the woman's head.
The woman probably died as a consequence of an injury and the helmet was placed on her head in death.
The image of her skull is that of a woman who was about 1.9 metres tall. She had a small head, with a narrow face.
Her teeth were also small. She was aged between 20 and 35 when she died.
In the archaeological literature there is no mention of a helmet like this being worn by women, although it is possible that this would not have been known in the past.
The face of the helmet is decorated with a pattern of four circles and a cross.
Stone Age helmets were unusual. Some have been found in Europe and in India, but this is the earliest one known.
The helmet has been dated to be from around 3200 BC, which means it was made around 5,500 years ago.
The skeleton of the woman was found next to the helmet. She was lying on her back with her head to the north. Her arms were crossed over her chest and her neck was bent back.
It seems that she was not thrown into the tomb as a sacrifice, but lay in the tomb for a while but was then deliberately placed on the floor.
The helmet has been described as a "significant discovery". It is remarkable that the helmet was found at all, and that it is so intact.
Archaeologists say it shows that the wearer of the helmet was a woman who was highly respected in her community.
The fact that the helmet was found in a stone burial chamber indicates the status of the wearer.
The chamber is the largest prehistoric burial chamber found in Scandinavia.
It had been excavated in 1870 and was open to the public.
The chamber was reopened in 2013 and the skeleton and helmet were found.
The discovery has been made public to help researchers study the woman and her death.
The helmet is currently on display at the Natural History Museum in Copenhagen, Denmark.

The label's name is a reference to the Zulu saying "Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu," which means, "A person is a person through other people."

They also work to provide financial support to young people who are interested in pursuing careers in journalism, law, and politics. Bishop Bricius 's chapter of eight clerics consisted of the dean , precentor , treasurer , chancellor , archdeacon and three or

four canons . The monks of the chapter can be traced back to 1066 , when the abbey held a second rank amongst the houses of the English church, after Winchester. On the death of the last Norman abbot , Hugh de Laci , the canons elected their first native Norman abbot , Robert de Courcy , a graduate of Oxford University . He was succeeded by Osbern Rufus (1122-1135), Robert de Tateshall (1135-1153), William de Monte (1153-1166), Robert de Rothwell (1166-1175), William de Bade (1175-1183), Richard de Lufford (1183-1209) and William de Lancastre (1209-1229). In 1229 , Bishop John de Gray , who had been appointed by King Henry III to the see of Norwich , removed the abbey from the care of the monks to that of canons . The suffragan see of Norwich was erected in 1101 by Pope Paschal II and was always dependent on the see of Canterbury . The subjugation of the monastery to the suffragan bishop was confirmed by Pope Clement II in 1143 . The abbey church was built in 1337 . A fire destroyed it in 1483 , but was promptly rebuilt by the abbot and his monks. It was destroyed in the 1644 , and finally the abbey and its church were demolished in 1822 .

Though he has been dead for more than 350 years, John Banister (1640-1689), the 'forgotten founder of American mycology', is still acknowledged as being the first American mycologist. In 1679, after studying for 11 years at the English School of Physic in London, he was ordained as a minister in the Church of England. Unable to find employment in England, he immigrated to the American Colony of Virginia where he became Minister of the parish of Jamestown. He was also the first naturalist in America and, as such, the first author of books on American natural history.
The first English settlers in America had brought with them a number of European plants and animals, including domesticated animals, which were well adapted to the local environment. However, the climate and animal life of the New World was largely unknown, so only a small number of the imported animals survived.
John Banister's ambition was to make America a suitable home for English agriculture. He was therefore particularly interested in native plants and animals, of which he kept detailed records, including 130 local plants and 200 animals. In 1680, he published an illustrated treatment of Virginia plants, Treatise of the Plants of Virginia. The next year he published a similar book on Virginia animals, A Brief Description of the Animals Found in Virginia. In 1705, these two books were combined and published as The Virginia Natural History. Widely admired for its pioneering scientific approach, it was translated into French in 1747 and German in 1752.
In the 18th century, the latest scientific thinking was that all plants and animals were created by God and that God had created them to be used as food, medicine and clothing. Hence, herbalists, who treated diseases with plants, were called 'physicians'. John Banister was one of the first physicians to point out that many of the plants, animals and insects in the New World had no counterparts in the Old World and were therefore incapable of being used as food, medicine or clothing.
Banister's interest in the natural world was not confined to Virginia. He was also a keen traveller. In 1682, he went on an expedition to the Dismal Swamp, which lies on the border between Virginia and North Carolina. On this trip, he was the first European to see the wild turkey and the American bison. He also witnessed the first recorded sighting of a bald eagle by a European. In 1683, he journeyed to the Atlantic coast of the Carolinas and, in 1685, to the Pacific coast of Mexico.
The first English settlement in America was at Jamestown, Virginia, in 1607. In 1680, the population of Virginia was only 4,000, but this had risen to 50,000 when Banister published his book Treatise of the Plants of Virginia in 1680.

It contains the remains of more than 6,000 people, including those of notable Argentines, including Generals Manuel Belgrano (the hero of the May Revolution), and José de San Martín , and the famous literary and intellectual figures, such as Adolfo Bioy Casares, Jorge Luis Borges , and Ernesto Sabato . ## Route description

SR 67 is a 19-mile (31 km) highway in the U.S. state of Arizona. It runs from the Tucson Mountains to the eastern end of the Rillito River Parkway. The roadway begins at a junction with SR 86, just south of the community of Sunset. From there, it heads north as an undivided two-lane highway. The route passes through the unincorporated community of Rillito as it enters the city of Tucson. Within the city, it has a short concurrency with SR 87. Afterward, it continues north as a divided four-lane highway, crossing the Rillito River and the Southern Pacific Railroad line. SR 67 turns to the northwest, passing more unincorporated areas and crossing the Santa Cruz River before it ends at a junction with SR 83/SR 84 east of the Tucson Mountains.

## History

SR 67 was established in 1959 as a renumbering of Southern Pacific's portions of Arizona 83 and 84.

## Major intersections

The entire route is in Pima County.

Ha ' K 'in Xook ( Mayan pronunciation : [ haʔ k ’ in ʃoːk ] ) , also known as Ruler 6 , was an ajaw of Piedras Negras , an anci

ently powerful city-state located in the Guatemalan department of Petén . He reigned from 771 to 798 .
The first known reference to Ha 'K'in Xook is from the tomb of Tzi-B'alam Ajaw , also called Tzi-B'alam II , at Tikal . The inscription was dated to 781 and is credited to Ha 'K'in Xook. The text reads:
"...[then] the king of Piedras Negras, who is Ha 'K'in Xook, the lord governor of the west, ..."
— Text from the Tomb of Tzi-B'alam Ajaw, Tikal, 781 CE.
Known as Ruler 6 in the hieroglyphic records of Piedras Negras , Ha 'K'in Xook, like his predecessors, was a Mayan ruler who reigned during the Late Classic Period . His reign is significant in that it bridges the transition from the Late Classic to the Terminal Classic periods . During his reign, the last of the great city-states was formed in the Petén region.
Ha 'K'in Xook, along with his predecessor, is an example of the elite ajawship , a role of authority and power, that he inherited from his father, Yajaw Teʼ Kʼinich , who ruled from 754 to 770 . Yajaw Teʼ Kʼinich was a co-ruler of Piedras Negras. He was responsible for the development and expansion of the city. When he died, his son Ha 'K'in Xook became the sole ruler, and he continued the expansion and development of Piedras Negras.
Ha 'K'in Xook was a member of a noble family that was descended from the Kaanul kingdom. The Kaanul kingdom was a powerful Maya state that controlled the area from the Pacific to the Caribbean in the era before the Maya Classic Period . It is also known that Ha 'K'in Xook was a descendant of the famous Kaanul ruler, Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat .
Ha 'K'in Xook is best known for his construction of a large palace and his expansion of the city. His palace, known as the South Acropolis , is one of the largest structures built in the Petén region during the Late Classic period.
During his reign, Ha 'K'in Xook maintained a number of contacts with other rulers. He maintained a close relationship with Tikal , which is a major city-state in the area. His relationship with Tikal is that of an inferior to the senior partner. Other cities he formed alliances with include Naranjo , Calakmul , and Yaxchilan .
The reign of Ha 'K'in Xook coincides with the period of decline of the Maya Classic Period. The exact cause of the decline is not known. One theory is that Ha 'K'in Xook saw a rapid decline in the number of tribute coming from his allies and vassals. This may have led to a reduced income for his city, leading to a decline in the city's power. The exact cause of the decline is unclear.
Ha 'K'in Xook is buried in the A Group complex at Piedras Negras . His tomb was discovered in 1982 by archaeologist Richard D. Hansen .
A tomb mound was excavated in the southwest corner of the A Group complex. The structure was built of limestone blocks, with a rectangular base and a pyramid shape. The mound was 5 m high and measured 29.5 m long.
Inside the tomb, researchers found the remains of Ha 'K'in Xook , his wife Lady Xook, and their children, along with their servants. The structure itself was decorated with murals. The murals were painted in red and black and depicted warriors, mythological figures, human sacrifices, and animals.
Ha 'K'in Xook's tomb was found to have been robbed twice. The first time, the tomb was robbed in the 10th century, and the second time, it was robbed in the 12th century.
Ha 'K'in Xook's tomb is one of the most significant finds in Mayan archaeology. The tomb, along with the murals, provides a rare window into the life and culture of the Mayans during the Late Classic period.

In 1845 , amateur geologists William Guybon Atherstone and Andrew Geddes Bain discovered several fossils near Dassieklip , Cape

of Good Hope, in what is now South Africa. They were sent to the Royal College of Surgeons in London , United Kingdom . There, they were examined by anatomist Sir Richard Owen , who described them as fossil turtles ; the find was reported in the 1846 issue of the Transactions of the Zoological Society of London .
In 1849, Owen assigned the fossils to a new genus, Neptunea , and described them as the oldest known fossil turtles. In 1854, Owen named the species Neptunea bainsi, after Bain. The Neptunea bainsi fossils are now housed at the Museum of Natural History in London, and are the only fossils of Neptunea known from the Karoo Basin .
In 1880, several fossil bones were discovered near Cabeça de Vaca , Brazil . They were sent to the University of Munich , where they were examined by paleontologist Louis Agassiz. He identified them as fossil turtles, and named the genus Neptunea after Owen's Neptunea bainsi . The species was named Neptunea brasiliana .
In 1992, paleontologist Robert L. Carroll suggested that Neptunea was a basal member of the superfamily Testudinoidea , which was named by Carroll in 1988 (it includes all living and fossil species of turtles). In 1993, Carroll and John J. Flynn proposed that the genus Neptunea was synonymous with the genus Trionyx , and that the fossil species were a single species, Neptunea bainsi. This was accepted by paleontologist Hans-Dieter Sues in 1996.
In 2007, paleontologist Lucas Kelley and colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, re-examined the fossils and reassigned them to the genus Trionyx. Kelley also described a new species, Trionyx minor, and concluded that the fossil species were members of the genus Trionyx , instead of Neptunea. Kelley's findings were published in the Journal of Paleontology in 2007.
According to Carroll, fossil species of the genus Neptunea have been found in South Africa, Namibia, India, and Brazil, but not in Europe. The fossils are between 170.5 and 151.5 million years old.

Early members of the ceratopsian group , such as Psittacosaurus , were small bipedal animals . Later members , including cerato

-saurs , were quadrupedal and had long necks and small heads. The largest dinosaurs , such as the gigantic _Diabloceratops ,_ were members of the Ceratopsia.
The most famous Ceratopsian is the ferocious Tyrannosaurus rex.
The Ceratopsia were the last of the dinosaurs. They survived until the end of the Cretaceous period , about 65 million years ago. During the last half of the Cretaceous , the Ceratopsia occupied a wide range of habitats , from the arid plains of western North America to the humid forests of Asia. They lived in herds , and fought each other for territory and mates. They also gave birth to their young, rather than laying eggs.
The ceratopsian skulls were distinctive in their paired, beaked horns. The meaning of the word _ceratops_ is "horned face." The horns and beaks were composed of bony material. Some had parrotlike beaks, while others had beaks similar to those of the duck-billed dinosaurs. The horns could be as long as the head.
The Ceratopsia were big-bodied animals that ranged from 1,000 to 5,000 pounds or more in weight. They were herbivores and grazed on plants. They could also browse on low-growing shrubs. They were bipedal, but were also capable of running on all fours. Some were quadrupedal.
#  **EARLY EVIDENCE FOR CERATOPSIANS**
The first evidence for Ceratopsia came from fragmentary fossils. These included the remains of the skull and horns of a dinosaur which was named _Psittacosaurus ,_ meaning "parrot reptile." _Psittacosaurus_ was first described in 1923. It was a small animal, about the size of a human, with a large skull and the horns of a parrot. Over the years, many more fossils have been found. They have been found in a number of places around the world, including China, Mongolia, and North America.
 A sketch of _Psittacosaurus_ , one of the first dinosaurs to be identified as a Ceratopsia. ( _Color by Dean R. Lomax_ )
Some of the fossils of _Psittacosaurus_ came from a place called Nemegt in Mongolia. Other fossils from Nemegt came from a Ceratopsian called _Kulceratops_ , which may be the same age as _Psittacosaurus_ , or perhaps slightly older. _Kulceratops_ was a small dinosaur, but some of its horns were as long as the skull. It had a beak, like a duck's bill, and a bony frill around the back of the skull.
Earlier fossils of Ceratopsia include _Talmana_ , from western North America, and _Dysalotosaurus_ , from China.
#  **LATE DISCOVERIES**
The late discoveries include _Protoceratops_ , from Mongolia, _Styracosaurus_ , from the United States, and _Titanoceratops_ , from Canada.
_Protoceratops_ was a small dinosaur. It had a large skull, small teeth, a frill, and horns. It was bipedal and had a parrotlike beak.
_Styracosaurus_ was a large dinosaur with a large frill and a single horn on the nose. It was bipedal.
_Titanoceratops_ had a large frill, two horns on the nose, and a horn on the snout. It lived in Canada and was somewhat larger than _Styracosaurus_.

The politics of Croatia are defined by a parliamentary , representative democratic republic framework , where the Prime Ministe

r is the head of government and the President is the head of state.
With its total area of 21,851 km2  (8,437 sq mi) , Croatia is the 127th largest country in the world and the 58th largest in Europe . Croatia shares a border with Slovenia to the north and northwest, Hungary to the northeast, Serbia to the east, Bosnia and Herzegovina to the southeast, Montenegro to the southeast, and the Adriatic Sea to the southwest.Due to its long coastline, the country’s territory covers 5,835 km (3,627 mi) of the Adriatic Sea.
Croatia’s name derives from Medieval Croatia , which was first recorded in the 7th century. Croatia officially became an independent state in 925. In the period between 925 and 1918 Croatia was part of various state formations, from kingdoms to republics and empires, and spanned in time the Early Middle Ages, the High Middle Ages and the Late Middle Ages. During the 19th century and the early 20th century, after the abolition of feudalism , the Croatian national revival developed into a political and economic movement. With the help of the Pan-Slavic movement, Croatia declared independence in 1918 during the breakup of the Austro-Hungarian Empire and subsequently became a part of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia . After the Axis invasion of Yugoslavia in 1941 , Croatia became a Nazi puppet state . During the war, most of the country was captured by the Partisans and other resistance groups, and was then annexed by the SFR Yugoslavia. After the dissolution of Yugoslavia at the end of the Cold War, the Croatian War of Independence resulted in the independence of Croatia in 1991.
Croatia is a member of the European Union (EU), NATO, United Nations (UN), the World Trade Organization (WTO), the Council of Europe and the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA). Since 2001, the Croatian government has committed to making the country a high-income economy based on tourism and the service sector.
The current Croatian Constitution , adopted in 1990, defines Croatia as a democratic and social state.
Croatia is a republic with a semi-presidential system of government. It is composed of 21 counties (hrustan), and further divided into 123 cities and 427 municipalities. The Parliament of Croatia (Hrvatski sabor) is unicameral . The parliament is elected for a four-year term. The President of Croatia is the head of state and is elected for a five-year term. The Government of Croatia (Vlada Republike Hrvatske) is the executive branch. It is composed of the President and the Council of Ministers of the Republic of Croatia , both of which are appointed by the President.
The courts in Croatia are split into civil, criminal, family, commercial, administrative and misdemeanour courts.
The Croatian governmental system is dominated by two political parties, the centre-left Social Democratic Party of Croatia (SDP) and the centre-right Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ). These two parties have dominated Croatian politics for the past 24 years, although numerous other parties are represented in the Croatian Parliament.
Croatia is a member of the Council of Europe , the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA), the UN , the OSCE and NATO. Croatia has signed the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages and has implemented the European Charter for the Promotion of the Culture of Peace, both adopted by the Council of Europe.
Croatia is a member of the Union for the Mediterranean .
Croatia has been a member of the World Trade Organization since 2000. It is a founding member of the Central European Free Trade Agreement.
Croatia is also a member of the UN’s 1540 Committee which seeks to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction . Croatia has been a member of the International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol) since 1990, and is a member of the Schengen Area .

Dylan's best-known works include "The Times They Are a-Changin'", "Blowin' in the Wind", "The Man in Me", "A Hard Rain's a-Gonna Fall", "Don't Think Twice, It's All Right", "Bob Dylan's Blues", "Bob Dylan's Dream", and "Oxford Town". . in Middlesex (Greater London). The first match was played on 22 March 1910 , with France drawing 3-3. The stadium was officially opened on 2 January 1923 , with England defeating France 15-0, although the stadium had been inaugurated on 27 January 1920 , with England defeating Ireland 14-10. In 1930 , the stadium hosted its first Five Nations match, with England defeating Scotland 24-3. The stadium hosted its first international rugby league match on 23 September 1932 , with England defeating France 18-5. Twickenham S. has since hosted 205 England international matches (as of 18 November 2012 ), including 175 Five Nations/RBS 6 Nations matches, 18 Five Nations/RBS 6 Nations Championship matches, 13 European Championship matches, 15 Rugby World Cup matches, 18 British and Irish Lions matches, 16 England Sevens matches and 1 Tri-nations match.
 The stadium has hosted 142 England national rugby union matches (as of 21 April 2012 ). This is the most of any venue in the world, and the second is Murrayfield S. (Edinburgh) with 137 matches. Tristan was a dark chestnut horse standing just under 16 hands ( 64 inches , 163 cm ) high , bred by Robert St Clair @-@ Erskin

Castle , Stirlingshire , Scotland , and was foaled in 1918 .
The horse was imported to Australia in 1923 by a Mr T A Doherty of Sydney , whose father , Mr T C Doherty , was the Sydney agent for the Scottish firm of Robert St Clair , and Tristan was the first of the Erksine horses to come to Australia .
Tristan was sired by St Clair's 1908 Derby winner 'Governor' , and his dam was 'Rosalie' , the product of 'Brio' out of 'Royal Flush' .
Tristan was trained by the famous Australian trainer Jack Holt , who as a jockey had won the 1900 Melbourne Cup , and who went on to train 10 horses to win Melbourne Cups , including 'Iranistan' in 1926 .
Holt was also a leading owner who raced horses such as 'Arnhem' (1918), 'Derry Vale' (1920), 'Glenvale' (1924) and 'Lochalsh' (1927).
Tristan was purchased privately for 250 pounds by Sydney businessman Bert Donaldson and raced in partnership with officers of the Australian Army Service Corps , who were based at Randwick .
Tristan's first race in Australia was a 10 furlong (2016 m) trial over the Sydney Racecourse on 24 October 1923 , his third race was the 1924 Sydney Cup over 3200 m (2 miles , 2 furlongs), and the horse finished second to 'Melbourne Cup' .
Tristan won 21 of his 51 starts , and placed 14 times , including a course record in winning the 1924 Stradbroke Handicap over 1600 m (1 mile) by 10 lengths .
The horse won the 1925 Melbourne Cup , the 1926 Sydney Cup , and the 1926 Melbourne Cup , and was ridden in the last of those races by jockey Jim Pike .
On 20 April 1927 , Tristan won the 1927 Sydney Cup , winning by 1 1/2 lengths from 'Bertie' with 'Tirol' 3/4 of a length behind in third .
The horse's last win was the 1927 Warwick Stakes over 1600 m (1 mile) at Randwick on 25 June 1927 , ridden by Jim Pike .
Tristan was retired from racing in 1927 and was sold to Mr C E Keys of Toowoomba , Queensland , for 3000 pounds , and was taken to the owner's stud .
Tristan's best progeny was stallion 'Wild Tristan' (1930-1937) , who was sire of 83 foals .
The horse's grandson was 'Wild Tristan' , who was sire of 35 foals , and the horse's first foals were born in 1938 .
'Wild Tristan' was foaled in 1930 , and was a dark bay horse standing 16 hands (64 inches , 163 cm) , bred by Mr J C Kays of Toowoomba , Queensland , and was sired by 'Tristan' out of 'Biggles' by 'Bran' , and his dam was 'Wanton' by 'Wildfowl' .
'Wild Tristan' was trained by the Australian trainer William N Dunn , who was based at Warwick , Queensland , and was ridden by jockey John 'Leader' Reid .
'Wild Tristan' won the 1933 Queensland Derby over 2400 m (1 1/2 miles) at Eagle Farm , and the 1934 Queensland Derby over 2200 m (1 3/16 miles) at Eagle Farm , and was sold to Mr H V McGrath of Toowoomba for 2000 pounds , and was retired to stud .
His first foals were born in 1938 .

Hellblazer was set in a contemporary world , albeit a world of magic and supernatural conflict behind the scenes . Although iss

uelength continuity was very much a part of the Hellblazer mythos, Garth Ennis and co-writer Jamie Delano did not always try to tie each story into the next, and a story could be read and enjoyed in isolation. However, there was a recurring cast of characters: John Constantine, the protagonist; his daughter, Chastity; John's mentor, Father Black; his girlfriend, Zed.
The four creators worked on Hellblazer together for the first thirty-seven issues, producing a cohesive and compelling series. The 1992 decision by DC to strip the series of its Vertigo branding was inspired, as it allowed for the escalating violence of the series to be read by a wider audience.
One consequence of the success of this series, however, was that DC tried to emulate it and sell it back to the market, often with disastrous results. Other characters who have appeared in Hellblazer have been the vampire John Constantine, the witch Astra Logue, the ex-cop Garth Ennis, and the werewolf Andrew Chambers.
The stories in Hellblazer frequently mirrored the zeitgeist of the eighties and nineties. For example, stories like "Showpiece" (issue 56) dealt with the child abuse scandal that rocked the United Kingdom in the mid-eighties. "The Witching" (issue 63) dealt with the occult crime that was prevalent in the back streets of London. "Uneasy Street" (issue 64) dealt with the racism that was evident in the United Kingdom in the wake of the 1981 riots. "A Slight Case of the Blues" (issue 91) dealt with the AIDS crisis. "Dangerous Habits" (issue 92) again took on the AIDS crisis. "Dangerous Habits" also dealt with the issue of homophobia.
Another strand that ran through the series was the conflict between John and his daughter, Chastity. This was a result of the "botched job" that Constantine had carried out on her conception. "The Children's Crusade" (issue 14) and "The Seed" (issue 15) saw Constantine's actions to conceal his mistakes have unforeseen consequences, forcing Constantine to accept full responsibility for his actions. Constantine's role as her father is also explored in "Dangerous Habits" (issue 92) and "Constantine" (issue 95).
The spiritual conflicts that John Constantine faces in Hellblazer are often presented in a very literal way. The character of Father Black is an example of this. Father Black is John's mentor and a constant presence in the series. He is also John's constant reminder of the consequences of John's own actions, coupled with the suggestion that Father Black is a manifestation of John's own internal demons.
An example of this is "Showpiece" (issue 56). Here Constantine is being punished by Father Black for his actions in the past, but at the same time acknowledges that his actions are necessary to protect those he loves.
One of the most important recurring motifs in the series is that of John Constantine attempting to protect those he loves. In "The Last Temptation" (issue 65), Constantine does this for his daughter, Chastity. In "Changers" (issue 67) he does this for his girlfriend, Zed. In "Dangerous Habits" (issue 92) he does this for his son, Jamie. In "The First of the Fallen" (issue 104), he does this for his wife, Livia. Indeed, the consequences of these actions are often shown to be far more damaging than the original "crime".
In terms of storytelling, Hellblazer was very much a comic that was concerned with telling a story. The style of storytelling was a combination of the traditional American comic book and European graphic novel. These stories were often a combination of supernatural horror and crime fiction. Constantine's world is one where we are often faced with the possibility of the supernatural occurring.

The International Olympic Committee ( IOC ) officially launched the bid process for the 2016 Summer Olympics and Paralympics on

16 May 2004. The IOC invited six cities to submit formal bids to host the Games: Chicago, Tokyo, Rio de Janeiro, Madrid, Moscow, and Prague. On 6 June 2004 the IOC voted to award the 2016 Summer Olympics and Paralympics to Rio de Janeiro, making it the first South American city to host the Olympic Games.
During the bidding process, which was dominated by the United States bid, Chicago, Tokyo and Madrid withdrew. In the end, Chicago withdrew amidst a lack of support from the local community and business leaders, and Tokyo and Madrid withdrew amidst serious concerns about the financial viability of their bids.

production, resulting in anemia. The AML cells also produce immature white blood cells, which are unable to fight infection. The leukemic cells also interfere with normal blood clotting, causing easy bruising and bleeding.

AML is more common in men than in women, and it is more common in people who are older than 65.

## Diagnosis

The diagnosis of AML is based on a blood and bone marrow test. To confirm the diagnosis, a bone marrow biopsy is performed. This is done by inserting a bone marrow needle into a bone and removing a small amount of bone marrow. The bone marrow is then examined under a microscope to look for leukemic cells. A bone marrow biopsy is important to differentiate AML from other types of leukemia.

### Staging

AML is staged according to the 2008 World Health Organization (WHO) classification of myeloid neoplasms . The WHO classification was published in 2008 by the World Health Organization (WHO) after a revision of the 2001 classification.

The staging system for AML is based on the French-American-British (FAB) classification system. It is a classification system based on the degree of maturity of the leukemic cells. The FAB classification system was published in 1982.

#### Criteria for staging

The WHO classification divides AML into eight subtypes, based on the degree of immaturity of the leukemic cells. The degree of immaturity is determined by the percentage of blasts present in the blood and bone marrow.

* M1: 0% to 15% blasts in the blood and bone marrow
* M2: 15% to 30% blasts in the blood and bone marrow
* M3: 30% to 45% blasts in the blood and bone marrow
* M4: 45% to 60% blasts in the blood and bone marrow
* M5: 60% to 70% blasts in the blood and bone marrow
* M6: 70% to 80% blasts in the blood and bone marrow
* M7: 80% to 90% blasts in the blood and bone marrow

In addition to the degree of immaturity of the leukemic cells, the WHO classification also takes into account the presence or absence of certain molecular markers (FLT3-ITD, NPM1, CEBPα and RUNX1-RUNX1T1).

### Prognosis

The prognosis for AML depends on several factors, including age, gender, and the presence of certain molecular markers. People who are older than 65 have a worse prognosis than younger people. People who are male have a worse prognosis than people who are female. The presence of certain molecular markers, such as FLT3-ITD, NPM1, CEBPα and RUNX1-RUNX1T1, is associated with a worse prognosis.

## Treatment

### Chemotherapy

Chemotherapy is the main treatment for AML. The chemotherapy drugs used to treat AML are often given in combination with other drugs, such as steroids and targeted therapy drugs. The most common chemotherapy drugs used to treat AML are cytarabine, daunorubicin, and idarubicin.

### Radiation therapy

Four main strategies have been used by translators . The first leaves all characters ' names unchanged and in their original sp

elling. The second attempts to use the name of the character as he or she is known in English, with no attempt at phonetic spelling. The third attempts to use the name of the character as he or she is known in English, but includes phonetic spellings where appropriate. The fourth attempts to use the name of the character as in the original text, but includes phonetic spellings where appropriate. More recently, there has been a tendency to use the first or second strategy, as they are more convenient for readers.
In the present book, I have used the second strategy, but have also included phonetic spellings where appropriate, in order to make characters easier to pronounce. The few Chinese characters that occur in the text are transliterated, not translated. I have also included a glossary of Chinese names, which is not identical to the traditional glossaries of Chinese names, which are usually arranged in hierarchical order.
The book is meant to be read by people who know no Chinese, but may also be of interest to the more advanced learner. Although the book is not meant to be a textbook, it does assume that the reader knows something about Chinese grammar. For the beginning learner, I recommend the traditional textbooks by H. N. Pearson and M. V. Wilkinson. For the more advanced learner, I suggest the textbook by M. A. N. Pridham, _Chinese Grammar_ (London, 1970).
On the whole, the present work is a revised version of my 1985 novel _Red Dragon,_ which is now out of print. The story is set in the period 1911–12, and describes the events surrounding the fall of the Ch'ing Dynasty. Some names have been changed, and some incidents have been slightly altered. The English-speaking reader will recognize many of the well-known names of the period, which are written as they appear in most English reference books on modern Chinese history. I have also renamed some of the characters to avoid the confusion that often occurs in Chinese historical romances.

The Jin – Song Wars were a series of conflicts between the Jurchen Jin dynasty ( 1115 – 1234 ) and Han Chinese Song dynasty ( 9

60 – 1279 ), which were the last of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period and the first of the Southern Song dynasty. The Jin dynasty had risen to power in northeast China in 1115 under Emperor Taizu, who had established a new dynasty after defeating his former imperial overlord, Emperor Huizong , a member of the Song dynasty. After a period of instability during the reign of Emperor Taizong (1123–1135), the dynasty was at the height of its power under Emperor Wanyan Huizong (r. 1135–1149). The Song dynasty was in a period of political turmoil during the reign of Emperor Gaozong (r. 1127–1162), who was the son of Emperor Huizong. The Song government was in a state of decline as it struggled to maintain control over the central plains, and the Song dynasty had been forced to cede control of much of the north to the Jurchen during Emperor Gaozong's reign. The Song government had largely abandoned its former northern territories, but some Song officials, including Emperor Gaozong's brother-in-law, Zhao Gou, continued to hold out against the Jurchen in the north, remaining loyal to the Song dynasty. Emperor Gaozong's son Emperor Xiaozong (r. 1162–1189) re-established control over the central plains of China during his reign, but the Song government was still unable to re-conquer the north from the Jurchen.

" Minutes to Midnight " is a song by American rock band Linkin Park , taken from their fourth studio album of the same name 2007 . It was released as the album's second single on January 29, 2008 . The song " Minutes to Midnight " has been described as an example of " rave - rock , " combining arena rock and aggressive electronic dance music .
The song debuted on the Billboard Hot 100 at number 25 , making it the band's highest-debuting single in 10 years . " Minutes to Midnight " debuted at number 17 on the Billboard Rock Songs chart , earning the band their second-highest debut ever . The song also debuted at number 10 on the Hot Modern Rock Tracks chart .
" Minutes to Midnight " was the band's first single to debut at number one on the Billboard Hot Mainstream Rock Tracks chart, where it ended the longest chart-topper streak in the chart's history.
The song has been a mainstay on radio stations in the United States . The album Minutes to Midnight has sold over 2.5 million copies worldwide .
The Minutes to Midnight is the second studio album by the American rock band Linkin Park , released on May 14, 2007 . It is the follow-up to the band's 2003 album Meteora , which sold more than 18 million copies worldwide.
The album was released simultaneously with the band's first live concert DVD, Road to Revolution: Live at Milton Keynes , which was recorded at the Milton Keynes Bowl in England during their Projekt Revolution tour in 2007.
Minutes to Midnight was preceded by two singles: " What I've Done " and " Shadow of the Day " . The album's third single, " Gossip ", was released on January 29, 2008 . " Leave Out All the Rest " was included in the soundtrack for the 2007 film Transformers , which also featured the band's 2004 song " Numb " . The album's fourth single, " New Divide ", was originally released as a digital download only and was released to radio on March 17, 2009.

An iTunes exclusive deluxe edition of the album was also released, which included a live version of " Given Up " , a live version of " No More Sorrow " , the band's 2007 live performance of " Numb " and the music video for " What I've Done " .
The first single from Minutes to Midnight, " What I've Done ", was released in March 2007. The song was also used as the theme song for WWE Raw . The song's music video features 6 scenes shot at the band's Projekt Revolution 2007 concert, and features various clips of the band performing at the concert.
The second single from the album, " Shadow of the Day ", was released on April 1, 2007, in the US and May 21, 2007, in the UK. The song was used in the trailer for 2007 film Transformers .
The third single, " Gossip ", was released on January 29, 2008. The song was used in an episode of the CW's television series Gossip Girl . " Gossip " was the band's last single from Minutes to Midnight.

On August 4, a ship reported that Carrie was located 35 mi ( 55 km ) west-northwest of Havana , Cuba , but the storm was not detected in satellite imagery until the following day. The storm was a weak tropical storm at the time, and it quickly weakened to a tropical depression as it rapidly moved to the northeast. The storm produced heavy rainfall in western Cuba, and some of the rainfall was aided by an upper-level trough that was located over the storm.
On August 8, the storm also produced torrential rainfall in southern Florida, with a peak total of 6.9 in ( 176 mm) reported in Palm Beach . The rain flooded streets and damaged some homes.

The Never Ending Tour commenced on June 7 , 1988 , and Dylan has played roughly 100 dates a year for the entirety of the 1990s

and all but a few of them in the 21st century. His performances are normally solo, but occasionally he is accompanied by a backing band. In recent years, Dylan's touring schedule has been at least as extensive as it was in the 1960s, and he has played to more people in the 21st century than ever before.
In 2008, Dylan released a live album called The Bootleg Series Vol. 8: Tell Tale Signs, which included performances from the Never Ending Tour.
The Never Ending Tour has received much media attention and has been subject to much speculation over the years. Dylan has acknowledged that he has no plans to stop touring.
The 2000s saw Dylan playing to some of the biggest crowds of his career. In 2000, he performed at the Roskilde Festival in Denmark, where he received a standing ovation of 20,000 people. At the O2 Arena in London in 2007, 16,000 people gave him a three-minute standing ovation after he finished his encore, causing Dylan to remark, "I have never performed for an audience like this before."
In the 1990s, Dylan played 150 shows in 1991, 148 shows in 1992, 133 shows in 1993, 137 shows in 1994, 100 shows in 1995, 106 shows in 1996, 105 shows in 1997, 101 shows in 1998, 77 shows in 1999, and 100 shows in 2000.
During the 2000s, Dylan undertook a tour that lasted one year and 200 days, playing 71 shows in 2001, 86 shows in 2002, 135 shows in 2003, 148 shows in 2004, 128 shows in 2005, 137 shows in 2006, 108 shows in 2007, 100 shows in 2008, 88 shows in 2009, and 58 shows in 2010. In 2010, Dylan played 11 shows in Australia, 11 shows in New Zealand, 25 shows in the U.S., and 20 shows in Europe.

The first spacecraft to visit Jupiter was Pioneer 10 in 1973 , followed a year later by Pioneer 11 . Aside from taking the firs

t close-up images of Jupiter, these spacecraft made comprehensive measurements of the energetic particles in the vicinity of the planet. Pioneer 10 was on its way to Saturn, and Pioneer 11 had to leave Jupiter for the sake of its relatively narrow trajectory. Both spacecraft, however, returned useful data; Pioneer 10 did not even reach Saturn, but it did help us understand Jupiter's magnetosphere.
The next spacecraft to visit Jupiter was Voyager 1 in 1979, followed a year later by Voyager 2 . They each flew by Jupiter in the same orbit, Voyager 1 passing to the north of the planet and Voyager 2 to the south. These spacecraft provided the first detail images of Jupiter's largest moons, and they helped us understand the details of Jupiter's atmosphere and its magnetic field.
The next spacecraft to visit Jupiter was Galileo in 1995. Galileo orbited Jupiter for eight years and has returned volumes of information on Jupiter's atmosphere, magnetic field, its large moons, and Jupiter's rings. This spacecraft also provided the first detailed images of Europa and Io, Jupiter's two icy moons, and helped us understand their geologic activity.
The next spacecraft to visit Jupiter is New Horizons, which flew past Jupiter in February 2007. This spacecraft is on its way to Pluto, but it will swing by Jupiter to help it on its way. It will provide new information on Jupiter's rings and the moons, but its main goal will be to study Jupiter's magnetic field and its aurorae.

s and youngsters . This is a painful and violent image , which in the end is a strong erotic one , but also a political one .
The most important thing is to get into the skin of the work . The violent pictorical language , the brutal gestures and the physical pain are all these details that transform the paintings in a strong political declaration . The violence that Busch portrays is not the result of a retaliation or a revenge , but rather a political violence , which at the same time is a parody of the Nazi violence . To say it in other words , the paintings of Busch are a ” counterviolence ” against the Nazi violent regime .
 In the same way , the paintings of Busch as well as the series of photographs of the ” Concentration Camps ” of the Nazi regime , are powerful political statements and they have a strong political and social impact .
 The artist was a prisoner of the Nazi regime and he spent a lot of times in jail . This is a part of his life that we can see in the paintings of Busch . The Nazi were strong enemies of the artist and the way the artist began to criticize the regime , was to paint the violence and the brutality of the regime .
 The paintings of Busch are violent and this is a theme that the artist begins to use in his works in 1933 and that will continue to use until the end of his life .
 Busch believed that the violence that was used by the Nazi against the society was the cause of the war , so he tried to make people aware of what the Nazi were doing and to criticize them .
 The Nazi were using violence against their enemies and also against the artists like Busch .
 The paintings of Busch are a strong political statement against the violence that was used by the Nazi .
 The Nazi did a lot of violence against all the people who did not belong to their ideology and to those who did not accept their political and social ideas .
 In the last stage of his life , Busch painted the images of the concentration camps of the Nazi regime , which was a protest against the violence that the Nazi were using against the society and, in particular, against the Jews .
Busch was an artist who was very sensitive to the political and social world that surrounded him .

The first part of the system was the 12-mile pipeline from Belmont to the Botanic Gardens. This was completed in 1897 and the next step was the construction of the Canning Dam.
The dam was to be built on the banks of the Canning River at Upper Swan. The first stage was the filling of the dam with water from the river. This required the construction of a settlement at Peron, where the pipeline from the river to the dam was to be joined by a pipeline from the dam to the treatment works at the corner of Adelaide Terrace and Mounts Bay Road. The settlement was planned by the architect William Lindsay and the builder John  E. Scott. The buildings were of brick, stone and iron and were designed to be attractive and permanent. With the exception of the new assembly hall, which was haphazardly added in the 1920s, the buildings are substantially intact.
The townsite was laid out in 1902 and the reservoir was completed in 1906. The water from the dam was pumped through the pipeline to the treatment works using steam pumps.
In 1906 the water supply was extended to the railway terminus at Fremantle. The pipeline was constructed to the north of the railway line and the track was raised on embankments paralleling the pipeline. The settlement at Peron was soon surplus to requirements and in 1909 the buildings were transferred to Fremantle. The townsite was closed and the area returned to bushland.
The treatment works have been relocated and extended several times. When they were first built they were situated south of the railway line. They were transferred to the eastern side of the line in 1935 to make way for the Belmont Viaduct and a new building was constructed. This was the first major relocation of the works. In 1955 the works were again relocated and the present building constructed. This was the second major relocation.
Pipelines and reservoirs were constructed over the next few years to provide water to the Perth suburbs of Bassendean, Floreat, Osborne Park, Crawley, Subiaco, Nedlands, Shenton Park, Tuart Hill, Mount Lawley, Bayswater, Maylands, Inglewood, Yokine and, later, Joondalup and Armadale.
The water supply system was completed in 1973 with the opening of the Roe 4 Dam. This was the first of a number of dams in the Canning River catchment and the water was connected to supply to the eastern parts of Perth.
The treatment works were relocated to the western side of the railway line and a new building was constructed in 1979.
Established in 1988, the network now has more than 935 kms of underground and overground pipelines and 20 reservoirs. In 2001 the network supplied 116 billion litres of water to 1.7 million people, 80 per cent of the population of Perth.
The works were closed on 17 October 2003 and the last reservoir was filled on 25 October 2003. The reservoirs were filled with water transferred from the main reservoir at the Roe 4 Dam. The Cogan Viaduct ( Welsh : Traphont Cogan ) is the most important element of the Cogan Spur as it crosses the River Ely with a

540-foot (160 m) span of 58 feet (18 m). It is Grade II listed building. The bridge is built on the cantilever method and is supported by two towers.
The bridge was built in 1906 by the Cambrian Railways and designed by Benjamin Baker. The design of the bridge is a variation of the Howe truss.
Following the closure of the Cogan branch line in 1962, the viaduct was disused. It was restored by the Cogan Spur Trust and reopened in 2001.
The viaduct is named after Sir George Cogan, who was MP for the constituency of Swansea from 1900 to 1910.
British search and rescue teams were the first to arrive in Léogane , the town at the epicenter of the quake , on 17 January .

They were drawn to the scene by the sight of an enormous cloud of dust that enveloped the mountains, and by the sounds of screams and the sounds of crashing buildings.  The task of finding survivors was made more difficult by the fact that the quake struck in the middle of the night, and by the fact that all the electric power and telecommunications were offline.
The _Guardian_ reported that the scale of the devastation was so enormous that it was difficult to comprehend.  "Many of the buildings in Léogâne and in the surrounding area were completely destroyed, including the local hospital and several schools.  The local police station, a brick building with a large wooden sign outside, was reduced to just a few pieces of charred debris.  The two nearby Catholic churches were left in ruins.  The majority of the buildings that survived were made of corrugated iron, and these were largely untouched by the earthquake."
The quake struck at a time when some 2000,000 Haitians were working in the Dominican Republic.  Many of them had built makeshift shelters, using discarded pieces of corrugated iron or wood.  They were killed by the quake, and more than 500,000 people who lived in the Dominican Republic lost their sources of income.  The quake also struck at a bad time for the Dominican Republic's economy, which had been struggling.  The day after the quake, one Dominican told the _New York Times_ that "we are just sitting here praying that nothing will happen.  We are scared.  We have no money.  We are all on the verge of starving."
The earthquake struck when Haiti was politically unstable, and the country was in the grip of a wave of political violence.  A general strike had been declared, and there was widespread violence; the Haitian government had declared a state of emergency and requested that UN troops be sent in to help contain the violence.  The earthquake struck just two hours after the state of emergency was declared.  The emergency had been declared after a week of violence, which started when protesters attacked the presidential palace on 5 January.  The attack was the latest in a series of protests by Haitians over the country's political and economic situation.  The attack was allegedly a response to a government crackdown on demonstrations against President Jean-Bertrand Aristide.  Aristide had recently been forced to flee the country, and he had been replaced by Prime Minister Gerard Latortue.  The protesters were demanding that Aristide be reinstated.
The UN had been planning to send peacekeepers to Haiti for several months, but the violence had intensified in the run-up to the general strike, which had been called to protest about the deteriorating political situation.  The UN had decided to send in the troops just two days before the earthquake struck.  The peacekeepers were intended to be a stabilising force in the country.  The earthquake struck just 20 minutes before the peacekeepers were due to arrive.  The force included 1800 troops, 1200 police officers, and 200 civilian staff.  The peacekeepers were drawn from Nepal, Jordan, and Bangladesh.  The peacekeepers were to have been stationed in the capital, Port-au-Prince.  They were not deployed in Léogâne, the town at the epicenter of the quake.

The plain maskray or brown stingray ( Neotrygon annotata ) is a species of stingray in the family Dasyatidae . It is found in s

ilt-laden waters around coral atolls and reef flats in shallow lagoons in the Indian Ocean . This flat, broad-bodied stingray measures up to 100 cm (39 in) across and is brown to chocolate brown in color. Its tail may be slightly darker and is marked with pale, broad, longitudinal bars. Its eyes have a large nictitating membrane.
The plain maskray is found in the Indian Ocean from the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden south to the Chagos Archipelago in the west and the Philippines in the east. It is a habitat generalist, occurring in a wide range of environments within its range, from coral reefs to mangrove swamps. It is a bottom-dwelling species found in shallow lagoons and reef flats in waters up to 10 m (33 ft) deep. It is a communal species that tends to form groups of a few individuals.
The plain maskray is harmless to humans but it is often eaten by humans. It is caught using handlines and in nets. The International Union for Conservation of Nature ( IUCN ) has assessed it as being of Least Concern.
