The newly constructed Minnesota and Northwestern Railroad across northern Illinois utilized trackage rights on the Illinois Cen

ral Railroad from Chicago to Kankakee. The ICR ran northwest from Chicago to Kankakee at the southern end of Lake Michigan, where the Illinois and Michigan Canal connected it to Lake Erie at LaSalle and to the Illinois River at Ottawa.
In 1886, the CB&Q purchased a 50% interest in the ICR, and the following year, it purchased the remaining 50%. Over the next few years, the CB&Q would acquire control of the Chicago, Ottawa, and Peoria (1888), the Chicago and Northwestern (1890), the Illinois Central Interurban (1899), and the Michigan Central (1906). By 1907, the CB&Q owned every railroad in Chicago except for the B&O and the PCC.
The ICR's main line from Chicago to Kankakee was known as the "North Main." The ICR leased most of its right-of-way along the North Main from CB&Q, and it had trackage rights on the CB&Q's main line from Chicago to Joliet. The ICR traced the North Main through an area of Chicago known as the "North Side" through the communities of Jefferson Park, Portage Park, Belmont Cragin, and Irving Park. The main line was double-tracked from Chicago north through West Ridge, Jefferson Park, and Portage Park to the Milwaukee Road's West Burlington Yard. From Burlington, the North Main was single-tracked north through Belmont Cragin and Irving Park to Joliet.
The North Side was the primary industrial center of Chicago. The North Main linked the area to the rest of the country and to other parts of the city. The communities along the North Main were generally poor and had been plagued by numerous fires, which had destroyed most of the area's businesses. The railroads had given the area a boost by locating their yards and many of their shops along the North Main. Despite the presence of the railroads, the area remained poor.
The North Side was also a major center of a burgeoning population of immigrants from Southern and Eastern Europe. Many of the new immigrants from Italy and Greece were forced to live in tenements near the railroads. As the area became more and more overcrowded, the railroads did little to alleviate the problems. By the early 1900s, the ICR and other railroads were facing a public relations nightmare on the North Main.
In response to the problems, the railroads began to make plans to relocate shops and yards to other areas of the city. In 1906, the B&O and C&NW, which had been operating the North Main since 1888, announced plans to build a new yard at Des Plaines. The announcement caused widespread fear among the residents of the North Side that the railroads would abandon the area altogether.
In April 1907, the Illinois Central Interurban, the ICR, and the CB&Q announced plans to build a new railroad yard at Chicago's 49th Street in the Bridgeport neighborhood. The new yard would be located on the North Side, but would be outside the area that the other railroads planned to abandon. The 49th Street Yard would be the largest railroad yard in Chicago and would cut through the poorest neighborhoods in the North Side. The news of the new yard caused rioting in the communities along the North Main.
Prior to the site selection for the 49th Street Yard, the ICR had planned to build its own yard in the area, but it would have been on land owned by the Norris Coal Company. During the selection process, the ICR had agreed to use the Norris Coal Company's land to build the yard. The Norris Coal Company was owned by the railroads that were selecting the site, including the ICR. The coal company's land was needed for trackage rights to the area. The ICR, and the other railroads, were aware of the conflict of interest when they agreed to use the Norris Coal Company's land.
The ICR and other railroads built the 49th Street Yard at Chicago's 43rd and 49th streets. The ICR was the first railroad to move into the yard, which was finished in 1910. The CB&Q and other railroads moved into the yard in 1911.

The black @-@ tailed jackrabbit plays host to many ectoparasites including fleas , ticks , lice , and mites , and many endopara

-site organisms, including coccidia , roundworms , and tapeworms . More than 100 ectoparasite species have been reported from jackrabbits , many of which are also parasites of other species. The black-tailed jackrabbit was the first host for a species of plague-causing bacterium, Yersinia pestis , and the first host for the West Nile virus . Transmission of the West Nail virus to humans may be the result of a jackrabbit being bitten by a mosquito . Jackrabbits also harbor viral diseases such as Myxomatosis and Rabbit Hemorrhagic Disease . Jackrabbits in the desert southwest are affected by several species of leishmaniasis-causing parasites, and they are also an amplifying host for parasites that affect humans and domestic animals. The black-tailed jackrabbit was the first host for the Epizootic Hemorrhagic Disease virus, which causes a hemorrhagic disease in white-tailed jackrabbits. A study of the gastrointestinal tract of jackrabbits found that 10% had parasitic worms. Of the worms found, 22 were tapeworms , 13 were roundworms , and 3 were flatworms . Some of the tapeworms were more than 150 cm long.
The black-tailed jackrabbit is a prey species for many predators, including hawks, coyotes, badgers, bobcats, and snakes. Sagebrush hares are an important food source for several species of snakes, and 21 species of snakes have been reported to eat jackrabbits. One species of snake, the Western diamondback rattlesnake , has a keen sense of smell and can detect jackrabbits from as far as 100 m (328 ft) away.

An important pathophysiological mechanism of leukemogenesis in AML is the epigenetic induction of dedifferentiation by genetic

and environmental changes in the bone marrow microenvironment [1–3].
Dedifferentiation is a reversible process in the cell cycle that leads to the loss of unique cell markers that distinguish one cell type from another, such as cell surface antigens, specific gene expression patterns, and morphology [4, 5].
Furthermore,  we found that differentiated leukemia cells and their precursors express CD34, a marker for hematopoietic stem cells and their precursors [6, 7].
CD34 is an important marker for hematopoietic stem cells and their precursors in the bone marrow .
In the light of the above mentioned studies, we postulated that the CD34 expression pattern in AML could be a useful tool to stratify patients with AML.
We therefore examined the expression of CD34 in freshly isolated CD34+ leukemia cells and their precursors in a large number of AML patients and correlated the expression pattern of CD34 with clinicopathological features and survival.
The study cohort consisted of 302 patients with AML, including 183 males and 119 females, median age 61 years (range 1–85 years).
The diagnosis of AML was established according to the WHO classification criteria .
The AML cases were subdivided according to the French-American-British (FAB) classification , CD34 expression , and the expression of clonal markers (M3, M4, M5, M6, M7, M1, M2, and M3-M20).
Patients were classified as having AML with CD34+ leukemia cells and their precursors (AML with CD34) or AML with blasts not expressing CD34 (AML without CD34).
The clinicopathological features of the patients were collected from the files of the Department of Hematology, Oncology and Clinical Immunology, University Hospital Mannheim, Germany.
CD34+ cells were isolated from freshly collected bone marrow aspirates or apheresis products from 10 mL of peripheral blood by using the CD34 MicroBead kit (Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany) according to the manufacturer's instructions.

## History

The first kelp crop was raised in 1768 by William Daniell in the Firth of Forth. Kelp was harvested in Arisaig, Lochaber, Fort William and Loch Rannoch. In the early 19th century the industry was important in the Hebrides and on the coasts of Lochaber, the Mull of Kintyre and the Tay. The first kelp works on the west coast of Scotland were at Lochaline and Carsaig. They were followed by works at Oban, Loch Awe and Loch Creran.

The industry was important in Elgin, Banffshire, in the 19th century and the kelp forests in the Moray Firth were among the largest in Europe. The area was over-exploited and the industry collapsed. The industry continued to thrive in the Sound of Mull.

## Regulation

The trade was governed by the Highland Society of Scotland which set the price and the maximum amount of kelp that could be harvested. The Society made sure that the landowners got their cut of the kelp trade. The first regulations were passed in 1736. A further regulation was passed by the Parliament of Scotland in 1756.

The noisy miner primarily inhabits dry , open eucalypt forests without understory shrubs . It is commonly found in open sclerop

horous forests from Sydney north to the Queensland border. A nesting site must be within 1 km (0.6 mi) of a food source. The noisy miner is predominantly a New South Wales and Queensland species, although it can be found in the ACT and Victoria. It is absent from Tasmania.
 The population size of the noisy miner is not known.
 The noisy miner was declared  a threatened species by the Australian government in 1996, due to declining numbers. The species is also listed as a threatened species in Victoria. The population size is decreasing.
 The major threats to the noisy miner are habitat loss and fragmentation.
The noisy miner is considered to be a conservation species.
The IUCN lists the noisy miner as being of Least Concern. It is also listed as a Conservation Dependent Species by the Commonwealth of Australia, a Protected Species by the state of Victoria, and a Priority Species by the state of New South Wales.
The noisy miner has been hit hard by introduced diseases, predation and competition for food and nesting sites.
Comair Flight 5191 , marketed as Delta Connection Flight 5191 , was a scheduled United States ( US ) domestic passenger flight

from Cincinnati / Northern Kentucky International Airport in Hebron , Kentucky , to Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport . On August 27, 2006 , the Bombardier CRJ200 , operating as Flight 5191 , crashed while attempting to land at the airport . All 47 people aboard were killed, along with a person on the ground. The National Transportation Safety Board ( NTSB ) concluded that the probable cause of the accident was the captain's failure to maintain airspeed after the aircraft encountered wake turbulence from a FedEx MD-11 , which resulted in the aircraft entering an aerodynamic stall from which it did not recover .
The NTSB determined that the captain, James Polehinke , had not received proper training in wake turbulence avoidance procedures, and that the first officer did not intervene adequately on the flight deck . As a result, the NTSB published an alert to air carrier pilots , urging them to receive additional training on wake turbulence avoidance procedures. On July 21, 2008, a settlement agreement was reached between the families of the victims and Comair.
The aircraft involved, N2137A , was a Bombardier CRJ-200 regional jet built in 2001 . At the time of the accident, it was owned by an Icelandic leasing company, and was operated by Comair as Flight 5191. The aircraft was delivered to Sterling Airlines on August 17, 2001. The aircraft was manufactured in 2001, registered as N2137A and delivered to Sterling Airlines on August 17, 2001. The aircraft was operated by Comair, in a capacity as a Delta Connection flight, from its hub at Cincinnati / Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG).
This was the second fatal incident in the history of the Bombardier CRJ-200. The first was the 1998 crash of Canadian Regional Airlines Flight 120.
The aircraft was on a scheduled flight from Cincinnati to Atlanta, with 47 passengers and four crew members aboard. The aircraft departed from Cincinnati at 8:20 a.m. EDT . While en route, the pilot reported a cracked windshield to air traffic control (ATC). The crew then requested to descend to 10,000 feet (3,050 m) as quickly as possible to avoid further loss of flight instruments . After requesting to descend, the captain requested to return to Cincinnati.
Shortly after the request, the NTSB reported that the aircraft had descended 2,000 ft (610 m) in about 10 seconds and was at 9,000 ft (2,700 m) when it struck the ground. The aircraft was flying at an altitude of 3,700 ft (1,100 m) and a speed of 204 knots (237 mph, 381 km/h). The aircraft struck the ground at a speed of 444 knots (509 mph, 819 km/h).
Passengers and crew onboard were not strapped in.
The aircraft was destroyed by impact and a postcrash fire. The wreckage came to rest in a wooded area near a road; the aircraft was damaged by trees and the impact.
There were 44 passengers and three crew members on board. All 47 people aboard the aircraft died, as well as one person on the ground.
Captain James Polehinke (aged 34) was the pilot in command (PIC) and first officer David J. Cox (aged 31) was the second officer. Polehinke was hired by Comair in 2003. On the day of the accident, he was scheduled to begin a new assignment as a pilot for Delta Air Lines . He had previously worked as a flight instructor and held a commercial pilot's license with Delta Connection (Delta affiliate airlines) ratings.
Polehinke had completed Delta Connection's wake turbulence avoidance training in 2005, but had not attended the annual refresher course.

Outside the sport , there were significant consequences for Anglo @-@ Australian relations , which remained strained until the

1 920s . The most important of these was the " Burke and Wills Expedition " of 1860-61 that was intended to be a scientific study of the two great deserts in central Australia ( the Great Sandy and Simpson Deserts ) .
Anglo - Australian relations were already strained over the question of the removal of Aboriginal peoples from their traditional lands , which was now gaining support among politicians and businessmen in Victoria . A committee of the Victorian Parliament , chaired by Sir John Young , recommended that the federal government should "resume and take under its control the whole of Australia " . The committee's report was widely circulated in the colony , and strongly supported by the governor , Sir Henry Barkly .
The expedition left Melbourne on 19 October 1860 , and reached the Gulf of Carpentaria on 10 December. The leader , Dr William Landsborough , was unable to find an overland route through the deserts , so the party went by ship. After a period of extended exploration , the expedition party returned to Melbourne by ship on 22 September 1861 . Landsborough had been joined in the Simpson Desert by the young German surveyor Ludwig Leichhardt , who had been sent north from Adelaide to explore the Darling Downs . Leichhardt and his party disappeared in the desert in 1848 .
The expedition had a major impact on the national consciousness in Australia , and was widely reported and commemorated in public art and literature . In Victoria , the government tried to dissociate itself from the expedition , but the report generated widespread public interest in the question of the removal of the Aboriginal peoples .
  In 1860 , the government of Victoria funded a second expedition to the interior of Central Australia , under the leadership of the explorer Thomas Mitchell . The expedition left Melbourne on 28 January 1860 , and returned to Melbourne on 14 January 1861 . As well as being an important scientific expedition , the Mitchell Expedition had a strong political dimension , and was seen as a response to the Burke and Wills Expedition . The Mitchell Expedition had a good scientific outcome . Mitchell discovered the Darling River , and the Lachlan River , and the 26 expedition members discovered a new route to the Darling . The expedition party travelled across country by bullock dray , and used the route to establish the first overland mail service from Melbourne to Sydney .

Croatia subsequently declared independence and dissolved ( Croatian : razdruženje ) its association with Yugoslavia on 25 June

1991. The Republic of Croatia was recognised as an independent state on 15 January 1992 by the UN Security Council Resolution 743 and on 7 May 1992 by the International Court of Justice.
During the war, the Croatian government sought to control all of Croatia's territory and fought with the Serbs in the Krajina region, the Serb-populated areas of eastern Slavonia, western Srem and the city of Vukovar. Croatian forces also fought with the Serbs in the eastern Herzegovina region of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Many Serbs fought along with the Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) and the paramilitary units of the Serb-dominated Yugoslav government. The war ended in January 1992 with the signing of the UN peace plan for Croatia. The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina lasted until 1995.
 Croatia has an area of 56,594 square kilometres (21,851 sq mi), of which 56,414 square kilometres (21,782 sq mi) is land and 180 square kilometres (69 sq mi) is water. Croatia's borders lie along the Adriatic Sea to the south, with Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro to the south-west, Serbia to the east and Slovenia to the north. The mainland is mostly hilly, with highlands in the north and south. The highest point is the 1,831-metre (6,007 ft) Dinara mountain in the southern part of the country. The north of the country is a gently hilly plain, in the area of Zagreb Valley. The northern parts of Croatia are part of the Pannonian Basin, and the southern parts are part of the Dinaric Alps.
The Croatian islands in the Adriatic Sea number 1,242, of which 48 are inhabited. The largest islands are Cres and Krk. Croatia also contains 468 smaller islands and islets. Croatia's biggest lake is Lake Vrana, situated in the delta of the Krka river in the central part of the country, while the largest waterfall in Croatia is the 10-metre (33 ft) high Krupa fall.
 Croatia has a Mediterranean and continental climate. The climate of Croatia is highly variable and the Adriatic coast experiences significantly milder winters and warmer summers in comparison with its inland. Croatia is a predominantly mountainous country and the vast majority of the territory lies between 100 metres (330 ft) and 600 metres (2,000 ft) above sea level. The southern tip of the Istrian peninsula reaches elevations near 1,000 metres (3,300 ft). The Dinaric Alps range is a highland that spans over 350 kilometres (220 mi) across Croatia and goes through the mountainous region of Lika. The largest mountain ranges are: the Gorski Kotar mountains and mountain ranges of Velebit and Paklenica, both stretching from the coast to the continental area in the interior, and Biokovo, islands of Cres and Krk and the Lika-Karawanken mountains along the border with Slovenia. The tallest mountain of Croatia is Dinara, at 1,831 metres (6,007 ft), located on the mainland, reaching elevations of over 600 metres (2,000 ft) in the mountainous areas, like Lika, Zagorje, Gorski Kotar, Zdenska Gora, and Kordun. The northern tip of Croatia lies on the Pannonian Plain, and this area is the lowest part of the country, at an elevation of 125 metres (410 ft). The largest river in Croatia is the Danube, which crosses the country in the north-east and flows into Hungary. In the south-west, the rivers are usually longer and flow into the Adriatic Sea. The Soča river is the largest Croatian river with a length of 138 kilometres (86 mi). The longest Croatian lake is the Vrana Lake, situated on the delta of the river Krka.

entrebane Road in the Roath district of Cardiff , Wales , to the southern end of Pentwyn Road in the Cathays district of the city. Several portions of modern NY 38 were originally part of turnpikes and plank roads during the 1800s . On April 13 , 1819 , the

62.96-mile (101.26 km) Chenango and Susquehanna Turnpike was incorporated to connect the state capital of Albany with the village of Binghamton . The company was authorized to lay out an 8-foot-wide (2.4 m) roadway, and the company's board of directors was to be elected from the counties of Broome, Chenango, Cortland, Delaware, and Tioga . The turnpike was to be 67 miles (108 km) from the Albany–Schenectady Road at the north end to the Tioga–Susquehanna Plank Road at the south end by 1827 . The portion of the road between the Schenectady–Albany Road at the northern end and the town of Chenango near the village of Binghamton was designated the Chenango Turnpike .
The Chenango Turnpike, running between Binghamton and Unadilla , was incorporated on April 11 , 1833 . The company was authorized to lay out a 20-foot-wide (6.1 m) turnpike, with the road to be located on the north side of the Chenango River from the village of Binghamton to the village of Unadilla . The Chenango Turnpike was one of the first roads incorporated as a turnpike in New York .
The Chenango Turnpike as it existed in 1840 and 1842 is not the same route as the Chenango Turnpike of 1833. In 1840, the Chenango Turnpike ran from Binghamton to New Berlin . It was incorporated to the south boundary of the town of Chenango, with the road running from the village of Afton to the Chenango River, running on the west bank of the river from the village of Afton to New Berlin . In 1842, the Chenango Turnpike was extended to the village of Smyrna .
The Chenango Turnpike was incorporated again in 1844, with the Chenango Turnpike extended to the town of Hancock . The portion of the road in the village of Afton was laid out on September 11, 1844 . The Chenango Turnpike was extended to the village of Lowville in 1845 .

### Tropical Storm Beryl

Main article: Tropical Storm Beryl (1981)

Beryl developed on August 28 as a tropical depression off the coast of Honduras , and subsequently strengthened into a tropical storm. Beryl moved northward, and on August 30 it made landfall on the Yucatán Peninsula in Veracruz. Beryl then turned to the northwest and struck Veracruz again on the 31st. The storm continued northwestward, and on September 1 it struck the Gulf of Mexico, and then moved into the central Gulf of Mexico. Beryl then curved to the west, and on September 4 it made landfall over the Florida Panhandle with winds of 60 mph (100 km/h). After landfall, the storm tracked across the southeastern United States , and turned to the north. Beryl then turned to the northeast, and on September 8 it dissipated over North Carolina .

### Tropical Storm Celia

Main article: Tropical Storm Celia (1981)

Celia developed on September 19 as an area of low pressure over the central Gulf of Mexico . The storm moved northward, and on September 20 it strengthened into a tropical storm. Celia then made a small loop to the east, and on September 22 it turned to the northwest. Celia strengthened into a hurricane, and then on September 23 it made landfall near Pensacola, Florida , with winds of 65 mph (105 km/h). Celia turned to the north, and on September 25 it made landfall over Georgia with winds of 60 mph (100 km/h). After landfall, the storm weakened quickly, and on September 27 it dissipated over the Atlantic Ocean .

### Hurricane Danielle

Main article: Hurricane Danielle (1981)

Danielle developed on September 28 over the central Gulf of Mexico . The storm moved north, and on September 29 it strengthened into a hurricane. Danielle then turned to the northeast, and on September 30 it passed over the Florida Keys with winds of 85 mph (140 km/h). The storm then turned to the northwest, and on October 2 it reached its peak intensity with winds of 100 mph (155 km/h). Danielle then turned to the north, and on October 4 it made landfall over Georgia with winds of 85 mph (135 km/h). After landfall, the storm turned to the northeast, and on October 6 it dissipated over the Atlantic Ocean .

### Tropical Storm Eloise

Main article: Tropical Storm Eloise (1981)

A tropical wave developed into a tropical depression over the Windward Islands late on September 30. Moving northwestward, the depression intensified into Tropical Storm Eloise early on October 2. Eloise became a hurricane later that day, and peaked with winds of 115 mph (185 km/h) on October 3. Eloise paralleled the southeastern coast of the United States, and became extratropical before striking Newfoundland on October 5.

### Tropical Storm Florence

Main article: Tropical Storm Florence (1981)

On October 13, a tropical wave developed into a tropical depression south of Jamaica. Six hours later, the depression became Tropical Storm Florence. The storm passed over the Cayman Islands, then moved to the northwest. On October 14, Florence became a hurricane. On October 15, Florence became extratropical and caused heavy rainfall in the Northeastern United States.

In the 1945 election , the Communists were unopposed because the other parties abstained . Once in power , the Communists intro

-duced a number of social security measures . These included old-age pensions and social insurance . The payments were made by means of vouchers which could be exchanged for food .
If the Soviet Union had not invaded the country , the people of Czecho-slovakia would have had to rely on the generosity of the West . In the summer of 1945 , the United States had agreed at a meeting in Moscow to allow the Soviets to occupy Czecho-slovakia . The Americans had no choice .
In the 1946 election , the Communists won a sweeping victory . The Czecho-slovak parliament voted to secede from the Western alliance and join the Soviet bloc . The U.S. chief of occupation in the country rejected the vote .
In 1948 , the Soviet Union demanded the return of the country to the Soviet bloc . The Czechoslovak parliament voted to comply . The Western allies refused to accept this .
 In 1968 , the Soviet Union began to exert its influence in Czecho-slovakia . The country became a Soviet satellite .
 In the 1970s and 1980s , the regime became increasingly repressive .
 In 1989 , the regime began to crumble . The first stirrings of dissent appeared .
 In November 1989 , the Communist Party was voted out of power .
 In 1992 , the country split into two : the Czech Republic and Slovakia .

" Crazy in Love " is a song by American singer Beyoncé from her debut solo album, Dangerously in Love ( 2003 ). It was released as the album's third single on February 12, 2004.
While " Crazy in Love " was a slower mid-tempo, "Bonnie & Clyde" was a fast-tempo R&B song. The lyrics describe the relationship between Beyoncé and Jay-Z, with Beyoncé singing lines such as: "Love is a dangerous thing / You might fall from the sky / I'm going down tonight / And I don't mind / 'Cause I'm crazy in love / Crazy in love / Crazy in love with you, baby." The song also makes references to the couple's private lives, with Beyoncé singing, "The house is so big / The rooms are so empty / You can't really see me / I'm looking at you... baby." The song was described as "an R&B song at heart," as well as being a "pop-infused" number.
The song's music video, which was directed by Beyoncé and Melina Matsoukas, was shot in Brooklyn, New York City and premiered on February 26, 2004. The video's concept was inspired by the 1991 movie New Jack City. The video features the couple in a speakeasy, and in a helicopter. The couple break into a dance floor, and Beyoncé is seen dancing with Jay-Z.

n Range. North of the North Fork Payette River, the forest is part of the Caribou Mountains. The South Fork Payette River flows out of the forest. The forest is approximately 100 miles north to south and about 60 miles east to west.
The forest is covered with mixed fir, pine, spruce, aspen and cottonwood. Blueberries, cranberries, huckleberries, bearberries and fireweed are found within the forest.
Throughout the forest, you can find a wide variety of wildlife, including deer, elk, moose, mountain lions, black bear, grizzly bears, wolves, coyotes, American martens and river otters, as well as many species of birds.
The forest is a wilderness area and is accessible only by foot, horseback or floatplane. Travel is discouraged in summer due to the abundant wildlife, but in winter, the forest is a prime area for cross-country skiing and snowmobiling.
The forest is divided among three ranger districts: the Salmon River Ranger District, the Sawtooth Ranger District and the Banks-Lowman Ranger District. The Salmon River Ranger District is located on the east side of the Salmon River, south of the town of Salmon. The Sawtooth Ranger District is located on the west side of the Salmon River, north of the town of Salmon. The Banks-Lowman Ranger District is located east of the Sawtooth Ranger District, north of the town of Banks.
The forest has developed a number of recreational sites, including Wild Horse Prairie, the Payette Wilderness, Payette Lake, Redfish Lake and Hell's Canyon.

In 1973, the Payette National Forest was designated as the Payette Wilderness Area , encompassing 550,282 acres. The Payette Wilderness Area is the largest wilderness area in Idaho.
The Payette Wilderness Area was designated to protect the North Fork of the Payette River, the Middle Fork of the Payette River, the South Fork of the Payette River, the West Fork of the Boise River, and their watersheds. The wilderness area was also created to protect the headwaters of the Weiser River and the Salmon River.
The Payette Wilderness Area is a part of the Idaho Primitive Area . The Idaho Primitive Area includes the Sawtooth National Forest, Idaho Panhandle National Forest, Payette National Forest, Caribou-Targhee National Forest, and Nez Perce National Forest. The purpose of the Idaho Primitive Area is to preserve the natural attributes of the area and to protect the wilderness experience.

The Payette River National Wild and Scenic Riverway includes the Payette River, Middle Fork Payette River, South Fork Payette River and West Fork Boise River. The wild and scenic designation was approved in 1980. The designation was created to protect the rivers and their adjacent scenic areas.
The Payette River National Wild and Scenic Riverway is located in the Payette National Forest. The riverway includes portions of the Payette National Forest and the Boise National Forest . The riverway is approximately 280 miles long.

, for courtship, or for communication among members of a herd, as in the case of elephants. Such a call would require a specialized system for creating air pressure and controlling the direction of the air flow.
The birds' vocal system is one of the most developed and complex of all vertebrates. The air sacs in their throats add volume and the syrinx (a structure like a small bell) adds a special quality to the call. All these features occur in Corythosaurus, even though the birdlike call is a fictitious one.
The crest is made up of several bony plates that are held together by ligaments. These plates were held in place by a system of muscles that are still poorly understood. The crest of Corythosaurus had a large air chamber within it. When the air chamber was filled, air pressure was released through the frill to create the call. The crest was probably used for social communication in the herds.
 Corythosaurus is the best known dinosaur with a crest, but there are others that have been found with crests, including the late-Cretaceous Saurolophus and some of the members of the pachycephalosaurid group. These are all herbivores, and the crests are probably used for social communication in the herds. Some of the ankylosaurs also had crests, but they are more like horns than frills.

The crests of ceratopsians may have been the first step in the evolution of the birdlike syrinx.

It is estimated that 7 to 8 million people , mostly in Mexico , Central America and South America , have Chagas disease as of 2

006.
 The disease is transmitted by triatomine bugs, also known as kissing bugs, but also can be transmitted to a human from a blood transfusion, organ transplant or congenitally.
 In 2014, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) and World Health Organization (WHO) called for intensified efforts to eliminate the disease.

## History

The disease was first discovered in 1909 by an Argentine doctor, Carlos Chagas, who discovered that people who lived in poverty were the ones who were more likely to have the disease.

There is still no cure for the disease, but there are medications that can be prescribed to those infected.

## Signs and symptoms

The symptoms of the disease vary from person to person. Often people who are infected with the disease do not show any signs or symptoms, until the later stages.

The symptoms of the disease are grouped in four stages. The first one is known as the acute phase, the second is the indeterminate phase and the third is the chronic phase.

In the acute phase, often known as the initial phase of the disease, the symptoms are often mistaken for other diseases and may include fatigue, fever, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, and muscle pain.

The second phase of the disease is the indeterminate phase. The indeterminate phase is known for symptoms such as fever, chest pain, eye inflammation, and heart palpitations.

The third phase of the disease is known as the chronic phase of the disease. It is known for symptoms such as heart failure, liver damage, stomach ulcers, and damage to the esophagus.

## Epidemiology

It is estimated that 7 to 8 million people, mostly in Mexico, Central America and South America, have Chagas disease as of 2006.

The disease is transmitted by triatomine bugs, also known as kissing bugs, but also can be transmitted to a human from a blood transfusion, organ transplant or congenitally.

In 2014, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) and World Health Organization (WHO) called for intensified efforts to eliminate the disease.

The character is also popular among gamers , especially Japanese and fans of the Final Fantasy series . Aerith has been include

in several video gaming guides on how to get the most out of your gameplay, including the book Final Fantasy VII Ultimate Strategy Guide (2002) by Shane Bettenhausen. Spin-off products include Aeris Gainsborough cosmetic cases and a ring by Takara (2005), as well as a figurine called "Aerith Gainsborough" by Kotobukiya (2006).

### Critical reception

Critical reception to Aerith in video games is positive. She has often been praised as an example of realistic female characters in video games. In 2005, GameSpot named Aerith one of the Top 100 Video Game Characters of All Time, ranking her as the 25th-best character in video games. GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann called her the most beloved female character in the Final Fantasy series. She ranked 34th in IGN's list of the "Top 100 Videogame Heroes" and 13th in GameSpy's list of "The Top 25 Female Characters in Games". She also ranked 10th on UGO.com's list of "The 10 Hottest Female Characters in Games" in 2009, and 19th on IGN's "Top 25 Final Fantasy Characters" list in 2012.

The character has been criticized for her sexualization. In 2009, a poll on GameDaily asked "Are you tired of the over-sexualization of female characters in video games?", 59% of the readers voted "yes". In 2012, a poll on GameDaily asked "What's the most over-sexualized videogame character of all time?", Aerith ranked third, with 7% of the votes.

Named after Bernardo de Gálvez y Madrid , Count of Gálvez ( born in Málaga , Spain ) , Galveston 's first European settlements

1729 and the first capital of the province of Texas .
Gálvez was born in Málaga , Spain on December 23 , 1746 .
His father , José de Gálvez y Gallardo , was a prominent member of the royal government and the Spanish nobility . In 1726 , he was appointed viceroy of Peru , where he served until his death in 1771 .
Gálvez was married to Ana Maria de Rojas y Fernández de Leyva . They had no children .
On the death of his father , Gálvez inherited his father's title of Count of Gálvez .
Gálvez's first service in the Spanish army was in 1760 in the Caribbean . He was thereafter a soldier in the Spanish army for the next 30 years . He fought in the Seven Years 'War and the American Revolutionary War. He was made a Captain and Major in the 23rd Infantry Regiment in 1778 . He commanded Spanish troops in the Mediterranean in 1780 .
Gálvez and his brother, Antonio María de Gálvez , served under Bernardo de Gálvez and helped to capture Pensacola in 1781 .
During the American Revolutionary War , Gálvez served as a Lieutenant Colonel in the Spanish army . He was promoted to Colonel in 1782 and given command of the 33rd Infantry Regiment .
He was made a Brigadier General in the Spanish army by King Carlos III in 1783 . He served in the Caribbean from 1783 to 1788 , and was promoted to Major General in 1787 .
Gálvez returned to Spain in 1788 . He was promoted to Lieutenant General in 1791 . He served in Spain until 1794 , when he returned to the Caribbean .
Gálvez received the title of Marqués de Sonora in 1796 .
He was made a Lieutenant General and Commander-in-Chief of the Caribbean in 1804 . He commanded Spanish forces in the Battle of Santo Domingo in 1805 . He was promoted to Field Marshal in 1806 , and fought in the west of the Spanish Empire in the years 1808-13 . He was given the title of Marqués de Bourbon during the Spanish War of Independence in 1811 .
Gálvez died in Madrid on September 21 , 1817 . His remains were buried in the Royal Pantheon of the Church of the Precious Blood of the Order of Montserrat in Madrid .
Gálvez was a close friend and ally of the Bourbon monarchs , and served both in the Spanish and French armies . He was an active supporter of the Bourbon cause in the Spanish War of Independence . His American Revolutionary War record was overlooked by the U.S. government when it decided to bestow awards on the Spanish officers who fought in the war .
Gálvez and his wife, Ana Maria de Rojas y Fernández de Leyva, had no children.

Guitar Hero: On Tour is the fourth game in the Guitar Hero series. The game was released on June 23, 2009 for the Nintendo DS and the Nintendo DS Lite . The game is playable with the Guitar Grip for the Nintendo DS. The DS game is set in a vertical orientation, unlike other games in the series.
The game features a career mode similar to Guitar Hero: World Tour. Career mode has the player take on the role of an up and coming guitarist. The player plays a series of shows at different venues. The player can also create their own guitarist using the in-game character creator.
In the game, the player can play with up to three friends with either Guitar Grip or the Nintendo DS stylus. The game features a total of 20 songs, of which 14 can be unlocked in the career mode and the remaining 6 in the challenge mode. Songs include " Don't Stop Believin' " by Journey, "Sweet Child O' Mine" by Guns N' Roses, and "Wonderwall" by Oasis.
Guitar Hero: On Tour has been met with mixed reviews. The game has a score of 65/100 on Metacritic .
The game was released on June 23, 2009 in Europe and on June 30, 2009 in North America.
Guitar Hero: On Tour is the first Guitar Hero game to be released on a handheld system.
Guitar Hero: On Tour was developed by Vicarious Visions and published by RedOctane . Released on June 23rd, 2009, the game was made available for the Nintendo DS, Nintendo DS Lite, and the Nintendo DSi.
The game is set in a vertical orientation, rather than the traditional horizontal setup that the other games in the series are.
Guitar Hero: On Tour features a career mode where the player starts out as an unknown musician hoping to make it big. The player performs in various venues and earns money to buy new gear for their character. The player can also unlock new characters by completing challenges.
When playing with friends, the game supports up to four players using either the Guitar Grip or the Nintendo DS stylus.
Guitar Hero: On Tour features a total of 20 songs, including "Don't Stop Believin'" by Journey, "Sweet Child o' Mine" by Guns N' Roses, and "Wonderwall" by Oasis.
Guitar Hero: On Tour was not as well received as the other games in the series. It holds a score of 65/100 on Metacritic, and was included in Game Informer 's list of the Top 10 Worst Guitar Hero Games.

Ryle's public life was divided between his work in Exeter and his role as a national figure in the Anglican Church. He was a lay preacher, and the author of many books, including the _Expository Thoughts on the Gospels_ , which he wrote for his own use and was not intended for publication. He was the first president of the National Assembly of the Church of England. His other presidential duties included chairing the Church Congress in 1888. He was an outspoken critic of the Liberal Party's efforts to separate religion from the state, and a staunch opponent of the notion of the 'separation of Church and state'.
As a distinguished theologian, Ryle was later invited to become the first president of the newly established Westminster Assembly of Divines.
Archbishop William Temple was the second president of the National Assembly. He was a distinguished theologian and a prolific author. He was also the second Archbishop of Canterbury since the Reformation.
Ryle and Temple were both keen to oppose the political secularisation of the Church of England and the disestablishment of the Church. They shared the view that the Church of England was the state church of England and that it was the duty of the state to protect the Church.
The National Assembly was formed in the summer of 1888 in response to the Church Disestablishment Bill, which had been introduced into Parliament by Gladstone's Liberal Party on 12 June 1888. The bill proposed a far-reaching reform of the Church of England, including the disestablishment of the Church, the removal of the role of the Church Commissioners and the Privy Council from the Church, the end of the establishment of the Church in the universities and colleges, the removal of the stipend of the Archbishop of Canterbury, and the change of the Church's name from the Church of England to 'the Church of Christ in England'.
At the same time, the Church was undergoing a period of considerable social and religious change, with a growing emphasis on the social ministry of the Church. This was, in part, a result of the work of the Ecclesiastical Commission, an independent body that had been established by the Church of England in 1836 to carry out  reforms within the Church. The Commissioners were appointed by the Privy Council, and they were independent of the Church. They reported to the Privy Council, which was the body responsible for the administration of the Church of England. The Commissioners were appointed to carry out reforms within the Church, in order to make it more efficient and to protect it from interference by the state.

After passing the entrance exam on his second attempt , in 1907 Wheeler was awarded a scholarship to read classical studies at

St John's College , Oxford , where he was a contemporary of and lifelong friend of Gerard Manley Hopkins . Hopkins's son , Robert , was Wheeler's godson .
While at Oxford , Wheeler came under the influence of the poet and critic W.B. Yeats , who had begun to lead a revival of the Celtic Twilight movement in Ireland . Wheeler's first published poem was for Yeats's magazine , The Irish Homestead , and he was later to write about the 1907 Yeats-Gregory tour of Ireland with his first wife . In 1909 , he graduated with a first-class honours degree.
In 1909 Wheeler was appointed to a tutorial post at Magdalen College , Oxford , where he came under the influence of  Maurice de Guérin , the "Wheelers' patron saint" . During this time he started writing poems under the pseudonym "Gerald" .
Wheeler's first book of poems Man and Bird was published in 1914 and included a poem dedicated to Maurice de Guérin .
In May 1915 the 19th Battalion of the Royal Fusiliers were shipped to the Dardanelles , and Wheeler was commissioned as an officer in the Royal Army Medical Corps. With the exception of a brief spell in hospital in Cairo , he remained at the front throughout the rest of the war, serving as a stretcher-bearer and medical officer with the 19th Battalion.
Wheeler was evacuated from Gallipoli to Malta in November 1915, and was appointed Medical Officer to the 38th (Welsh) Division.
In 1917 he was awarded the Military Cross for his work during the Second Battle of Gaza .
In 1918 he was moved to the Italian Front , where he was awarded a bar to his Military Cross for his actions during the Battle of the Piave River .
In 1919 he was awarded the Order of St. George of the Fourth Class (fourth degree) for his services.
Wheeler was demobilised at the end of 1919 and returned to Oxford , where he became a Fellow of Magdalen College.
In 1920 Wheeler married the novelist  Barbara Reynolds and took up a teaching post at the University of Liverpool .
Wheeler's second volume of poems, Ancient Light , was published in 1923.
Wheeler's next volume, Between the Dark and the Daylight , was published in 1934 and included a poem dedicated to his old friend Gerard Manley Hopkins .
Wheeler's next volume of poems, Oblations , was published in 1939. The title is based on the Latin term oblatio , which in Roman law refers to a gift voluntarily given to the state .
Wheeler's last book of poetry, The Lost Land of the Living , was published in 1952 and included a poem dedicated to his son , Timothy .
Wheeler was appointed to a professorship at the University of Leeds in 1946 and became Professor of Poetry at Oxford in 1950 .
In 1952 Wheeler was made a Fellow of the British Academy , and in 1957 he was awarded the Queen's Gold Medal for Poetry .
Wheeler was appointed a Knight Bachelor in the 1958 Birthday Honours and he was also appointed Professor of Poetry at Oxford for a second term .
Wheeler was a President of the Poetry Society from 1961 to 1963.

On December 3, 1889, the first Italian Catholic bishop of Italian Somaliland was appointed. The parish church in the city of Mogadishu was registered as an independent parish church in 1893. In 1902, the church was permitted to build a cathedral in the city.
The cathedral was built in 1928 on the site of the church. It was built in the Baroque style. The church was consecrated on October 13 of that year. The church was named the "Cathedral of Mogadishu", and the bishop of Italian Somaliland was also named "the bishop of Mogadishu".
On October 15, 1939, the cathedral of Italian Somaliland was promoted to the status of a diocese. The bishop of Italian Somaliland was promoted to the title of "bishop of Mogadishu". The cathedral was the seat of the Diocese of Mogadishu .
In 1960, Somalia declared its independence. The cathedral continued to be the seat of the local bishop.
On October 15, 1973, the diocese of Mogadishu was elevated to the rank of archdiocese.
In 1991 during the Somali Civil War , the cathedral was attacked by the Somali militia. It was completely destroyed.

The album of the film was released on 29 August 2009 under the banner of T-Series. The music of the album is composed by Chandan Shetty and the lyrics are penned by Nilesh Moharir and Ram Marathe. The song "Ab Kis Liye" became a chartbuster, with the music video featuring Riteish Deshmukh and Genelia D'Souza . The song won the Best Song of the Year award at Zee Cine Awards 2010.

## Reception

The film received mixed reviews from critics. Taran Adarsh of Bollywood Hungama gave it two stars out of five, describing it as "dramatic and terribly cliched" and praised the performances of Riteish Deshmukh and Genelia D'Souza in the film.

Sukanya Verma of Rediff gave the film two stars out of five and wrote, "Even though the film is in B & W, don’t expect a period drama. This may well be a reincarnation, but it’s not remotely classical in approach. In fact, it’s a typical contemporary romance. The only difference is that the woman is a ghost and the man is a reincarnation of her lover."

In an attempt to lure out and destroy a portion of the Grand Fleet , the German High Seas Fleet with 16 dreadnoughts , six pre

1910 battleships and a large number of cruisers, advanced to the mouth of the Firth of Forth on 29–30 May 1916 for a battle with the British Grand Fleet . The British Grand Fleet was at Scapa Flow in the Orkney Islands at the time, and no fleet was available at Rosyth.
 The Germans were detected by a British seaplane flying at about 6,000 ft (1,800 m) which spotted them at 8:00 am. The British Admiralty cancelled the fleet air service's patrols and ordered all ships to steam to sea.
General Haig, the British Army Commander-in-Chief , ordered the British Expeditionary Force (BEF) to move all its guns to the Forth, so that any attack by the German Fleet would be fired at by all possible guns.
The German fleet was spotted at 9:20 am by four seaplanes , but no action was taken against them. At 11:00 am the British Admiralty ordered the Grand Fleet to leave Scapa Flow and patrol the entrances to the Forth. They were ordered not to engage the Germans unless the Germans attacked first.
The German fleet headed south towards the North Sea and was attacked by British submarines and aircraft. The German fleet turned and headed north back to Germany. The British fleet was still at sea and followed the Germans north.
The German fleet headed for the English coast. The British fleet was still following them, but the German fleet was heading for the North Sea at a much higher speed . The British fleet was not ordered to attack the Germans until they were closer to the English coast than they were to the Forth.
The Germans were spotted by British aircraft at about 1:00 pm, when they were about 20 mi (32 km) off the coast of East Anglia , about 50 mi (80 km) from the Forth. The British fleet was ordered to attack the Germans, but it was too late. The Germans had already turned for home.
The Germans were heading for the Dutch coast. The British fleet was still following them, but the Germans were heading for the North Sea at a much higher speed. The British fleet was not ordered to attack the Germans until they were closer to the Dutch coast than they were to the Forth.
The Royal Navy had lost control of the situation. At about 4:00 pm, the Admiralty ordered the Grand Fleet to return to Scapa Flow, and the Royal Air Force (RAF) was ordered to cease patrols.
Haig ordered the BEF to return to France.

Historian Edward Hasted , in the third volume of The History and Topographical Survey of the County of Kent published in 1798 ,

wrote that: "The Abbey of St. Wites, founded by King Ethelbald, and dedicated to the Virgin Mary, was a cell to Rochester, and a collegiate abbey. It was a very rich abbey, and had a very large revenue, in the reign of King Edward the First, amounting to 300l. a year, and the abbots were usually great benefactors to the church."
The abbey was founded in the 8th century by King Ethelbald, who was the first bishop of the diocese of Rochester. The abbey was then dedicated to St. Wite (also spelt Wita, Witae, Wyt, Wita or Hewit), who was an Anglo-Saxon saint and the daughter of King Ethelbert of Kent. She was also the sister of St. Mildred. King Ethelbald initially wanted to make St. Wite a nun, but she decided to become a hermit instead. She was subsequently canonised and her relics were kept in a shrine at Minster-in-Sheppey.
The abbey is recorded in the Domesday Book in 1086 as Abathi, with the entry recording that it was the property of the abbey of St. Wite. The entry records that the abbey was assessed at 10 hides. The abbey was assessed at 12 hides in 1199.
The abbey was granted to the Knights Templar in 1141 by King Stephen, after the Knights had assisted him in his war against his rival, King Henry of Anjou. The abbey remained in the possession of the Knights Templar for the next 200 years. The Knights Templar were themselves disbanded in 1312. The abbey was then transferred to the Knights Hospitallers, who initially lived within the cloisters of the abbey. The Knights Hospitallers were later renamed the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, and the abbey became the headquarters of the Order. The Order was dissolved in 1540 and the abbey was granted to the Croyland Abbey in Lincolnshire.
According to Hasted (1798) the abbey was originally situated "on the opposite side of the river Medway ... but is now washed away by the encroachment of the tide, the remains of which are still visible." The abbey was situated to the east of the present-day town of Sheerness and the ruins of the abbey are now submerged by the River Medway.
The abbey was granted to Croyland Abbey in 1540. The abbey passed into the possession of the Crown and was granted to the Dean and Chapter of Canterbury in 1547. The abbey was subsequently let to various tenants.
The abbey was sold to Sir Henry Goodricke of Ribsden Holt in 1589. The abbey subsequently passed through various owners, until it was purchased in 1743 by the 5th Duke of Richmond. The duke employed architect Thomas Ripley to carry out repairs to the abbey. The main body of the abbey was subsequently demolished and the abbey became a farmhouse.
The ruins of the abbey are within the parish of Minster, Isle of Sheppey, in the county of Kent. The ruins are a Grade I listed building and a scheduled monument. The ruins are located on the east bank of the River Medway, 1 mile (1.6 km) northwest of the town of Sheerness, 3 miles (4.8 km) south of the village of Minster and 3 miles (4.8 km) south of the town of Queenborough. The ruins are situated in private grounds, which are at one with the grounds of the nearby Elmley Marshes Nature Reserve. The ruins are accessible by a path that starts from the River Medway. The path is signposted from the road known as The Street.
The ruins are located within the Isle of Sheppey Local Nature Reserve. This local nature reserve was established in 1987 and is 161.5 acres (65.3 ha) in size. The local nature reserve is managed by Kent Wildlife Trust on behalf of the Ministry of Defence, and the local nature reserve was designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest in 1998. The local nature reserve is situated on the Isle of Sheppey, which is the largest of the islands in the Thames Estuary

In this book I am concerned with the period from the time of the founding of Jamestown in 1607 to the time of the First Congregational church in 1630. In the chapter on the First Congregational Church I will cover the period 1630-1638. The chapter on the Puritan migration is concerned with 1638-1643. I am not concerned with the period 1644-1660. The important events of the mid-seventeenth century took place in England and in the New England colonies, but not in Plymouth.
I have examined the journals of the leaders of the colony, the pilgrim leaders, William Bradford and John Winthrop, and the _Mayflower_ passenger, Edward Winslow. I have examined the journals of the Puritan leaders, John Cotton, Thomas Hooker, and John Davenport, and their diary, the _New Haven Colony Records_. I have examined the journals of the Dutch, the _Nieuw Nederlandts_ , by Peter Minuit and the early Dutch governor, Pieter Stuyvesant. I have also examined the journals of the early French explorers, Champlain and de Mons.
It is my hope that this book will be useful to the general reader, to the pilgrim, to the Puritan, and to anyone interested in the history of the American colonies.

#  JAMESTOWN
The first English colony was founded by the Virginia Company in May 1607. The first settlement was on Roanoke Island off the coast of North Carolina. The settlement was called Jamestown. On August 13, 1607, the first colonists, led by Captain John Smith, set out in three ships, the _Susan Constant_ , the _Godspeed_ , and the _Discovery_. The colony was a commercial venture. Its purpose was to find gold, silver, and precious stones, to find a northwest passage to China, and to find a route to the Pacific Ocean. The colonists had very little understanding of the native peoples. They did not even know about the existence of the Indian tribes. The English had been in North America for only thirty years and did not have a clear idea of the extent of the continent.
The first winter in the New World was a terrible one. The colonists lived in a fort made of timber driven into the earth. They had no fresh water and had to rely on salt water in iron buckets. They had no livestock, no farming tools, and no supplies. They were starving. The colonists had a terrible time. They were without food and without hope. The Indians were friendly at first but after a time became hostile. They fell upon the colonists, killed them, and took their weapons and supplies. The colonists survived the winter, but lost nine out of four hundred and forty men.
The next summer the colonists went in search of food. In October 1608, Captain Smith, the leader of the expedition, went on an expedition to the lands of the Chesapeake Indians. He discovered the site he believed to be the site of a rich Indian town. He called the place Jamestown after King James. The settlement was a commercial enterprise. The colonists were to work the land and mine the gold. The first governor was Lord Delaware.
The settlement was a disaster. Captain Smith described the settlement as a "hell" and a "thousand hells." One winter the colonists were without food and without hope. The Indians were hostile and killed many of them. The settlers lived in a fort made of timber driven into the earth. They had no fresh water and had to rely on salt water in iron buckets. They had no livestock or farming tools or supplies. They were starving.

The company was to be able to exert control over the colonies. The company was to be able to appoint their own officials and to have a monopoly on the trade in the colonies. The company was to be able to tax the colonies.

The land, which is now a private property, has been worked by the same family for many years.
Many archaeological remains have been found in the area of the house.

The digging is of great importance for the archaeologists, as it has given a good picture of the daily life of peasants in the Roman Empire.
The amphorae unearthed in the house can be dated to the second century AD, according to the archaeologist, Florian Jeannot.

The 10 Freeway was originally conceived in the early 1960s as a way to relieve congestion on a heavily traveled coastal route of U.S. Highway 101. The first segment of the freeway to be completed was a 12-mile (19 km) stretch from Beverly Hills north to Hollywood Boulevard, which opened on August 21, 1964. The freeway was originally proposed to run north to Sepulveda Boulevard , but the route was changed to the current one. The freeway was completed in 1993 with the opening of the Foothill Freeway (SR 210) from the Ventura Freeway (SR 134) in downtown Los Angeles through the San Gabriel Valley to the Chino Valley.
When the 10 Freeway was originally proposed, public controversies arose over the freeway's impact on the San Fernando Valley . The freeway was opposed by many residents on environmental grounds, but supporters of the highway emphasized that it was needed to relieve congestion on U.S. 101 and the Hollywood Freeway (SR 170), which were increasingly becoming congested. Many residents in the San Fernando Valley, which was then an unincorporated area of Los Angeles County, opposed the freeway's construction, arguing that it would destroy the valley's remaining open spaces and harm the environment. As a compromise, a freeway tunnel was approved for the Sepulveda Pass, which would run underneath the San Fernando Valley. However, this was scrapped in 1967, and the freeway was routed through the valley. In the 1970s, a portion of the freeway was diverted around the University of California, Los Angeles, after students protested against its construction.
The 10 Freeway was originally intended to be a toll road, but the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) was not authorized to collect tolls. In the 1990s, a plan to convert the freeway into a toll road was revived. The 2008 budget included $30 million for the conversion and toll collection. The conversion was approved in January 2008 and the road was tolled on March 2, 2008, at 5:00 am . The tolls are $2.50 for cars and trucks, $5 for motorcycles, and $10 for RVs and Buses. The tolls are collected on express lanes, which are signified by the word "Express" on signs. The tolls are collected by a camera system .

Above the level of the photosphere is the stellar atmosphere . In a main sequence star such as the Sun , the lowest level of th

e atmosphere is called the photosphere and is the surface where most of the Sun's energy is emitted. The temperature of this region is about 5,700 K, and it is opaque to visible light . The transition from the photosphere to the chromosphere is abrupt, and lines of strong spectral absorption or emission are visible. The chromosphere extends up to an altitude of 1,000 km (620 mi). The transition from the chromosphere to the corona is less abrupt, and the corona extends to high altitudes of 1 to 10 million kilometers (620,000 to 620,000 mi) above the photosphere. The corona is composed of a tenuous plasma that is nearly a perfect vacuum. Temperatures in the corona can reach about 200 million degrees K (30 million degrees C). In the Sun, the corona is about 100,000 times hotter than the photosphere. The corona is only visible during a total solar eclipse, when the Moon covers the disk of the Sun and the sunlight is scattered into space.
Surface features on the Sun can be seen by examining changes in the light spectrum. In general, the energy of the light is related to the temperature of the emitting or absorbing body. When light is absorbed it becomes heat. The Sun's spectrum changes because of the absorption of light. Sunspots , regions of low temperature, appear darker in the spectrum, and the corona, which is hotter than the photosphere, appears brighter.
The Sun's surface and atmosphere together are referred to as the solar photosphere . The photosphere is about 5,000 km (3,100 mi) thick. The Sun's interior is much hotter than the photosphere, and is heated by nuclear fusion reactions that occur within the Sun. The hot interior is not visible because the light produced is absorbed by the photosphere. The Sun's atmosphere remains hot to distances of about 100,000 km (62,000 mi) above the photosphere.
The Sun is a main sequence star . It is made up mostly of hydrogen, with a small amount of helium. The Sun is a typical main sequence star. It is about 30 percent larger than the Earth, and it is about 330,000 times more massive. The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old, and it will remain a main sequence star for another 5 billion years. It will end its life as a red giant.
The Sun's mass is 333,000 times that of the Earth. The Sun's diameter is 1,400,000 kilometers (870,000 mi) and is about 109 times the diameter of the Earth. The Sun is about 99.86 percent hydrogen, 0.12 percent helium, 0.6 percent heavier elements, and 0.001 percent unknown elements. The Sun radiates energy at a rate of 3.847 × 1026 watts, almost three million times the world's total energy consumption. The Sun's gravity is about 28 times that of Earth. The Sun's rotation period is about 25 days, and its rotation axis is slightly tilted, which is why the Sun has an apparent north-south direction.
Atoms of hydrogen, the most common element in the universe, are constantly combining to form helium. In the Sun, about 600 million tons of hydrogen is converted into helium each second. The Sun's core temperature is about 15,000,000°C (27,000,000°F). The core of the Sun is a ball of 75,000,000°C (1,300,000,000°F) gas and plasma (a state of matter in which a gas is ionized).

Clarkson described her vocal style on 25 as " [having] a little bit of a jazz influence in some songs, and a little bit of a pop country influence in other songs " . Billboard described her vocals as " warm, inviting, and powerful " , and Vibe wrote that they " showcase [Clarkson's] dynamic range " . The album's lyrical content is " nostalgic, fun, and sometimes witty " , according to The New York Times ' Peter Robinson .
Clarkson has said that, although the album is not intended to be a Christmas album, she wanted it to " feel like Christmas " . The album's sound is a mixture of " old and new " . The album is a mixture of Christmas standards and " newer hits " . The album also contains two original songs, " Under the Mistletoe " and " Glow " .
The album contains a cover of " Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas " , a song that Clarkson has sung many times in concert. She first sang it in 1999, while a contestant on the first season of American Idol . Clarkson's version of the song appears on the 2001 compilation album American Idol: The Great Holiday Collection , and in 2006 she sang it on the Idol Christmas album . Clarkson has said that the song " has been on my Christmas list forever " . She said the song's lyrics are " so sad, but so beautiful " , and that they " make you think of someone who's not there " .
" Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas " is a duet with The Band Perry , a country music trio that Clarkson had previously collaborated with on the single " Don't Rush " . The song was written in 1943 by Hugh Martin and Ralph Blane , and was first performed by Judy Garland in the 1944 film Meet Me in St. Louis . Clarkson and The Band Perry's version of the song is a duet, and was released on November 16, 2014, by RCA Records and Sony Music Nashville .
Clarkson's version of " Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas " was well received by critics . Jon Pareles of The New York Times called it a " creamy, elegiac duet " , while Sarah Rodman of The Boston Globe described it as " a classic " . " Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas " also received a nomination for Best Country Duo/Group Performance at the 57th Annual Grammy Awards .

In addition to the storms which attained at least tropical storm strength in 1940 , five additional tropical depressions were a

part of the 1940 season. A tropical depression in the southern Gulf of Mexico which formed on September 10, 1940, was located too far south to contribute much to the season's activity. A second tropical depression on October 31, 1940, formed just south of the Yucatan Peninsula , but dissipated the same day without ever developing into a tropical storm. The third tropical depression of the season formed on November 13, 1940, in the southwest Caribbean Sea , and moved northward toward the Yucatan Peninsula. It dissipated on November 16, 1940, while still hundreds of miles from land. The fourth tropical depression of the season formed in the southwest Gulf of Mexico on December 15, 1940, but dissipated the same day before reaching tropical storm strength. A fifth tropical depression formed on December 19, 1940, in the Gulf of Mexico near the mouth of the Mississippi River , and moved northward into the northeastern Gulf of Mexico. It did not reach tropical storm intensity before dissipating on December 20, 1940.

The poem contains a complicated use of assonance ( the repetition of vowel sounds ) , as evident in line 19 , " O why did ye no

speak to me ? " and line 23 , " Ugly and sore and sad . " Also, end rhymes in lines 3 and 4 , 6 and 7 , 9 and 10 , and 11 and 12 .
 This poem is a villanelle. A villanelle is a poem made up of 19 lines. Lines 1-3 and 5-7 are repeated, as are lines 9-11 and 13-15. The first and third lines are also repeated as the final couplet at the end. There is a repeating refrain that occurs in lines 2, 4, 6, and 8. The last line, line 19, is unrhymed. There are two variations of the villanelle form: the Italian and the French. The Italian villanelle is written in tercets (three-line stanzas). The French is written in five-line stanzas.

In the 1840s, the potato crop failed in Ireland and as a result of this, the Irish people starved. As a result of this, the people of Britain were forced to feed large numbers of Irish people and in 1846, the Irish famine commenced.
The first World War was fought from 1914 to 1918 and was a period of great hardship and loss for the people of Britain.

Although it is very much a minority view , three prominent twentieth @-@ century masters claimed that White 's advantage should

be assessed as greater, on average, than that of Black . This author has no difficulty in accepting the general validity of this minority view (it seems to be supported by anecdotal evidence), but it is not something that can be proven with the certainty that is demanded by the "scientific method".
 (1) In the first place, each of the three masters who held this view is one of the most outstanding players in history.
 (2) Each of them was an individualist in his interpretation of the game, and this individualism was reflected in his assessment of White 's advantage.
 (3) The masters who held this minority view were, in a sense, philosophically opposed to the mainstream of chess theory, which has tended to favour Black .
Each of these three masters was a person of enormous stature in the world of chess.
Alekhine (he was born in 1892) was at the height of his powers in the 1920s, and was world champion (1927-35). He was a prolific author, in addition to his chess career, and wrote a great deal about chess theory.
Spielmann (1886-1965) was a player of great strength, a former British champion (1914), and at one time rated as the tenth strongest player in the world (1922). He was especially a fine analyst.
Keres (1906-1975) was one of the greatest players of the twentieth century. He was a former Soviet champion (1945) and world challenger (1948). His style made him a popular player. He was an outstanding author, and was also a poet and writer of science fiction.
Each of these three masters was an individualist in his interpretation of chess.
Alekhine was a highly controversial personality. He was a Russian émigré, and had been an ardent admirer of the Bolshevik revolution. He later became a Nazi sympathizer. He was widely respected as a player, but was unpopular with many of his contemporaries.
Spielmann was a somewhat reserved personality, but one who had strong opinions on various matters. His best friend was the great English master, George Alan Thomas, and this friendship was a subject of some controversy.
Keres was an outgoing personality, who had a strong sense of humour. He had a great love of music, and was a poet and science-fiction writer in his spare time.
Each of these masters was opposed to the mainstream of chess theory.
Alekhine was the first to publish a theory that Black 's advantage could be greater than White 's. He was writing in 1924, in the book _My Best Game of Chess_. This book was a collection of ten "best games" selected by Alekhine himself. It is no coincidence that Alekhine's selection included many games in which White had an advantage, and Black 's advantage was therefore less; and that Black 's advantage was greater in the games in which Alekhine was playing White. Alekhine's book was an outspoken attack on the mainstream of chess theory, which had favoured Black .
Spielmann, too, was a person of strong views. He had a lifelong interest in spiritualism, and in 1922 published a book on the subject, _The Problem of Life After Death_. In 1944 he published the first of his two books on chess, _The Art of the Attack_. Tropical Cyclone Herbie originated from an area of low pressure on 17 May 1988 northwest of the Cocos Islands . Later that day

0000 UTC, the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) classified the system as Tropical Low 03S. Tropical Low 03S moved westward into the Australian region, and the next day 0600 UTC the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) classified the system as Tropical Cyclone Herbie. The system continued to strengthen, and at 1200 UTC on 19 May the JTWC upgraded Herbie to a Category 1 typhoon. Herbie continued to strengthen, and at 0000 UTC on 20 May the JTWC upgraded Herbie to a Category 2 typhoon. At 0600 UTC the same day the BOM upgraded Herbie to a Category 2 cyclone. Herbie continued to strengthen, and at 1200 UTC on 21 May the JTWC upgraded Herbie to a Category 3 typhoon. Herbie continued to strengthen, and at 0000 UTC on 22 May the JTWC upgraded Herbie to a Category 4 typhoon. At 0600 UTC the same day the BOM upgraded Herbie to a Category 4 severe tropical cyclone. Herbie continued to strengthen, and at 1200 UTC on 22 May the JTWC upgraded Herbie to a Category 5 typhoon. At 0000 UTC on 23 May the BOM upgraded Herbie to an extremely severe tropical cyclone. At 1200 UTC on 23 May the JTWC upgraded Herbie to a Category 5 typhoon. Herbie continued to strengthen, and at 0000 UTC on 24 May the JTWC upgraded Herbie to a Category 6 typhoon. At 1200 UTC the same day the BOM upgraded Herbie to an extremely severe category 5 severe tropical cyclone. At 0000 UTC on 25 May the JTWC downgraded Herbie to a Category 5 typhoon. At 1200 UTC the same day the BOM upgraded Herbie to a Category 5 severe tropical cyclone. At 0000 UTC on 26 May the BOM downgraded Herbie to a Category 4 severe tropical cyclone and at 0600 UTC the same day the JTWC downgraded Herbie to a Category 4 typhoon. At 1200 UTC on 26 May the BOM downgraded Herbie to a Category 3 severe tropical cyclone. At 0000 UTC on 27 May the BOM downgraded Herbie to a Category 2 severe tropical cyclone. At 1200 UTC on 27 May the JTWC downgraded Herbie to a Category 1 typhoon. At 2000 UTC the same day the BOM downgraded Herbie to a Category 1 severe tropical cyclone. On 28 May Herbie transitioned to an extratropical cyclone, and the JTWC issued their last warning on Herbie at 1200 UTC. Herbie continued to weaken, and at 0000 UTC on 29 May the BOM issued their last warning on Herbie. On 29 May the remnants of Herbie continued to the north-northeast.

## Confirmation

The Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) confirmed that Herbie was the worst cyclone in the history of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, killing 10 people. The worst damage was on the islands of North Keeling and Direction Island.

Music has been in evidence in Ireland since prehistoric times . Although in the early Middle Ages the church was " quite unlike

the strict theocracy that it has since become," Irish musicians were "considered to have been among the best in Europe." As recently as 1780, the historian Henry Hallam thought that the Irish were "the most musical people in Europe." Of course, such a judgment might be challenged by Slavs, Greeks, or Spaniards, but it is an indication of Ireland's musical past.
In the nineteenth century, though, the Irish people were said to be losing their traditional musical skills. It was thought that "the old Irish music, which had been so full of life and vigour, was gradually dying away." On 31 July 1862 , under the command of Lieutenant Charles H. McBlair , Atlanta conducted her sea trials down the Savannah River

and into the Atlantic Ocean . The ship was found to be seaworthy and the crew was judged to be competent.
On 21 August 1862, the ship departed Savannah to join the CSS H. L. Hunley , CSS Lafayette , and the gunboats CSS Jackson and CSS Chicora in a raid on Port Royal, South Carolina . On 22 August, the vessels were sighted by the blockading forces and a battle ensued.
On 24 August, Atlanta came about in an attempt to escape the enemy and was struck by the stern of the blockading steamer SC Pawnee . The hull was breached and water rapidly entered the engine room, putting the ship's engines out of commission.
By 25 August, the ship was drifting in a southeasterly direction. The crew abandoned ship, but three of the crew were killed when another vessel was sighted. The remaining crew was rescued by USS Wabash .
On 27 August 1862, Atlanta was reported as having sunk in the Atlantic Ocean.

Andrew Johnston ( born 23 September 1994 ) is a British singer who rose to fame when he appeared as a boy soprano on the second

series of BBC One singing competition The Voice UK, making the final of the show.
Johnston was born in Hertfordshire, England, and was raised in Claydon, Suffolk. He attended Claydon Primary School and Great Cornard High School and he was a chorister in the choir of St Mary the Virgin Church, Lavenham. When Johnston was ten years old, he began learning how to play piano and guitar.
In 2010, Johnston appeared on the ITV talent show Britain's Got Talent and got a dance group through to the semi-finals. He also sang the song "O Come, All Ye Faithful" on the ITV Christmas day television programme The Queen's Christmas Message.
In 2011, Johnston sang the national anthem at the FA Cup Final at Wembley Stadium. He also sang "If I Were a Carpenter" on the BBC Two talent show Last Choir Standing.
In 2012, Johnston reached the final of The Voice UK. He was one of the youngest participants on the show and the youngest finalist in the show's history.
After singing his version of "Hallelujah", Johnston was eliminated from the competition by his mentor Jessie J.
His final performance of Leonard Cohen's "Hallelujah" was released on 2 June 2012 on iTunes. The single reached number 17 on the UK Singles Chart.
In 2016, Johnston appeared on the BBC talent show All Together Now and reached the final but was eliminated.
On 23 April 2014, Johnston appeared on the British game show The Chase during the spring edition of the show. He was one of the "chasers" and was chosen by the chaser Anne Hegerty to compete. He was chosen as one of the contestants because he had once been a contestant on the show, and he had won £17,500. He was eliminated in the first round of the show.
