Turner and Outram, famous for their work on the docks and railways, were the forerunner of Balfour Beatty, a name which has become synonymous with Britain's transport infrastructure. For the first fourteen years of their partnership they were based in the City of London, but in 1827, having acquired the title of Civil Engineers to the City of London, they moved to a more prestigious location, 122 Fenchurch Street.
The move to Fenchurch Street coincided with the shift of the centre of gravity of the City from the East to the West, and the building itself was a clear sign of the growth of the City's power. It was, however, an inauspicious start for the partnership as Turner died in 1832 and Outram was declared bankrupt in 1833. John Outram, however, was a determined character and continued the business, incorporating it the following year as Outram and Co. In 1835 he appointed Abraham Stott as his partner and the company prospered.
In 1845 Stott left Outram and Co. to set up his own firm, and the following year he bought a house in Hulme, across the River Irwell from Manchester. A few years later he moved to a house in Crescent Road, Sale, in a building which still stands today. A new firm, Stott and Sons, was formed, and the company prospered under the direction of his son, John, and grandson, also named John. By 1891 they were contracting on the London and North Western Railway, the Midland Railway, the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway and the Manchester Ship Canal, and had built a new shipyard at Barrow-in-Furness, Cumbria.
In 1915 the company was nationalised as part of the Government's war effort, but they continued to operate as Stott and Sons until 1965, when they were amalgamated into Morrison-Denny.
Oliver Stott was born in 1863 and was educated at Sale Grammar School. From an early age he was involved in the family firm, and served his apprenticeship with the company between 1875 and 1880. He left the firm to become a clerk at a firm of engineers in Manchester, but returned to Stott and Sons in 1888, when he was made a partner, specialising in the design and construction of bridges. In 1897 he was appointed chief engineer and partner in the firm, and in 1913 he became chairman of the company. He was in charge of the company when it was nationalised, and was appointed, as Stott and Sons was, as a partner in Morrison-Denny.
In 1920 Stott was elected MP for Stretford and Urmston, and served until 1922. He continued to serve on the board of Morrison-Denny, and was chairman of the board from 1934 until his retirement in 1947.
Galveston Island was originally inhabited by members of the Karankawa and Akokisa tribes who called the island Auia . The Spani

In 1816, the first Anglo-American settler, John Rosborough , arrived and purchased 2,000 acres (8.1 km 2 ) of land. He named the island "Galveston" in honor of his home in Galway , Ireland . In 1836, the Republic of Texas declared independence from Mexico and Galveston became the capital of the new republic. However, by 1839, the capital was moved to Houston and Galveston's population began to decline.
In 1865, Galveston was the site of the famous "Galveston Hurricane" which killed over 10,000 people. In 1900, the city was struck again by a deadly hurricane which killed 8,000 people. Between these two hurricanes, population on the island grew to about 40,000. In 1901, the United States Congress approved an Act of Congress for the construction of the Texas Seacoast Fortification System. This system included the construction of a fort on Galveston Island. In 1917, the United States Department of War took over the fort from the Army and began using it as a prisoner of war camp. The Galveston County Courthouse was completed in 1912 and is now listed on the National Register of Historic Places .

All of the surviving megalithic tombs from the Early Neolithic period have suffered from neglect and the ravages of agriculture

. They have also been subjected to countless acts of vandalism and destruction. Some of the most extensive damage has been caused by souvenir hunters who have hacked off stone slabs to remove decorative motifs carved into them. This is especially true of the best-known monuments in Britain, including Maeshowe in Orkney and Newgrange in Co. Meath, Ireland, plus the smaller and less-known sites such as the West Kennet Long Barrow in Wiltshire.
The first major survey of megalithic tombs in Britain was made by the noted Victorian antiquarian Sir John Lubbock, who published his findings in _Prehistoric Times as Illustrated by Ancient Remains, and the Manners and Customs of Modern Savages_ (1865). Lubbock's pioneering surveys, which covered many of the best-known sites in Britain, helped to establish the importance of these monuments and, consequently, their value as archaeological sites, which could be explored and preserved for posterity, rather than being treated as 'national curiosities'. Yet, despite Lubbock's personal efforts to prevent the destruction of megalithic monuments, it was not until 1919 that the first legal protection was given to them.
In 1919 the Archaeology (Scotland) Act was passed in the Scottish Parliament, followed by the Ancient Monuments Act in 1925. The latter restricted the removal of stones from megalithic monuments and other ancient structures. The Ancient Monuments Act was amended in 1931 and again in 1937, when the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Areas Act was passed. This extended the protection given to ancient monuments to include ancient monuments and archaeological areas (defined as 'sites of national importance'). It was the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Areas Act that made it an offence to unlawfully interfere with, or damage, any ancient monument or archaeological area, punishable by a fine of up to £2,500.
In the 1930s and 1940s, a number of important discoveries were made, including the site of the Neolithic village at Skara Brae in Orkney, and the remains of a hunter-gatherer settlement at Star Carr in the North York Moors. In the 1950s, more important discoveries were made, including the barrows at Thornborough and the early Mesolithic settlement at Flag Fen.
In 1979 the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Areas Act was amended again, to create a new category of national monument, the registered monument. Any monument that was not yet protected under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Areas Act, including scheduled monuments, could be registered under the new legislation. This was a consequence of the growing interest in archaeology, which had been fostered by the television series _Time Team_ , which began in 1994.
Another important change to the legislation was the introduction of the Scheduled Ancient Monuments Consent Order in 1999. This gave local authorities more control over the planning process, allowing them to make decisions about development that affected scheduled monuments. As a result, the number of scheduled monuments increased, from 6,198 to 8,900.
Despite the legislation, many of the best-known megalithic monuments in Britain continue to suffer from neglect, despite the fact they are now nationally protected. The Barrow Clump long barrow in Wiltshire, for example, is one of the best-known megalithic monuments in Britain, yet it has been vandalised on numerous occasions. Most recently, in July 2016, around 200 of the stones in the roof of the tomb were taken.
In Britain, megalithic tombs are mostly found on the west coast of Wales, in the south-west and in the west of England. The sites are generally considered to be of Irish origin, since many of them were built at a similar time to the large passage tombs in Ireland.

Aston Villa Football Club /əˈstɒn ˈvɪlə/ is a professional football club in Birmingham, England. Founded in 1874, they have played at their home ground, Villa Park, since 1897. They are the second-most successful club in the history of the Second Division of the Football League, having won the title a record six times. The club have also won the top-flight League Championship six times, the FA Cup seven times, and the League Cup five times. As a result, they are one of only five clubs to have won the "double" of the League and FA Cup, which they achieved in 1887–88 and 1895–96, and also one of only three English teams to have achieved a "treble", winning the League Cup, FA Cup and the European Cup in 1981–82.They are the second most successful team in the history of the Football League Cup, the third most successful team in the history of the UEFA Champions League and one of the most successful English clubs in European competitions overall.
Aston Villa scored the first ever European Cup goal at the hands of Gary Shaw in the 1971–72 UEFA Cup Final against Bayern Munich . The Villains are also one of only five English clubs to have reached a UEFA cup final, winning the competition in 1981–82.

The only internationally recognized authority for naming celestial bodies is the International Astronomical Union ( IAU ) . A n

organization known as the Planetary Society has lobbied to change the organization's official definition of "planet" in order to try to include Pluto as a planet. The IAU has refused to do so, and continues to use the original definition which excludes Pluto as a planet.
1. A planet is a celestial body that is in orbit around the sun, has sufficient mass for its self-gravity to overcome rigid body forces so that it assumes a (nearly) round shape, and has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit.
2. A dwarf planet is a celestial body that (a) is in orbit around the sun, (b) has sufficient mass for its self-gravity to overcome rigid body forces so that it assumes a (nearly) round shape, (c) has not cleared the neighborhood around its orbit, and (d) does not meet any of the other criteria for planethood.
The IAU has not included Pluto in its official list of planets. The IAU definition has been used by the U.S. Board of Geographic Names, the U.S. Department of State, and most international organizations dealing with the classification of celestial bodies.
The IAU definition has been criticized by many people, including a group of scientists who wrote an open letter to the IAU in August 2006. This group includes the astronomers Alan Stern, Chad Trujillo, and David Rabinowitz.
The IAU has responded to the criticisms of its definition in two ways. First, the IAU published a paper in 2006 that clarified the definition of a planet. Second, the IAU commissioned a committee to review the definition. This committee will reportedly make a final decision about the definition of a planet at the General Assembly of the IAU in Prague in August 2006.
 For a more complete explanation of the IAU definition, see "Definition of Planet."

was first found in 1976 by a Finnish mycologist named Harri Peck, who observed it growing on decaying wood in a Finnish forest .  A German patrol torpedo boat had sunk on 17 November 1914 the 1,400-ton British merchant ship Etruria near the English coast. In retaliation, the British Admiralty ordered the German trawler Hela to be sunk. A Royal Navy flotilla commanded by Godsal, consisting of the destroyers HMS Brilliant, HMS Bulldog, HMS Sparrowhawk, and HMS Pigeon, was ordered to stop her and sink her. It was a difficult task since the German vessel was heavily armed, but the mission was successful.
The British patrol was on a mission to stop and search German shipping off the Dutch coast. The flotilla sailed in line ahead, with the destroyer HMS Brilliant leading. The flotilla was approximately fifteen miles from the mouth of the German port of Emden when the Germans spotted them and were warned by the Germans to turn back. Godsal, who was in command of the flotilla, refused to turn back and pressed on toward Emden.
The Germans countered by launching a torpedo against the British patrol. The torpedo hit HMS Brilliant and damaged her badly. The ship lost control and sank. The other ships in the column picked up the survivors, but it was too late for Godsal. He was trapped in the sunken British destroyer. The Germans, who had been watching the operation from shore, were able to rescue him from the destroyer but he died soon afterwards from his injuries.
The sinking of the Brilliant was one of the first known successful uses of the counterattack tactic. The Germans continued to use the tactic as the war progressed and it became known as "wolf pack" tactics.

The 2007 Sheraton Hawaii Bowl was a post @-@ season college football bowl game between the Boise State University Broncos from

2007 NCAA Division I FBS football team and the Hawaii Warriors of the University of Hawaii.The game was played on December 23 at Aloha Stadium in Honolulu, Hawaii. At the time, the stadium seated 50,000 people, but the game was not a sellout.
The Broncos won, 41-14, led by quarterback Jared Zabransky and running back Ian Johnson.
The Broncos were invited to play in the 2007 Hawaii Bowl after winning the 2007 Mountain West Conference Championship Game. The game was the Broncos' first bowl game in three years after ending their two-year bowl ban in 2006. The Warriors were invited to the game after winning the Western Athletic Conference Championship Game, where they defeated Fresno State 41-40. The game was Hawaii's fourth bowl game in five years.
This game came only five days after the Broncos' former defensive coordinator, Jerry Pettibone, was fired for allegedly accepting money for recruiting violations.
The Broncos scored on their first drive of the game, starting the game with a 7-yard touchdown pass from Ian Johnson to Jerard Rabb, giving the Broncos an early 7-0 lead. Hawaii answered with a 51-yard touchdown pass from Tyler Graunke to Ryan Grice-Mullen to tie the game at 7. The Broncos responded immediately with a 62-yard touchdown run by Ian Johnson, going up 14-7.
Hawaii scored on their next drive with a 4-yard touchdown by Michael Lotulelei, tying the game at 14. Hawaii would kick a field goal to make it 17-14, but the Broncos would answer with a 1-yard touchdown run by Ian Johnson, putting the Broncos up 21-17. On the next drive, the Broncos would intercept Graunke, taking the ball to the Hawaii 5. The Broncos would score with a 3-yard touchdown run by Ian Johnson, going up 28-17.
In the fourth quarter, the Broncos scored again when Jared Zabransky ran in a 10-yard touchdown, extending the Broncos lead to 35-17. The Broncos would score again on a 5-yard touchdown run by Ian Johnson. The final score was 41-14.

## Plot

Thakur Baldev Singh ( Dara Singh ) is a powerful but ruthless landlord with a large estate and a strong army of henchmen at his disposal . He is also the guardian of his godson Ramgarhia ( Sanjeev Kumar ) , who lives in a nearby village protected by a large wall .

One day, while Baldev is away in Delhi , Ramgarhia's younger brother Vikram Singh ( Amitabh Bachchan ) and his friend Jai ( Dharmendra ) , a small-time thief who has been in jail for a few years , break into the house in search of food . Vikram is a quiet and peaceful man who lives in his brother's shadow , while Jai is a boisterous and fun-loving man who is always thinking of ways to make money .

The two men , who are introduced to the house by an attendant , escape the house unnoticed and flee .

That night , Ramgarhia's wife, Urmila ( Hema Malini ) , disguises herself as a man and leaves the house to meet her lover at a nearby pond . When Baldev arrives home and discovers Ramgarhia's wife is missing, his men are unable to find her . Baldev thus believes his nephew was kidnapped by Ramgarhia's brother and sends his men to the village to bring Ramgarhia to him .

Ramgarhia's village is on the way to the fort where Ramgarhia is to be taken . Jai and Vikram are eager to help the local villagers in their fight against Baldev, and they form an alliance with them.

Baldev's men arrive at the village and demand that Ramgarhia be handed over to them. But the villagers refuse to give up their leader, and a small skirmish ensues. The villagers are defeated, and Ramgarhia is taken to Baldev's mansion.

Meanwhile, Urmila , in her guise as a man named Ram , has been reunited with her lover , but is shocked by Baldev's state of mind after he discovers that Ram is not his nephew . Baldev's men try to silence Ram by forcing him to drink poison , but the women decide to save Ram's life . Urmila is sent to Baldev's house to spy on him, while Meena (Nirupa Roy) returns to the village to inform the people of Baldev's intentions .

Baldev, who is initially suspicious of Ram, begins to trust him after Ram proves himself to be brave and loyal , and he decides to adopt him as his son . However, the villagers have not forgotten Baldev's attack on their village, and they are determined to retaliate .

The ties with the _Daily Mirror_ resulted in the most powerful newscast on television, and an early realization by DuMont that television was not just a medium for entertainment but could also be a powerful tool for communicating with the public. In March a contract was signed between ABC and Associated Television (ATV) for the American broadcast rights to the series, with a first airdate set for September.
The American series was produced by Filmation, a company which also produced cartoons for television. Filmation's studio was located in New York City , where the company had been formed in 1963. The contract specified that the episodes produced by Filmation had to be made to the same standard as those produced by ATV .
The contract was signed on 2 April 1966, and Filmation began production of the first batch of 13 episodes on 1 May. These were to be combined into one 90-minute show for broadcast in the autumn of 1966. Filmation was given a weekly allowance of $50,000 to produce the episodes.
The first 13 episodes produced by Filmation were aired on ABC on 16 September 1966, beginning with "Lady Penelope's Flying Car". The opening credits were changed to include the words "An American Production" (in the form of a banner) and were made slightly different in each episode. In the UK, the first 13 episodes were broadcast on ATV in January 1967, two months after their American premiere.
In addition to the 13 episodes made for ABC, Filmation also produced 13 one-off episodes over the next three years, of which all but one (originally on a separate contract) are considered to be part of Series Three . The episodes were broadcast in the USA between 1967 and 1969.
The American version was broadcast in syndication in the USA in 1967, and was also shown in Japan on the NET network.
In 1967, following the cancellation of the original series, Filmation were commissioned to produce six additional episodes of the series, in connection with the first Thunderbirds feature film, Thunderbirds Are Go. The first of these, "The Cham-Cham", was broadcast as part of the regular series on 29 September 1968, and the remaining five were broadcast in the USA in 1969 as part of Series Four .

Planning by Dade County for an expressway, initially named the "Snapper Creek Expressway", was underway as early as 1958. However, the county was unable to move forward with this project.

In 1972, the Florida Legislature created the Snapper Creek Expressway as a proposed highway from Southwest 104th Street at Red Road to the Rickenbacker Causeway. The highway was projected to cost $136.5 million and was to be financed with tolls. The expressway was planned to be completed by 1980.

In 1974, the state legislature amended the bill to designate the highway as the Snapper Creek Expressway. In 1976, the state legislature removed the Snapper Creek Expressway from the state highway system.

Ownership of the road was transferred to the Florida Department of Transportation in 1978. The Snapper Creek Expressway became part of Florida State Road 836 after the department resurfaced the road in 1981.

He had a reputation for being unorthodox and was a keen amateur ornithologist and a skilled painter.
When Meinertzhagen arrived in the Sinai in March, he was greeted by a scene of anarchy. The sheikhs were divided into two main groups, the Qarsa and the Kataba, and the members of each group were constantly trying to take over the other's territory. Meinertzhagen had to try to persuade them to form a united force. He was also faced with the problems caused by the Bedouin who were smuggling , and the problems posed by the Bedouin themselves. Most of the Bedouin were illiterate, uneducated and unruly tribesmen who had no experience of dealing with the European way of life.
Meinertzhagen had to deal with the problems in the Sinai and the camel corps with barely any resources and an inefficient bureaucracy. He had to persuade the Bedouin to support him in his efforts, but he soon discovered that the Bedouin were not very interested in the British military. The men who served in the camel corps were constantly trying to find ways to circumvent the rules which were set down by the British. The British found that they had to deal with an unruly and rebellious force, and the methods that were used to try to deal with their problems would have serious consequences for the war.

Established in 1891 with one building and fewer than 50 students , today the University of Texas Medical Branch ( UTMB ) campus

is one of the most prestigious institutions of higher learning in the United States. The school has grown to include seven health science schools, and today has more than 2,200 students from all 50 states and 78 countries.
The campus is located on Galveston Island, 50 miles southeast of Houston , Texas , and covers more than 100 acres of land. The campus is separated into three sections: the 67-acre main campus, the 15-acre Shriners Burn Hospital, and the 25-acre UTMB Health Center at League City . On the main campus are the School of Medicine, the School of Nursing, the Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, the School of Public Health, and the Institute for Translational Sciences, which houses the Institute for Human Infections and Immunity and the Institute for Human Genetics.
The School of Medicine began in 1891, when the city of Galveston donated $15,000 and a five-acre lot for a medical college. The school opened in May 1891 with nine students and one building. The first classes at the school were held in a downtown building that had formerly been the academy of the Sisters of the Incarnate Word.
In 1900, the school moved to the southwest corner of Sealy and 15th Street, where it remained until 1906. At that time a new building was constructed on Broadway and 15th Street, where classes continued until 1930. In 1930, a new building, designed by Edward Durell Stone, was constructed on the main campus on Broadway and 15th Street.
During the 1930s the school began to expand. The School of Laboratory Medicine was established in 1930, the School of Allied Health Sciences was established in 1940, and the School of Graduate Studies and Research was established in 1944. In 1944 the school moved to the main campus, where the buildings were designed by the firm of Roy O. Allen and Harvey Hines. The School of Graduate Studies and Research became the Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences in 1952. A Research and Biology Building was constructed in 1958, and the School of Graduate Studies and Research moved there, followed by the School of Laboratory Medicine in 1960 and the School of Allied Health Sciences in 1963.
In 1963 the University of Texas System assumed control of the school. The UT System is a state-funded system of 13 state universities that was established in 1967. At that time, the medical school on the Galveston Island campus became the University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB). The school was accredited by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools in 1977.
In 1969 the School of Medicine became part of the University of Texas System. At that time the school also became known as the University of Texas Medical Branch. The name change was made to emphasize the school's affiliation with the University of Texas System. The school also expanded, opening a new School of Allied Health Sciences in 1981. The School of Laboratory Medicine was divided into the School of Pharmacy and the School of Health Professions in 1986. In 1986, the School of Nursing was established.
The School of Medicine also expanded in the 1980s, establishing the School of Public Health in 1986 and the School of Graduate Biomedical Sciences in 1988. The School of Graduate Biomedical Sciences was established to coordinate the work of the departments that offer graduate-level instruction and to provide a centralized graduate admissions process. The school was also established to coordinate the work of the research and educational departments.

In early 2007 , the DePaul Political Science Department voted nine to three , and the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences Pers

pectives Committee voted unanimously, to recognize the DePaul University College Republicans as an official student group. DePaul University is a private, Catholic university in Chicago, Illinois. Founded by the Vincentians in 1898, the university now has more than 23,000 students enrolled, primarily in its undergraduate programs.
In the spring of 2007, DePaul University College Republicans president Colin O'Malley received a letter from the university's Dean of Students, stating that the university would not recognize the DePaul College Republicans as an official student organization because the group's "purpose is not in line with the University's Mission." The letter added that the group was not eligible for funding because its "purpose is not in line with the University's Mission." The letter also stated the group would be subject to "discipline" if it continued to present itself as an official student organization after March 15, 2007.
On April 20, 2007, the DePaul College Republicans, led by president Colin O'Malley, filed a federal lawsuit against DePaul University in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, Eastern Division, alleging violations of the First and Fourteenth Amendments to the U.S. Constitution.
The case attracted national attention for its allegation that a private university had violated its students' First Amendment rights.
On January 23, 2009, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois issued a decision in DePaul University v. College Republicans of DePaul University (Case No. 07 C 5532) denying DePaul's motion to dismiss the lawsuit, finding that the College Republicans had stated a valid claim that DePaul's action had violated their First Amendment rights.
On March 18, 2009, DePaul University filed a motion for summary judgment in the case. On July 27, 2009, U.S. District Court Judge Ronald A. Guzman denied DePaul's motion for summary judgment and denied DePaul's motion to dismiss the case. The Court held that the DePaul College Republicans' "purpose and activities, both as a whole and on their face, are protected speech" and that DePaul's denial of recognition was a violation of the First Amendment. The College Republicans had also alleged that DePaul's actions violated the Fourteenth Amendment due process clause. The court held that the College Republicans had stated a claim for violation of their due process rights.
DePaul then appealed the decision to the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit. On July 26, 2010, the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the District Court's decision.
The case was then appealed to the Supreme Court, which denied certiorari on April 18, 2011.
On November 29, 2011, U.S. District Court Judge Ronald A. Guzman issued an order requiring DePaul to recognize the DePaul University College Republicans as an official student organization.
In its 2012-13 annual report, DePaul University reported an operating budget of $791,631,368 and a physical plant budget of $436,347,649.
The DePaul University College Republicans received $1,051.29 ($1,129.41 in 2014-15) in funding from the university for the 2012-13 academic year, according to the 2012-13 DePaul University Student Organization Allocation Report, which was released on January 24, 2013, and the 2013-14 DePaul University Student Organization Allocation Report, which was released on January 23, 2014. The College Republicans received $1,115.47 in funding for the 2013-14 academic year.
The organization also received $1,500 in funding from the College Republicans National Committee (CRNC) for the 2012-13 academic year. The CRNC is the fundraising arm of the College Republican National Committee (CRNC), the official political arm of the College Republican National Committee, the official political arm of the Republican Party.

The west part of the Strand was in the parish of St Martin in the Fields and in the east it extended into the parishes of St Cl

ere, St Clement Danes, St Bride, St Clement Eastcheap, and St Martin Ludgate.
St Mary-le-Strand, 1592.
The Strand was the site of some of the greatest country houses of London. In 1592, The Honourable Thomas Sackville, Earl of Dorset, built Somerset House here on the site of the old Savoy Palace. In 1604, on the site of the old abbey of St Mary Overie at Southwark, the monarch James I granted land to his wife, Queen Anne of Denmark, who built Denmark House. To the west of the Strand, where there had been a palace of the Bishop of Ely, Queen Elizabeth I built Whitehall. It was one of the largest private houses in England and it was the first building in the world to have over 100 rooms. In 1637, Charles I bought the old manor house of the Bishops of Lincoln that was here. The king called it York House and it became the main London residence of the royal family. It was here that the courtier John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester, wrote some of his scurrilous satires. Rochester's poem 'The Strand' was the most popular song in London in 1672.
The Strand in 1675.
In 1649, during the Civil War, the fifth earl of Dorset was executed and the property reverted to the Crown. The king sold it to William Cavendish, 1st Duke of Newcastle, who demolished Whitehall and built a larger house. This was called The Strand House and it was later called The Savoy. The Strand House was the largest house in the country, until it was surpassed by Blenheim, built for the Duke of Marlborough. In 1702, the duke of Somerset sold the property to Charles II's illegitimate son, the Duke of Monmouth. The duke demolished the building and built a new house, which he called the New Somerset House.
The New Somerset House.
In 1726, New Somerset House was bought by Sir Richard Steele. He had been part of the Kit-Cat Club, which met at the Turk's Head Tavern. When the Turk's Head was demolished in 1721, the club chose the New Somerset House as their new home. The club was named after the poem 'The Vanity of Human Wishes', which was written by the club's member, William Congreve. The club's members included many famous writers, including Alexander Pope, John Gay, Jonathan Swift, and Samuel Johnson. We will meet them in more detail in the next chapter.
In 1745, the club was in the process of moving to Gresham College when it was destroyed by fire. The club relocated to the New Somerset House and in 1753 it was joined by the Kit-Cat Club. The club was now called the Kit-Cat Club and the Holy Club. The club elected a steward, who was to be the 'honest man of the company'. The club met on Sundays and on Wednesdays, when it was known as the 'dining club'. The club was the first to hold regular dinners with a menu and it had a wide range of cuisine, including French, Italian, and English food. The club was one of the first to have a wine list. The club was dissolved in 1754 after an argument between Steele and his wife.
The New Somerset House was demolished in 1756 and the site of the house is now occupied by Somerset House. The old house was replaced by a new building that was designed by William Chambers for the builder George Colebrooke. The new building was called the New Somerset House.
Somerset House, 1766.
In 1781, the building was bought by the Duke of York and deployed as the headquarters of the Royal Navy. In 1791, it was used as the venue for Prince William Henry's wedding to Princess Frederica of Prussia.
In 1798, the Duke of York sold the building to the War Office. During this period, Somerset House was used as the headquarters of the Royal Military Engineers. In 1803, it was used as the headquarters of the Royal Artillery. In 1829, the War Office moved to Wellington Barracks and the building was then used as a barracks by the Royal Artillery.

## Life

Robert Browning Harris (1850–1906) was an English poet and writer.

Harris was born in London to Mr. and Mrs. John Harris. His father was a member of the London Stock Exchange. He left school at the age of fourteen and joined the army, but was discharged on medical grounds after serving for only a few weeks. He then became an apprentice to a lithographic printer, and was able to travel to Malta, Italy, and Germany.

Leaving school without his family's knowledge, he made the decision to fight in the Civil War in August 1862. Despite his miraculous survival, he was never able to break free from the memories of the war. At the age of twenty-one, he published his first poem in a local newspaper—"Song of the Shirt"—and was quickly recognized as a brilliant poet. His first collection of poems, The English Poets, was published in 1862, and a year later he published his second book of poems, The Poems of Robert Browning. Harris continued to write poetry throughout the years, and in 1878 he published his last collection, Love's Labour's Lost. He died at the age of forty-nine. His son, Robert Browning Harris, also became an important writer.

### Marriage

Harris was married twice. He married his first wife, Margaret, in 1878, after meeting her on a visit to Wales. They had one child together, a son named Robert Browning Harris. Margaret died in 1880, and in 1884 Harris married his second wife, Emily.

### Death

Harris died in 1906.

The common starling has about a dozen subspecies breeding in open habitats across its native range in temperate Europe and west

Asia. They differ in appearance, laying eggs in different months of the year, and vocalizing at different times of day and night.
The starling's non-breeding range extends from North Africa to southwest Asia and east to the Himalayas and China. Some birds are permanent residents, but others are migrants and move to more temperate areas in the winter.
Starlings are gregarious. They forage and roost in large, noisy, sometimes raucous flocks, but they pair up to breed.
Starlings are opportunistic omnivores, eating a wide variety of plant and animal material. They will eat insects, earthworms, snails, seeds, fruit, acorns, and grain. They can be found in open areas, but they also adapt to a variety of urban habitats.
Starlings breed in the spring and summer. They are monogamous. Males and females sing to attract a mate, but singing males may have only a single mate, while females may have multiple mates.
When courting, males will often sing to a female and then fly through, just above her head, creating a "star-like" pattern in the sky. Successful copulation may take place as they are flying through the air.
Males defend territories that include a nest site and foraging areas. They may defend the nest site with characteristic swooping flight displays. The display begins with the male raising and lowering his tail feathers in a series of fan-like motions. He then darts forward and rises, with his wings held in a shallow V and his tail pointing downward.
The male provides food for the female. He gathers insects and spiders, scratches the ground for seeds and worms, and may steal food from other birds.
Both males and females construct the nest. The nest site may be near human habitation, such as a building or a streetlight, and may be in a tree or on the ground. The nest is made of grass, moss, leaves, lichens, and twigs, and is lined with finer materials such as feathers, wool, and hair.
The female lays three to six eggs that are incubated for about two weeks. Both parents feed the young for another two weeks. The young leave the nest when they are about 14 days old, but the parents continue to feed them for another two weeks. Starlings disperse by the time they are about one month old.
The starling's population is increasing, and it is considered a pest species, especially in Europe and the United States. They are often associated with the spread of diseases, such as West Nile virus, and they are often considered a nuisance because they gather in large flocks and can damage crops and ornamental plants.

#  RANGE
The common starling breeds in Europe, western Asia, and northwest Africa, and it is a year-round resident in southern Europe, western Asia, and northern Africa. It is a migratory species in the rest of its range, and winters south and east of its breeding range.
#  HABITAT
The starling breeds in open country, such as grasslands, fields, and roadside habitats. It also breeds in agricultural areas, where it nests in buildings and barns, in trees, and on the ground.
The non-breeding range of the starling extends from North Africa to southwest Asia and east to the Himalayas and China. Some birds migrate south to more temperate areas in the winter.
#  DIET
The starling is a generalist omnivore that eats a wide range of plant and animal material. It eats insects, earthworms, snails, seeds, fruit, acorns, and grain.
#  REPRODUCTION
The starling breeds in the spring and summer. It is monogamous. Males and females sing to attract a mate, but singing males may have only a single mate, while females may have multiple mates.
When courting, males sing to a female and then fly through, just above her head. They try to create a "star-like" pattern in the sky. Successful copulation may take place as they are flying through the air.

One tropical wave was present in the northeastern Atlantic Ocean on September 1. This wave reached the Lesser Antilles on September 3 with a 20% chance of tropical cyclone formation. On September 6, the wave developed into Tropical Depression 13 with the formation of a closed surface circulation. The depression remained a weak tropical cyclone for the next couple of days, but strengthened to a minimal tropical storm on September 8. By September 9, the storm had developed an eye and became a hurricane, and was named Hilda by the National Hurricane Center. Hilda continued to strengthen and became a Category 2 hurricane by September 11, attaining peak winds of 105 mph (165 km/h). Hilda turned to the north and began moving away from the United States. The storm reached its peak intensity on September 12. However, Hilda weakened back to a tropical storm by September 14 and degenerated into a tropical wave. The system dissipated over the open sea.
As a tropical cyclone, Hilda had little impact on land. The storm developed offshore and remained at sea during its entire life cycle. It did have an impact on Hurricane Hunter flights, as Hilda was used to test the new P-3 aircraft. Hilda was the first hurricane in the 1964 Atlantic hurricane season.

In April and May 1978 , Dylan took the same band and vocalists into Rundown Studios in Santa Monica , California , to record an

album of original music titled Street-Legal . The album was well received upon its release in May 1978, but not a commercial success.  The album peaked at #28 on the Billboard 200 chart.  It also became one of the few Dylan records to not produce a hit single.
The album received mixed reviews from critics.  Allmusic critic Andrew Viner wrote: "Street-Legal ranks among the most overlooked of Dylan's entire catalog, and with good reason: It's a big, sprawling album, its hooks are often subtle, and it's hard to spin while driving."  Viner praised the musicianship on the album, particularly the guitar, piano, organ, and backing vocals of the musicians.  However, Viner called the lyrics of the album "fuzzy."  Author Oliver Trager wrote in his book Keys to the Rain: "Street-Legal is admittedly Dylan's least commercial album, but it's also one of his best."  He added: "The songs are metaphorically dense and the lyrics are dense with references to other writers, obscure books, and philosophers. It's also the only Dylan album without a single hit song."  In 2010, the album was ranked #230 on Rolling Stone magazine's list of The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time.  In a 2012 interview with Rolling Stone , Dylan described Street-Legal as one of his worst records.

The gradual switch from amateur to professional continued in 1968 , when for the first time the chorus was supplemented by a sm

attering of professional musicians, mostly drawn from the Royal Opera House orchestra. The new regime lasted for just two years before the director, Deryck Cooke, decided to return to a more traditional amateur set-up, with the help of professional musicians for the first night performance. For the rest of the season a string quartet was employed to accompany the choir, but on the second night the chorus was backed by the Royal Opera House orchestra.
The year 1968, which saw the introduction of the new format, was also the year in which it was decided that future Christmas performances would be in aid of charity.
The first of the Royal Opera House choral concerts had taken place at the Royal Albert Hall in 1952, in connection with a performance of Handel's _Messiah_. The concert was repeated in 1953, and again in 1954, this time in aid of the Royal Opera House orchestra. In 1955, the second night performance of _The Death of J.S. Bach_ was held in aid of the Royal Opera House orchestra, but it was not until 1969 that the Royal Albert Hall became the permanent home of the event.
The Royal Albert Hall concerts continued to benefit the Royal Opera House orchestra, until 1987, when the proceeds went to the Association of British Choral Directors. The first concert in the series to benefit the ABCD was in 1988. In 1990, the ABCD decided to donate all the money raised over the course of the year to the London Chorus, a charity set up to find and provide work for homeless and unemployed Londoners. The charity was formed in 1989 by the then director of the Royal Opera House orchestra, the composer and conductor Sir Colin Davis. It is now known as the London Choral Society.
Since 1994, the ABCD has used the proceeds from the annual concert to fund its own charity, the ABCD Bursary, which awards scholarships to choral directors.
In 2009 the Christmas concert was held at the Royal Festival Hall, with proceeds going to the ABCD Bursary.
The London Symphony Orchestra has played at the majority of the Royal Albert Hall concerts, but in 1994 a new partner was found in the shape of the English Chamber Orchestra. In 2005 the ECO was replaced as principal orchestra by the BBC Symphony Orchestra.
The conductors of the London Symphony Orchestra and the English Chamber Orchestra have included Sir Charles Groves, Sir Malcolm Sargent, Sir John Barbirolli, Sir Colin Davis, Sir Roger Norrington, Sir Simon Rattle, Sir Antonio Pappano and Sir Roger Norrington.
The conductors of the Royal Opera House orchestra have included Sir Thomas Beecham, Sir John Barbirolli, Sir Charles Groves, Sir Malcolm Sargent, Sir Colin Davis, Sir Roger Norrington and Sir Simon Rattle. The Royal Philharmonic Orchestra has also made an appearance, with Sir Malcolm Sargent, Sir John Barbirolli and Sir Colin Davis conducting.

If G is a DAG , its transitive closure is the graph with the most edges that represents the same reachability relation . It has

the property that every reachable vertex in G is reachable in the transitive closure of G.
Given a graph G , the transitive closure of G can be computed in polynomial time using dynamic programming. The transitive closure T of G is a graph with the following properties:
 Edge t ∈ T iff there is a path from u to v in G such that t is an edge on that path.
 T is a DAG .
 For all edges t ∈ G, either t ∈ T or all edges on the path from u to v in G that include t are also in T .

### Example

The transitive closure of the graph below is:

```
        u
      / \
     /   \
    v     w
  / \  / \
 a   b  c
```

### Definition

The complexity of transitive closure is O(|V|+|E|).

### Implementation

The transitive closure of a graph can be calculated in \(O(V^{2}E)\) time by a simple depth-first search preorder traversal of the graph.

## Applications

### Shortest path

A shortest-path problem can be solved if the graph has a transitive closure. The shortest path from a source to a destination is found by following the transitive closure from the source to the destination.

### Graph coloring

An algorithm for finding the chromatic number of a graph can be expressed as a series of transitive closures.

### Equivalence checking

The transitive closure of a graph can be used as a data structure to check for equivalence of permutations.

### Finding a matching

A matching in a graph is a set of edges that are not adjacent. When a matching is found, adding it to the transitive closure of the graph can be used to find a maximum matching.

### Connected components

A connected component of a graph is a subgraph where vertices are connected by paths. When a graph is decomposed into connected components, the transitive closure of the graph can be used to find the connected component with the maximum number of vertices.

### Other applications

The transitive closure can be used to detect acyclic dependencies in a software program, or to find the longest path in a network.

The Scythians , ancient warriors who dominated the Pontic steppe and semi-desert tracts of southern Russia between the 7th and 4th centuries BC, are perhaps the most famous people of this region. Scythian nomadic tribes are known to have traveled along the shores of the Black Sea and into the Mediterranean as far as Spain and Greece.
The name of the Black Sea is derived from the Greek Acheron ("unfruitful") and the Scythian name for sea, "Melas". This was probably in reference to the Sea of Azov.
During the Greek Classical period , the northern coasts of the Black Sea were the site of many Greek colonies , including Panticapaeum , Heraclea Pontica , Sinope , Olympiopolis and Tyras.
The coasts of the Black Sea formed the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire , the coasts became the eastern frontier of the Byzantine Empire . With the decline of Byzantium , the Black Sea region gradually came under the control of the Kipchak Turkic peoples , who were gradually converted to Islam .
In the 11th century, the Black Sea became an important trade route for the Crusaders , who began to use the sea as a trade route to Constantinople and Asia Minor , and later to the Holy Land . The city of Genoa established colonies on the Crimean Peninsula and the coasts of the Black Sea in the 13th century.

The third storyline is concerned with the thoughts and motives of Rafael Leónidas Trujillo Molina himself . The chapters concer

ne the Dominican dictator's actions during the last three years of his life, and examine how these actions reflected on his character, personality and outlook on life. Trujillo had surrounded himself by an impenetrable wall of secrecy and lies. Hernández-Reguant tells us that Dominicans had always called the dictator "El Jefe," meaning "The Boss." But he also uses the Spanish word _jefe_ to translate the word _chefe_ , which is used in Haiti to translate the English word _chief_ , the one who heads a tribe. By this metaphor, Trujillo was both _el jefe_ , the boss of the nation, and _el chefe_ , the chief of a tribe. The latter connotation was particularly apt for a man who considered himself the reincarnation of Christopher Columbus, who thought himself a "tribal chief"—guiding his nation to progress. But there was more to it. Trujillo's Haitian ancestry had made him an outsider in the Dominican Republic. He always felt the need to prove his racial and national superiority, and therefore resorted to an authoritarian regime to do so.
The fourth and last storyline is concerned with the _ruling class_ of the Dominican Republic, which was a term used by the dictator to describe the country's elites. Trujillo had surrounded himself by a small, privileged group of rich and powerful people. They were the ones who benefited from his reign, and they were the ones who were in charge of the "totalitarian machinery" that kept the nation under control. Brooks discussed the cultural influences on the novel . He claimed inspiration from " The Good War " : An Oral History of World

War II , by Studs Terkel, and from his own experiences as a college student during the 1960s. 

## Overview

The book is a novel rather than a true memoir. The author says that some of the events are true, but many are not. 

The book is set in the 1950s and 1960s and is the coming-of-age story of a Jewish college student, whose parents had immigrated from Poland to the US during World War II.

The main character, "Sonny", is a college freshman who is fighting his own battle with religious faith and looking for meaning in life. He is involved in the civil rights movement and the anti-war movement. He is also involved in a love triangle with a black classmate and a white former classmate. He justifies his involvement in the civil rights movement by saying that Jews were treated badly in America and should know about discrimination. He says that he does not care whether he is Jewish or not.

The story is told in part through the eyes of a fictitious author who is writing a novel about Sonny. The author is the son of a rabbi. The author also has a love triangle involving a much older woman and the son of an immigrant.

The book is a satire of the cliches used by many college students in the 1960s and 1970s.

The book was made into a movie in 2011, directed by Stephen Hopkins.

## Reception

The book received positive reviews.

"A funny, touching and poignant book that captures the kaleidoscope of passions of the sixties." —NY Times

"A touching, funny and exquisitely realized novel of a young man's search for meaning, and a love story that is an homage to, and a critique of, the best of American fiction." —The Boston Globe

"A brilliant, funny and moving novel. Brooks has rendered a world of people in a way that is both tender and pointed." —The Washington Post

The opening production of the National Theatre was Hamlet in October 1963 , starring Peter O 'Toole and directed by Olivier . O

'Toole was a brilliant choice, having achieved fame in the role already on Broadway, but in a slightly different version, directed by John Houseman at the American Shakespeare Festival in Stratford, Connecticut, in 1955. The play had been a hit on Broadway and when Houseman agreed to direct the film version, the director had to be persuaded to allow O 'Toole to play the role again.
The film was made on the roof of the Mayfair Hotel in downtown Los Angeles, from which a Helicopter could almost be seen. The actors were crammed into the tiny hotel room, its tiny window overlooking the street, where they had to spend the day and night on location. The film was a hit.
O 'Toole's Hamlet subsequently became a legend in its own lifetime. It was the star turn of a star who was, at the time, one of the most famous actors in the world. The film was made in 1964 and its single-take, 90-minute, 24-hour sequence was shot over five days. The set-up was simple. O 'Toole was to play the role for 12 hours, but after being shot in the chest by his mother's lover, he was to "die" and the film was to continue without him. But O 'Toole was so exhausted that he fell asleep. After twelve hours, the film ended; but the actor had been so exhausted that he was unable to wake up and continue.
The film was a box-office success and the material was subsequently reworked for the stage. The result was a new production of Hamlet , first performed at the Globe Theatre in 1965 and then taken to Broadway, where it won the coveted Tony Award for Best Play. Olivier, who had been the director of the original production of the play, had been cast as the ghost of Hamlet's father. The play had been a hit and it achieved a new immortality when it was filmed for television in 1964. It was so successful that it was made into a musical.
One of the reasons for the success of this production was that it played with the boundaries of theatrical realism. They had a number of U-boats stationed in the area and these were ordered to patrol the south-western coast of Scotland to stop any invasion fleet trying to get into the Atlantic. As a result, the U-boats picked off the Lend-Lease ships coming from the US for the invasion as they approached the coast and a further convoy was lost.
The main body of the invasion fleet, which was supposed to be landing in the Lochs of Scotland, was now heading to the Irish coast, but since the Germans didn't know where it was, they ordered U-boats to patrol the Irish Sea to intercept it.
The U-boat commanders were not impressed with their orders and some of them decided that the safer thing to do was to return to base. However, this decision proved to be very unlucky. On the morning of 26 April 1943 a German U-boat, _U-124_ , was attacked by an American B-24 Liberator bomber near the Norwegian island of Romsdal. The bomber had been on a practice training flight and it was only by chance that it had met the U-boat. The American crew torpedoed and sank it. It was the first time that a U-boat had been sunk by an American-built plane.
This was the signal that the Germans had been waiting for. On 26 April 1943 they ordered all U-boats in the Atlantic to leave their patrol lines and head for the Canadian coast. This was the beginning of Operation _Paukenschlag_ , a German offensive in the Atlantic that was to last for the next two years.
The Germans had once again correctly identified the weakest point in the Allied war effort – the supply lines. They had already been successful in the Battle of the Atlantic and now they were going to make it even more difficult for the Allies to bring supplies to the European and North African theatres.
In the summer of 1943 the Germans started to use a new and deadly weapon in the Atlantic – the _Schnorchel_ , or snorkel. This was a tube that enabled submarines to surface and take in air without having to come up to the surface, which would have made them a target for Allied aircraft. This made the U-boats much more dangerous and the Allies had to change their tactics to stop them.

The COIC was given access to all the Allied intelligence sources – ships' logs, radio intercepts and reports and sightings from aircraft and aircraft patrols. Their job was to track down U-boats and then to pass information on to the navy and the RAF to enable them to find and destroy them. The COIC would also act as a clearing house for all the information that the Allies had about U-boats.
The COIC was a great success. It was able to find and destroy numerous U-boats and it was also able to provide information about the U-boats and their movements to the navy and the RAF.
The COIC was staffed entirely by volunteers from the three services, and its staff was drawn from all three services. The code-breakers and other staff volunteered from the Royal Navy, the RAF and the British Army.
The COIC was divided into two sections. The first section was responsible for finding and destroying U-boats, and the second section was responsible for keeping track of them.

The name Gustav was retired from the list of Atlantic hurricane names by the World Meteorological Organization in 2010. The name was replaced by Gert.
Hurricane Gustav made landfall in the United States on September 1, 2008, near Cocodrie, Louisiana, as a Category 2 hurricane, over a month before the official start of the 2008 Atlantic hurricane season. The storm left 79 dead, over 400 injured, and caused billions in damage in the United States.
Hurricane Gustav's origins were traced to a tropical wave that exited the west coast of Africa on August 28. The system moved westward across the Atlantic Ocean without development. The wave was forecast to enter a region of favorable environmental conditions, and on August 31, the system became a tropical depression. The NHC gave the system the name Gustav, the seventeenth named storm of the season. The next day, Gustav strengthened into a tropical storm. As it moved north-northwestward, the storm turned westward and began to intensify. The storm intensified into a hurricane on September 2. By late September 2, Gustav was located over the central Gulf of Mexico, and as the storm intensified, the NHC issued a hurricane warning from Morgan City, Louisiana to the Mississippi-Alabama state line.
Hurricane Gustav made landfall over Grand Isle, Louisiana, near Cocodrie, Louisiana, around 11:10 AM CDT (16:10 UTC) as a Category 2 hurricane, with maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 km/h). Gustav continued northwestward and weakened to a tropical storm, and made landfall in Alabama later that day. It continued northwestward and weakened further to a tropical depression. It continued to weaken and degenerated into a remnant low pressure area on September 5. The remnants of Gustav turned eastward and dissipated over western Mississippi on September 7.

In essence , the lbw law remained the same between 1839 and 1937 , despite several campaigns to have it changed . An 1863 propo

sition from the MCC to the Marylebone Cricket Club that lbw should be called if the ball pitched outside the off stump and was then bowled , it was a proposal which was rejected . The Marylebone Club had pushed for a change in 1879 , when it was felt that the law should be further revised to allow for the lbw to be called if the ball pitched outside the off stump , _and_ had hit the stumps before being bowled . This concept was rejected in favour of the so-called 'stumped' law that was introduced in 1889 .
ay
The stumped law was abandoned in 1890 , along with the lbw law itself , but the MCC had to wait until 1900 before it was able to reintroduce the lbw law .
 The 1900 law stipulated that lbw be called if any part of the batsman's bat touched the ball after it had pitched or bounced more than half-way towards the wicket , but the ball had to be struck before it had pitched or bounced .
 The 1900 law also made it clear that it did not apply to a batsman who was 'blocking' , and this remained the case until 1923 .
 The 1926 ICC meeting decided that lbw be called if the ball pitched outside the off stump and was then bowled , and that the law should apply to a batsman who was 'blocking' .
In 1937 the ICC decided that lbw should no longer be called if the ball struck the bat more than half-way towards the wicket , and that the lbw law should not apply to a batsman who was 'blocking' .

The main area of inhabitation of Bantu ethnic minorities in Somalia has historically been in village enclaves in the south , pa

ired with a nomadic lifestyle in the northern parts of the country. The majority of the remainder of the population are ethnic Somalis, descendants of ancient Cushitic peoples. They are further divided into four major clans—the Dir, the Darod, the Hawiye, and the Rahanweyn.
During the 19th-century conquests of Somalia, the Majeerteen Sultanate and Sultanate of Hobyo were established in the northern and central parts of the country by the Issa and Gadabursi Somalis, respectively. In 1884, after the Berlin Conference, British and Italian military officials partitioned the coastal territories of Somalia between them. The northern coastal region was administered as British Somaliland, a protectorate of the British Empire, while the southern and more strategic region became an Italian colony known as Italian Somaliland. In 1941, during World War II, Italian Somaliland was captured by British and Indian forces, with British Somaliland gaining independence in 1960.
Somalia thereafter remained a member of the British Commonwealth as the Somali Republic, until the government was overthrown in 1969 by a coup d'état backed by the U.S. and Soviet Union, and became a socialist dictatorship under the Somali Democratic Republic (Somalia, officially the Somali Democratic Republic). In 1981, after four years of civil war, Somalia collapsed into clan-based warlordism, which persists to the present day. The capital was moved to Baidoa in 1993, before returning to Mogadishu in 2000.
After the fall of the Barre Government in 1991, the country's first multi-party elections were held in 1992, but they resulted in the ousting of President Ali Mahdi and the subsequent beginning of the Somali Civil War. The United Nations Security Council thereafter authorized the establishment of UNOSOM I, which was followed by the nation's first major clan-based civil conflict. In 1993, a two-year UN arms embargo was lifted to allow the Course of the Somali Civil War. In 1994, UNOSOM II was established, which permitted the creation of a new transitional national government.
In 1995, with the aid of UNOSOM II, the transitional government assumed control of most of the nation's southern and central regions, but by the end of the year, it had lost control of southern and central Somalia to the Somali National Alliance (SNA). In 1998, the SNA split into the Alliance for the Restoration of Peace and Counter-Terrorism and the United Somali Congress, leading to the start of the Second Somali Civil War.
In 2000, the transitional government was forced out of Mogadishu, which then was ruled by the Islamic Courts Union (ICU), a coalition of Islamist courts introduced in 2006. In 2006, following the Ethiopian intervention, the Transitional Federal Government (TFG) again assumed control of the nation's major urban centers, but by 2008, virtually all government institutions had collapsed and by the end of 2008, the nation had descended into anarchy.
In 2009, TFG President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed stepped down from office and was replaced by former Prime Minister Abdirahman Mohamed "Farole" to serve as Acting President, while former Foreign Minister Omar Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke became the Prime Minister. In 2010, the TFG and the ICU formed an interim federal government (IFG), which assumed control of the entire nation. In 2012, the IFG collapsed, and its successor, the Federal Government of Somalia (FGS), re-established control over most of the nation's central and southern regions.

Alkan was not always remote or aloof . Chopin describes , in a letter to friend , visiting the theatre with Alkan in 1847 to se

ethe new _La Juive_ by Jacques Fromental Halévy:
Alkan was more than enthusiastic for the _Juive_ . He came back with us and sang the airs of the _Juive_ over and over again. He seemed to be very much in love with them. The house was quite empty and we were alone in the box . He sang the _Juive_ with so much sentiment and such a _fraîcheur_ of voice that I was quite breathless.
Another source of enthusiasm for Alkan was the music of Liszt , whose style he admired greatly and whose fame was at its zenith in the early 1840s . Alkan was known to have played Liszt's _Piano Sonata in B Minor_ (S.178) and transcribed some of his works for the organ . He also published a massive compilation of his own transcriptions of 36 of Liszt's works for piano (51 in all) . These transcriptions are of great interest as they show Alkan's own distinctive writing style and his many innovations as a transcriber .
Alkan was not only a fine pianist , but he was also an accomplished organist . He successfully competed for organist posts in Cologne (1829), Strasbourg (1833) and Paris (1841) – the latter position he held for the rest of his life . Alkan was also known to have played Mozart's organ concertos transcribed for piano by his first teacher, Vicente Rodriguez .
Alkan's method of transcription, like that of many other transcribers, was to first play the work on the piano and write down the pitches of the notes . He then added the pedal marks . The pedal marks were not always obvious in the score and Alkan often had to improvise the pedaling on the piano – a skill that he must have acquired in his early years as a church organist in Paris .
Alkan's transcriptions were sometimes criticised by the musical establishment of the time , who tended to prefer transcriptions of the works of well-known composers such as Beethoven , Schubert and Schumann . Chopin , who was a great admirer of Alkan's work, was one of the few composers who supported the transcriber . He once said that Alkan was the 'pianistic genius of the age' .
Alkan's transcriptions are still performed and recorded today and his influence can be heard in the music of contemporary composers such as Pierre Boulez and Olivier Messiaen .

The Peach Bowl was the final game as head coach of Virginia Tech for Bill Dooley , who had accumulated a record of 62 – 38 – 1

over seven seasons. The game was the Hokies' fifth consecutive bowl appearance and their third consecutive appearance in the Peach Bowl, which they won in 1989 and lost in 1990.
In the 1991 season, the Hokies finished with a record of 9–3, with their third consecutive Top 20 finish.
The Miami Hurricanes finished the season with a 9–3 record, which included a 5–2 record in games played away from The Orange Bowl, where they lost to the Florida Gators, 41–21.
The 1991 Peach Bowl was a rematch of the 1990 game between the same two teams in the same bowl, the first time this had occurred since the 1983 Cotton Bowl Classic (also known as the Hall of Fame Classic) between the University of Texas and West Virginia University.
This was the 44th edition of the Peach Bowl.
This game was the first in the series to be televised by ESPN. It was one of the first games to be televised by the network, having been established in 1979.

The San Francisco Bay Area was severely damaged by the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake. The quake caused much of the damage to the Embarcadero waterfront, which was reconstructed. The Golden Gate Bridge was closed to traffic for a week.
The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake (also known as the Loma Prieta quake), was a major Southern Californian earthquake on October 17, 1989, with an epicenter near Loma Prieta in the Santa Cruz Mountains, California and a maximum Mercalli intensity of IX (Violent). The quake killed 63 people, injured more than 3,700, and caused approximately $6–10 billion in damage.
The earthquake was felt across large parts of central and northern California and western Nevada. It has been described as "the worst natural disaster in the history of Northern California." Major stretches of the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge and Nimitz Freeway were severely damaged, causing them to be closed for several days. The quake also damaged or destroyed many buildings and homes in San Francisco, Berkeley, Oakland, and many smaller surrounding communities, as well as in San Jose, Santa Cruz, and other cities in the Bay Area.
The quake occurred at 5:04 pm local time on October 17, 1989, and had a magnitude of 6.9–7.1 on the Richter magnitude scale. The epicenter was in the Santa Cruz Mountains, near Loma Prieta, about 10 miles (16 km) northeast of Santa Cruz, California, and 4 miles (6 km) east of the city of Santa Cruz. The hypocenter was at a depth of 3 to 6 miles (5 to 10 km).
The earthquake struck during Game 3 of the 1989 World Series, which was being played at San Francisco's Candlestick Park, and was broadcast on television nationwide. The postgame coverage delayed in some cases by a half-hour after the quake was televised on CBS. The quake also struck during the 1989 National League Championship Series, with the Giants playing at the St. Louis Cardinals.
The earthquake was the worst natural disaster to strike Northern California since the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, and it was the worst natural disaster in California since the 1971 San Fernando earthquake.
The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake was the first earthquake to be recorded and felt by the San Francisco Bay Area's population since the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. According to the USGS, the magnitude 6.9 earthquake was felt over a wide area of northern California (from the San Francisco Bay Area to the Oregon border) and western Nevada. It was also felt as far north as Portland, Oregon, and as far east as Reno and Carson City.
The earthquake occurred at a time of high traffic for the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge, and it caused severe damage to the bridge. Approximately 100,000 cars were crossing the bridge during the time of the quake, and two of the 115,000-ton (104,000-ton; 104,000-metric ton) suspension towers toppled into the bay. One of the towers struck the Yerba Buena Island tunnel and fell partially onto the island, which was connected to the mainland by a small causeway. The other tower fell partially into the bay, with some of its pieces landing on the bridge deck.
A section of the Nimitz Freeway (Interstate 880) collapsed. The collapse killed 42 people and injured 200.
The earthquake was the largest in the Bay Area since the 1906 San Francisco earthquake.
The earthquake caused extensive damage, and knocked out power to a large area. The quake caused major damage to buildings and homes, particularly in the Bay Area, San Jose, and Santa Cruz. Much of the damage was caused by the collapse of chimneys, which killed 29 people and injured 1,000.

The activities and structures of proteins may be examined in vitro , in vivo , and in silico . In vitro studies of purified pro

-teins are used to understand the folding and other characteristics of isolated protein molecules. The use of in vivo studies with living organisms is used to understand how proteins function in vivo . The use of in silico (computer) models allows scientists to study properties of proteins which are too large or too complicated to study in vitro or in vivo .
The large number of chemical building blocks that can be combined to create proteins combined with the large number of ways in which these building blocks can be arranged provides a nearly infinite number of possible protein structures.
The observations that most proteins fold into a specific three-dimensional structure and that the structure is consistent with the amino acid sequence of the protein are known as the principle of structural homology. The term homology refers to the similarity between the structures of related proteins. For example, the protein fold of an enzyme is similar to the fold of all other enzymes. The principle of structural homology is important because the fold shapes the protein's function.
Each protein fold is associated with a three-dimensional structure. Scientists recognize a protein structure when they identify the structural features of a protein that are similar to those of other proteins with similar functions. For example, Figure 1.1 illustrates four protein structures that belong to the same group, known as the TIM-barrel fold.
Protein structures are also associated with a particular amino acid sequence. The sequence of amino acids in a protein determines the primary structure, or basic structure, of a protein.
The primary structure of a protein is the sequence of amino acids. The sequence of amino acids in a protein determines the primary structure, or basic structure, of a protein.
The secondary structure of a protein consists of the local folding of peptide bonds within the protein.
The tertiary structure of a protein consists of the larger, overall folding of the protein.
The quaternary structure of a protein consists of the complex arrangement of multiple protein molecules.
Many proteins are composed of multiple protein molecules. The quaternary structure of a protein consists of the complex arrangement of multiple protein molecules.
The functional structure of a protein is the way in which the protein's structure and functional sites are arranged to perform its biological function.
There are two general ways in which proteins can be classified. The first is by function. Proteins can be classified based on their function. The second way is by structure. Proteins can be classified based on their structure.
Proteins can be classified by both function and structure. The way in which proteins are classified depends upon the type of information available. For example, it is possible to classify proteins by sequence similarity, which is to say, by their sequence of amino acids. However, almost all proteins have a similar sequence. Therefore, proteins are more commonly classified by function before they are classified by structure.
Structural proteomics is the study of proteins by their primary and tertiary structures. Structural proteomics is an important area of study because proteins are the molecular machines of the cell.
The location of the functional sites and how they interact with the protein's structure are two important issues in protein structure analysis.

Ralph Merrifield ( 1913 – 1995 ) was born and raised in Brighton , and , following an education at Varndean Grammar School , he

was for many years a teacher at the City of Brighton & Hove Grammar School. In 1952 he was appointed the first Honorary Curator of the Town 's Museum ( now the Booth Museum of Natural History ) , and he was to fill this position for some 32 years until his retirement in 1984. His passion for Brighton 's history led him to become a founder member of the Brighton & Hove Archaeological Society in 1967 , and in 1983 he was elected as the first President of the Brighton & Hove County Local History Society .
In his retirement he was the author of several books on Brighton 's history and heritage. He also had a lifelong passion for collecting local photographs and ephemera, which he generously donated to the Brighton & Hove County Local History Society . Most of these items are now housed at the Brighton & Hove Archives & Local Studies , whilst others are housed at the Booth Museum.
The work presented here is a selection of his photographs, to which he added descriptive captions. The selection is of course highly subjective , and the author apologises to those whose work he did not include.

In different eras , various gods were said to hold the highest position in divine society , including the solar deity Ra , the

elephantine deity Amen (the consort of the sun god Ra), and the lunar deity Thoth , the consort of the goddess of the moon, Maat (or Ma'at). All three were members of the supreme divine court of the god Horus , whose own consort was the goddess Isis .  Horus became the patron of the pharaohs, who were said to be the earthly representatives of the divine court in the human realm. Some of these deities could be regarded as the equivalent of the Greek deities Hermes and Athena , or the Roman deities Mercury and Minerva .
Each of these gods had many different aspects, which were interpreted by humans in all kinds of myths. They were also worshiped in many different locations, and each was linked with specific ritual acts. In this sense, the worship of the various gods was not a simple religious ritual or a single act of devotion. It was a complex system of devotion and beliefs that was sometimes based on magical principles, and at times was also based on a deep understanding of the mysteries of nature.
As a result of the outstanding importance of these gods, they were also worshiped in the afterlife. This was a time when they were no longer regarded as earthly deities but were seen as the gods who were already part of the divine court, which had descended into the underworld. In this way, the gods became the gods of the dead and the gods of the living.
In many instances, the gods themselves also took on other aspects and were worshiped in the form of animals. Thus, the god Re was worshiped as a ram , and the god Horus was worshiped as a falcon . Even the goddess Isis became a vulture . Another example is the goddess of wisdom, Maat, who was worshiped as an owl.

The mind meld begins and Picard is taken to the past. He sees himself at the height of his career, serving with William Riker aboard the USS Excelsior in 2293. Picard, Riker, and the rest of the crew are called to the bridge, as the ship is being hailed by the USS Enterprise. Riker decides to go to the ship's Warp 5 engines to meet the Enterprise. Kirk orders Riker to return to the Enterprise's position, and Riker is forced to retrace his steps back to the bridge. Picard is angered at Kirk's decision, as he feels that Riker is being punished for a mistake.

The Enterprise-B is called to a meeting where it is revealed that the Starfleet ship they destroyed was the Enterprise. Admiral Cartwright explains that the Enterprise was sent on a mission to rescue a Federation officer who was being held in a Klingon prison, as well as to determine why the Klingons were attacking Starfleet ships. Starfleet Command has discovered that the Enterprise has returned to Earth, which in turn means that Kirk is still alive. The Enterprise crew is shocked to see Picard, as they thought he was dead. Picard explains that he is from the future. Kirk is ordered to take the ship to the Klingon Empire, as the Enterprise has recently been informed that the Klingons are preparing to attack Earth.
The Enterprise reaches the Klingon homeworld, and the crew is surprised to find that the Klingons are in control of the planet. Kirk orders the ship to be disguised as a Klingon vessel, and the Enterprise stealthily enters the Klingon capital of Qo'noS. The Central State Normal School , established to train teachers for central Pennsylvania , held its first classes in 1877 at a

two-story brick building in Boiling Springs , Cumberland County , when it was known as the Penn State Normal School. It was the first normal school to be founded in the United States . In 1923, the school's name was changed to Central State Teachers College and moved to its new campus in Bellefonte , Centre County .
The College was chartered by the Pennsylvania General Assembly on March 23, 1877, as the Penn State Normal School and Business Institute to prepare teachers for central Pennsylvania . It was established on the recommendation of the Select Committee on Public Schools, which was formed by the General Assembly in 1876 to study the public school system in the state.
The school was granted a charter for a minimum of 10 and a maximum of 20 years, and the first classes began in 1877 with 11 students.
In 1885, the General Assembly authorized the Normal School to confer degrees. The school conferred its first bachelor's degree in 1886.
In 1888, the General Assembly authorized the Normal School to offer a three-year curriculum, leading to a bachelor's degree, as an alternative to the four-year curriculum.
The General Assembly abolished the Normal School's Institute and reduced the maximum number of students that could be enrolled to 160. The General Assembly also required the Normal School to grant a bachelor's degree to at least half of its graduates.
