In 1904, the General Assembly authorized the Normal School to grant a three-year curriculum leading to a bachelor of science degree.
In 1909, the General Assembly authorized the Normal School to begin offering courses in agriculture.
In 1923, the General Assembly changed the name of the school to the Central State Teachers College.
In 1950, the General Assembly authorized the Central State Teachers College to offer graduate programs.
In 1961, the Central State Teachers College was authorized to offer courses in the arts and sciences, and in 1963, the General Assembly authorized the Central State Teachers College to offer courses in engineering and technology.
In 1963, the General Assembly authorized the Central State Teachers College to begin offering courses in education for graduate students.
In 1969, the General Assembly authorized the Central State Teachers College to begin offering courses in business, and in 1970, the General Assembly authorized the Central State Teachers College to begin offering courses in nursing.

Gaelic football , hurling and handball are the best @-@ known of the Irish traditional sports , collectively known as Gaelic ga

els games . They are played in Ireland and by Irish communities around the world , by about 2 . 5 million people . Along with association football , rugby union and cricket , they are the most popular sports in Ireland . Gaelic games are organised by the Gaelic Athletic Association ( GAA ) , which is responsible for the promotion and regulation of these sports . The GAA was formed in 1884 , and has since grown to a worldwide membership of over 600,000.
Gaelic football and hurling are played by teams of 15 and 17 players on a rectangular grass pitch . The objective is to score by driving the ball through the opponent's goalposts , or by placing it over the opponent's goal line , above or under the crossbar . The other major form of Gaelic sports is Gaelic handball , is played by two players who pass a ball with their hands against a wall . The game is played within 68-foot-wide (21 m) rectangular courts by men and women.

Rich Sisler, a professional baseball player for 13 years and a vice-president of A.G. Edwards and Sons, died of cancer yesterday in St. Louis at age 58.
Mr. Sisler stopped playing baseball after the 1945 season but remained a spokesman for the game, serving as an officer of the National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum in Cooperstown, N.Y.
Mr. Sisler was a right-handed first baseman who played for the St. Louis Browns from 1933 to 1942 and for the Chicago Cubs and Philadelphia Phillies from 1943 to 1945.
He was the first player to hit 40 or more home runs, 100 or more runs batted in and collect 100 or more runs in a season, all in one year. That feat was accomplished in 1920, when he hit 41 homers, scored 107 runs and batted in 167.
After his baseball career, Mr. Sisler became an executive with the investment firm A. G. Edwards and Sons for more than 30 years, reaching the position of vice-president.
He is survived by his wife, the former Elizabeth E. McDowell, whom he married in 1947; two sons, Richard Jr. and Mike; a daughter, Susan, and two grandchildren.
Rich Sisler, an outfielder who slugged 40 or more home runs six times and batted in 100 runs or more 10 times, died on Friday at his home in St. Louis. He was 78 years old.
In an era when the game was played almost exclusively by veterans, Sisler made his major league debut with the St. Louis Browns on Sept. 10, 1933, as a 22-year-old rookie. He was a five-time American League All-Star and finished second in the American League batting race three times, hitting .368 in 1933, .368 in 1936 and .345 in 1939.
He was the first major league player to hit 40 home runs, 100 runs batted in and collect 100 runs in a season. That feat was accomplished in 1920, when he hit 41 homers, scored 107 runs and batted in 167. He was the only player in major league history to have 100 or more R.B.I.'s in three different seasons: 121 in 1930, 108 in 1931 and 114 in 1936.
Sisler was a member of the 1934 World Series champion Browns. He was traded to the Chicago Cubs in 1944 and played for the Philadelphia Phillies in 1945. He retired in 1945 after playing in 1,808 games.
He was an original member of the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1939 and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1953.
Sisler's accomplishments did not go unnoticed by his contemporaries. In 1920, Walter Johnson, the Hall of Fame pitcher, said: ''He's the greatest hitter I ever faced. He hits everything.''
Sisler worked for A. G. Edwards and Sons from 1946 until his retirement in 1978 and served as an executive vice president from 1963 until 1972.
Surviving are his wife, the former Elizabeth E. McDowell; a son, Richard Jr.; a daughter, Susan, and two grandchildren.

During the Song dynasty , the city of Bianjing had three enclosures : the outer city wall , the inner city wall , and the palac

eless inner city. The main gate to the inner city was called Qingmen, a location where numerous offensives were launched against the Mongols during the Jin-Yuan Wars.
The Wanli Emperor ( 1573–1620) of the Ming dynasty, who reigned at Bianjing for 47 years, loved hunting in the Yongding Mountains . He used the Bianjing Hunting Pavilion to entertain guests; and the Wuyuan Garden was built as a strolling garden.
After the Ming dynasty fell, the Manchu conquest of China was announced by the Qing dynasty , which moved the imperial court to Beijing. The Ming palace and imperial gardens were made inaccessible to the public. Most of the city was now composed of shops and residences.
During the Republic of China era, the Qing dynasty Forbidden City remained intact. However, the city had fallen into disrepair and was in dire need of renovation. In 1924, the first phase of renovation began. The walls were repaired and the city was renamed Zhongdu ( 中都 ). The old Ming buildings were renovated and the city was planned for approximately 100,000 people. The second phase began in 1936, and the work was completed just before the Second Sino-Japanese War.
The Japanese invasion of Northeast China in 1931 forced the Kuomintang (KMT) government to move the capital to Hankou, but they returned to Northeast China in 1937 and occupied the city on 10 October 1938. The Japanese renamed the city as Chungking (中央) on 18 October 1938. It was also used as the name for the Japanese puppet government. On 16 October 1945, the city was renamed back to Zhongdu.
 The city survived the Second Sino-Japanese War , but was devastated by the Northeast China Campaign , which destroyed the city's infrastructure.
The city was invaded by the People's Liberation Army in 1948. The Kuomintang government and the Kuomintang Army retreated to Taiwan , while the city was renamed as Shijiazhuang ( 石家庄 ) in 1949.
The Cultural Revolution was initiated by Mao Zedong in 1966. The city was heavily damaged by the Red Guards, and the city and nearby areas were renamed as "Shengping" ( 盛平 ). In 1969, the city was recaptured by the People's Liberation Army, and the city was renamed as Shijiazhuang.
On 1 January 1983, the city governments of Shijiazhuang, Yi County, and Nanpi County were merged into the city of Shijiazhuang.
Under the 11th Five-Year Plan, Shijiazhuang became a National High-Tech Industrial Development Zone .
Shijiazhuang has a monsoon-influenced humid continental climate (Köppen Dwa) with four distinct seasons. The annual average temperature is 12.5 C (54.5 F), and annual precipitation is 551.4 mm (21.7 in). Monthly mean temperatures range from −2.1 C (28.2 F) in January to 27.3 C (81.1 F) in July, and from 14.7 C (58.5 F) to 23.4 C (74.1 F).
The city has an annual average of 1,757.4 hours of sunshine, and the annual average relative humidity is 73.4% .

During the early phase of the Battle of Passchendaele , Andrew 's battalion was engaged in fighting around the village of La Ba

iley. The 1st Battalion, Northumberland Fusiliers, had been forced to fall back, leaving many wounded behind. Andrew's company had been sent forward to help and the following account was written by the battalion's official historian, Major H.C.B. Robertson .
The first casualties were to the right, where a platoon of the Northumberland Fusiliers, which had been posted in the adjoining trench to act as a flank guard, was caught in the open and had to fall back. A party of thirty or more men was cut off and captured by the Germans.
The German gunners were firing incessantly at the village, and from time to time white flares of burning shrapnel rose from the streets. From one of the houses, the German machine-gunners directed a murderous fire upon the advancing troops, and the Northumberland Fusiliers suffered severely.
The German barrage commenced to fall upon the centre of the road about 7.30 a.m. ... The Northumberland Fusiliers had been plunged into a heavy barrage of shrapnel and machine-gun fire from the direction of the wood ... The line was broken. The Northumberland Fusiliers were driven back, and the battalion on their left had retired to the edge of the village.
Two platoons of the Northumberland Fusiliers, which had been in the adjoining trench on the right, and to which the situation was at once explained, at once came forward. The first platoon, under Lieutenant E. Pickering, rushed forward up the slope, and was at once checked by a hail of bullets. It had to retire, and was withdrawn to the sunken road behind. The second platoon, under Lieutenant A. Hall, having carried out a similar rush, also fell back to the sunken road.
The companies of the 1st Battalion, York and Lancaster Regiment, under Captain C.T.T. Wade and Captain A.J.R. Gibbs, had now arrived, and at 8.30 a.m. they were ordered to attack. They were to hold the sunken road and the trench beyond it; and as they advanced along the sunken road, the Northumberland Fusiliers were to come up to them on the left, and the 11th Battalion, West Yorkshire Regiment, were to come up on the right.
It was not until 8.30 a.m. that the 1st Battalion, Northumberland Fusiliers, were again able to advance, and their attack was delayed while the country was being swept by shell-fire.
The left-hand platoon of the Northumberland Fusiliers was working up the valley towards the village, and as it emerged from behind the stakes was exposed to a heavy cross fire from the wood. Lieutenant Pickering, who with a party of about 20 men had rushed forward and was making his way towards the village, was hit and fell dead.
Lieutenant Hall, who had already been wounded in the head and arm, and was unable to lead his platoon forward, was now ordered to retire. He asked for a volunteer to take his place, and a man named Laidlaw stepped out of the ranks and took the platoon forward. Hall, who had been slightly wounded in the eye, was hit in the chest and fell dead.
The position of Lieutenant Hall was very dangerous, and no one could blame him for wanting to retire. It was his duty to take his platoon forward, and so he had done. He had made himself a target for the enemy, and had been killed. We could not have expected him to do more.

The Dark Ages or Dark Age (Latin: saeculum obscurum) is the periodization of European history from the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century to the Renaissance period of the 14th century.
The Dark Ages or Dark Age (Latin: saeculum obscurum) is the periodization of European history from the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century to the Renaissance period of the 14th century. This periodization is essentially a European one, and is an invention of the Renaissance. It was unknown in the Middle Ages itself, which instead referred to itself as classicus saeculum (the classical or "normal" century).
The Dark Ages also refers to the late Roman Empire, or Post-Classical Antiquity, characterized by a decline in population, cultural achievements, and technology. There is no scholarly consensus as to what caused the decline, with proposed causes including social upheaval and invasions, climatic changes, economic changes such as delayed trade, and plague. The term "Dark Ages" was first used in a self-critical manner by the Italian historian Giovanni Lanza in 1834 in his book Storia della letteratura italiana, and by the French writer Jules Michelet in his 1840 Histoire de France.

## Plot

The game follows the adventures of two friends, the thief and trickster Meredy and the young swordsman Chester. They are both in search of a legendary castle in the center of a large forest. In the castle they find a mysterious girl named Anges, who is trying to find her missing sister. The two friends promise to help her, and they take her on their search for the castle. On their journey they encounter the bizarre knight Exca, who lives in a floating castle. He also joins the group, and the two friends and Anges set off to find the castle that has eluded them for so long.

## Gameplay

Tales of Eternia is a Japanese role-playing game with action elements. The gameplay is similar to Tales of Symphonia, in that the player can freely move their characters around the environment, interacting with NPCs and enemies. The player can attack enemies by using the characters' weapons to strike the enemy, or by using special techniques that use the elements of wind, lightning, and earth. The character's health and magic points are displayed on the top of the screen, and the player can use items to restore health and mana.

A tropical wave spawned a tropical depression between the Lesser Antilles and Cape Verde on August 7 . It slowly strengthened a

little farther to the east and became Tropical Storm Harvey on the 11th. By the 12th, Harvey was rather well-organized and was forecast to become a hurricane. By 1800 UTC on August 12, Harvey strengthened into a hurricane, becoming the third tropical cyclone of the season. Harvey rapidly intensified, reaching Category 4 status by August 14. On the 14th, Harvey became a Category 5 hurricane, but its peak of 160 mph (260 km/h) winds only lasted four hours. Harvey weakened back to Category 4 on the 15th. Harvey weakened quickly, falling back to Category 1 status on the 17th and weakening to a tropical storm on the 18th. Harvey's remnants became stationary, but the National Hurricane Center continued to issue advisories on the system. On August 21, Harvey was downgraded to a tropical depression and was last noted at 0330 UTC that day.
Harvey caused widespread flooding in the Bahamas, though little damage was reported. Harvey was the first hurricane to make landfall in Cuba since 2005 and caused significant damage in the westernmost region of the country. Damage in Cuba was estimated at $200 million. In Florida, Harvey caused minor damage and only one death.

In October 1891 , upon the formation of the first constitutional government in Zanzibar , Mathews was appointed First Minister

(Hakim) by Sultan Khalid bin Barghash. He was the first to hold that office. The office of First Minister was abolished upon the assassination of Sultan Khalid bin Barghash in 1896, and on the accession of Sultan Hamud bin Muhammad in 1896, Mathews was appointed Minister of Finance , a position he held until 1902. In 1902, Mathews was made a member of the Privy Council (Majlis-e-Shura) by Sultan Hamud, and was appointed Minister of Foreign Affairs, positions which he held until his death in 1924. The post of Minister of Foreign Affairs was a novelty at the time.

### Death

Mathews died on 31 December 1924. His grave is located on the grounds of the St. Augustine's Church, located in the Zanzibar district of Mtoni.

Germany and the _Germantown_ sailed to Newport News, Virginia, to join the Atlantic Fleet. On 24 July, she was rammed by the destroyer _Bainbridge_ because of inadequate lookout and failed communication between the two ships. While the _Germantown_ was under repair at Norfolk Naval Shipyard, she was reassigned to the Pacific Fleet.
 On 19 October 1917, the _Germantown_ set sail from Norfolk for the west coast, and after stops in San Francisco and San Diego, she arrived in San Pedro on 15 November. A few months later, she was assigned to the Pacific Fleet's Battle Fleet and patrolled the coast of Central America.
 On 25 April 1919, the _Germantown_ steamed off the coast of Mexico with a fleet of sixteen battleships and fourteen destroyers. Early the next morning, the flagship, _Oregon_ , was struck by a magnetic mine and sank in ninety seconds. The _Germantown_ picked up 449 survivors of the _Oregon_ and the battleship _California_ , transferred them to the cruiser _Chicago_ , and then escorted the cruiser and the damaged _New Mexico_ to San Pedro.
 While the _Germantown_ was at San Pedro, she was reassigned to the Atlantic Fleet, where she was converted to a seaplane tender. She was redesignated CV-12 on 14 November 1920 and departed San Diego on 21 January 1921 for the east coast.
 The _Germantown_ was overhauled at Philadelphia and then assigned to the Training Squadron, Atlantic Fleet. She visited Central and South America, and in 1923 sailed for the Asiatic Station, where she was assigned to the Asiatic Fleet's Scouting Force. After a year in the Far East, the ship returned to the Philippines, where she remained for more than four years. The _Germantown_ was decommissioned at Cavite, and while awaiting disposal, she was loaned to the Philippine Navy in 1928. She was returned to the United States in 1931, sold to the Philippine Navy in 1932, and returned to the United States in 1934.
 In 1935, the _Germantown_ was recommissioned in the United States Navy and assigned to the Reserve Fleet, where she remained until she was stricken from the Navy List on 24 March 1937, and sold to Bethlehem Steel Corp. in Baltimore.

Discovered by Fox et al. in 2002 , paraspeckles are irregularly shaped compartments in the nucleus ' interchromatin space . Fir

ms of paraspeckles, which are generally 20–50 nm in size, are densely clustered in the nucleus and are mutually exclusive. They are predominantly located at the nuclear periphery, with some paraspeckles extending to the inner nuclear membrane. The number of paraspeckles is cell cycle dependent and is increased by changes in the cell cycle status. These changes are caused by phosphorylation of the paraspeckle-associated protein PSPM1 , which has an amino-terminal kinase domain and a C-terminal WD40 repeat domain .
Although the functions of paraspeckles are largely unknown, their presence in the nucleus has been linked to different cellular activities. For example, PSPM1 knockout mice exhibit aberrant lymphocyte development and a reduced number of peripheral T and B cells . Furthermore, paraspeckles have been implicated in cellular responses to stressors, as the absence of paraspeckles has been shown to increase cells' sensitivity to DNA damage . Finally, paraspeckles have been linked to cell proliferation and tumorigenesis, as a reduction of the number of paraspeckles is found in tumor tissues .
In this study, we show that paraspeckles regulate cell cycle progression in a manner dependent on the cell cycle status. This regulation is accompanied by a decrease in the number of paraspeckles in G1 cells and an increase in their number in S cells. Moreover, paraspeckles are required for cell cycle progression in S and G2 cells, but not in G1 cells. In G2 cells, a decrease in paraspeckle number results in a reduction of the number of centrosomes and a reduction of centrosome amplification. In addition, PSPM1 overexpression results in a reduction of centrosome amplification. Finally, paraspeckles are required for G2 progression. In summary, our results demonstrate that paraspeckles accompany cell cycle progression and exert a homeostatic control on centrosome number.
Paraspeckles were first discovered in mammalian cells by Fox et al. . They are generally 20–50 nm in size, spherical, and can be distinguished from other nuclear structures by their irregular shape and their distribution in the interchromatin space, at the nuclear periphery, and in the nucleoplasm (Fig 1A). Paraspeckles are associated with but do not necessarily co-localize with the heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) family, which includes HP1α and HP1β . PSPM1 is a paraspeckle-associated protein that is shown to be involved in paraspeckle assembly and maintenance .

In the early 1950s , working in Hanford and Savannah River Sites , Reines and Cowan developed the equipment and procedures with

which they discovered the neutrino in 1957.
In 1980, as associate director of research at Los Alamos National Laboratory , Reines founded the Laboratory's Center for Particle Astrophysics , which was dedicated to the study of astrophysical particles such as cosmic rays , neutrinos , and dark matter. Reines was the associate director of the Los Alamos Neutrino Laboratory (LANL) from 1987 to 1990. He was co-author with John N. Bahcall of the first paper describing cosmic ray spectra due to the annihilation of dark matter.
From 1991 to 1995, Reines headed the Division of Physics, Mathematics, and Astronomy at the National Science Foundation . He was a member of the Committee on Science, Engineering, and Public Policy of the National Academy of Sciences , chaired the 1999 NAS study on the science and technology of the worldwide neutrino program, and served on the Advisory Committee to the Assistant Secretary for Science and Energy in the Department of Energy. Reines served on the Committee on Science and Technology in the Department of Defense in 2003-04 and was a member of the Committee on Science and Technology Policy, National Institute of Science and Technology. He was a member of the Executive Board of the American Physical Society (APS) from 1995 to 1997 and served as chairman of the APS Division of Astrophysics in 2001-02. Reines was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1975 .
The paper by Reines and Cowan (1956) established that the neutrinos were of antielectron type (i.e. they had a negative electric charge, as opposed to those of the electron, which have a positive charge). However the first, and still the only, detection of a neutrino of a different type was made in 1965 by Ray Davis and Frederick Reines at the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNO) in Ontario, Canada. Their detector had two strings of 1000 light bulbs, one containing only deuterium and the other containing only tritium, where, if neutrinos passed through the strings, they would cause a scintillation in the tritium bulbs and not in the deuterium ones. The experiment was, however, frustratingly difficult to interpret because the flux of energetic muon neutrinos from the Cretaceous Era solar system and the resulting background radiation from the Earth were so strong.

The clear @-@ cutting of forests in the 19th century adversely affected the ecology of the Plunketts Creek watershed and its water quality. With the onset of the industrial age, the effects of pollution began to take a toll on the health of the river. The capacity of the local and state governments to deal with these problems was limited by inadequate staff and resources. In addition, the manufacturing businesses themselves are not always motivated to invest in pollution control equipment. By the 1960's, the Plunketts Creek watershed was subject to the detrimental effects of soil erosion, deforestation, and pollution. It was at this time that the Plunketts Creek Watershed Association, a non-profit organization, was formed to deal with the myriad of problems and to try to find solutions. The lines of communication between the Association and the various state and local agencies were not always smooth. The Association's role was to act in an advisory capacity. The various agencies, such as the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Resources, were responsible for planning and enforcement. The position of the Association was that the local people should be involved in the decision-making process. The Association sponsored town meetings and involved citizens in the evaluation of environmental conditions. The Association also sponsored the development of a master plan for the Plunketts Creek watershed. Although the master plan did not provide a comprehensive solution to the many problems of the watershed, it was a first step in the development of a cooperative approach to solving environmental problems.

It is ordinarily used as a reproach, but with more regard to the effective use of terms than to their philosophical meaning. There is, then, a meaning of 'ideology' in which it is synonymous with 'philosophy,' in the sense of a coherent system of ideas, or a system of generalizations, for a determinate purpose. It is used in this sense, for example, in the phrase 'ideology of modern science,' which refers to the general system of ideas or beliefs that is in accord with some particular phase of the development of the sciences.... The term 'ideology' is sometimes used in a second, and a more legitimate, sense, namely, as a term of reproach, to indicate the extent to which a system of ideas may be used for the purpose of concealing realities or making them appear in a false light. In this sense, the term 'ideology' is applied to systems of thought which are, in their origin, intimately connected with the interests or the political and social life of a nation or a class" (1927, 12–13).
 There are, of course, many other possible approaches to the concept of ideological critique. For example, one might attempt to develop a more systematic, unified theory of ideology that would reveal the mechanisms of ideology's production, reproduction, and transformation (see, for example, Gross 1997).
 The term "theoretical-activist" is meant to evoke the idea that theorists can and should be actively involved in political struggles. This is not to suggest that theorists should dissolve themselves into activist groups or that activists should become theorists. Theorists should maintain their own identity, as theorists, and also should continue to develop their theory. Theorists might develop their theory by working with activist groups, but they should not do so in a manner that submerges their own identity.
 While the theoretical-activist is concerned with the ways that they are connected to each other, the activist-theorist is concerned with the ways that they are connected to the world.

## Background

The title of this episode was revealed by Jeffrey Combs on his Facebook profile on 11 August 2011. In a Facebook post, Combs, who portrayed Shran, stated, "Next week I'll begin shooting 'The Maltese Crusher'! My first scene is also my last scene! I'm looking forward to working with the cast and crew and will miss my dear friends, Jeffrey, Jolene, and the gang!"

## Plot

On the Enterprise, Shran and Tucker speak about the Maltese Falcon, a starship that Shran believes is in Federation custody. Shran plans to find it, but Tucker, not wanting to arouse any suspicion, advises him to keep it a secret. When Enterprise arrives at the planet Deneva, Tucker and Shran discuss the Maltese Falcon. Tucker tells Shran that it is impossible to find, and Tucker, who is known as a "savvy" investigator, tells Shran that the starship was destroyed in the Battle of Donatu V. When Tucker and Shran go to the bridge, they encounter Admiral Forrest, who is in command of the fleet.

Shran and Tucker's conversation is overheard by Captain Archer, who gives Shran a tour of the ship. When Shran is done, he and Tucker go to the ship's cargo hold, where they discover the Maltese Falcon, which is being used as a storage facility. When Shran and Tucker are done investigating the ship, the admiral orders Shran and Tucker to escort the Maltese Falcon back to Earth.

Critic Jamahl Epsicokhan gave the episode a mostly positive review. He said the plot was "pretty good", but that he found the episode to be "mostly forgettable." He did however say that he enjoyed the episode, and that "it's always fun to see Shran."

The episode aired on September 29, 2011 on Syfy in the United States. It remained in that country until May 16, 2012, when it was released on DVD and Blu-ray. In the United Kingdom, "The Maltese Crusher" aired on April 19, 2012 on Sky1.

Busch was a frequent visitor to the house of Franz von Stuck, on his travels to the artist's house in the Bavarian countryside, near Murnau am Staffelsee. Busch was also an admirer of the artist's wife, Fanny Lewald, who wrote novels under the name Fanny von Stuck. Fanny von Stuck was a noted folklorist, and Busch was an enthusiastic supporter of her literary and artistic work.

Busch died in Munich in 1915, in the wake of the First World War.

The 1947 UN Partition Plan in late November 1947 designated Haifa as part of the proposed Jewish state . Arab protests over tha

plan led to the 1947–1948 Civil War in Palestine and the 1948 Arab–Israeli War , after which Haifa became part of Israel.
In 1934, Haifa had 97,967 inhabitants, of whom 13,552 were Jews and 84,415 were Arabs. During the 1948 war, Haifa was captured by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) in Operation Horev on 21 October 1948. The war was over by 15 May 1949. With the war's end, 150,000 Arabs became refugees. Haifa's Arab and Jewish populations were exchanged, with the Arabs fleeing to the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, while most of the Jews fled from the Arab countries to Israel.
The city's population growth, and the growth of the Israeli population as a whole, were aided by an influx of immigrants, many of whom arrived in Israel illegally. These immigrants, mainly Jewish refugees from the Middle East and North Africa, came to be known as the Mizrahi community, and their arrival in Haifa is often dated to the mid/late 1950s.
During the 1950s, Haifa was chosen to host major projects, such as the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology , Carmel Market and the National Maritime Museum .
In the 1960s, the city expanded and began its shift from an industrial to a service-oriented economy. The city's port was expanded and the Carmel Tunnels were built. The 1960s were marked by development of the city's northern areas and by the construction of its first skyscraper, the Haifa Tower, an engineering landmark, which was completed in 1965.
The 1970s saw the establishment of the Baháʼí World Centre in the northern part of the city. In 1974, the city was the site of the Haifa Conference, one of the most important Baháʼí gatherings in the 20th century.
In the 1980s, Haifa continued its development, including the extension of the Carmel Tunnels, the establishment of the Hadar HaCarmel neighborhood and the Haifa Development Project (HDP). The HDP was intended to rehabilitate the city's poorer neighborhoods and to revitalize the city's northern edge. The city's first master plan, which was drawn up in 1959, was updated in 1985 to include the HDP.
Since the 1990s, Haifa has become increasingly multicultural and multiethnic. In 1997, the city had 250,000 Jews, 190,000 Arabs and 20,000 Christians. In 2008, the city had 276,000 Jews, 133,000 Arabs and 15,000 Christians.
Haifa is located on the slopes of Mount Carmel, which rises to 550 m (1,800 ft) above sea level. The Carmel Range is a continuation of the Lebanon mountain range and the highest peak in Israel, Mount Hermon, is 1,230 m (4,035 ft) high. The coastal plain is narrow, and Haifa's suburbs, including Kiryat Haim, Kiryat Motzkin and Kiryat Ata, stretch along it.
The city is bordered by the Mediterranean Sea to its west, the Jezreel Valley to its east and the Carmel Range to its south. Haifa is 90 km (56 mi) north of Tel Aviv, 50 km (31 mi) south of Akko and 30 km (19 mi) northeast of Netanya. Haifa Bay is one of the largest natural harbors in the world.
Haifa is a major seaport and an industrial center. The city has a large oil refinery and petrochemical complex, both of which serve as a center for the distribution and export of petroleum products. Haifa is also home to Israel's largest port, which is the country's main port for imports and exports and the only one that serves both its Mediterranean and Red Sea ports.

After her mother's remarriage in 1978, Fey and her family moved to Wynnewood , a suburb of Philadelphia .  Fey met fellow Saturday Night Live writer and performer Tina Fey , then known as Tina Henschell, at the Second City . Fey and Henschell became friends when they were both hired by Second City in 1993. Henschell later gave birth to Fey's godson. Fey married Jeff Richmond , a composer and lyricist, in 2001. On July 11 at 2: 26 PM, United Airlines Flight 93 crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania after passengers and crew attempted to take control of the aircraft from hijackers. The hijackers had diverted the aircraft to the Washington, D.C.-area to target the White House or the U.S. Capitol. Passengers learned of the other hijackings and decided to attack the hijackers. The passengers attempted to retake control of the aircraft from the hijackers, but they failed. The hijackers then deliberately crashed the aircraft into a field near Shanksville.
The plane crashed just 32 minutes after takeoff from Newark International Airport  It was the longest flight in the air at the time of the crash. The victims of the crash included four passengers ( Edward P. Felt, Jr., Thomas E. Burnett, Jr., Jeremy Glick, and Deora Frances Bodley) , three flight attendants ( Renee M. May, Louis J. Nacke, and Sandra W. Bradshaw) , and all four hijackers ( Satam al-Suqami, Mohammed A. al-Qahtani, Ahmed al-Haznawi, and Ahmed al-Nami) .

The song was used in the 2008 film Tropic Thunder and the 2009 television series The Mentalist .

## History

" Dog Eat Dog " was written by Talking Heads member David Byrne and Tina Weymouth.

The song was released as the lead single from the band's fourth album Speaking in Tongues (1983). The single was released in the United States on September 21, 1983.

In 1984, the song was featured in the film Repo Man.

In 2008, a cover version of "Dog Eat Dog" was used in the opening scene of Ben Stiller's film Tropic Thunder.

In 2009, a cover version of "Dog Eat Dog" was used in the opening scene of the CBS television series The Mentalist.

The book reviews in Super Science Stories were of a higher standard than elsewhere in the field , and historian Paul Carter reg

retted that they were "the only serious reviews" in the genre press. Other reviews were written by fans, such as the editor of Science Fiction Adventures , who in 1955 wrote that the magazine "represents the best of modern science fiction".  The editor of IF , however, complained that "The standard of SF magazine reviews is very low, particularly in the 'biggest' magazines. It's a pity that reviewers do not take more trouble over their work before publishing it."
Science fiction magazines were also reviewed elsewhere. The magazine Science Fiction Review was the first to review the genre, noting in its debut issue in 1939 that "we are now reading and discussing science fiction seriously". It reviewed novels and short fiction in the United States and Britain, and even included a section on current science-fiction films. It was also the first magazine to include reviews of science fiction films, starting in its second issue. Other magazines devoted to science fiction analysis included John Carnell's Science Fantasy in the United Kingdom and the British Science Fiction Association Bulletin . In the United States, fans of the genre also produced fanzines, which reviewed science fiction stories and books.
 Other magazines reviewed science fiction, such as the popular American magazine Life , which in 1941 featured a science fiction section and in 1949 reviewed several science fiction magazines. In 1957, the British science fiction magazine Science Fantasy published a review of Life in which the magazine's editor noted that Life's coverage was "a good deal more thorough" than its own.
 The editor of IF also noted that "the science-fiction field in the U.S.A. is better served by its magazines than it is by the book reviews as a whole". American science fiction magazines also included "Letters to the Editor" sections, where readers could share their opinions of the fiction they had read in the previous issue.
In 1947, the British magazine Science Fantasy began publishing a "Books Received" section in which it listed recently published science fiction and fantasy books and magazines.
 Extrapolation was the first academic journal devoted to the study of science fiction. It was founded in 1958 by Sam Moskowitz, Paul Carter, and Bob Sandall and first published in 1959. Its first issue included a review of the first volume of The Foundation Trilogy by Isaac Asimov. The review noted that Asimov was not a professional writer, but a "technical writer, a science-fiction fan, and a recognized authority on science fiction". The editor of Science Fiction Adventures complained that the review was "too generous".
In 1964, Asimov published a book titled Before the Golden Age , which included over 400 reviews of science fiction.

In the week following the Capitol One Bowl victory , several changes were made to the Alabama coaching staff . Defensive line c

oach Billy Neighbors resigned to become head coach at Southern Cal, while running backs coach Danny Sheridan left to become head coach at Utah.
The first change was the hiring of Coach Lloyd Carr to be the Offensive Coordinator and Quarterback Coach . Coach Carr comes to Alabama with 11 years of coaching experience, all at the Big Ten level. Prior to coming to Alabama, Carr was the offensive coordinator and quarterback coach at Ohio State for the last nine years.
The second change was the hiring of Coach Chris Beatty to be the Running Backs Coach and Assistant Recruiting Coordinator. Coach Beatty comes to Alabama with seven years of coaching experience. In 1996, Beatty was named offensive coordinator at the University of Tennessee.
The third coach hired was Coach Terry Bowden to be the receivers coach and offensive coordinator. Coach Bowden comes to Alabama with 14 years of coaching experience. Prior to coming to Alabama, Bowden was the head coach at Auburn for two years and at Samford for seven years.
Although the changes made to the coaching staff were significant, the year 2000 was not without its problems. The first problem was the preseason No. 1 ranking that Alabama received.
At the beginning of the season, Alabama was ranked No. 1 in the nation. This preseason ranking led to several problems that the team had to overcome. As the regular season progressed, Alabama began to struggle with being No. 1.
This was especially evident during the Iron Bowl , a game that Alabama lost to Auburn 31-20.
The second problem, which was related to the first, was the lack of respect that the team received.
"I think it was a little bit of a distraction," said linebacker Keith McCants . "It was a big year for Alabama. We were picked to win the SEC. We had a lot to live up to. I think we played with that added pressure and that's why we had some problems."
The addition of Coach Carr, Beatty and Bowden brought a new offensive attack to Alabama. The team was ranked second in the nation in passing offense and third in total offense.
However, the team was ranked 109th out of 115 teams in rushing offense.

# The 1984 San Diego Padres:
# A Season of Firsts
> _The Padres have had a great year. Things are going their way. It's a lot of fun to be a part of that._
> 
> —Tony Gwynn, 1984
After nearly thirty years of the San Diego Padres being in existence, the 1984 season was the first for them to play in a World Series. The team had been affiliated with Major League Baseball since 1969, and had been playing its games in the Padres' own stadium since 1980, but it was not until that October that San Diego was able to experience the thrill of playing for a championship.
Few baseball fans would have predicted that the Padres would reach the 1984 World Series. The team was in first place during the 1983 season, but was far from being one of the league's best teams. After the 1983 season, the Padres lost their best player, Tony Gwynn, who was traded to the San Francisco Giants. The team also lost its manager, Dick Williams, who left to manage the Oakland Athletics.
In 1984, the Padres were led by a new manager, Dick Williams, the man who had led the team to the 1983 Western Division title. Before the season began, the team made two trades that greatly improved its chances of winning. On June 11, the Padres acquired Joe Cummings from the Cleveland Indians. Cummings was a relief pitcher who had led the American League in saves three years earlier. The Padres also acquired Bill Robinson from the Detroit Tigers. Robinson was a first baseman who had played for the Padres from 1975 to 1982.
The 1984 season began on April 11 with the Padres playing the Houston Astros in San Diego. San Diego lost the opener, but won the next three games, including the final two in Houston. San Diego won eight more games before losing another one, against the Los Angeles Dodgers on May 1.
On May 20, the Padres were in first place with a record of 18-12. The team lost five of its next eight games, however, and were in second place with a record of 22-20 by June 9. The Padres were still in second place on June 26, but with a record of 30-29, were only two games behind the Dodgers.
The Dodgers and the Padres were battling for the division lead until the middle of August when the Dodgers, who were in first place, lost their lead. The Dodgers had a record of 54-43 on August 18 and finished the regular season with a record of 84-78. The Padres, who were in second place, had a record of 70-56 on August 18 and finished the regular season with a record of 92-70, one game ahead of the Dodgers.
Dollo 's specimens allowed him to show that Owen 's prehistoric pachyderms were not correct for Iguanodon . He instead modelled

the skeleton on the basis of the skull and teeth, the evidence for which was actually much stronger than for the rest of the skeleton. But here the fossil record was remarkably rich, with many bones coming from the same part of the body and with apparently complete skulls.
The most important fossil of all was the complete skull of a big pachyderm from the Weald of England. It was not unlike modern elephants in its bulk, with a huge, domed skull, but something was wrong. The lower jaw was completely different from that of an elephant. The teeth were also strange. There were no tusks, but the front teeth were large, curved and tipped with a concave crescent. And they were very far apart, with none actually in front of the others. It was clear that these could not be elephants. But what could they be?
It is not too much to say that the problem of the pachyderms was one of the greatest puzzles facing nineteenth-century palaeontologists. What kind of animals had these huge, elephantine beasts been?
Dollo 's solution was a stroke of genius. The lower jaw was unlike anything seen in elephants, he reasoned, because it was not elephantine at all. It was more like that of a rhinoceros, and so were the teeth. Elephants were mammals and rhinoceroses were mammals, so why not assume that this was the same animal? The front teeth were not actually in front of the others, he argued, because the whole lower jaw was curved downwards. The crescent-tipped teeth were not feeding tools, he pointed out, but used as a defence against other animals. The animal could be identified, he concluded, as a rhinoceros-like mammal, a rhino.
Dollo 's solution was not the last word on the pachyderms. As we have seen, anatomical arguments later forced a change in the interpretation of the fossil remains, and in the process the pachyderms were shown to be dinosaurs, their skeletons reflecting the growth of the bones of the skull and body, not of the teeth. But there was a gap this time, and that was the problem of the teeth. These could never be explained by traditional ideas about rhino-like animals. They were too dumb.
There were, in the end, a number of solutions to the problem. The most successful was to make the animal a giant, with big, elephantine teeth. And, in terms of the fossil record, the most successful was the idea that these animals were cynodonts.
The cynodonts were not dinosaurs, but they were a very important group of therapsid animals, which had been the dominant land animals in the world during the Triassic. They had lived on the Earth for nearly a hundred million years, and their fossils were much more abundant than those of the dinosaurs. They could be found in sediments of every age between the Permian and the early Cretaceous. Indeed, they were so abundant that they could even be found in the coal measures of the Carboniferous. They were the most successful group of vertebrate animals since the Permian, and had lost their competitors, the archosaurs, during the Triassic extinction.
In a way, the cynodonts almost became victims of their own success. As their fossils became more and more common, palaeontologists began to realise that they were not always the same. Some of them were small, and others were big, and some of them had large, elephantine teeth. So it was natural that the early palaeontologists should assume that the large-toothed animals must be the cynodonts. But they were wrong.
The dinosaurs, of course, had been around for a long time, and were thought to be related to the cynodonts. But nobody had ever seen a dinosaur before the invention of the term in the 1850s. Nobody had ever seen a dinosaur fossil, and there were no claims of dinosaur fossils until the 1870s. So, if you wanted to explain the large-toothed animals, the dinosaurs were not an obvious choice.
And that is why the cynodonts were so popular. They were so widely distributed in the geological record, some fossils of them even being found in the coal measures, that people simply assumed they had been around for a long time

The churchyard is on high ground immediately outside the churchyard and entrance to the churchyard is through a porch.  The churchyard is enclosed by a yew hedge in which there are 12 yew trees.  One of these trees is very old and has a trunk 15 ft in diameter .  The churchyard is of interest for the quality of the medieval monuments , including the Boothby tomb and the churchyard cross .
The churchyard cross stands in the churchyard and  is 15 ft high .  It is a red sandstone cross dated 1610 .
The tomb of Sir John Boothby and his wife is 14 ft long and 3 ft high and is 16th century .  The tomb is carved with the Boothby arms and is now partly ruined.
The churchyard is the burial place of the Reverend Thomas Bray, 1656-1730, who was the founder of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts.  Bray was a native of Tattershall, and was the Rector of St Mary's Church, Cripplegate, London.  He was buried in the churchyard at Tattershall on 6 October 1730.  Bray's tomb is on the inside of the churchyard wall.  The inscription on the tomb reads "In memory of Sir John Boothby, Bart. who died 22nd day of December 1714, aged 55. Also of his wife, Margaret his wife, who died 9th day of February 1730, aged 56. Also of the Revd Thomas Bray, Rector of Cripplegate, London, Founder of the Missionary Society in Foreign Parts, who died October 6th 1730, aged 73, and was buried at Tattershall, Lincolnshire, the place of his birth."
The churchyard of St Mary's Church stands high above a stream which flows through the village.  The churchyard contains the tallest ancient yew tree in England, a 25-metre (82 ft) high organically shaped tree with a trunk 15 ft in diameter .  One of the largest yew trees in the world , it is the second largest in Europe and the third largest in the world after those at Lewis in the Hebrides and Bardsey in Wales .
The churchyard is still used for burials.  The current parish priest is The Revd Canon Beamish .

The Great Coastal hurricane of 1806 was first noted far east of the Lesser Antilles on 17 August . Weather historian David M. L

esser (1963) named the storm Dorian, although he was not the first to do so. In 1806, the hurricane was essentially unknown to the public and, consequently, little was written about it. There are only a few brief accounts of the storm in newspapers of the day, which provide no information about the hurricane's track.
The storm was first noted by the British Admiralty's _Weather Log_ , which was kept under the direction of Admiral Sir James Saumarez, commander-in-chief of the Jamaica Station. No information is available about where the storm was when it was first noted. The _Weather Log_ noted an unnamed hurricane, and reported that the storm "was passing the south end of Cuba at 6 p.m. with violent gusts of wind, and squalls of rain."
The storm was noted on the morning of 23 August by Commodore Horatio Nelson, the second-in-command of the British fleet in the West Indies, who was on a voyage to Jamaica from the United States. Nelson reported that the hurricane was "about 10° south latitude, and about 50° west longitude, which is 680 leagues [2,600 km] to the west of the Magdalena River." The storm was 1,250 km (780 mi) east of Trinidad and 1,400 km (870 mi) east of Barbados. The storm was noted by Nelson as a "tropical gale" on 23 August, at which time it was moving east at 24 km/h (15 mph). Commodore Nelson reported that the storm was "very violent, and would be very destructive to the shipping."
By 1 pm on 24 August, the hurricane was still moving east at 24 km/h (15 mph) and was located about 9° north latitude, 58° west longitude, some 1,300 km (800 mi) east of the island of Trinidad. The storm was moving more east-southeast than the 210° direction of the hurricane, which was recorded on a 180° compass.
The storm was first mentioned in a U.S. newspaper report on 28 August. The _New Orleans, Louisiana_ _Daily Advertiser_ reported that "a most tremendous hurricane" had "passed over the Bahama Islands [Bahamas]," and that the storm "fell on the eastern coast of Cuba." The _Advertiser_ also reported that the storm had "done considerable damage in the Bahamas," and that "the towns of Jamaica and Turks Islands were all laid level."
The storm was also first mentioned in the London _Times_ on 28 August. The _Times_ reported that the storm was "in the latitude of the Bahamas" and was "probably the same" hurricane that had "been so destructive on the islands of the West Indies." The _Times_ article also noted that the storm was "reported to have done much mischief to the shipping in the Gulf of Mexico."
The storm was first mentioned in the _New Orleans, Louisiana_ _Advertiser_ on 31 August. In the article, the storm was referenced as "the late hurricane" and was said to have "inflicted great damage on the coast of Cuba."
In his account of the storm, David M. Lesser (1963) correctly pointed out that the storm was not the same one that had ravaged the northern coast of Puerto Rico on 20 August. Lesser's account of the storm was based on an article in the _New York Evening Post_ of 1 September, which was the first hurricane of 1806 to be reported in the _Post_. The Picts were a tribal people of uncertain origin, but were likely descended from a group of tribes of eastern and northern Britain who settled the area after the Roman withdrawal. They were probably a mix of peoples from across the north of Britain but had a distinct identity by the fifth century, when they began to gain in strength.
The Pictish elite had a tendency to be more Gaelicised than the population as a whole, and there is a possibility that some of the Hebridean population were Gaelic speakers. Their Gaelicisation may have been enforced at a very early stage, since the Gaelic expansion into the north of Britain may have begun as early as the fourth century. The Picts themselves are believed to have been first Gaelicised by the Irish.
The Picts were never a unified people, however, and kingdoms often fought each other. The Picts' isolation made them the perfect target for such aspirants, and fortified settlements, such as the Broch of Mousa in Shetland, were frequently attacked. The Picts were also attacked by the Scots, who seem to have been living in the eastern Highlands by the early middle ages, and they were constantly threatened by the Vikings, who began to raid the islands from the eighth century.
The first written record of the Picts is in the History of the Britons by Nennius, written in the ninth century. He describes the Picts as being divided into three parts, the _Picti Scoti_ , the _Picti Caledonii_ and the _Picti Orcadonii_ , the first of which were the inhabitants of what is now Scotland, and the second and third of whom were the inhabitants of the Orkneys and Shetlands respectively. This division is still reflected in the names for the people of Scotland and the Orkneys, _Scotti_ and _Orcadians_ , respectively, although the names are not used any more.
The Picts were organized into tribes known as _clans_ 1 and consisted of a number of families. The term _clan_ is used nowadays to describe a modern Highland family group, and this is the sense in which it is used in the following narrative. The clans were the basis of the Pictish army, which consisted of a series of units drawn from the clans, each of which was commanded by a chieftain. Most of these chieftains were godi (or _king_ ) of their particular clan, but some were mere _ceannard_ 2 (or _leader_ ). The population of the clan was organised into tribes, each of which was led by a _chieftain_ or _leader_ , with a council of elders called _Taighe_ 3. The chieftain was usually elected by the elders, although some were hereditary.
The clans had a sense of collective identity, and many clans had their own _Senachie,_ or hereditary historian. The following narrative is based on the traditions of one such clan, the _Senachie_ of the MacIain MacLeod Clan.

Determination of Pitman 's final fate has been aided by a 1914 article in the _New York Evening Telegram_ , and letters between Pitman 's widow and the War Department. I have their letters enclosed, and would respectfully ask of you that you will use your influence to have them returned to me." The letter from Colonel Pierce stated, "I have the honor to acquaint you that your husband, Major J. F. Pitman, was well known and highly esteemed in the department of this office. He was captured by the enemy at the battle of Gettysburg and died in this hospital, January 19, 1863 . I deeply deplore his death, as I knew him to be an officer of good character and patriotism, and a brave soldier."
In a letter dated February 2, 1863 , Colonel Pierce to Pitman 's wife stated "I enclose you the death certificate of your husband, which I have prepared according to the existing regulations of the Confederate States. I have the honor to be, dear madam, yours respectfully."

Bridges' division would have to hold the beaches until the rest of the Australian forces, the British 25th Division , arrived. The Australians would be in France from March 1916 onwards, but this was the first time they had been on the same front as the British Expeditionary Force.
The 52nd (Lowland) Division , commanded by Major General Douglas Haig , was the next to land. The 156th Brigade had recently returned from Gallipoli and was the first to disembark. Although not fully equipped, they were still organised into battle order and had suffered few casualties. The 154th Brigade , which had been serving at Salonika, was the last to land. They had been assigned to the 15th (Scottish) Division , commanded by Major General Douglas Niven . Both these divisions were being reinforced by troops from the British Isles.
On the first day of the invasion, more than 4,000 British soldiers were killed, wounded or missing. The Germans lost 2,700 men, of whom 745 were killed. In the following days, the Allies gained a small advantage and the Germans were driven back across the Somme. The Somme would be the first action in which General Robertson had command of the Expeditionary Force. It was also his first chance to see the latest addition to the British Army – the tank.
The tanks had been developed by Major Winston Churchill , the Minister for Munitions, and Captain Walter Gordon Wilson . The first of them were built by William Tritton of William Foster & Co. Ltd. in Lincoln. They were designed to break through the barbed wire and shell-holes that had slowed the infantry advance and the guns that had held them back. The first tanks were the Mark I, weighing 28 tonnes. They had caterpillar tracks instead of wheels and were armed with a machine gun and a small artillery piece. They could only travel at 3 miles an hour and were limited to a range of 30 miles.
The tanks were tested on the Salisbury Plain in 1916 and proved their worth. The first tank attack would be at Flers on the Somme on 15 September. They were under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Ernest Dunlop Swinton and the commander was Captain George McElroy . The tanks were a success and were followed by a cavalry charge during which the Germans were overrun.
At the end of the Somme campaign, the British Empire had gained 8 miles of ground and the French had gained 6 miles. By then, the Germans had lost more than 440,000 men, while the British and French had lost just over 400,000 men. The Germans had also lost 1,500 guns, 78 tanks and 197 aeroplanes.
The Germans were exhausted and had reached the limit of what they could do with the troops they had. Loose received generally positive reviews from music critics ; it holds an average score of 71 out of 100 at aggregate website

Metacritic. It debuted at number 31 on the Billboard 200 with 8,000 copies sold in its first week.
Critical reception to the album was generally positive. At Metacritic, which assigns a weighted average score out of 100 to reviews from mainstream critics, the album received an average score of 71, based on 10 reviews.
Billboard magazine critic Margaret Wappler called the album a "solid effort", but felt that it was weaker than the band's previous effort, including "a few repetitive and stale tracks". Drowned in Sound's Sean Adams gave the album 8 out of 10, commenting on Loose's "audacious" nature and compared it to the group's debut, 2005's Babel.
Pitchfork Media's Ryan Dombal and Amy Phillips gave the album a positive review, calling it "an amalgam of glam and slick pop, and manages to avoid the slickness of the former or the pop of the latter." The Guardian's Caroline Sullivan called the album "a textured, intelligent, accomplished work, which is why the band is a million miles away from the pretty boy vapidity of the boy bands." Ian Mathers of Stylus magazine gave the album 8 out of 10, comparing the album to the disco record "Donna Summer's I Remember Yesterday", and stating that the album is "a record that doesn't sound like anything else you've heard this year." However, he did criticize the album, calling it "the kind of weirdly earnest, self-important, and self-pitying album that hides the kind of self-loathing so many creatives are hiding."
"The Good Life", the album's first single, was released to radio stations on February 20, 2007. In the UK, the song debuted at number 46 on the UK Singles Chart. The song has also been used in the trailer for the film The Lookout. The album's second single, "This Is the New Year", was released to radio stations in Ireland on February 24, 2007. The song debuted at number 20 on the Irish Singles Chart.

Probably the most well known of the many Dutch East India Company ships was the _Amsterdam_ , which was captured by the French in 1672 and became the mainstay of the Franco-Spanish fleet at the Battle of the Four Days Fight off the Dutch coast . _Amsterdam_ was captured again in 1673 and _Zeeland_ was built as a replacement .
The Dutch East India Company (Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie Dutch abbreviation: VOC, Polish abbreviation: KVOC, abbreviated "VOC" in Dutch literature) was an early megacorporation founded by a government-directed amalgamation of several rival Dutch trading companies. It was established in 1602, when the States-Provincial of the Netherlands gave it a 21-year monopoly to carry out operations in Asia. The VOC was the first company to issue stock and the first recorded company to pay a dividend. The VOC was dissolved in 1800 when Napoleon Bonaparte's French Empire invaded Holland, and the Dutch republic was re-established.
The VOC was a major force in the Dutch Empire for more than 200 years, and the world's first multinational corporation. The VOC was directly involved in the colonisation of Indonesia, where it formed a colonial administration that ruled most of Indonesia. The VOC lands in Indonesia, with the exception of those in present-day Malaysia, were ceded to the Dutch government in 1800, and the Dutch East Indies were established as a formal Dutch colony.
As one of the first major trading companies, the VOC was active in trade with India, China, and Japan, and was involved in the slave trade until it was abolished in 1800. The VOC was also involved in the spice trade, and in the early 18th century, the company hired Johann Reinhold Forster to build a maritime botanical garden at its base in Batavia (present-day Jakarta), in an effort to produce new varieties of spices.

In June 1390 , Alexander Stewart , Robert III 's brother , burned the cathedral , manses and burgh of Elgin . This fire was ver

balized as vengeance for the death of Alexander's young son , Alexander , who was killed in 1389 by the MacKay clan at the Battle of Inverurie .  The city was rebuilt, and the cathedral was reopened in 1411 .
 noting that, although the parish church of Elgin had a long and distinguished history, the cathedral had been built only in the 1390s .
In 1619, the parish of Elgin and the cathedral were united , with the cathedral becoming the parish church.
 The cathedral was destroyed by the Gordon clan in 1645 .
In 1661, during the Restoration period , the cathedral was repaired and dedicated to St Andrew, but was subsequently lost in a fire in 1711 , while undergoing further restoration.   The building was demolished in 1712, and a new cathedral , which was designed by William Adam , was built nearby.  The new cathedral was completed in 1722, and dedicated to St John the Baptist.
The cathedral was destroyed by fire again in 1803 , and was restored and expanded . The new building was dedicated in 1815.
Elgin Cathedral in 2003 The cathedral was severely damaged in 1857 by fire, and the roof and interior were rebuilt in the Gothic Revival style by George Gilbert Scott .  The cathedral was re-dedicated in 1866.
The organ was built in 1907 by J. W. Walker & Sons Ltd. and rebuilt in 1960 . The organ has a single manual and pedal.
In the late 20th century , the cathedral underwent several renovations, including a major re-ordering in the 1980s, which included the moving of the altar from where it was to the centre of the chancel, with the removal of the pipe organ to the balcony.  A major renovation was completed in 2003, which included the installation of a new metal roof.
The cathedral is on the Scottish National Inventory of Historic Battlefields at the site of the Battle of Elgin of 1645, when the cathedral was attacked and burnt by the Royalist Army.

roides (which is the type genus of the family Therosauridae ). In 1835, he added the specific name velox , meaning "swift" in Latin , in reference to the rapid movements of the animal.
 The genus name was changed to Mochlodon by German paleontologist Friedrich von Huene (1877-1962) in 1932. The name was changed back to Emausaurus by Huene in 1940. This genus was later synonymized with a genus that Haeckel had erected, Emausaurus.
 The genus name was changed to Emausaurus in 1941 by American paleontologist Charles Lewis Camp (1893-1963) due to "internal reasons". It was changed back to Mochlodon by Argentine paleontologist Osvaldo Reig (1906-1989) in 1946.
 The genus name was changed to Mochlodon in 1975 by Camp and Argentine paleontologist José Fernando Bonaparte (1928-2014) due to "internal considerations". Some authors believe Emausaurus to be the correct name for this genus, and the genus Mochlodon to be a junior synonym of Emausaurus.

After the war Wiśniowiecki engaged in a number of conflicts with neighbouring magnates and nobles . Jeremi was able to afford a

number of palaces and manors. He was also a patron of the arts. He commissioned the construction of the Drohobycz Castle in Drohobycz in 1701 and the Olesko Castle in Olesko in 1712. His protégé was Jan Chryzostom Paska, a notable architect who was responsible for the construction of the two palaces. Wiśniowiecki also owned the nearby Pidhirtsi Castle. In 1704 he purchased the Mykulyn Palace in Uhniv from Stanisław Hozjasz Sapieha. In 1710 he purchased the nearby Przemyśl Castle from Franciszek Sapieha who became the voivode of Podolia. Wiśniowiecki also possessed the nearby Przemyśl Castle (now in Ukraine). He also built two palaces in Warsaw. The first was the Wiśniowiecki Palace on the Rościsławska Street which was later purchased by the Polish Sejm. The second was the Wiśniowiecki Palace on the Długa Street which was purchased by the Polish King Augustus II the Strong who later used it as his living quarters. On 24 July 1715 Wiśniowiecki died.
After the death of his father, Jeremi Wiśniowiecki inherited the Mykulyn Palace in Uhniv. His son, Jerzy Wiśniowiecki, later inherited the palace and owned it until 1725. After Jerzy died, the palace passed to his widow Maria Zamoyska who was the daughter of the Hetman of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland Stanisław Jan Jabłonowski. Maria died on 2 October 1754, and her eldest son, Franciszek Wiśniowiecki, inherited the palace. He was the father of the future Hetman of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland, Franciszek Ksawery Wiśniowiecki. When Franciszek Ksawery became the Hetman of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland he became a leading magnate in the country. In 1782, he married the daughter of Józef Pułaski. After the death of both Franciszek Ksawery and his wife, the palace was inherited by their son Józef Ksawery Wiśniowiecki. He resided in the palace until 1800. On 14 June 1800 the palace was purchased by the Polish King Stanisław August Poniatowski. After the third partition of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, the palace passed to the Austrian monarchy.
The palace remained in the possession of the Austrian Empire until the end of World War I. After World War I the palace was passed on to the Ukrainian People's Republic. When the UPR was divided into western and eastern Ukraine, the palace was transferred to the Eastern Ukraine. In 1922 the palace was nationalized and turned into a museum. During World War II, the palace was heavily damaged by the German military. After World War II the palace was repaired and reopened as a museum. The museum currently displays Ukrainian historical and art objects.

Aerobatic competitions take place for both powered aircraft and gliders , with up to 30 events each year in the UK and Ireland

and between 100 and 200 events internationally.
The Royal Air Force has a display team, the Red Arrows , which performs at air shows worldwide.
Organised forms of model flying have been in existence since the First World War and the 1930s, with the first international contest at the 1936 Berlin Olympics.
A group of air enthusiasts formed the British Model Flying Association (BMFA) in 1931. It is based in Grantham, Lincolnshire and is affiliated with the British Air Display Council and the International Aeromodelling Federation.
There are 50,000 registered BMFA members and 350 affiliated clubs who maintain 88 flying sites across the UK. The BMFA is the largest sport flying association in the UK and has over 900 volunteer instructors.
The BMFA regulates the use of model aircraft and has issued over 100,000 certificates.

The plain maskray is a mobile species that tends to move in schools.
The plain maskray is an omnivore. The plain maskray eats small crustaceans, small fish, and other invertebrates.

Thaksin Shinawatra

On 24 August 2006, Saprang led a group of demonstrators to the offices of the Thai Rak Thai party (TRT) in Samut Prakan to protest against TRT's alleged illegal financing of the party. Saprang demonstrated outside the party's offices, while some in his group allegedly vandalised the offices and set them on fire.

On 4 September 2006, Saprang was arrested for the arson attack on the TRT offices. He was released on 16 October 2006 on bail of 100,000 baht. On 29 November 2006, Saprang was again arrested, this time on charges of insulting a Thai monarchy after he allegedly called Thaksin a "traitor" and "traitor's king".

On 23 January 2007, Saprang was found guilty of arson of TRT offices and sentenced to 20 years in jail. On 24 January 2007, he was also found guilty of insulting the Thai monarchy and sentenced to two years and 150,000 baht in fines. The sentences were later reduced to 10 years in jail and 150,000 baht in fines. Saprang has appealed against the sentences.

During the SETI program , Earth 's scientists send out transmissions ( shown to be the Arecibo message ) with information about

the planet and its inhabitants, in the hope that extraterrestrial life will respond. The Arecibo message (Spanish: Mensaje de Arecibo) was a radio message sent to members of the Global Seti Institute (GSI) from the National Astronomy and Ionosphere Center (NAIC), located at Arecibo Observatory in Arecibo, Puerto Rico on November 16, 1974. The message was a sequence of numbers and letters that formed part of an attempt to communicate with extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI). The message was based on a design by the GSI, while the Arecibo Observatory provided the technical means of transmitting and receiving the message. The Arecibo message was broadcast using the 305-metre (1,000 ft) Arecibo radio telescope, which was used to send a signal to the globular cluster M13, 25,000 light-years away. The 1,679-bit message was transmitted at a rate of 10 bits per second over a period of 20 minutes.
The Arecibo message is one of the first unambiguous messages aimed at extraterrestrial life, and it is the first interstellar radio message. It was the first to be confirmed as having been sent to an extrasolar system. The message is the most famous or publicized interstellar radio message to date.
The Arecibo message contains a diagram of the human form, drawn to scale using the hydrogen atom as a unit of measurement, which is inaccurate due to the Earth's rotation. The message includes the atomic numbers of the 15 chemical elements which are most likely to be found on other planets and some of their most common isotopes, and a mathematical sequence representing a prime number . The main sequence of the Sun's life cycle is also included as a graphic. The message ends with the digits of π and a representation of the genetic code, which is a sequence of nucleotides (adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine) that represents the amino acids of life. There are seven of each amino acid, as they are the most common. The message also contains a summary of basic information about Earth, including information on its physical dimensions, its solar system, basic information on the human body, and humanity's technical abilities.
The Arecibo message was sent in response to a recent paper written by Frank D. Drake, Carl Sagan, and Iosif Shklovsky that described how a message could be transmitted to alien civilizations. According to a paper written by Drake in 1961, the Drake equation, the chances of alien life are one in a thousand.

18 th Dynasty kings, the ruler of Kush known as Senkamanisken , launched a series of raids into Egyptian territory. On one occasion, he crossed the southern frontier with his army and attacked the city of Cush . During the reign of Djedkare, Senkamanisken launched his second attack, this time against the city of Elephantine. The details of this attack are known to us from the record of one of Djedkare 's officials, a scribe named Senemut, who was serving as mayor of Elephantine. The city was under siege, but Senemut had managed to send a messenger to the king in Thebes. Senemut's messenger arrived safely, and Djedkare dispatched a relief force to save the besieged city. The Elephantine archives contain a complete account of the battle which took place between the Egyptian king's forces and the army of Senkamanisken; the Egyptian forces won the battle, and Senkamanisken's army fled back across the border into Kush.
The battle was a major success for Egypt, but Djedkare was not content to leave things at that. The king of Kush had set a precedent, and he would not tolerate future violations of the agreed upon border. During the subsequent peace negotiations, Djedkare demanded that his southern border be respected by Senkamanisken, and the Kushite king agreed to the terms.
Djedkare 's reign was also marked by one of the earliest recorded defeats of the Egyptian navy. In the region of Canaan, a people known as the Sherden have been mentioned in the records of several Egyptian kings. These Sea Peoples appear to have been a western Mediterranean nation composed of Phoenicians and other, related peoples. The Sherden were originally allies of the Egyptian king, but they rebelled against Egypt during the reign of Djedkare. A large fleet of Sherden ships crossed the Mediterranean to raid Egyptian coastal cities, and the Egyptian navy was defeated by the rebels. The fleet of Sherden ships sailed south along the coastal towns of Egypt, destroying and looting as they went. Djedkare was forced to mobilize the entire Egyptian army to defend the coast. The Sherden raiders were eventually defeated, but not before they had destroyed a number of coastal cities, including the port of Tjaru .
Djedkare was also involved in a dispute with the Hittites, an empire which had expanded its territory to the far reaches of the Anatolian plateau in modern Turkey. In a letter to the Egyptian ruler, the Hittite ruler Mursili I asked Djedkare to send his son, Djedkare-Nebsekh , to Hatti to be trained as a hostage. Djedkare refused the request, stating that he was concerned that the Hittites would use the hostage to manipulate him. Instead, he sent his son to Egypt's ally, Mitanni, to be trained as a hostage.
Djedkare 's reign was not without its problems at home. There is evidence that a man named Neferhotep was involved in a plot to overthrow the king. The evidence against him can be found in a papyrus document dating from Djedkare's reign. In the papyrus, a scribe named Ipi describes the events of a court trial in which Neferhotep was accused of treason. If Neferhotep was guilty of the charges, he would be put to death, and his holdings would be confiscated. Ipi's name suggests that he was a member of the royal court, and he may have been one of Djedkare's officials.
Ipi's testimony in the trial provides us with a glimpse of life in ancient Egypt. The trial itself was held in a courtyard in Thebes, and Ipi described the scene in detail:
The trial took place in the courtyard of the Palace of the Queen, and everyone in the city was in attendance. The accused was brought to the courtyard, where the two judges were already seated. As two series of inscriptions on the foundations of the monumental podium attest , construction of the sanctuary 's podium did

not begin until 1336/7 , well into a reign that had lasted for 16 years.
The monumental podium of the sanctuary is a series of limestone blocks, roughly square in shape and varying in height between 1.6 and 1.8 metres, of which 15 remain. Each stone is made up of two main components, the upper part being a broad, flat block and the lower part being a thick rectangular block from which the upper block was cut.
The series of inscriptions on the podium stones records the donation of the materials used in the construction of the podium by a number of noblemen of the city of Nicopolis ad Istrum. These inscriptions are so numerous that they also give a complete account of the names of the families who formed the nobility of the city, their titles and offices (at the time of the foundation of the sanctuary, the city of Nicopolis ad Istrum was under the authority of the Byzantine Empire).
It is not known how many stones had to be removed to build the monumental podium of the sanctuary of the god Mithras. However, it is certain that the donation of the materials was very costly both in terms of the materials themselves and the time required to transport them. The donation of the materials was probably made in exchange for a promise of the favour of the god Mithras.
 The first record of the existence of a temple dedicated to the god Mithras in the city of Nicopolis ad Istrum dates from 241 .
 The temple of Mithras was built on a very large scale, and the podium on which it stood, the foundations of which are still visible, was built around the same time as the temple itself, in 241 .
 Construction of the temple was probably carried out under the supervision of the architect Dionysius of Athens. He also designed the temple of the goddess Roma and the nearby monumental podium, on which the temple of Mithras was built.

After Edward 's death on 6 July 1553 Northumberland undertook the enforcement of the King 's will . Lady Jane Grey accepted the

crown, but the nobles who supported Northumberland had no interest in seeing her rule. The northern nobility, led by the Duke of Suffolk, the Earl of Westmorland, and the Earl of Pembroke, supported the Lady Mary, and Northumberland's arrest of them was their signal for rebellion. The two sides met at Northampton, where the northerners defeated the King's forces. Northumberland was captured at Welbeck, but the leaders of the rebellion refused his offer to join them; instead, he was imprisoned at Wallingford, where he died in late November 1553.
As Northumberland had lost his power, so also had the King's council. The Duke of Somerset, who had been the driving force behind the King's reforms, was tried and executed for treason. The Council of State made the Duke of Northumberland its president, but he had little influence over the King.
The King died on 6 February 1554, and the Duke of Northumberland was appointed regent on the same day. He ruled for nearly a month, during which he made some decisions without the advice of the Council. However, he considered himself to be the King's father, and he felt that he should rule in the King's name. It was only when the Duke of Suffolk and the Earl of Pembroke landed in the north that his authority was reduced in the last days of his reign.
 The King's will was read out at Hampton Court on 21 February 1554, and the Duke of Northumberland insisted that Lady Jane Grey should be the new Queen. The Duke of Suffolk, the Duke of Somerset, and the Earl of Pembroke refused to acknowledge her and instead declared the Lady Mary to be the rightful Queen. The Duke of Northumberland was forced to abdicate, and the Lady Mary was crowned Queen on 19 March 1554.
