1.2 Nearshore buoys
1.3 Coastal buoys
1.4 Marine Haze Observations
2 List of buoys
Offshore buoys[edit]
Offshore buoys are operated by the National Data Buoy Center and are a part of a larger network of buoys called the Automated Tropical Disturbance Monitoring System. The offshore buoys are used to monitor tropical weather and they provide information on the location of tropical cyclones.
Nearshore buoys[edit]
Nearshore buoys are maintained by the National Weather Service and are a part of a larger network of buoys called the National Data Buoy Center Coastal Ocean Observing System (COOS). The nearshore buoys are operated by the National Weather Service and are used to monitor weather in the nearshore regions, and they provide information on wave height, wind speed and direction, air temperature, air dew point, air pressure, relative humidity, and water temperature.
Coastal buoys[edit]
Coastal buoys are operated by the National Data Buoy Center and are a part of a larger network of buoys called the National Data Buoy Center Coastal Ocean Observing System (COOS). The coastal buoys are used to monitor coastal weather, and they provide information on wave height, wind speed and direction, air temperature, air dew point, air pressure, relative humidity, and water temperature.
Marine Haze Observations[edit]
The NOAA also operates a network of buoys that are used to monitor marine haze. The buoys provide information on the concentration of particulate matter in the air along the coast.

The Washington Senators were founded in 1901 as the National League Washington Senators. A subsequent Senators franchise joined the American League in 1903, and the two coexisted for six seasons (1901–1907). In 1905, then-owner Clark Griffith moved the team to Minneapolis, Minnesota, and renamed it the Washington Nationals. The Senators name was revived in 1909, when Griffith moved the team back to Washington.
The team was known as the "Senators" in reference to the U.S. Senate , which occupied the same building in Washington, D.C. The team's nickname was not a reference to any particular senator.
In 1954, the Senators moved to Arlington, Texas, and became the Texas Rangers .

In gathering inspirations for Wrapped in Red , Clarkson started by listening to Bing Crosby 's and Rosemary Clooney 's soundtra

cks for White Christmas (1954). She later expanded her music library to include the likes of Dean Martin, Frank Sinatra, Nat King Cole, and Ella Fitzgerald . The album's sound is influenced by both contemporary and classic pop music;[15] the album's first single, "Underneath the Tree", was described as a "contemporary take on an old-fashioned Christmas song" by Rolling Stone .[16]
  "Underneath the Tree" was released through digital download on September 17, 2013, as the lead single from Wrapped in Red . The song was written by Clarkson and Greg Kurstin. It was later added to the deluxe edition of the album on November 18, 2013. "Underneath the Tree" was a commercial success, reaching number four on the US Billboard Hot 100, and number six in Canada. Internationally, it became a top 40 hit in New Zealand and the United Kingdom. "The Greatest Gift of All" was released on November 22, 2013, as the second single from Wrapped in Red . It was written by Clarkson, Chris DeStefano, and Sia. The song became a top 40 hit in the United States, and a top 10 hit in Canada. The album's third single, "Wrapped in Red", was released on March 31, 2014. The song was written by Clarkson and Martin Johnson. It became a top 30 hit in the United States, and a top 20 hit in Canada.
 Wrapped in Red received generally positive reviews from music critics. At Metacritic , which assigns a normalized rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream critics, the album received an average score of 61, based on 17 reviews, which indicates "generally favorable reviews". Jon Pareles of The New York Times called Wrapped in Red "a holiday album that's a little more grown-up than the usual stuff: warm and melancholy, not saccharine or cloying" and stated that it is "a charming album that's mainly warmly nostalgic and not too schmaltzy."[22] Stephen Thomas Erlewine, writing for AllMusic , said that "Clarkson turns in a respectable performance on this holiday album, but it's hard to get excited about a set without any surprises."[23] Leah Greenblatt of Entertainment Weekly gave the album a "B" and wrote that "Clarkson doesn't necessarily make a case for herself as a pop mistress, but she's at least learned to sound like she believes what she's singing."[24]

## Commercial performance

In the United States, Wrapped in Red debuted at number two on the Billboard 200 with first-week sales of 273,000 copies, behind Justin Timberlake 's The 20/20 Experience – 2 of 2 .[26] The album was later certified platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) for shipments of at least one million copies in the United States.[27] In Canada, Wrapped in Red debuted at number one on the Canadian Albums Chart with first-week sales of 25,000 copies, marking Clarkson's second number-one album in the country.[28] The album also topped the US Top Holiday Albums chart, becoming Clarkson's third number-one album on the chart.[29]

In 1972 a testimonial match was organised by Everton on Lawton 's behalf to help him pay off his debts of around £ 6 @,@ 000 .

The game, which was played at Goodison Park on 29 April, was between Everton and a Rest of the World team. 'Lawton was in awe of the reception,' recalled his international team-mate Peter Osgood. 'I think it was the first time he had really appreciated the love that the Everton fans had for him. It was a very special day for him, and a wonderful moment for me to witness.'
As a footballer, Lawton was a complete player. His strengths were his vision, his timing, his intelligence, his pace and his reading of the game. He was also a player who scored goals of beauty. Lawton had moved to Everton as a boy of sixteen and, although the club had loaned him out to Carlisle, he had returned to Goodison Park. He had been with Everton for eight years and, in that time, had scored 108 goals in 283 matches.
Lawton was born in the mining village of Higher Walton, near Wigan, on 19 December 1943. He was brought up by his mother, Doris, in a modest home in a back street off Walthew Street, a few hundred yards from Walton Park. It was a house he would remember for the rest of his life.
His father, William, had been killed in action. He had met Doris before the Second World War and their son was born nine months later. 'I was born the day before the war ended,' said Lawton, 'and my father was killed the day after the war ended. He was a flying officer in Lancaster bombers and was killed when they came back from Germany.'
In the 1950s, still a boy, Lawton watched Everton regularly at Goodison, but he had another boyhood hero. It was not another footballer but a white-flighting racing driver, Stirling Moss. Moss was four years older than Lawton and had been born in 1929, when Lawton was five. He had driven for Mercedes and Maserati and had won the French Grand Prix at Montlhéry. Everton, he felt, were already his team, but he had a further reason for supporting the club. 'I loved Stirling Moss, and I used to watch him driving,' said Lawton. 'I think it was because my mum was a nurse and she used to look after him when he was ill.'
Lawton was encouraged to play football by his uncle, a local Everton supporter, and he started playing for Higher Walton Boys Club. He was spotted by the Everton scouts and was signed up to the club. His first season was as an amateur and he played in the reserves. 'I loved it,' said Lawton. 'I was playing regularly in the reserves and I was playing for their first team in the Lancashire Junior Cup. I was lucky to be playing, but I was still an amateur.'
Lawton was signed professional in October 1960, and in the same month he played his first first-team game, against Nottingham Forest in the League Cup. He was eighteen years old. The following week he made his first Football League appearance, coming on as a substitute against Sunderland.
He always maintained that he did not consider himself to be a professional footballer until he had signed a professional contract. 'I was paid £ 1 0 @,@ 000 as an amateur, and that was for 45 weeks a year,' he said. 'I used to work on other jobs during the summer holidays, and I didn't consider myself to be a professional footballer until I signed a professional contract, and I did that at eighteen.'
Lawton formed a partnership with Jimmy Husband, who had played for Everton as a junior. They were both teenagers and they were signed to help fill the void left by the departure of Derek Temple and Roy Vernon. As the years passed, Lawton was the one who became the more popular of the pair. He was a more flamboyant player and, as he became older, found it easier to express himself.
'Jimmy was a good player, but he was a bit shy,' said Lawton. 'He was a good lad, and I got on well with him, but he was more of a quiet character. I was more flamboyant, and I played a lot of games for England and I was more confident about that. I was more confident. I was more confident of my own ability.'

Murphy and Falchuk are also the executive producers of the show. The first season was produced by 20th Century Fox Television.
The show is a musical comedy-drama, which follows a group of students who participate in the Glee Club at McKinley High School in Lima, Ohio. The show has a series of storylines that intertwine with each other and display aspects of the characters' personal and professional lives.
The show has received widespread critical acclaim and has been called "a game-changer" by critics. It has been praised for the quality of the show's music, its subject matter, and its characters. The show has won numerous awards, including the Golden Globe Award for Best Television Series – Musical or Comedy, the Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Comedy Series, and the Emmy Award for Outstanding Casting for a Comedy Series.
In the first season, the Glee Club's main storyline revolves around the attempts of Mr. Schuester to revive Glee Club at McKinley High School. The main characters of the show are the Glee Club members, and they are all students in the school. The Glee Club members are Finn Hudson, Rachel Berry, Kurt Hummel, Artie Abrams, Tina Cohen-Chang, Mercedes Jones, and Quinn Fabray. The secondary characters of the show are the members of the Cheerios, the students of the school, and the parents of the Glee Club members.

McNichol graduated from junior footballer and apprentice motor mechanic in his native Scotland to a professional contract with

2nd placed Dumbarton.

## Early career

McNichol spent eight seasons as a junior footballer, playing for Rangers, Dumbarton and Partick Thistle before joining Dumbarton in 1951. After 42 games and 10 goals in his first season, McNichol was signed by Third Lanark and spent the next three seasons with the club, making 119 appearances and scoring 32 goals.

## Rangers

In 1955, McNichol signed for Scottish league champions Rangers, making his Scottish league debut in a 7–2 home win against Celtic in January 1956. He made 10 league appearances in his first season at Ibrox, scoring twice. After just one league appearance in his second season at Ibrox, McNichol was sold to Hearts, making the move to Tynecastle in March 1957.

## Hearts

In the 1957–58 season, McNichol spent two-thirds of his time on the bench, only getting a regular run of games from October to December 1957. He was sold to 2nd Division Dunfermline Athletic in March 1958.

## Dunfermline Athletic

McNichol joined Dunfermline in early 1958 and scored 15 goals in his first season at East End Park. He was transferred to Celtic in May 1958 for £7,000.

## Celtic

McNichol joined Celtic in May 1958 and scored on his debut, a 2–2 home draw against Hearts on 23 August 1958. He spent two seasons at Celtic Park, scoring 14 times in 69 appearances.

## Later career

In January 1960, McNichol joined Third Division Stenhousemuir and scored 13 goals in 23 appearances before joining Second Division Raith Rovers in September 1960. McNichol played for Raith Rovers, making 14 appearances and scoring 6 goals, before joining Newcastle United in November 1960.

McNichol spent one season at St James' Park, making 13 appearances and scoring 1 goal, before returning to Scotland with Dunfermline Athletic.

### Dunfermline Athletic

McNichol made 15 appearances and scored 3 goals before being released in July 1962.

## Later career

McNichol had brief spells with Hamilton Academical and Cowdenbeath before retiring from playing in 1963.

## After retirement

McNichol spent several years as a coach with Dumbarton and Hamilton before retiring from the game in 1969. He died in December 2017 in Glasgow aged 81.

Loss of habitat is the other major threat to the corn crake . Apart from the reduced suitability of drained and fertilised sila

, this has been attributed to the loss of wet heath, such as that of the New Forest, or the replacement of wet grassland by intensive farming. There has also been a decline in the shelter-belt of woodland in East Anglia that used to be available in winter as a flight refuge.
Nevertheless, the corn crake remains one of the most characteristic and widespread of our summer migrants. It is a symbol of the natural history of the English countryside, and it deserves our care and protection.
The American version of the corn crake, _Zapornia americana_ , has been well described by Herbert Spencer, in his _Natural History of the United States of North America_ (1841): 'It is a little bird about the size of a sparrow, which, when seen on a branch, is a very pretty object, having a soft, silvery grey coat, with a jet black head and wings. It is a very noisy bird, both in the daytime and at night, and is a great favourite with the Indians. They have a number of very pretty songs, and the music of the "Chickadee", as it is called by the Indians, is very soothing and pleasant to the ear of the skilled hunter, especially at night, when the notes come to him with a peculiar distinctness and loudness, and, as it were, almost a human tone.'
The Corn Crake has a long history in literature. It was first mentioned in _Gawain and the Green Knight_ , and it has been the subject of many later poems.
The theme of the poem 'The Corn Crake' by James Elroy Flecker (1884–1915) was inspired by a visit to the New Forest in 1909.

Phoenicians of the coast towns of Canaan are described as having migrated to the Western Mediterranean, particularly to the island of Sicily, which was called the "Phoenician Isle." This migration was part of a phenomenon which caused the progressive displacement of the Canaanites by the Israelites.
The name "Phoenician" has now been replaced by "Carthaginian." The Phoenicians were the first peoples to use the alphabet, the oldest of which was found in the royal tombs at Ugarit (Syria) and dates back to the fourteenth century BC. The first alphabet, called the "Ugaritic alphabet," had only twenty-two letters. The alphabet was adapted to other languages, including Greek.
The Phoenicians were expert seamen, and their ships were used to carry out the expeditions of the Assyrian kings, Babylonians, Persians, and Greeks.
Among the Phoenicians of the coast towns of Canaan there were rival cities, each with its own fleet of ships. These cities were Sidon, Tyre, Byblos, Berytus (Beirut), and Arwad.
The Phoenicians founded trading colonies in the Western Mediterranean, including Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily, and Malta.
During the reign of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon, the king of Tyre, Hiram I, sent a fleet to the coast of Spain to intercept the merchant ships of the Phoenician city of Cadiz, which was a prosperous commercial city.
Among the kingdoms of the West, the Phoenicians of Sidon were the most enterprising. They established a colony in the city of Carthage, which became a wealthy trading city.
Hanno, the Phoenician sailor who made the exploration of Africa in the second century BC, was born in Carthage.
Several peoples of the Egyptian delta, who had settled there in prehistoric times, and the Libyans who immigrated there later, became known as "Egyptians."
The Egyptians of the delta, who were also called "Masri," were the earliest settlers of the Nile valley. The first capital of Egypt was called "Memphis."
The Egyptians had a complex religion, which can be divided into four periods, and which also influenced the religion of nearby kingdoms, such as the Canaanites and the Jews.
The first period began with the unification of Egypt by Narmer, who established the city of Memphis as capital.
The second period of Egyptian religion began with the Old Kingdom, which had its capital at Memphis, and ended with the Second Intermediate Period.
The third period began with the New Kingdom, which had its capital at Thebes, and ended with the fall of the kingdom.
The fourth period began with the spread of the "Ptolemaic" dynasty in Egypt, and ended with the conquest of Egypt by the Romans in the first century AD.
The Egyptians were a warlike people. The first Egyptian king, Narmer, was a conqueror who unified his country by defeating and killing the king of the neighboring kingdom of Upper Egypt. The Egyptians called this king "the first king of the two lands."
The Egyptians were also known as "the people of the papyrus."
The Egyptians were the first people to use hieroglyphs, which were developed by the Egyptians and became the basis for writing.
The Egyptians are known as the first inventors of the calendar. It is said that it was the Egyptians who invented the wheel, and the pharaohs of the sixteenth dynasty were the first people to use saddles.
The Egyptians were also famous for their art, architecture, and jewelry.
The Egyptians were a pagan people. Their god was called Amun-Ra, the sun god.
The first Egyptian temples were built in the form of pyramids, to protect Egypt's dead pharaohs.
The Egyptians called their country "Kemet," which means "black land."
The Egyptians were also called "Asiatics" in classical Greek. They were also called "Libyans," because they were from Libya.
The Egyptians also had a complex system of writing, which was used by the Greeks and later by the Romans.
The Egyptians were also famous for their obelisks.

The film was controversial upon its release, and the American Jewish Committee, the Simon Wiesenthal Center, and the Zionist Organization of America all strongly criticized the film as an attack against Israel. Jeffrey Goldberg, editor-at-large of The Atlantic, called the film a "hagiographic portrait".
The film was nominated for Best Documentary Feature at the Jerusalem Film Festival.
The film was released in 2007 and is in the public domain.

 But in 1864 Busch was able to move into the field of writing and illustrating for children. Next to the works of Wilhelm Grimm, it was the writings of Friedrich Froebel that influenced Busch. Froebel's kindergarten system of educational play emphasized the spiritual and psychological development of children and encouraged the use of the arts and crafts in the education process. The illustrations in Busch's Kinder-Album (1864) were done in colored etchings and lithographs, but the pictures do not have the "cute" look of so many of the other children's books of the time. His drawings for the book are as charming as his drawings for the Munich magazine, but they are meant to be more than just pretty pictures.
From 1864 to 1868, Busch wrote and drew the stories for the Kinder-Album, Kinder-Lustspiel-Album (1865), and Kinder-Abenteuer-Album (1867). He also supplied the pictures for a number of other children's books. He was so successful in writing and illustrating for children that he decided to concentrate on just that.

Two films featuring Olivier were released in 1960 . The first — filmed in 1959 — was Spartacus , in which he portrayed the Roma

gladiator-turned-slave-rebel. Spartacus was a major box-office success, and it won four Academy Awards, including Best Director.
The second film was The Entertainer, a grim and depressing British drama based on the play of the same name by John Osborne. The film, directed by Tony Richardson, was less of a success, and it was not nominated for any Academy Awards.
This was refreshing for Olivier, who had won four Academy Awards for acting, but had never been nominated for one for directing. He also hoped it would bring him critical acclaim. "I'm looking to prove to people that I'm not just another ham," he said.
Olivier was given more than a fair share of ham in The Entertainer, which follows Archie Rice (Olivier), a washed-up music-hall performer. He is living in a small town in the north of England with his wife Phoebe (Janette Scott), daughter Jean (Judith Furse), and son Frank (Sean Barrett), a would-be performer.
Frank, a failed music-hall comedian, has not been home in several years, and Archie has been trying to get him to come back to the family. When Frank finally does return, he discovers that Phoebe has a new boyfriend and that Archie is being treated for alcoholism. After an argument, Frank decides to leave again.
It is a bleak film with a bleak message.
Although Olivier had won four Academy Awards for acting, he had never been nominated for one for directing.
Before the film was released, Olivier appeared on several talk shows to promote it. At one of these, he was asked what he thought when he saw the film for the first time. "I thought it was good," he said. "The cameraman and the editor were good . . . I thought the actors were really good . . ."
The film was released in the United States in November 1960. Olivier's performance was well received, but the film's bleak tone left audiences cold.
Olivier was nominated for the Golden Globe for Best Director, but lost to Stanley Kubrick for Spartacus and Richard Brooks for Elmer Gantry .

Since about 1900 , the Black Canyon and nearby Boulder Canyon had been investigated for their potential to support a dam that w

ou1d produce hydroelectric power. After the 1913 flood, irrigation systems were put in place, and the government acquired the land along the river for the purpose of storing water for power and irrigation. After a thorough investigation, the Black Canyon site was chosen as the most promising for a dam.
The government then enacted the long-standing Boulder Canyon Project Act of 1928, which authorized the construction of a dam at the Black Canyon. The government sought the services of the Bureau of Reclamation (BOR), the federal agency in charge of water projects. The BOR, in turn, sought the services of the Iron Mountain Dam Company, a private company, to construct the dam. The Bureau of Reclamation hired the firm of John A.L. Waddell, which in turn hired the firm of McKenzie and Hancock to design and build the dam. The firm of J.A.L. Waddell hired John W. Stevens to serve as the project manager.
The project manager was responsible for seeing that the project was built, within budget, on time, and according to specifications. He was assisted by a staff of engineers and other technical personnel, many of whom were also with the Bureau of Reclamation. About 500 additional people were hired to work on the project.
During the construction, the project manager's task was to see that all the work was completed, so that the dam could be put into use and the project could be turned over to the Bureau of Reclamation. At the end of the construction, the project manager was responsible for recording the results of the work, in the form of a manual and drawings. The manual was submitted to the Bureau of Reclamation, with the drawings for their archives.
The project manager's manual was a collection of all the technical information needed to operate and maintain the dam and its appurtenant works. The manual was written in a way that it could be used by the BOR personnel to operate and maintain the dam.

Simone Live is the nineteenth album by American singer Nina Simone, released in 1978 by Myrrh Records. It was recorded at the Town and Country Resort Hotel, San Diego, California on April 28, 1978. It is Simone's first album to be released by Myrrh Records.
The album features live performances of some of Simone's greatest hits, including "My Baby Just Cares for Me", "I Shall Be Released" and "I Wish I Knew How It Would Feel to Be Free".
The album was recorded at the Town and Country Resort Hotel in San Diego, California on April 28, 1978 and was produced by Larry D. Aikman. It was released on January 1979 by Myrrh Records.
The album was met with positive reviews from critics. Martin Williams of The New York Times described it as "a spirited performance... a joyful occasion". In a review for AllMusic, critic Brian Mansfield wrote, "It's a glorious set that captures Simone at the peak of her powers."
The album has been certified gold by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA).

Recorded originally as Watergate and Waterhead Milne , it was for a long time a hamlet in the parish of Oldham that formed a si

utated a parish of its own from the late 18th century until the early 20th century.

## History

The name Waterhead is a dialect version of Waterhead Mill.

The hamlet was situated at the northern end of Stalybridge, 2 miles (3.2 km) south of Chadderton Green.

Waterhead mill was built in 1779 as a cotton mill. It was then demolished in the 1880s and a new mill was built in its place.

The hamlet was a separate parish until 1904, when it was merged into Stalybridge.

The railway station, Waterhead railway station, opened in 1875 and closed in 1959.

The hamlet had a population of 120 in 1891, and 101 in 1901.

## Notable people

Sir Arthur Conan Doyle lived at 3 Waterhead Terrace, Stalybridge from 1895 to 1909, where he wrote the Sherlock Holmes novels.

Anthony Burgess, the author of A Clockwork Orange, was born on 25 February 1917 at 5 Waterhead Terrace, Stalybridge; the house is no longer standing.

The brigade traces its lineage back to an engineering regiment active during World War II , but the brigade itself did not see

combat until 1965 when it was deployed to Vietnam to construct the new air base at Da Nang.

## History

The 3rd Brigade was the only other US Army engineering brigade that did not trace its heritage to a regimental headquarters. It was active for most of the Vietnam War, and was tasked with enlarging the Da Nang Air Base.

The 3rd Brigade was stationed in Germany from 1976 to 1992, taking part in the Berlin Airlift of 1989. It was inactivated in 1992 and reactivated in 1996, first serving in Bosnia and Herzegovina, then in Kuwait as part of the Iraq War. The unit was deactivated on 15 September 2006.

### Vietnam

The 3rd Brigade was activated in August 1965, and was assigned to the 18th Engineer Brigade. The brigade's first mission in Vietnam was to construct the Da Nang Air Base. The brigade was then assigned to the 1st Cavalry Division to construct a new base at Chu Lai. From there, the 3rd Brigade constructed the Dong Ha Bridge and the Dong Ha Bridge Support Bridge, which were under constant attack by the People's Army of Vietnam. The brigade also constructed the large base at Phu Bai.

### Cold War

The brigade was deactivated in Germany on 29 July 1992, and reactivated on 1 October 1996. The brigade was deployed to Bosnia in 1996, where it engaged in reconstruction efforts. The brigade was later deployed to Kuwait during the 2003 Invasion of Iraq.

The 3rd Brigade was inactivated in 2006.

The jackrabbit will have a home range that may cover as much as 45 square kilometers . This large home range is probably the result of protection from predators that may be found in all habitats. The rabbit often hides in the burrows of prairie dogs , badgers , and coyotes .
Food is mainly vegetables and grasses. Rabbits that live in dry areas live off of the vegetation like grass, while those in moist areas live off of vegetation, fruits, and berries . There is no set time for the rabbit to eat, as it often is found to eat in the morning, afternoon, and evening.
Rabbits are often preyed upon by a wide variety of animals, such as foxes, coyotes, badgers, eagles, hawks, owls, snakes, and many others.
Black-tailed jackrabbits are very wary animals that are often found to be hiding in their burrows. They may also use a wide variety of burrows, both natural and man-made. Jackrabbits are not usually aggressive, but are quick to flee when they are approached.
Several subspecies of the black-tailed jackrabbit are found throughout South America, from the southern tip all the way to central Mexico . The jackrabbit is found in the forests and the deserts of the United States, and has been introduced into New Zealand, Australia, and many other places around the world .

Ross was born January 13 , 1885 , in Naughton , Ontario . His father , Thomas Barnston Ross , was the head of a Hudson 's Bay C

ompany Trading Post at that time. Ross is believed to have been born in the old Ross Mansion , located on the grounds of the present day Naughton Community Centre . The family resided on the property for generations.
In 1893 , the family moved to the village of Nipigon , Ontario . Ross studied at the local public school , and later attended the Owen Sound High School . In 1905 , he worked for the Dominion Land Survey Company , in the office of the Department of the Interior , in Ottawa.  In 1906 , Ross became a clerk with the Department of Immigration and Colonization , in Ottawa.
During this time Ross began writing poetry and was published in magazines and newspapers. He also began writing short stories. His first story for children , " The Treasure Trove ," was published in 1910 in the Canadian Magazine and earned him a modest sum of $ 20.00.
In 1911 , Ross left his position with the Department of Immigration and Colonization and accepted a position with the Department of Education , in charge of the school libraries of the Department. On March 28, 1911 , Ross married Edith Humphrey in Toronto .
In 1912 , Ross was transferred to Montreal to take charge of the Department of Education lending library. Ross began to write for the Montreal Children 's Hospital , producing stories and poems for the children of Montreal.
In 1913 , Ross decided to leave Montreal and move to Toronto to work with the Department of Education and the Toronto Public Library . He was also appointed the editorial director of the Canadian Sunday School Magazine , where he published most of his early works. In 1914 , Ross wrote " Scarface Cree ," a novel for boys dealing with the adventures of Billy Timmins and his dog Scarface in the Canadian west. In 1917 , Ross was appointed the editor of the Canadian Junior Standard , a magazine for young people.
In 1919 , Ross joined the Canadian Red Cross as a writer. In 1920 , Ross traveled to England and France to cover the war for the Canadian Red Cross. Ross returned to Canada in 1921 and published a book of war poetry entitled " Canary in No Man 's Land ," and a book of short stories for children entitled " The Adventures of a Canadian Boy ."
In 1922 , Ross returned to London , Ontario , to take a position as head of the Department of Education. In 1923 , Ross moved to Los Angeles , California where he worked for the Department of Education and an organization called the Child Welfare League of America .
In 1924 , Ross returned to Canada and moved to Vancouver, British Columbia , where he accepted a position with the Vancouver Public Library. In 1925 , Ross was appointed director of the Vancouver Public Library . Ross also continued to write stories for children and adults. In 1927 and 1928 , Ross wrote a series of short stories for an American magazine called " The Wonderful World of Oz ."
In 1930 , Ross was appointed director of the B .C . Provincial Library . Ross had a long and distinguished career with the B .C . Provincial Library until his retirement in 1953.
Ross married Dorothy Mary Bond in 1930 . They had two children , Barney Ross (1931 - 1992) and Rosemary Ross (1933 - 2001).
Ross died May 14 , 1965 , in Vancouver.
The Ross Collection consists of correspondence, documents, book drafts, and photographs. The collection was donated to the University of Saskatchewan Archives by the estate of Ross 's daughter , Rosemary Ross , in 2004 .

The first Japanese troops landed at 1400 hours on the beach at Kota Bharu , a small town on the east coast of northern Malaya , on the north-east corner of the British peninsula of Malacca. In all, 15,000 Japanese troops landed in the area, with 200 aircraft and 160 armoured vehicles. The main attack came in the north-west of Peninsular Malaya, at Sungai Ujong. The British 18 th Division, which had been expected to hold the area, was engaged in a counter-attack in the Thailand / Burma border area. The Japanese troops met little opposition, and by the end of the day the Japanese had pushed the British out of Sungai Ujong. The Japanese advance was further impeded by the fact that they had no maps of the Malay jungle. Nevertheless, they had won a great victory in the space of 24 hours.
In Singapore , the British garrison was a little more prepared for an invasion than it had been in Malaya. The 8 th Army, under the command of Lieutenant-General Percival, consisted of Indian, Chinese, Australian and British troops. Overall command of the defences of the island rested with Sir John Northcott , the Governor of Singapore. The Japanese, under Lieutenant-General Yamashita Tomoyuki , landed at 0400 hours on 8 February. Their attack was concentrated on the north-west of the island. They were opposed by the 18 th Indian Infantry Brigade and the 18 th Australian Brigade, and on the first day they made little progress. By the end of the day, however, they had forced their way through the southern coastal area to a point on the northern coast. They continued to advance, and by 12 February had pushed the British back to the south-east of the island. The Japanese had a clear run to Singapore , and by the end of the day Major-General Percival had surrendered the island.

They also improved their tactical position in the war, and, on the strategic level, they had increased the pressure on the Allied forces in the South-East Asia Command.
The Japanese invasion was also a great failure. The Japanese had underestimated the strength and quality of their opponents, and their plan of forcing the Allies to use all their strength in Malaya and Singapore was not successful. The Japanese forces in Malaya and Singapore were badly led and showed little initiative. The Japanese army was not yet the formidable fighting force it was to become. There had been no preparation for the invasion of Malaya and Singapore , and the Japanese had not taken sufficient account of the terrain in the area. The Japanese had not planned for the resistance they would meet, and they did not have a clear idea of the Allied strength in the area.
The Japanese had not succeeded in destroying the Allies in the South-East Asia Command. The British had lost Malaya and Singapore , but they had not lost the war. The Allies had not been defeated in the South-East Asian Command. The Japanese had lost a great number of men, and they had made a costly mistake.

"The regimental museum in Hamilton has a copy of a letter that General Mario Roatta sent from his headquarters in September 1943 to the 48th Highlanders," the officer said. "The letter has a map attached, which Roatta used to thank the 48th Highlanders for their assistance during the battle and that it was due to their remarkable courage and efficiency that the enemy was not able to cross the river. # SAN LEONARDO, SEPTEMBER 1943
FOUR DAYS BEFORE THE LETTER WAS SENT, the 2nd Battalion, Royal Canadian Regiment, was involved in a battle in and around the town of San Leonardo, a few kilometres west of the Adriatic coast. While the town and its surroundings were no longer important military objectives, the 2nd Battalion was ordered to secure the area as a precaution. The order was given by Lieutenant Colonel L.M. "Tubby" Stinson, the commanding officer of the 1st Canadian Infantry Division, who said it was "too important a terrain feature to be left to the enemy."
The town had been captured by the Allies during the summer, but the Germans had retaken the town in August. It was no longer important, but it was important that it not be retaken.
The Royal Canadian Regiment was ordered to seize the town by surprise at daybreak. "We were to clear the town of all enemy forces and then we were to dig in, and this was to be completed before dawn," recalled Lieutenant (later Colonel) R.A. (Al) Edwards of the 2nd Battalion. "We were to dig in along the banks of the Sangro River, which was an arm of the Adriatic Sea. It was only about 100 feet across and about 10 feet deep. It was to be a good defensive position, as the town was built on a hill. We were to be able to look right across the Sangro River and beyond it for some distance."
The town of San Leonardo was an important objective, but it was not an objective that would be defended by the Germans. The Germans had no intention of defending it or any other town on the Italian coast. They would not fight what they believed was a lost war.
The 1st Canadian Infantry Division had been ordered to the Italian Adriatic coast, principally to prevent German forces from crossing the river and attacking the Allies' positions on the other side. The Allies had forces near the town of Civitella del Tronto on the west side of the river and the town of Ortona on the east side. San Leonardo was on the west side of the river, and the 2nd Battalion was to secure the town so that the enemy could not cross the river.
The 2nd Battalion consisted of 26 officers and 953 other ranks. It had only been in Italy for eight days, and then had only one day of combat experience. "To the left of the 2nd Battalion was the West Nova Scotia Regiment, to our right was the Seaforth Highlanders of Canada," recalled Edwards. "The South Saskatchewan Regiment was to be on our left flank, but for some reason it never got there. We were on our own, with the exception of the West Nova Scotia Regiment, when we were ordered to attack San Leonardo."

Typical of Meyerbeer 's innovative orchestration is the use in Robert le diable of dark @-@ toned instruments – bassoons , timp

ani , trombones – to imitate the sounds of bells and church clocks in the third act.
The opera is said to have been written for the dancer Marie Taglioni, who was soon to become a famous ballerina, and for the ballerina herself the dance sequences are central. In the third act the ballet of the Devil and his demons, the dance of the court ladies with their male partners, and the single pas de deux of the principal characters are all important. The orchestra is sometimes merely a background to the dances, as in the duet 'Je t'ai vue' ('I saw you'), in which Robert is heard from far off in the distance, and is soon lost in the crowd. In the ballet the orchestra is a continuous accompaniment, and here the violins and woodwind are used as much for their special effects as for their tonal colour. The violins are of the greatest importance, and have the most individual roles. They are used for their individual tone-colours, however, as much as for their orchestral technique, and this is true in general of Meyerbeer's orchestration as a whole.
The orchestra of the first act of the opera includes piccolos, D-flutes, A-flutes, B-flutes, oboes, English horns, E-flat clarinets, B-flat clarinets, bass clarinets, bass oboes, bassoons, contrabassoons, alto horns, tenor horns, trumpets, trombones, timpani, kettledrums, triangle, and cymbals. In the second and third acts the orchestra includes piccolos, flutes, B-flutes, English horns, clarinets, two bassoons, contrabassoon, four horns, two trumpets, three trombones, timpani, and cymbals.

Jan Kiepura was born in 1902 into a family of Polish-Jewish origin in the Austrian-ruled city of Lemberg. In 1920 he was living in Breslau. From 1925 he studied singing at the Hochschule für Musik in Berlin and was a regular soloist at the Deutsche Oper in Berlin from 1929. In 1935 he moved to Paris. In 1937 he was engaged by the Royal Opera House Covent Garden in London and was appointed to the position of Kammersänger in 1939. He was taken prisoner by the Germans in 1941 and released in 1942. He continued his career in New York and Hollywood. In 1945 he was deported to Dachau. He was released again in 1947 and returned to Berlin. He was appointed to the position of Kammersänger at the Deutsche Oper in Berlin in 1949 and became a guest soloist at the Deutsche Staatsoper in the same city from 1950. In 1953 he was appointed to the position of Kammersänger at the Staatsoper in Vienna. In 1956 he was engaged by the Bavarian State Opera in Munich, where he performed until his death in 1966.

In 1927 he was appointed to the position of Kammersänger at the Deutsche Staatsoper in Berlin. In 1936 he became a guest soloist at the Deutsche Oper in Berlin. He was incarcerated in the Sachsenhausen concentration camp in 1939 and the Dachau concentration camp from 1945. In 1940 he left Berlin for New York. He made his first appearance in the United States in 1942. In 1946 he was appointed to the position of Kammersänger at the Metropolitan Opera in New York. The Derfflinger @-@ class ships were armed with eight 30 @.@ 5 cm ( 12 in ) SK L / 50 guns in four twin gun turrets , two forwa

rd and two aft . The forward turrets were mounted on the fore and main decks . The aft turrets were mounted on the upper deck .
The SK L / 50 naval gun was a 50.8 caliber naval gun developed by the German firm Krupp . The gun was capable of firing a 32.5 pound shell over 20,000 yards . The weight of the gun was 14,500 pounds .
The Derfflinger was laid down on 5 May 1910 and launched on 26 May 1912. The ship served with the German High Seas Fleet until the end of World War I on 24 October 1918 when she was scuttled in the North Sea to prevent her capture by the British Royal Navy.
The ship was raised in 1928 and scrapped in 1930.
The Derfflinger was named after the French 74 gun ship of the line L'Herault .
The number of guns on the Derfflinger was reduced by two to six.
The forward turrets were removed in 1914.

Much of the ecology of the watershed has been affected by wildfires and forestry , and is considered to be in a seral phase . T

he ecosystem is in a dynamic state , and a high level of ecological variability is expected.  Monitoring of springs over time is required to understand the hydrological, geomorphological, and biological changes that have occurred.
Springs provide unique habitats for many different species of flora and fauna. The springs in the watershed are considered to be of high ecological value, and are being monitored to determine the impact of the fires on the aquatic communities .
The quality of the water in the springs has been monitored for the past 12 years.  The water quality data from the springs are used to evaluate changes in water quality as a result of the fires, and to determine the hydrological impact of the fires on the springs.
Recent research has focused on the effects of the fires on the springs.
This study is a survey of the fish species found in the springs of the watershed. The survey was conducted by the Southeast Kootenay Springs Monitoring Program (SKSM) as part of its efforts to determine the impacts of fires on the aquatic ecosystems of the watershed.
The purpose of this report is to provide a description of the fishes found in the springs of the watershed.
All of the fish species found in the springs of the watershed were observed by the SKSM during the 1996 and 1997 field seasons. Fish were collected for identification and to determine population density.
The watershed springs are located within the southwest part of the Meadow Creek watershed, east of the town of Castlegar and west of the community of Fruitvale, British Columbia. The springs are located in the main stem of the Meadow Creek and its tributaries, including Kootenay Lake, West Fork Meadow Creek, Elk River, and Bullmoose Creek. The springs are located on the valley floor and in the valley sides. The springs are located in a variety of environments, including meadows, riparian areas, wetlands, and forested areas.

In January 2014 it was announced that David Goyer and Daniel Cerone were developing a TV series based on Hellblazer and that NB

T Entertainment was developing the series. The series was being shopped to cable television networks, with Channel 4 and Syfy being two of them. It was also announced that the series would be a "dark fantasy series, similar to Game of Thrones. Goyer wanted to make the series "bizarre and terrifying", which would be "hard to do" because of the "legacy of the character. Goyer explained, "If you're going to do Hellblazer, you have to be true to the character, but also [have] a new take on it. I think the character will change from what it was. Think of the difference between Watchmen, the graphic novel, and the movie. It's the same character, but it's a different story." He revealed that they were attempting to find out what was "in the dark" with the series. He explained, "I think the series is going to be a little bit darker than what people are used to. The TV series will be a little bit more intense. It's not a kids' show, and it's not a comedy. It's a show where you really feel like you're getting into the dark corners of the human psyche."

In May 2014 it was revealed that the series, titled Constantine would be premiering in October 2014. It was also revealed that it would be on NBC, not Channel 4 or Syfy. NBC ordered 13 episodes in May 2014, with the pilot being written by Goyer and Cerone, and Mark Sullivan as an executive producer. It was announced that John Shiban, the creative consultant for Supernatural, would be serving as an executive producer and a writer for the series and that the series would be produced by God, Seriously and Berlanti Productions.

### Casting

On May 14, 2014, it was announced that Matt Ryan would star as John Constantine. On June 2, 2014, it was announced that the series would be executive produced by Daniel Cerone, David S. Goyer, and Jeremy Carver. On June 10, 2014, it was announced that Angelica Celaya would star as Anne Marie. On June 11, 2014, it was announced that Charles Halford would star as Chas. On June 12, 2014, it was announced that Harold Perrineau would star as Manny. On June 13, 2014, it was announced that Charles Parnell would star as Detective Jim Corrigan. On June 16, 2014, it was announced that Jeremy Davies would star as Dr. Isaac, a character that was created for the series. On July 2, 2014, it was announced that Michael James Shaw would star as Detective Robert Sale. On July 10, 2014, it was announced that Rupert Evans would star as Gary Lester.

### Filming

In Los Angeles, California it was announced that the pilot for the series was being filmed. The pilot was filmed on a soundstage at Warner Bros. Studios, Burbank, with filming starting in June 2014, and was completed in July 2014. According to a New York Times article, the series was originally planned to be filmed in Vancouver, but due to the filming of Arrow and The Flash, it was decided to film the series in America.

### Cancellation

On May 7, 2015, NBC announced that Constantine had been cancelled, after only one season. The series was released on Blu-ray and DVD on March 15, 2016.

## Reception

### Reception

Critical reception for Constantine has been mixed. On Rotten Tomatoes, the series has a rating of 45% with an average rating of 5.62/10, based on 21 reviews. The site's consensus reads, "Constantine is a serviceable adaptation that doesn't quite capture the spirit of the comics, but it's still worth a look for fans of the character." On Metacritic, the series has a score of 50 out of 100, based on 5 reviews, indicating "mixed or average reviews".

In 1968 , R. Gordon Wasson proposed that A. muscaria was the Soma talked about in the Rig Veda of India , a claim which receive

some support in 2004, and most recently by an article that appeared in New Scientist in 2007 .
 In 1978, Wasson and his wife Valentina Pavlovna took psilocybin and ibogaine with a West African shaman, and notes that: "The experience in every detail was identical with that I had with the Mazatec shaman. I felt as if I had been born in a homeland where I could live forever." This article has been criticized as being a morality tale of the Wassons' own drug use.
 By 1986, Wasson was working with the Mazatec shaman María Sabina, who had developed a method for using psychoactive mushrooms without intoxication. This method was described in the book "Sacred Mushroom of Visions: The Divine and Visionary Artists, Shamans, and Mystics".
 Wasson died on 23 April 1986, aged 84.
 Wasson has been criticized for mixing up the descriptions of the mushrooms used by the Mazatec to induce visions with those of the mushrooms used by the Zapotec to induce trance.
 Maria Sabina's technique of drinking the decocted mushroom extract, which Wasson calls "the purified brew," rather than ingesting the mushrooms themselves, is now the most common use of psilocybe mushrooms.
 Wasson claimed that he had tried "a dozen varieties" of mushrooms, but he had actually only tried psilocybe mexicana, psilocybe mexicana var. caerulescens, psilocybe oaxacensis, psilocybe tampanensis, and psilocybe caerulipes.
 Wasson also claims to have taken psilocybe cubensis and psilocybe subaeruginosa, which psychoactive species of mushroom are not found in Mexico but are found in Cuba and the Florida Everglades, respectively.

Mathews was born at Funchal on Madeira on 7 March 1850 . His father , Captain William Matthews was Welsh , and his mother Jane

was from the Royal Navy . He had three younger brothers and a sister.  His family was close to the local Anglican clergyman , the Reverend George Townsend .
His father moved to Madeira around 1845.  His younger brother Charles was born at Funchal in 1851 ,  and his two other brothers were born in the mid 1850s.  His father was the local pilot , and lived in a house in the village of Funchal.  His mother died in 1853 , when he was three years old.  His older brother John was born at Madeira in 1852 , as was his sister Jane .
The family lived in the village of Funchal , and in 1861 were living on the main street in the parish of São Martinho in the parish of Funchal .  His father was the local pilot , and the family lived in a house in Funchal.  By the time of the 1871 census he was living in the parish of São Martinho at Funchal . His father William was living in the village of Funchal .  His father died in 1875 .  His eldest brother John was living in the village of Funchal , and his younger brother William was living in the village of Belmonte .
His father was a pilot , and he inherited his father's position as pilot.  He was appointed to the position in 1877 .  He was the pilot who had brought the fleet of HMS Zealous into Madeira when they arrived in 1882 .  He was promoted to the position of Inspector of Pilots in Madeira in 1882 .  When he was appointed to the position of Inspector of Pilots , he was the youngest pilot in the world , at the age of only 25 years , and the first ever Inspector of Pilots to be appointed by the British Admiralty .  He was also the first pilot to be appointed by the British Admiralty .  He was then appointed by the British Admiralty as the Inspector of Pilots in Newport , Isle of Wight .  He was then appointed by the British Admiralty as the Inspector of Pilots on the River Mersey .  He was appointed by the British Admiralty as the Inspector of Pilots in Dover .  He was appointed by the British Admiralty as the Inspector of Pilots in Dartmouth .
He married Dorothy Anne Georgina Baker at St Margaret's church in Westminster on 2 June 1882 .  Her father was Captain George Baker , who had been the captain of HMS Zealous .
He was appointed by the British Admiralty as the Inspector of Pilots in Portsmouth .  He was appointed by the British Admiralty as the Inspector of Pilots in Plymouth .  He was appointed by the British Admiralty as the Inspector of Pilots in Swansea .  He was appointed by the British Admiralty as the Inspector of Pilots in Falmouth , where he was living when he died .  He was the son of the local pilot there , and lived with his family in the village of Falmouth .  He was living in Melville Terrace , Falmouth , when he died .

## Plot

The film is set in the fictional town of Abrighton, England, where all of the shops and businesses are owned by one family, the Baines. The Baine family includes the patriarch, Henry Baines (Frank Lawton), his wife, the matriarch, Jessie (Renee Godfrey), and their son, Peter (George Chandler), a man-child who has a pet wolf.

One day, a young woman named Helen (Irene Ware) shows up at the Baines' doorstep, claiming that she is the daughter of a recently deceased and wealthy man named Charles Baines (also Lawton), who was thought to have been killed in a car accident. The Baines family are overcome with joy at the thought of having found a long-lost relative. The only problem is that Charles Baines is not dead. He is alive and well and living in London with his wife, Maude. Charles and Maude had decided to separate some time ago, and Charles had thought that Helen had been killed in a car accident, so he had left her money to be given to her in the event that she would ever show up. Charles and Maude are baffled as to how the Baines family could have thought that Helen was their daughter, since Helen has no resemblance to Charles or Maude.

Maude goes to London to investigate the situation, and discovers that the Baines family are only too willing to believe Helen's story. Peter immediately falls in love with Helen, and the Baines family seems to have forgotten that she is a stranger in their midst. Charles, on the other hand, adores Helen, but Maude is tormented by the situation, since she does not know how she can get Helen out of her home. Peter soon discovers that Helen has been lying to the Baines family and that she is actually a former chorus girl named Olive. Peter is heartbroken, and is about to expose the truth, but Helen/Olive tricks him into marrying her.

The Baines family is crushed at the thought of Helen's deception, but the marriage makes everything worse. Helen is furious that Peter has married her, and she leaves her husband at the altar. She even tries to leave the town, but is stopped by Maude, who is determined to get Helen out of her home. A man named Henry (Alan Napier), whom Helen had been secretly dating, shows up, and the two confess their love for each other. Just when Peter and Helen seem to be reconciling, Henry is struck by a car and killed. Helen and Peter are devastated, but they soon realize that they love each other and reconcile.

This crake migrates to Africa along two main routes : a western route through Morocco and Algeria , and a more important flyway

via the Iberian Peninsula.  These routes are used by many other waterbirds (e.g. waders) and some have been shown to be important as stepping stones along migratory routes. The two main routes are apparently used by different populations and it is thought that some populations may be resident in the Mediterranean. 

## Etymology

The English name "white-winged crake" is from the Greek φερειν (pherein), "to carry" and πτερυγος (pterygos), "wing". The specific dedicator "rubricatus" is a Latin adjective meaning "reddish".

## Description

The white-winged crake is a rather large member of the family Rallidae, ranging from 23 to 26 cm (9.1 to 10.2 in) in length. Its plumage is cryptic, with the back, rump and flanks being a rich brown, the throat, breast and belly being buff and the tail being blackish, with white tips to the feathers. It has a very short bill, with the upper mandible black, the lower one yellowish, and the iris is golden-yellow. The female is similar to the male, but duller, the yellow on the bill being replaced by buff. 

## Distribution and habitat

The white-winged crake breeds in central and southern Europe, Asia Minor, and north-western Africa from Tunisia to Mauritania and Senegal. It is a migratory species, wintering in western and eastern Africa, west and south Asia, and Australasia.

## Behaviour

The white-winged crake is generally solitary and nocturnal, but tends to seek cover during the day. The male's song is a harsh rattle, repeated frequently, produced primarily by inflating the crop. The call is a high pitched "kleek".

Ethnically , the Middle Colonies were more diverse than the other British colonial regions in North America and tended to be mo

re multicultural than even New England. By the mid-eighteenth century, the major religious denominations were the Anglicans (Episcopalians), Presbyterians, and Quakers. There were also large numbers of Catholics in Pennsylvania, and the Dutch Reformed, Lutheran, and Moravian denominations. German settlers also established their own congregations.
**Law and Government:** The Constitution of Pennsylvania, adopted in 1776, was based on the model of the English-American constitution and provided that "the people have, and of right ought to have, full and free liberty in religious matters." In New Jersey, the constitution of 1776 "maintains the liberty of all religions." New York's constitution of 1777 provided the same.
**Religious Life:** The Quakers, who had been established in New Jersey since the 1680s, were the most influential religious group in the Middle Colonies. The colony of Pennsylvania was named for William Penn, the Quaker leader who had been granted almost ten million acres of land by King Charles II in 1681.
The Middle Colonies were also home to the German Reformed Church (1725) and the Moravian Church (1741). In 1709, the first Methodist congregation formed in the southern Middle Colonies.
**Economy:** By 1760, the Middle Colonies had developed into a fairly prosperous region, thanks to the leadership of Pennsylvania's Benjamin Franklin, who promoted the building of canals, later developing the first steam-powered engine.
**Social Life:** Because of the region's diversity, the Middle Colonies were more progressive than New England in their social customs. They were considered "refined," of "higher class" than the other colonies, and were more tolerant of differences.
**Women:** Pennsylvania had a reputation for being the most progressive colony for women. Its laws and mores gave women the right to own property, to pursue whatever education they desired, and to work outside the home.
#  **Colonies in the West**
The nine colonies in the West were Kentucky, Mississippi, Tennessee, Arkansas, Missouri, Iowa, Louisiana, Wisconsin, and Minnesota.
**Overview:** In the 1760s, the French were the dominant European power in North America, with their territory stretching from Canada to the Gulf of Mexico. But in 1763, Britain defeated France in the French and Indian War, and in a treaty that followed, Britain gained control of much of French territory west of the Alleghenies.
**Geography:** The area was mountainous, and the streams and rivers were difficult to navigate. The land was fertile, with good soil.
**Economy:** Economic activity was primarily based in the farming sector. Because of the distance from major transportation routes, farmers in the West usually either grew products suitable for their region or produced them on a small scale for local markets.
**Social Life:** Because of isolation and the remoteness of the region, the West had a more rural quality than the other colonial regions.
**Women:** In the West, women's role in society was generally defined as "helpmeet" to their husbands.
#  **Colonies in the South**
The 13 colonies in the South were Virginia, Maryland, North and South Carolina, Georgia, and Delaware.
**Overview:** The South was a British colony from 1607, when the English settlers at Jamestown, Virginia, arrived. Unlike the other colonies, the South had no regional leader.
**Geography:** The South was more fertile and productive than other regions, thanks to its warm climate, level land, and mineral deposits.
**Economy:** The South was the wealthiest of the colonies, thanks to its plantations (established in the 1670s) and the slave labor that produced tobacco, cotton, and rice.
**Social Life:** Because of the slave economy, the South was the most stratified region, with a social hierarchy that included a group of wealthy, powerful planters and a group of poor, desperate slaves.
**Women:** Most women were not considered useful for anything but childbearing. Even in Virginia, women were regarded as second-class citizens.

The Missouri 's nickname , the " Big Muddy " , was inspired by its enormous loads of sediment or silt – some of the largest of

any river and the largest of the western rivers .
The term " Big Muddy " has come to be associated with the Missouri River in popular culture and by the media , but it has no official status.
The Missouri River is the longest river in the United States , flowing 2,341 miles (3,770 km) in the central United States .
It rises in the Rocky Mountains of western Montana, near the city of Three Forks . It is formed by the confluence of the Jefferson , Madison and Gallatin rivers near Three Forks . The river then flows southeast for 1,371 miles (2,207 km) through the states of Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, Iowa, and Missouri, eventually joining the Mississippi River at St. Louis , Missouri.
The Missouri was once a major transportation artery in the United States . Before the advent of railroads and the internal-combustion engine, riverboats carried thousands of settlers westward. The Missouri also has the distinction of being the river most responsible for the settlement of the northern Great Plains . The river is the source of the largest floods on record in the United States , though flooding is not primarily caused by heavy rainfall but by the melting of mountain snowpacks.
Much of the lower stretch of the Missouri River is now part of the Big Muddy National Fish and Wildlife Refuge, which was established in 1996.
The Missouri River has a number of major tributaries: the Marias River and Teton River in Montana, the Yellowstone River in Montana and Wyoming, the Bighorn River in Wyoming and Montana, the Powder River in Wyoming and Montana, the Little Missouri River in North Dakota, the Cheyenne River and the White River in South Dakota, the Niobrara River in Nebraska and South Dakota, the Platte River in Nebraska, the James River and the Grand River in Iowa and the Kansas River in Kansas.
The Missouri River drains a vast watershed of 585,300 square miles (1,517,000 km2) (38% of the United States) and is the country's largest drainage system north of the Rio Grande. Its total watershed area is larger than the combined watersheds of the next seven largest U.S. rivers, the Mississippi, St. Lawrence, Ohio, Colorado, Hudson, Saginaw,  and Susquehanna rivers.

This was a pointed statement, one of many in the song, as well as an allusion to a common image of a nation's teachers as the most stalwart and steadfast of its citizens.
This association of teachers with the struggle for national independence and freedom is one that goes back at least as far as the American Revolution: many early American schoolteachers were also involved in the struggle for independence and freedom, and furthermore, the schools were often used as places for the instruction and indoctrination of young people in the "new" national ideology of individualism, liberty, and equality.
In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the natural progression of this tradition was to see teachers, in almost every country on earth, as "patriots" and "nationalists." In these countries, both public and private schools served to perpetuate the values of the national society, including its national character, national identity, and national culture. Schoolteachers were seen as the guardians of the nation's education, and therefore of its cultural and national values.
In most countries, teachers were also the most powerful group in their societies, at least in the sense that they had the most power to define the values and ideas that were taught in the schools, and to influence the young. Given this powerful role, teachers were often perceived as having a special responsibility to be committed to their country. The doctrines of anekāntavāda and syādavāda are often criticised on the grounds that they engender a degree of hesitancy and un

trustworthiness in the individual. The claim is that, unless one adopts a single, unambiguous world-view, one is constantly likely to shift one's position in order to avoid the risk of being wrong. The reason for this is that the multiple standpoints imply that one is never in a position of certainty. In the face of contradictory premises, the only way in which to resolve the contradiction is to suspend judgement.
The criticisms are not without foundation. However, if one takes a closer look at the various texts that have been used to justify the claim, one finds that the texts do not represent a clear and coherent understanding of the doctrine. Rather than a coherent criticism, we have a series of statements that have been taken out of context and which, as such, are inadequate for the task at hand.
The statements that have given rise to the criticism are usually taken from the Ānandavardhana's _Dharmakīrtiśāstra_ , the Kashmiri scholar's exposition of the Buddha's teachings. The statement that has caused the most consternation is the following:
> When one is going to speak, one should not be dogmatic, for there is no single path to the truth. When one is going to act, one should not be inflexible, for there is no single path to the truth. When one is going to decide on a course of action, one should not be inflexible, for there is no single path to the truth.
> 
> (Dharmakīrtiśāstra 1.1.5)
Here, Dharmakīrti does not say that a person should be indecisive in all things. Rather, he is referring to an _epistemological_ strategy, as is clear from the following statement:
> In the case of a view, it is such that the view may be true, or that it may be false. If there is an understanding of it, in that case it is true, and if there is not, it is false.
> 
> (Dharmakīrtiśāstra 1.2.2)
And again:
> Because of the view of the ultimate truth, which is such that it is to be understood as that it may be true, or that it may be false, if there is an understanding, in that case it is true, and if there is not, it is false.
> 
> (Dharmakīrtiśāstra 1.2.3)
In other words, the statements that have given rise to the accusations are to be understood as applying only to the epistemological problem, not to the issue of action.
The issue of action is dealt with in the following statements:
> In the case of the truth of action, there is no single path, for the path of action is different according to the circumstances.
> 
> (Dharmakīrtiśāstra 1.1.5)
And, yet again:
> If an action is to be done, it is such that there is no single path to it, for it is different according to the circumstances.

Complementary to the field of structural genomics , protein structure prediction seeks to develop efficient ways to provide pla

usible structures of unknown proteins. The field is much younger than structural genomics, which has its roots in the 1990s. Predicting protein structures is still much more challenging than predicting nucleic acid structures.

## History

Since the first protein structure was determined by X-ray crystallography in 1958, proteins have remained a difficult target for structural prediction. This was due to a number of factors, including the heterogeneity of protein structure, the large size of proteins, the large number of atoms in proteins, the large number of protein degrees of freedom, and the fact that many proteins have no known structure.

### Methods for Protein Structure Prediction

Structural modeling was first attempted using homology modeling , often called template-based modeling. This technique relies on the assumption that proteins sharing sequence similarity have similar structural similarity. Homology models are constructed by taking as a template a structure of a similar protein, and by replacing each amino acid in the sequence using the most similar amino acid in the template. Many homology models were constructed for proteins of known structure in the 1970s and 1980s. However, these models suffered from the large sequence to structure distance problem.

In 1983, Abrahams and Sali developed threading , a method of modeling proteins using the most similar structure in a threading database. This was followed by the development of the ExPASy Protein Structure Database in 1997, which contains proteins with known structure, as well as their sequences. In 1996, threading was combined with homology modeling to create iterative threading and folding, or I-TASSER. I-TASSER is the most successful method for protein structure prediction to date.

#### Neural networks

The use of neural networks in protein structure prediction dates back to 1986. Neural networks are a class of machine learning algorithms which allow for the learning of patterns and dependencies. A neural network trained on a dataset of protein structures can then predict the structure of an unknown protein. Many neural network methods have been developed for protein structure prediction.

#### Model-based

Model-based methods are based on the assumption that a protein has a "rule-based model" or "potential energy function" (PEF) that describes its structure. Model-based methods rely on the knowledge of the PEF of the protein to predict the structure.

### Aims of protein structure prediction

Protein structure prediction is concerned with the determination of protein structure from the amino acid sequence. The process of protein structure prediction is divided into two phases. The first phase is the protein sequence analysis, which consists of the identification of potential protein sequence homology. The second phase is to identify the potential folding of the protein.

### Use in structure-function analysis and drug discovery

Protein structure prediction software is widely used in protein structure-function analysis and drug discovery. It has been used to identify potential targets for drug development.

Limited computer power : There was not enough memory or processing speed to accomplish anything truly useful . For example , Ro

chester's computer was 14,000 times slower than the current fastest supercomputer .
Three-dimensional computer graphics were not yet practical (see Figure 15-1).
 _Figure 15-1._ A computer graphics scene from a film based on _The Lord of the Rings._
The original Rochester computer had a 24,000-word memory and a 30-second processing time. (A word represented six bits , or six binary digits, or six numbers ranging from 0 to 1.) For example, if the computer had to process a series of n numbers , n > 24,000 , it would take well over 30 seconds to process the numbers, and the results might not be accurate. Today , the fastest supercomputer at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign can process 200,000,000,000,000,000,000 (200 quintillion) calculations in 25 seconds .
To make matters worse, the original Rochester computer had no way to store data or programs. It had to be reprogrammed after each calculation. The process was so slow that it was not economical to perform even simple calculations, such as finding the roots of quadratic equations. Programming the computer therefore was not practical for researchers who wanted to solve mathematical problems .
The next leap, from slow to fast, came around 1956 , when the transistor was invented . The transistor , unlike the vacuum tube, was small enough to be embedded in a computer chip . This increase in speed made it possible to do useful things with computers .
Although the transistor was invented in 1947 , it took more than 10 years for it to gain acceptance . In the 1950s , it was not commercially practical to build a computer using transistors .
The first computer to use transistors was built by Ken Olsen of Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) in 1957 . It was a special-purpose computer, an "early digital machine," which was used to calculate the trajectories of artillery shells .
Because it was a special-purpose computer, the DEC computer could be built in a very compact way . It was built into a desk with a keyboard and a display screen. The machine was about the size of a refrigerator and weighed a ton. It had 16 bit-manipulating units, each of which was capable of performing 2000 multiplications or division a second . (A bit is the basic unit of information in a computer. It can have a value of 0 or 1.) This was a great leap forward in computer speed.

y conversation, and that understanding the intent behind utterances is critical to understanding the purpose behind the conversation.

for the museum's premises. But the building was now too small for Serbs and Croats to share. Historical tensions between them did not make the situation easier, and the Serbs in the municipality of Vukovar , especially those in the Civic League (SL), wanted their own museum. They decided to build one of their own.
The Serbs and Croats in Vukovar , and the rest of the country, found themselves in a new and uncharted situation. They were sharing a square which had previously been a military base, secure in the knowledge that the city was surrounded by the River Danube . The United Nations had been deployed to monitor the situation and prevent any incidents from happening between the two sides. The situation was volatile and dangerous, because although the agreement was signed by representatives of both sides, the Croatian government was reluctant to give up any territory, especially in the region of Slavonia . When the Croatian government agreed to the UN resolution on 25 September 1991, the Croatian parliament was not yet in session, and the president had not yet signed the agreement.
 The Serbs and Croats were very different. The Serbs were a minority in Croatia , and had been living alongside the Croats for years. In an effort to eliminate French support Commodore William Cornwallis , the British naval commander in the region , stationed a

squadron of a dozen battleships off the coast of Maine in March 1813. The British warships anchored in the Penobscot River , at the entrance to the Bay of Castine , Maine , and began shelling the American town, which was home to 2,000 inhabitants. Commodore John Rogers , commander of the American squadron, had only three ships and one gunboat to defend himself. The British squadron was led by Sir Thomas Hardy. Their ships included the frigates _Confiance_ and _Apollo_ , and the vessels _Pomone_ and _Tigress_ , the latter of which was led by Commodore Hardy. At 8 a.m. on July 1, 1814, Sir Thomas Hardy and the British ships entered the Penobscot River and headed toward the fortified town of Castine.
As the British stepped ashore, the American sailors commenced firing their cannons. The British charged the American defenses, led by Hardy, and after several hours of fighting the American forces were forced to retreat. The British now held the fortified town of Castine and the American squadron was left with only two ships. Commodore John Rogers was forced to return to the safety of the open seas, leaving his entire squadron behind.
One hundred years later, on August 14, 1914, the British Royal Navy's newest battleship, HMS _Dreadnought_ , was commissioned. This vessel was not only the pride of the Royal Navy — she was the first of a new class of battleships. She had all the features of a modern battleship, including the first all-big-gun armament. The _Dreadnought_ was a revolutionary design that changed the face of naval warfare.
The _Dreadnought_ had a displacement of 18,000 tons and was armed with ten 12-inch guns and eight 4-inch guns. With a top speed of 21 knots, she could destroy any ship in her class. At the time of her commissioning, Britain was the world's only superpower and the _Dreadnought_ marked the beginning of Britain's naval dominance.
As the Royal Navy exploded in size, the United States was left behind. When the United States entered World War I in 1917, the U.S. Navy was outgunned, outmanned, and outclassed by the Royal Navy. In the following decades, the United States found itself in the same predicament during World War II. The United States Navy lacked the numbers, the equipment, and the experience to match the Royal Navy. During World War II, Britain and its commonwealth countries were the only forces in Europe capable of blocking the Axis advance. The number of U.S. naval vessels paled in comparison to the Royal Navy and the Royal Canadian Navy.
In 1941, the United States was in dire need of naval vessels that were superior to the Royal Navy. To solve this problem, the United States launched its own program to build large battleships. Four of these new battleships were built, and each was named after four of the largest cities in the United States: the USS _Indiana_ , the USS _Massachusetts_ , the USS _New York_ , and the USS _Washington_.
The USS _Indiana_ was laid down on June 17, 1941, at the Bethlehem Shipbuilding Corporation in Quincy, Massachusetts. The USS _Indiana_ was launched on June 29, 1941, and commissioned on May 28, 1942.
The USS _Indiana_ was 732 feet long, 112 feet wide, and displaced 35,000 tons (the same size as the _Dreadnought_ ). She was armed with nine 16-inch guns and eighteen 5-inch guns.
The USS _Indiana_ was the first of the new generation of American battleships. She was equipped with the same sophisticated technology as the Royal Navy's battleships. After an initial period of training, the USS _Indiana_ was assigned to the fleet and spent several months in the Pacific waters.
