Eventually, Busch's uncle conceded to the suggestion that he should study, and so, before the end of 1826, Busch left the Lüthorst family home and moved to Munich , where he intended to live for two years.
Between 1827 and 1830, Busch attended the Munich Academy. During this time, he worked as a draftsman, often working for the painter Peter Cornelius , and painted small-scale portraits for a living.
In the summer of 1830, Busch went to Berlin to see a performance of Robert Schumann's oratorio, The Prophet , which had been produced in May of that year. During this trip, Busch met with the artist Eduard Gaertner, who suggested that Busch should travel with him to Italy. Together, Busch and Gaertner travelled to Venice , where Busch was able to study the works of Tiepolo and other eighteenth-century Venetian painters.
In the summer of 1831, Busch returned to Berlin . During his stay in the city, he met with the painter Karl Friedrich Schinkel . Together, they visited the castle of Finkenwerder , where Busch was inspired to paint a landscape he showed at the Berlin Academy in 1833. Following this visit, Busch travelled to Dresden , where he visited the works of Caspar David Friedrich and Adam Friedrich Oeser at the museum. He was also able to see the works of Peter von Cornelius. In 1832, Busch returned to Berlin , where he painted a portrait of the poet and playwright Friedrich Hebbel .
In 1833, Busch and Schinkel travelled to Dresden, where the latter was appointed director of the city's academy. At this time, Busch was commissioned to paint a landscape of the castle of Finkenwerder, which he showed at the Berlin Academy in 1834.

The noisy miner is also known as the "Australian drongo" , because of the fact that many of the honeyeater species are known to "mine" trees .
The noisy miner is found in various habitats, including grasslands, woodlands and occasionally forests.

Le souper de Beaucaire was a political pamphlet written by Napoleon Bonaparte in 1793 . With the French Revolution into its fou

-tenth year, the rift between the Convention and the Jacobins was already severe, and as the dissension deepened, Bonaparte's position as commander-in-chief of the Army of Italy was increasingly in jeopardy. The pamphlet was the first in a series of political and military works Bonaparte published in his attempt to refute the allegations of Henri Grégoire , Bishop of Blois , who accused Bonaparte of having caused the death of his superior, Lazare Hoche .
Le souper de Beaucaire is a satirical and obscene diatribe against Grégoire, with Bonaparte taking on the persona of a male prostitute, who takes great delight in making fun of his opponent's weakness for young boys. Bonaparte's diatribe also has a more serious side: it is a vicious attack on Grégoire's character and his alleged sexual perversions. The satire also has an ulterior motive: by attacking Grégoire, Bonaparte hoped to discredit himself in the eyes of the Jacobins and thus avoid being brought before the Revolutionary Tribunal.
In March 1793, the French Army of Italy was preparing to cross the Alps and invade Italy. Bonaparte was in command of the army's right flank, with a large force of 38,000 men. The left flank was commanded by Lazare Hoche, with a smaller force of 18,000 men. The Army of Italy was to attack the Austrian forces in Italy in order to relieve pressure on France's southern border. The Austrians were occupying a position that Bonaparte and his army had to cross in order to enter Italy.
Jean-Marie Collot d'Herbois , a Jacobin deputy and a friend of Grégoire, had been given the task of preparing a petition to the Convention to have the Army of Italy split in two. The petition was based on an allegation that Bonaparte had prevented Hoche from attacking the Austrians at Verceil , Italy, and that Hoche had died as a result. The petition, which was signed by Bonaparte's enemies, was presented to the Convention on 25 March 1793, and a vote on it was scheduled for 27 March. Bonaparte was arrested on 26 March 1793; he was charged with "failure to obey a superior officer's orders" and "attempting to subvert the republic." The Convention later voted to send the case against Bonaparte to the Revolutionary Tribunal.
While in prison, Bonaparte had little contact with the outside world. Grégoire frequently visited Bonaparte in prison, and it was during these visits that the two had their first discussions about Le souper de Beaucaire . Bonaparte's first version of the pamphlet was written in prison, and was in the form of a pamphlet. On 14 April 1793, the pamphlet was sent to the editor of the Caveau de la République. On 9 May 1793, the editor of the Caveau de la République published the first version of Le souper de Beaucaire . The second version of Le souper de Beaucaire was written by Bonaparte during the night of 17–18 May 1793. The second version of the pamphlet took the form of a letter addressed to the Jacobin Club, and was published in the Caveau de la République on 20 May 1793 . The two versions of the pamphlet were substantially different, and the second version is the one that is most often referred to in current literature.
Bonaparte was released from prison on 15 May 1793, and was immediately appointed the commander-in-chief of the Army of Italy.

The use of condoms to prevent STD transmission is not specifically addressed by Catholic doctrine , and is currently a topic of

controversy within the church. Catholic tradition has generally condoned the use of condoms in certain situations, such as for male prostitutes , and the church hierarchy has historically favored this position. But the church has also opposed the use of condoms in certain situations, such as for female prostitutes, and in the past few years it has reaffirmed this opposition in various statements.
In the summer of 2006, Pope Benedict XVI, in his first papal trip to Africa, endorsed the use of condoms as a means to prevent the spread of HIV among prostitutes. "It is not true that the only thing we can do for people who are suffering is to give them drugs; on the contrary, we can bring them hope and comfort," he said in a speech to a group of AIDS sufferers in Cameroon.
A few months later, however, Cardinal Renato Martino, the Vatican's chief representative to the United Nations, contradicted the pope's comments, saying that the church still was opposed to condom use even to prevent the spread of HIV. The Vatican also withheld its backing from an AIDS conference that was scheduled to take place in Kenya in 2007, which was attended by U.S. President George W. Bush. The Vatican apparently opposed a U.S. proposal that called for more money to be given to Africa to fight AIDS, and which also urged greater use of condoms.
In 2007, senior Vatican officials further reaffirmed the church's opposition to condom use by HIV-infected prostitutes. The Vatican's position is based on the belief that the AIDS epidemic is a consequence of immoral sexual behavior, and that the spread of HIV can be prevented by promoting abstinence and fidelity. This position was endorsed by an influential group of Catholic theologians in January 2009, although the theologians also acknowledged that the church should not "stigmatize" prostitutes or other people with "unconventional sexual lifestyles."
A few months later, Papal Nuncio to the United States Archbishop Pietro Sambi, echoing Pope Benedict XVI, said that the church has a duty to speak out against the use of condoms in certain situations, including prevention of the spread of HIV. "The Catholic Church is opposed to the use of condoms as a means to combat the spread of AIDS, since it is not scientifically proven to be effective," Sambi said in a statement.
The debate has continued to rage in recent years, with some Catholic groups calling for greater use of condoms to prevent the spread of HIV, while other groups argue that the church's position is rooted in an outdated and outmoded opposition to birth control.

Silver Bullet is a western @-@ themed steel inverted roller coaster designed by Bolliger & Mabillard located at Knott 's Berry

Farm in Buena Park, California. The ride is a clone of the coaster X² at Six Flags Magic Mountain as well as another clone located at Hard Rock Park, which closed in 2008. The ride opened on July 19, 2008. At the 2011 Golden Ticket Awards, Silver Bullet was awarded Best New Roller Coaster.
Silver Bullet is built on a plot of land formerly occupied by the Dodge City & Calico Railroad. Nearby rides include the calico mine train, bigfoot rapids, and the Timber Mountain Log Ride.
Silver Bullet's theme is based on old west stories of a silver bullet, a more traditional theme than the other two B&M inverted coasters at Knott's, which have space-oriented themes. The ride features an on-ride soundtrack of western music, which plays throughout the entire ride.
The ride features 10 inversions, which include a vertical loop, a corkscrew, and a zero-G roll.
Silver Bullet's train is a B&M U-shaped model, or "Wing Coaster", that features four cars with two rows of two seats each, for a total of eight riders per train. Each row has two shoulder harnesses.
The ride begins with the train pulling out of the station and going around a small banked turn. Then, the train enters the lift hill and begins to load. Once loaded, the train begins to move toward the top of the lift, where it begins to turn 180 degrees and moves toward the station. The train then begins to descend the 131' drop. After this, the train enters the 131' vertical loop. This is followed by a cobra roll and an Immelman, then the train enters the zero-G roll. The train then enters an overbanked turn and pulls into the station.
Silver Bullet was the first of three roller coasters built for Knott's Berry Farm by Bolliger & Mabillard. The others are HangTime (which opened in 2018) and Fuel Rod Run.

Aniston 's performance in Friends has been praised since her first appearance in its pilot . Entertainment Weekly 's Ken Tucker

called her the "funniest person on television"  and a "comic genius". Her character, Rachel Green, was selected by TV Guide as one of the 50 greatest TV characters of all time, calling her "one of the most endearing characters ever to pass through a television screen".  She also won two Primetime Emmy Awards  and two Golden Globe Awards  for the role. Of her performance, Aniston said: "I feel incredibly lucky to have gotten the chance to do this show, and I feel incredibly lucky to have gotten the part that I did. I think I got a little bit of a head start because of the fact that I was labeled the pretty one."
 After Friends ended in 2004, Aniston took a role in the romantic comedy The Break-Up (2006) with Vince Vaughn. The film was a box-office hit, earning $206 million worldwide.  The following year, Aniston had roles in the romantic comedies Marley & Me (2008) and He's Just Not That into You (2009). She was praised for her work in the latter, with The Hollywood Reporter saying that "she's the glue that holds the movie together" and "delivers possibly the best performance of her career."  The following year, she starred in the romantic comedy Horrible Bosses (2011). The film grossed $209 million worldwide and received positive reviews, with Ann Hornaday of The Washington Post saying that "it's a pleasure to watch Aniston in a role that doesn't require her to be self-deprecating or zany, and in which her considerable comedic skills can take center stage."  Of her performance, Aniston said: "I think I'm a better actress now because I've done comedy. It's a good challenge, and it's not as easy as it looks."

In 2014, Aniston had a voice role in the animated film Turbo (2013) and appeared in the science-fiction romance Cake (2014). The latter saw her nominated for the Golden Globe and SAG Award for Best Actress.  In 2015, she starred in the comedy We're the Millers and the drama Cake (2014); for the latter, she received a third Golden Globe nomination for Best Actress.  She had voice roles in the animated films Storks (2016) and Office Christmas Party (2016). Aniston also reunited with Vaughn in the comedy sequel The Break-Up 2 (2017); she said the film had been a "long time coming" and that she was "thrilled" to be working with Vaughn again. ## Life

He was the son of Jeremi Wiśniowiecki and Laura Czetwertynska, and was born on 24 August 1625. He participated in the election of Władysław IV Vasa as King of Poland on 11 April 1632.

### Diplomatic career

In 1643, he was appointed ambassador to the court of the Elector of Saxony in Dresden and Upper Palatinate; he had to negotiate the alliance of the Polish–Saxon–French alliance against the Swede. His mission was successful, and in 1644, he was appointed Polish ambassador to the court of Louis XIV in Paris.

### Then military career

On 28 April 1648, he was appointed General of the Crown Lithuanian Cavalry. He commanded a cavalry brigade during the First Northern War against Sweden during the Battle of Jankov and the Battle of Khotyn in 1649.

### Political career

He was of a pro-French orientation, and was one of the political leaders of the anti-Swedish faction.

He was elected the voivode of Bratslav in 1648, and in 1649, he was elected the castellan of Podolia.

### Litigation

In 1648, he was implicated into the unsuccessful attempt to elevate Miron Kowno to the polish throne, as king.

In 1651, he was implicated into the conspiracy, organized by the grand chancellor Jeremi Wisniowiecki, to murder the king John II Casimir, who wanted to renegotiate the treaty of 1648 with the Swedes. He was arrested at the same time with Wisniowiecki.

### Death

He died in 1651, while imprisoned.

## Family

He was married to Dorothea Barbara de Beauvais, daughter of Philippe de Beauvais, Count of Noailles, and Catherine de la Baume Le Blanc de La Vallière.

Ceratopsia or Ceratopia ( / ˌsɛrəˈtɒpsiə / or / ˌsɛrəˈtoʊpiə / ; Greek : " horned faces " ) is a group of herbivorous , beaked

dinosaurs that lived in what is now North America (and possibly Asia) during the Cretaceous Period , about 100 million years ago. There were many different species, and they are a member of a larger group called Neoceratopsia .
Ceratopsia is one of the most common groups of dinosaurs found in the fossil record. The earliest known species is dated to about 110 million years ago, during the late Jurassic. Ceratopsia diversified rapidly, and by the end of the Jurassic, there were many different species. They survived into the Cretaceous, where they became the dominant herbivorous dinosaurs in North America. Ceratopsia were widespread in the Northern Hemisphere, but they are rare in the Southern Hemisphere , where they were replaced by similar dinosaurs, the Ornithopoda . However, a few species are known from Australia, including the famous Gondwanatherium .
The first known ceratopsian was a species of Psittacosaurus . Psittacosaurus was a small, fairly primitive genus. During the early Cretaceous, another genus, Yinlong , gained a very large fanfare (between 1 and 2 meters). The early ceratopsian dinosaurs were small and primitive, and they were not true ceratopsids. Rather, they were more closely related to the horned dinosaurs, like Triceratops . The early ceratopsian dinosaurs gave rise to the horned dinosaurs like Triceratops , so the early ceratopsian dinosaurs are considered the "ancestors of ceratopsian dinosaurs".
The ceratopsian dinosaurs probably evolved from a group of dinosaurs called basal ceratopsians. The basal ceratopsian dinosaurs were a diverse group of small, primitive, and often bipedal dinosaurs. During the Georgian era Bath became fashionable . The architects John Wood , the Elder and his son John Wood , the Younger laid

out the streets of the city and built elegant Palladian houses that were the talk of Europe.
 The Pump Room , created by John Wood , was built in 1797 and soon became a popular place to meet and talk. By the early 19th century, the novelist Jane Austen was part of the local community. She described the city in her novels, such as Northanger Abbey , and her letters contain references to the "Hell Fire Clubs" that met in Bath.
 The city was popular with artists and writers, including Robert and Elizabeth Barrett Browning and Thomas Hardy. The city was a popular place for suffragettes to gather, including Emmeline Pankhurst , who founded the Women's Social and Political Union there.
When World War II broke out, the city was an obvious target for German bombers. During the Blitz , Bath was frequently bombed and this damaged many of the fine buildings. The Bath Blitz of 25 April 1942 was the deadliest night of bombing, when 163 people were killed and 160 people were seriously injured.
During the late 20th century, the city became a tourist destination. At the beginning of the 21st century, Bath was a Victorian City with a Georgian Face.

Wales change strip – also known as the alternative strip – is black jerseys , shorts and socks although there have been various changes to this over the years, with white socks being introduced for the Home Nations.
the tradition of the alternative strip first came to the fore when Wales reached the semi-finals of the 1958 World Cup, which they did by beating England in the quarter-finals.
Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, Wales changed strips for home matches, usually opting for the all-black strip.
This would often be paired with black outfield boots and white goalkeeping boots.
The white jersey with red trim was worn for the matches at the 1976 European Championships in Yugoslavia, which Wales reached by beating Northern Ireland in a qualifying play-off.
It was also worn at the 1978 World Cup in Argentina.
Wales wore the all-black strip once again in 1985 for a European Championship qualifier in Norway, a 4-0 defeat.
In 1988, Wales changed their strip twice more, when they played a friendly in Australia.

Various wuxia novels and folk legends have endowed Zhou with different kinds of martial and supernatural skills . These range f

rom abilities to detect magic and speak to animals to the power of a thunderbolt to discharge lightning from the palm .
The character Zhou Zhiruo was first introduced in the _Shui hu zhuan_ (Water Moon Records) and _Zhuang zi shi_ (Record of the Strange Tales of Zhuang Zhou), two popular stories of the Western Jin dynasty . Zhou's supernatural powers were inherited from her father Zhou Xing  , and her comic antics and elegant speech were inherited from her grandmother, the beautiful and intelligent Zhou Yue  , a legendary figure in Chinese history .
In the _Shui hu zhuan_ , Zhou is a young girl who lives with her father and stepmother in the town of Jianye . When her stepmother dies, her father remarries and has a son . Zhou is not in good terms with her father's new wife and the two even fight to the death .
 Zhou left her father and stepmother and went to live with her grandmother, Zhou Yue . She eventually marries a handsome young man named Zhuo Yuanjin  . When her husband's mother dies, Zhou takes over the role of a stepmother to her husband's younger brother and sister . Zhou Zhiruo and her husband are later persecuted for their knowledge of the supernatural and are both murdered .
In the _Zhuang zi shi_ , Zhou is the daughter of Zhou Xing, a man of supernatural powers who is also a famous poisoner . Zhou Xing is a master of the "philosophy of no-man" and he has a son and a daughter . However, his son Zhou Zhongze is not very fond of his father and was once poisoned by him . Zhou's daughter, Zhou Zhiruo, is next in line to take over the poisoning business and is often taunted by her brother . Zhou's father dies of illness and she receives the offer to inherit his poisoning skills from a mysterious traveller . Zhou is seduced by this traveller and she agrees to become a poisoner .
Zhou Zhiruo, the daughter of Zhou Xing, is also featured in other wuxia novels, such as _Shui hu zhan sheng_ (Record of the Strange Tales of the Water Moon), _Ba ba zhi ji_ (Eight Diagram Pole Fighter) and _Ding shi zhuan_ (Record of the Strange Tales of the Ding Family) . In these novels, Zhou is portrayed as a beautiful and virtuous young woman who is pure of heart and is surrounded by a number of loyal and devoted retainers .
 Zhou Zhiruo's most famous appearance is in the _Meng xiang xi ling_ (Dream of the Red Mansion). Zhou is the first love of the protagonist, Jia Baoyu . The two are playmates as children and share a close relationship . However, when Zhou grows up she develops feelings for the scholars Xue Baochai and Tan Yang . She marries Xue and is later murdered by Tan .
Zhou Zhiruo's character is very versatile and she has been adapted for a wide range of films and television series . In the 1980s television series _Xiao zhan sheng_ (Romance of the Great Tang), Zhou was interpreted by Zhang Xiaoqiong . In the 1990s television series _Shui hu zhan sheng_ , Zhou was interpreted by Feng Min . In the 1985 film _Zhou zhiruo, xue baochai_ (Zhou Zhiruo, Xue Baochai), Zhou was interpreted by Zhao Xiaobing .

The Missouri River is the longest river in North America . Rising in the Rocky Mountains of western Montana , the Missouri flow

ed through the central Plains for more than 2,500 miles , past eight states, and into the Mississippi River near St. Louis . It was the lifeblood of the "Great Plains," the vast grassland between the Rockies and the Mississippi, and it was also the "Main Street" of the West. In the middle part of the nineteenth century, the Missouri was an important highway for the millions of emigrants who traveled westward to settle the West. But the river was also a barrier to settlement, because it was blocked by rapids, waterfalls, and other obstacles that made it difficult to navigate.
In the early part of the nineteenth century, James Mackay was a Scottish farmer who emigrated to America to help his brother-in-law establish a farm in the United States. The Mackay family spent the winter of 1816-17 around the mouth of the Missouri, in what is now the state of Iowa . While he was there, Mackay witnessed the first attempt to navigate the Missouri by steamboat. The boat was called _Enterprise_ , and it had been built in London. The boat's captain, Thomas McKenney, had been a United States army officer in the War of 1812 and had been present at the surrender of the British at Detroit . After the war, McKenney served as a topographical engineer on a survey of the Missouri River. He was the first to navigate the river as far as Omaha, Nebraska , and became the first to take an American flag to the far West, at Fort Mandan in the Dakotas. But because of the obstacles in the river and the danger of Indian attack, McKenney did not return home. Instead, he stayed on the Missouri to trade with the Indians. Mackay and other emigrants who came to the area asked McKenney to take them back to St. Louis, and on September 28, 1817, seventeen of them climbed aboard the _Enterprise_ , which had been loaded with trade goods.
Mackay's description of the voyage is brief but interesting. He says the river was about four hundred yards wide and that the _Enterprise_ was built for six or eight passengers and a crew of six. The boat had no deck, and the men and the passengers sat or stood on the gunwales. As the boat came to the falls at Bellevue, Iowa , Mackay says he thought the boat was going to turn over. The crew made a "landing" at what is now Omaha, Nebraska , but the boat was damaged and had to be towed to St. Louis. Mackay and the other emigrants went on to Missouri. His account of the voyage gives us some idea of the difficulties that boatmen like McKenney faced as they attempted to navigate the Missouri and other rivers of the West.

of a few weeks . The eggs are oval in shape and have a diameter of about 0.7 mm. The eggs are deposited in a white wax-like substance which protects them from the environment, and are attached to twigs in the tops of trees. Each female can lay up to 1,000 eggs over a period of their lives. The eggs hatch in about 10 days . A larva hatches from each egg, and can grow to a length of about 12 mm over a period of about 14 days. It then passes through a pupal stage for about 10 days, after which it emerges as a fully grown adult. The adults often live for about a year, but can live for up to 2 years in favourable conditions .

### Food and feeding

The eggs and larvae live on the eggs of birds and other insects. The adults feed on pollen and nectar .

### Habitat

The larvae live in trees, and the adults live on trees and bushes .

### Distribution

The species is found in tropical and subtropical regions around the world. It is found in eastern Africa, in the south-western Indian Ocean, in south-eastern Asia, in the south-western Pacific and in northern Australia .

After the PTC 's statement , Julianne Escobedo Shepherd of AlterNet wrote that the group seemed to employ a double standard ; i

.e., fail to condemn all forms of violence in the name of religion , but condemn only those that conflict with the group's own beliefs .

### Media coverage of the statement

The statement was covered by many media outlets. The Associated Press reported that the PTC had made the statement by email, and quoted PTC chairman Tim Winter. The Washington Post commented that the PTC had made its statement following the Obama administration's announcement that it would remove a ban on federal funding for embryonic stem cell research. The Tampa Tribune, the Minneapolis Star-Tribune, the Charlotte Observer, the Rocky Mountain News, and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer reported that the PTC had warned that the statement could be seen as religiously motivated.

The Washington Post and the Tampa Tribune quoted Winter as saying that the group's statement was meant to combat a "false narrative" that the media was spreading about the PTC's stance on the issue. The Charlotte Observer and the Rocky Mountain News quoted PTC member Brent Bozell as saying that the media had used the PTC's statement as an excuse to "bash conservatives as 'against science' and 'anti-knowledge.'" The Rocky Mountain News also quoted the PTC's statement of July 13 as saying that "the more than 100 groups who have signed [the PTC's statement] represent the views of millions of Americans who are concerned about the growing trend of hostility toward religion in our culture."

### Criticism of the statement

In a blog post, Jonathan Merritt of The Atlantic questioned whether the PTC's statement was "an attempt to showcase the organization's religious diversity or a public-relations blunder?" He wrote that the statement "only made sense if the PTC's goal was to make itself seem less conservative." He also wrote that the statement "demonstrates an epistemological provincialism and an unreasonable conflation of religion with conservative politics."

In a blog post , John Cole of Balloon Juice wrote that "the PTC is cynically attempting to blur the lines between science and religion to make it appear as if they are concerned about science when in fact they are concerned about theocracy."

On the PTC's website, a blogger identified as "Girl in a Baseball Cap" wrote that the PTC was "trying to get away with saying that they are for science and against religion, while at the same time saying that they are for religion and against science."

In a column for the Orange County Register, Erick Erickson of RedState wrote that the PTC's statement "is a blatant lie" and that the PTC could not claim to support both science and religion. He wrote that "the PTC's 'religious' statements are made up of anti-science statements."

The Turing test was proposed by British mathematician Alan Turing in his 1950 paper Computing Machinery and Intelligence, which is often credited with being the first paper to discuss the concept of artificial intelligence. In his paper, Turing proposed three tests to distinguish between machines and humans: one is to ask the machine to write a story, the second is to ask the machine to play chess, and the third is to ask the machine to engage in a conversation. The third test is known as the Turing test. The test involves a human judge, with no knowledge of the machine's capabilities, conversing with two other entities, one human and one machine. Turing proposed that if the judge is unable to determine the machine from the human, the machine is said to have passed the test.

The interior is divided into two parts by a lofty screen of Ionic columns and a triumphal arch. A choir of 15 semicircular stalls and a rood screen of oak with stained glass and statues of the Virgin and Child, St John the Baptist and St George were installed at the end of the eighteenth century. There are monuments to Henry Thynne (1739–1796), Baron Carteret (1712–1765), James Wolfe (1727–1759) and his wife Jane (died 1794) by Sir Francis Chantrey, and to Sir Astley Cooper (1768–1841) by his son.
The church has a 14-bell carillon made by Whitechapel Bell Foundry, now housed in the neighbouring church of St Clement Danes. The organ, built by Forster and Andrews in 1842, was rebuilt in 1878 by Hill and Son.
The church was re-ordered in 1972 by Edwin Lutyens and Richard Austin.
The church is Grade I listed.

Australian and English bowlers tended to pitch the ball up, so that the batsman had to play to the pitch of the ball, and the fielders were expected to stay well back. In this period there was no such thing as a 'silly point', where the batsman was liable to a leg before or leg before wicket decision if he played at the ball with his leg.
The next specific change occurred in 1891 when the 'pivot ball' was introduced. This was a rule devised by Lord Harris to stop batsmen playing the ball on its way out of the hand of the bowler. The batsman would be adjudged out if he were to deliberately play at a ball which was not pitched in his area. The pivot ball was intended to protect the bowler and the batsman, but it was found to be a blunt instrument and it was soon abandoned.
The next change came in 1895 when 'stumping' was introduced. This allowed the wicketkeeper to claim the batsman if he caught the ball before it pitched and the batsman was out of his ground. This change was made because the bowler was finding it too easy to have the batsman out lbw, so that the batsman had to do no more than make a small defensive prod to be out, although the bowler was in theory expected to claim the batsman by his head.
The next notable change came in 1900 when the run-out rule was introduced. It was designed to bring about a quicker game by allowing the bowler to claim a batsman who was out of his crease when the ball was bowled. The umpire could only adjudge a batsman out of his ground if he was in the act of running, so that 'backward running' was not allowed.
The next change came in 1902 when the 'leg before wicket' rule was introduced. The umpire would decide whether or not the batsman had hit the ball with his leg before the ball had pitched. This rule provided a more level playing field between bowler and batsman for the first time. The leg before wicket rule was not very well understood at first, and it was soon found that bowlers and umpires alike were making decisions too liberally, so that the wicketkeeper and the fielders were doing most of the bowler's work.
The next change came in 1905 when 'dead ball' was introduced. This was a rule which allowed the ball to be replaced when it went out of play, and it was intended to make the game quicker. The batsman was allowed to re-enter the field of play without the ball being out. A dead ball was also placed on the field when a batsman went to the pavilion to get treatment for an injury, and the ball was replaced when the umpires were changing ends. The rules governing the dead ball were soon found to be an unfair burden on the bowler, so that at the end of the season the dead ball was removed from cricket.
The next change came in 1921 when the 'golden duck' was introduced. This was intended to speed up the game by allowing the batsman to leave the field without the ball being out. This rule was unpopular with both umpires and the spectators, and it was soon abandoned.
The next change came in 1925 when the 'silver duck' was introduced. This was intended to speed up the game by allowing the batsman to leave the field without the ball being out. However, the batsman was not allowed to leave the field without the ball being out, and the batsman was allowed to re-enter the field of play with the ball still in play. The silver duck was allowed to stay in place for a couple of years after which it was abandoned.
The next change came in 1939 when the 'D' LBW was introduced. This was intended to bring the game into line with the 'leg before wicket' rule by allowing the batsman to be out lbw even if he did not play at the ball with his leg.
The next change came in 1949 when the 'D' LBW was replaced by the 'leg before wicket' rule. This was intended to bring the game into line with the 'leg before wicket' rule by allowing the batsman to be out lbw even if he did not play at the ball with his leg.

Congress eventually passed a watered @-@ down version of the original plan put forward by Bedell and Senator Pete Domenici . Th

e 1996 Farm Bill did not contain the $5 billion in conservation funding originally proposed, or the provision that would have forced the Conservation Reserve Program to acquire 40,000 acres of grasslands each year. The only significant change to the Committee's original proposal was that it required the secretary of agriculture to consider the effects on state and local government budgets in deciding how to allocate the money. But even this nod to fiscal responsibility was not required to be a factor in making decisions.
As the 1996 Farm Bill was being debated, a coalition of conservation and environmental groups led by the Environmental Defense Fund and the National Wildlife Federation. along with the National Association of Counties, launched a campaign to pressure Congress to support the full conservation program that Bedell and Domenici had enacted.
The coalition met with senators and congressmen from both parties, and in the end their efforts paid off. Both the House and the Senate passed versions of the farm bill that contained provisions similar to the original proposal. But the legislation was stalled in the conference committee, where all the major issues could be resolved. When the committee finally issued its report on August 22, 1996, the conservation provisions were gone.
The next day, a coalition of environmental groups that included the Environmental Defense Fund, the National Audubon Society, the National Wildlife Federation, the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Sierra Club, the Wilderness Society, and the Nature Conservancy sent a letter to the president warning that "the failure to enact a meaningful and broadly supported conservation bill will, at a minimum, be viewed as a bad omen with respect to the ability of the new Administration to reform and improve the entire federal regulatory and policy making systems."
The groups also warned that the failure of the farm bill to encourage conservation would "diminish the capacity of the federal government to protect and manage our natural resources in the future," and that the American public "will view the failure to pass a strong conservation title as an indication of a lack of political will to deal with environmental issues."
In their letter, the conservation groups told Clinton that if he wanted to restore the economy and improve the environment, he would have to use the farm bill as a vehicle for enacting major environmental initiatives.
In the end, the coalition's efforts paid off. On November 28, 1996, President Clinton signed the 1996 Farm Bill into law. The bill contained a variety of provisions that would help farmers. But it also contained major conservation measures that would help conserve the environment. The legislation provided $7.7 billion for conservation programs over the five-year life of the bill. And it mandated that the secretary of agriculture set aside 30 million acres of grasslands, wetlands, and other environmentally sensitive areas for protection.
The 1996 Farm Bill was a major victory for environmentalists and conservationists. But it also proved that these groups could not always rely on the president to support their efforts. In fact, the president's support was crucial in getting the bill passed. And while President Clinton helped to create a bipartisan coalition in Congress, he resisted the efforts of environmental groups to pressure him to support their legislative agenda.

Because of the possibility of subsurface liquid oceans on Jupiter 's moons Europa , Ganymede and Callisto , there has been great speculation regarding the potential habitability of these icy worlds. In particular, Europa and Ganymede have been identified as the most likely bodies in the Solar System other than Earth to support life. The habitability of these moons is a function of the total energy input and the chemistry of the hydrogen ocean. This review describes what is known about the chemistry and structure of the icy interior, and the energy input from the Sun, Jovian magnetosphere, and Galactic cosmic rays. The review also summarizes the astrobiological implications of these icy worlds as potential habitable environments.

This book contains 22 papers presented at a symposium held at the University of Arizona in Tucson on November 8-10, 1979, which explored the recent scientific results from the Voyager 1 and 2 flybys of Jupiter's moons Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. The Symposium was sponsored by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) as a followup to the 1977 meeting of the International Astronomical Union (IAU) Working Group on the Moons of Jupiter. The symposium, attended by 90 scientists, was a major forum for the presentation and discussion of scientific results from the Voyager 1 and 2 flybys. The papers presented at the Symposium are grouped into four sections: (1) Jupiter, (2) Europa, (3) Ganymede, and (4) Callisto. The chapters of each section are arranged in approximate order of presentation at the Symposium. The topics covered range from the interior structure of Jupiter to the thermal properties of Europa, and on to the investigation of Callisto's surface. The picture of Jupiter that has evolved from the Voyager flybys indicates that the planet is composed of a gaseous outer layer, an oceanic layer, and a rocky core. The planet's atmosphere is composed of hydrogen, helium, and traces of other gases, with a surface pressure of about 450 kPa. The surface of the planet is composed of a transparent, cloudy layer of ammonia crystals that has a temperature range of about 100-180 K. Beneath the surface, the planet is believed to be composed of a layer of hydrogen and helium, followed by a layer of water and ammonia, and a rocky core. The moons Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto are also believed to be composed of these layers, although their relative thicknesses are believed to be different from those of Jupiter. The moons also have a variety of interesting features on their surfaces.

In addition to the smaller @-@ scale expeditions described earlier , Mathews embarked on two much larger expeditions to the Afr

icanders, in 1818 and 1820. These expeditions were unique in that they were carefully planned, well organized, and, in the case of the 1820 expedition, were intended to bring an end to the wars with the Africanders. They were also unique in that they were failures.
The 1818 expedition was organized by Sir John Cradock, the Governor of the Cape, with the goal of removing the Africanders from the Castle of Good Hope and other British forts in the Western Cape. Mathews was named in the expedition as its highest-ranking officer, a position he shared with Lieutenant-Colonel William Farquhar of the Royal Engineers. The two men were ordered to take control of the Castle, and to remove the Africanders from other British forts, including Swellendam, Wynberg, and the Dutch Reformed Church of St. George in the Hout Bay. Mathews and Farquhar were also ordered to arrest any Africanders who sought refuge in the Cape's Dutch Reformed Churches.
Despite the fact that it was an act of war, the expedition was carried out in a manner that was intended to diminish as much as possible the suffering and loss of life. Mathews and Farquhar, supported by a large force of British soldiers, were instructed to treat any hostile actions by the Africanders with patience and forbearance. The Africanders should be given time to surrender, and should only be fired upon after all other means had been exhausted. The British were also forbidden from using greater force than necessary to capture any of the Africanders.
The expedition was a failure. Mathews and Farquhar were taken prisoner while attempting to take the Castle of Good Hope. When the British forces who had been sent to liberate the two men arrived, they found that the Castle had been surrendered to the Africanders. The British forces then proceeded to the next objective: the Dutch Reformed Church of St. George, which was also defended by a small group of Africanders. The church was captured, and a number of Africanders were taken prisoner.
Mathews and Farquhar were then taken to the Cape Town Exchange, where they were held prisoner until they were released the following year as a gesture of good will by the new Governor of the Cape, Sir Lowry Cole. It was a measure of the respect that the Africanders had for Mathews that they had treated him so well during his time in captivity.
The 1820 expedition had a similar purpose—to remove the Africanders from the Castle of Good Hope—but it was intended to be a peaceful, diplomatic mission. The mission was organized by the British government, and was led by Sir Benjamin D'Urban, the Governor of the Cape, and Sir Robert Craig, the British ambassador to the Cape. Mathews was named as the highest-ranking officer of the force, which was made up of British and German soldiers.
The expedition was also a failure. Mathews and the other British officers were taken prisoner upon their arrival at the Castle of Good Hope. They were released soon afterward, but the rest of the expedition was a failure.
After the two expeditions, Mathews returned to the Cape of Good Hope, where he remained for most of the next decade. During this time he was involved in several other expeditions to the Africanders, including an attempt to capture Africander leader Andries Schermerhorn, who had been declared a traitor by the Cape government. The expedition was a failure, and Mathews and the other British officers involved were taken prisoner and held for several months.
Mathews remained in the Cape until 1830, when he returned to England. During his time in the Cape, Mathews was involved in several other expeditions and skirmishes with the Africanders. He was also involved in several other expeditions to the Africanders, including an attempt to capture Africander leader Andries Schermerhorn, who had been declared a traitor by the Cape government. The expedition was a failure, and Mathews and the other British officers involved were taken prisoner and held for several months.

Yingzao Fashi is a technical treatise on architecture and craftsmanship written by Li Jie , an architect and official at the Di

anshan Gate of the palace during the Song Dynasty. Fashi simply means manual or treatise. This is the first architectural treatise in China and was written in 1103. It was published by the Chinese government in 1104 to instruct craftsmen on good building practices. It has been translated into English by Frank Ching, an American-Chinese architect, and is published by the John Wiley & Sons.
This book is a general reference guide to building construction, including designs for temples, palaces, military structures, and residential buildings. It has been translated from the original Chinese. The original is a 235-page document with 130 illustrations. It is cited in the book Chinese Architecture (ISBN 0-415-23934-9) by A.D.K. Briggs.
It is the most important book on architecture in China, and is the earliest complete book on architecture. It is one of the most important books in Chinese history. It was written around the same time as the Domus by Vitruvius.
The book provides the first known descriptions of a standardized Chinese unit of measurement, the fen.
Most of the book consists of photographs of the various buildings, with detailed descriptions of each. The book covers many topics such as roofs, walls, pillars, doors, windows, and construction techniques.

Norbert was the most intense hurricane in the 1995 Atlantic hurricane season. Norbert's large size and intensity made it one of the most damaging hurricanes in the 1995 season.
 Norbert moved west-northwestward before making a large loop to the north. Norbert was situated in a very favorable environment for intensification and as a result, Norbert strengthened and intensified rapidly. Norbert moved to the north as it approached the islands of the Lesser Antilles and was moving away from the Lesser Antilles as it intensified to a Category 5 hurricane. Norbert's track was possibly influenced by the strong steering currents associated with Hurricane Opal. Norbert weakened as it moved towards Puerto Rico and made landfall as a Category 1 hurricane. Norbert weakened further as it moved towards the Dominican Republic and made landfall as a tropical storm.

Barker 's sketches , drawings , and paintings of children were given to friends or to the parents of the subjects , donated to

the University of Washington , Seattle , Washington , donated to the Museum of Modern Art , New York , or returned to the child's family. In 1985 , the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington , D.C. , acquired Barker 's entire collection of sketches , which the Kennedy Center labeled as photographs , in order to sell them. The Kennedy Center claimed that Barker had given permission for them to sell the photographs. The Center also claimed that the photographs had been made public in a magazine article.

## Critical reception

In 1956, in a review of Barker's exhibition at the Kootz Gallery, critic Clement Greenberg wrote:

Barker's pictures are incidental to the discourse of their time in another way. They are not about the discourse, they are not intended to be about the discourse, or possibly not. They are not about the discourse of their time in the sense that they do not contribute to it, or even, in their own way, comment on it. They are not about the discourse of their time in the sense that they are not on the surface of their own time, but of another time, a past time. They are not incidental to the discourse of their time in the sense of being uninteresting to it. They are incidental to it in the sense that, as the incidental music in a film is incidental to the film, but is not uninteresting to it.

The incidental music in a film, as incidental photographs, is not uninteresting to the film, but is not of the film. It is like the musical accompaniment to a play: it is not of the play, but it is not uninteresting to it. The music, moreover, is not incidental to the play in the sense that it does not contribute to it or does not comment on it; it is incidental to it in the sense of being of another time and place.

2-dimensional gel electrophoresis (2-DE) has been used for many years to identify individual proteins in vitro, the method has been used to analyze protein expression in vivo only recently . This is in part due to the lack of suitable antibodies that can be used to detect proteins in situ. In addition, the proteins of interest are often found in small quantities, and in a highly heterogeneous distribution. However, new antibodies have recently become available that can be used to detect proteins in situ, and a number of methods have been developed to increase the sensitivity of in vivo analysis by immunocytochemistry.
The use of immunocytochemistry for in vivo analysis of proteins has been greatly facilitated by the development of new antibodies against proteins of interest. One of these is the polyclonal, anti-Hu antibody. This antibody is specific for the Hu antigen, a 22 kD protein found on the surface of mammalian cells that is also known as the gp150 polypeptide (gp150) . The Hu antibody is also capable of recognizing a number of other proteins, including the 22 kD antigen found on the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria (the H antigen), and proteins of the rhesus macaque Rh system .
The ability to recognize a number of proteins other than the Hu antigen has been exploited to prepare polyclonal antibodies against proteins that are found in high amounts in cells of a specific tissue . This has been done by immunizing animals with an extract of the tissue, which contains all of the proteins of interest. In this way, a number of antibodies have been prepared against proteins of interest in the testis, brain, and heart .
A number of different techniques have been developed to increase the sensitivity of protein detection in vivo by immunocytochemistry. One of the most common techniques is the use of antibodies conjugated to biotin (Fig. 1). This results in the formation of a streptavidin-biotin complex that can be detected by immunofluorescence microscopy with a fluorescent dye that binds to streptavidin. The streptavidin-biotin conjugate has been used to detect proteins in situ in a number of different tissues, including the testis (Fig. 2) .
Although antibodies conjugated to biotin are highly sensitive, they are often not specific for the protein of interest. This is because the antibodies may cross-react with proteins with a similar epitope, or proteins with very similar amino acid sequences. One way to overcome this problem is to use antibodies that have been raised to a protein sequence that is completely different to the protein of interest. This type of antibody is known as a phage antibody. A phage antibody is produced by injecting whole phage into an animal. The antibodies are later isolated from the animal and used to raise a specific antibody by immunizing animals with a small amount of the protein of interest. In this way, phage antibodies can be raised against proteins that are found at extremely low levels in the tissue. For instance, phage antibodies have been used to detect proteins in the testis that have been found only once among all the testes that have been analyzed .
Another common technique for increasing the sensitivity of protein detection in vivo by immunocytochemistry is the use of antibodies conjugated to horseradish peroxidase (HRP) (Fig. 3). This has been used to detect proteins in the testis , and in the heart . However, a potential problem with HRP conjugated antibodies is that the antibodies may cross-react with proteins with a similar epitope. This may be overcome by using an antibody that has been raised to a protein sequence that is completely different to the protein of interest, as in the case of phage antibodies.
A further potential problem with antibodies conjugated to HRP is that they are often not specific for a single protein. This is because HRP can bind to a number of proteins, including antibodies. The antibodies may also react with other proteins, such as the proteins that are present in the cell membrane. This problem can be overcome by using antibodies conjugated to avidin (Fig. 4). After a brief stay in Boston , Bradstreet made his first residence in Newtowne ( later renamed Cambridge ) , near the Dudleys i

.e. the New England Company's primary settlement. In 1632, he was appointed public notary of the Massachusetts Bay Colony . He also served as an official of the General Court and president of the colony's highest legislative body, Plymouth Colony , during its first two sessions. During his tenure in Plymouth, Bradstreet wrote one of his most famous poems, "The Courtship" (1633), which was a satirical description of his marriage to Dorothy Dudley. After the death of his first wife, he married Hannah Alden, a widow with five children.
 Bradstreet's poetry, unlike the work of many of his contemporaries, was influenced by the literary traditions of the Metaphysical poets , particularly John Donne and George Herbert . He was also influenced by the Cavalier poets, in particular Richard Lovelace , Henry Vaughan , and Richard Crashaw . In 1645, Bradstreet moved with his family to Salem, Massachusetts (now a part of Danvers, Massachusetts ), where he became a judge and was appointed to the General Court. He was also appointed postmaster of Salem. He died there in 1657 and was buried in the burying ground of Salem's Old South Church.
 Some of Bradstreet's lines were quoted by Benjamin Franklin in Poor Richard's Almanack (1733–1757). Franklin's translation of Bradstreet's lines in The Way to Wealth and Poor Richard's Almanack (1733) read, "Fools choose to ramble in the road, And idlers make the road their home."
 In 1927, American poet Robert Frost wrote a poem about Bradstreet entitled "The House Divided", which is about Bradstreet's decision to leave his position as a judge in Salem.
 Bradstreet was one of the first American poets to use the sonnet structure in his work.

In September 2008 , it was reported that " Oldham Town Hall is only months away from a major roof collapse " . A tour taken by

600 guests highlighted the decaying state of the building, and led to the formation of a trust to save it.
The town hall was built in 1887 and designed by George Deaville of Manchester. It is a Grade II listed building , and is described in the national listing as being "a large neo-classical building in pale gritstone with a slate roof, four low Ionic columns supporting a cornice and entablature, all on a rusticated plinth. The principal façade is symmetrical with an entrance portico on the east front with four paired pilasters and a pediment above on which is a clock. The east side has a large arched window with a keystone and the west side two large arched windows. The south side has a half-round arched window on the ground floor and a round-arched window on the first floor. The north side has a round-arched doorway with a keystone and a round-arched window on the first floor. The roof is hipped.
The town hall was designed in the neo-classical style, and is a good example of its type.
It was built as Oldham's town hall, but was the third town hall to be built on the site, replacing a neo-Romanesque building from 1868 , which was in turn replacing an earlier building from 1823 .
The front portico was removed in 1930.
The town hall was listed in July 1972 as Grade II*, and was listed in the same grade in January 1985 . The listing has a 2002 amendment that states that the town hall is "externally of special interest as a good example of a neo-classical town hall of the 1880s".
The town hall is now occupied as offices, and is not open to the public.

## Effects

### Dominican Republic

In the Dominican Republic, the storm caused 13 deaths. Most of the damage came from flooding, which caused the deaths of 10 people. The storm also caused widespread crop damage.

### Saint Lucia

In Saint Lucia, the storm caused much damage to the island. In Castries alone, the winds uprooted many trees and caused severe flooding. The storm also caused damage to buildings, and destroyed crops and livestock.

### Antigua

In Antigua and Barbuda, the storm caused two fatalities. The storm also caused damage to buildings, and uprooted trees.

### Puerto Rico

In Puerto Rico, the storm caused one fatality, and also caused damage to buildings and the Puerto Rico Central Railroad.

Boise National Forest 's 2010 forest plan recognizes that fire and other disturbances play important roles in maintaining the c

olonial  bee  squirrel  ecosystem  (forest plans  are  the  legal  documents  that  guide  natural resource  management  on  National  Forest  System  lands).  The  plan  outlines  the  reason  and  need  for  conservation   of  the  squirrel  population  and  their  habitat.  There  is  also  a  provision  in  the  plan  that  requires  the  management   of  the  squirrel  habitat   to  support  the  squirrels  and  their  food  source,  the  cones  of  pinyon-juniper  and  ponderosa  pine  trees.  It  is  up  to  the  USFS  to  determine  how  this  would  be  accomplished.  Some  options  include  using  prescribed  fire  to  burn  the  brush  to  create  an  open  meadow  for  the  squirrels  to  use,  or  letting  the  squirrels  naturally  control  the  habitat  through  their  own  actions.  The  squirrels  are  suspected  to  be  responsible  for  a  large  percentage  of  the  fires  in  the  forest.
As  of  June  2012,  no  action  has  been  taken  on  the  Forest  Plan  to  manage  the  squirrels  and  their  habitat.  Although  the  plan  was  for  the  squirrels  to  be  managed  by  the  USFS,  a  collaborative  group  of  citizens  is  currently  working  with  the  USFS  to  develop  a  plan.  The  group  has  been  meeting  since  March  2011  and  is  currently  working  on  a  final  draft  of  the  plan.  The  plan  is  expected  to  be  completed  by  August  2012.  The  plan  is  available  at  www.bcfirefocus.org.

On August 29 , 2006 , Dylan released his Modern Times album . Despite some coarsening of Dylan 's voice ( a critic for The Guardian ) the album was well received. On November 22, 2007, Dylan and The Dead performed together for the first time at the Beacon Theatre in New York. Dylan and the Dead went on to play 11 more shows during the 2007–2008 tour. In 2009, Dylan and the Dead performed at the New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival. In 2010, they embarked on another tour , and in May 2011 they performed at the Hollywood Bowl . In 2015, they did another tour.
One of the classic songs that Dylan performed with the Dead is "All Along The Watchtower". Dylan was inspired by a painting by artist Jimi Hendrix , who recorded his own version of it in 1967.

Joyce Kilmer 's reputation as a poet is staked largely on the widespread popularity of this one poem . " Trees " was liked imme

asurably more than any other of his poems by his contemporaries, and it is still widely read and anthologized. This fact, combined with its simple subject matter, its plain-spoken diction, and its insistence on the reader's identification with the speaker, has led to a certain condescension toward it. Many of the poems in this volume, however, have more depth than "Trees" has been given credit for, and this volume provides an opportunity to see the full range of Kilmer's poetry.
 Kilmer's poetry is based on a belief in the sanctity of the natural world. His romanticism is of the Transcendentalist variety, but he also shares with the Romantics a tendency to see nature as a metaphor for human emotion. His best poems are intensely personal, full of feeling and with a sense of directness that makes the reader feel as if he, too, has seen what he describes.
 Kilmer has been called a "poet of the people," and he is indeed popular. This is partly due to the fact that his poems are widely anthologized and often repeated aloud by children in school. But there is more to it than that. There is a directness and simplicity in Kilmer's work that is endearing, and it appeals to the child in us all. This simplicity, however, does not lessen the depth of the poems. His best poems are powerful and moving, and the reader is left with the feeling that he has lived through experiences that are intensely real.

Oldham 's town centre contains the highest concentration of retailing , cultural facilities and employment in the Metropolitan

Borough . The town has a number of retail centres, including the Oldham Centre, the Broadway Centre, and the King Street Centre.  The town also features a number of public houses, nightclubs, shopping centres, restaurants, cafes, and sporting venues. Soap  Factory  museum , which is a listed building and Grade II* listed , is located in the town centre.
Oldham is home to the Oldham Coliseum Theatre , which was founded by Sir  Frank  Birley in 1923.  The theatre hosts a wide variety of productions including family shows, pantomimes and live music. The theatre is often used as a setting for BBC dramas.
Oldham has a number of annual events, including the Oldham Carnival , which is held on the last Saturday of May; the Oldham Lights  Festival  which is held on the first Saturday of December; and the Oldham Food and Drink Festival which is held in October. GREENSBORO, N.C. (AP) — Trey Wolff kicked a 29-yard field goal with 2:11 remaining and East Carolina beat North Carolina A&T 37-29 on Thursday night.
Wolff’s 29-yard kick came after ECU (5-3) recovered a fumble at the Aggies’ 45-yard line. East Carolina turned the ball over on downs at the Aggies’ 28-yard line with 5:32 remaining. The ECU defense held on downs at midfield with 2:38 remaining, and the Pirates were able to run out the clock.
East Carolina was outgained 579-381, but the Pirates made big plays when they had to. ECU was 5 of 11 on third down and 3 of 4 on fourth down.
East Carolina also held A&T to two field goals in the second half after the Aggies (4-4) had scored touchdowns on their first four possessions in the third quarter.
Jaleel Scott had seven catches for 154 yards and a touchdown for ECU.
A&T quarterback Lamar Raynard completed 25 of 37 passes for 299 yards and two touchdowns, but he was also intercepted twice.
Four A&T receivers had at least 83 yards receiving, led by Elijah Bell’s 122 yards on five catches.
The Aggies had 164 total yards in the first quarter, but scored only three points. East Carolina took a 17-3 lead before A&T scored a touchdown on an 8-yard run by Marquell Cartwright early in the second quarter.
East Carolina: The Pirates had their sixth straight victory against an FCS team, dating back to 2009. ECU’s win over North Carolina Central in 2012 was vacated because of NCAA sanctions.
North Carolina A&T: The Aggies’ record against FBS opponents is 1-22. They lost to Clemson 41-7 in 2011, lost to North Carolina 35-21 in 2013 and lost to East Carolina 35-7 last year.

North Carolina A&T: The Aggies will be at Delaware State on Nov. 5.

The Tempest maintains much of the horrorcore lyrical content ICP is known for , as well as their humorous perspective . Unlike

their previous albums, the duo enlisted a number of guests to appear on The Tempest , including Twiztid, Tech N9ne, and E-40 .  The album's first single, " Ghetto Nights " , was released on July 23, 2007 .
Lyrically, The Tempest is centered on the trials and tribulations of ICP's life in the rap industry, as well as their encounters with law enforcement, fans, and their critics . While The Tempest is primarily a concept album, the overall theme is more in the realm of  fantasy than reality .  The album is also the first ICP album to include clean versions of the songs.  On June 17, 2007,  ICP announced the release date for The Tempest,  and teased  the album's title track in early June. On June 27, 2007, ICP premiered the song " The Tempest " on the Gathering of the Juggalos  event in New Orleans, Louisiana .  On July 2, 2007, the song " Ghetto Nights " was made available for streaming on the ICP website.
The Tempest was preceded by a short film, ICP: The Motion Picture , which premiered on June 25, 2007, as a lead-up to the release.  The motion picture is divided into two sections, "Ghetto Nights" and "The Tempest", and contains the same story as the album.  The film also includes the music video for " Ghetto Nights " , the song " Ghetto Nights (Remix) ", and " Ghetto Nights (Ruff Rider's Club Remix)" .  The film was directed by ICP member Joey C.  The film was released on DVD on August 28, 2007.  ICP: The Motion Picture was originally intended to be a full-length feature film, though the final version is only approximately an hour long.  The film was distributed by Rap-A-Lot Records , and released on DVD on August 28, 2007.
The Tempest received positive reviews from most music critics.  Pitchfork Media's Mark Richardson, who gave the album  a "Best New Music" rating, said "The Tempest is more musically  adventurous than any of their previous efforts, and the lyrics are as detailed and compelling as any they've ever written."  The album was ranked at number 3 in the annual Pitchfork Media's Top 50 Albums of 2007 list.  While The Tempest has been described by some critics as the band's "most cohesive album yet", and "their best album to date",  the album was also criticized by some reviewers as being "all over the place" .

awartha Trans Canada Trail ) and a short jaunt along a paved trail leading to Victoria Beach . This section is mostly within the City of Kawartha Lakes. The trail is well maintained and well used by walkers, cyclists and cross-country skiers in winter.
 The trail continues north of Lindsay to Fenelon Falls . The trail follows the former railway bed ( now the Kawartha Trans Canada Trail ) and crosses the waterfront of Fenelon Falls.The trail then crosses through the small village of Belmour before arriving in Bobcaygeon.
 The trail then leaves Bobcaygeon and heads north, crossing the Trent River , continuing on to Campbellford.
 The trail then crosses the Trent River and heads onto Cobourg . This section of the trail is heavily used by walkers, cyclists and cross-country skiers in winter.
From there it heads north to Port Hope where it crosses the port.
The trail then crosses Highway 401 and follows along the east side of Owen Sound to Wiarton .
The trail then heads west and south along the Bruce Peninsula , passing through Wiarton, Tobermory and ending at Lion's Head .
There is a proposed extension of the trail north of Lindsay to Peterborough .

Woodhouse was born in Beverley and raised in Driffield . His father , Bernard Woodhouse , died at the age of 51 after he had a

17-year battle with cancer. He was educated at Nunthorpe Grammar School , where he became a prefect and was awarded sportsman of the year. He left school with four A-levels in French , German , history and chemistry and was offered a place at Leeds University to study medicine . However, he decided to pursue a career in law and went to the University of Sheffield to study law, gaining a 2:1 degree and being awarded a prize for the best law student in his year. He was called to the bar by Gray's Inn in 1976.
 In 1977, Woodhouse was appointed as an assistant recorder in York and in 1982 was appointed as a recorder in the Crown Court . He became a Deputy High Court Judge in 1983 and a High Court Judge in 1990. He presided over the 1996 trial of the Birmingham Six , who were wrongly convicted of the IRA Birmingham pub bombings , where a total of 21 people were killed and more than 200 injured in 1974. He was the presiding judge in the 1997 trial of the football hooligan John Fashanu, who was convicted of the manslaughter of his 17-year-old lover, Myra Adams. Fashanu was found to have suffocated Adams and was jailed for six years.
Woodhouse was appointed the Master of the Rolls in 1999 by Lord Irvine of Lairg , the then Lord Chancellor . The Master of the Rolls is the senior common law judge in England and Wales and is responsible for the constitution and management of the Chancery Division of the High Court. He is the principal judge of the greater number of cases in Chancery and is the principal authority on the practice of the division. Woodhouse was appointed to the Privy Council in 2008.
 Woodhouse's judicial responsibilities included the 2003 trial of the killer Stephen Griffiths , who murdered Mary McLoughlin, Rhiannon Roberts and Susan Rushworth. In 2004, he condemned the "outrageous" behaviour of a woman who had repeatedly sent her abusive boyfriend threatening letters and text messages, saying that he would kill her family. In the same year, Woodhouse turned down an appeal by a man who had been convicted of the murder of 12-year-old schoolboy Stuart Thomas in 1986. In 2005, he was responsible for the trial of an 11-year-old boy who had stabbed a 16-year-old boy to death.
 In 2007, he was the judge in the trial of 20-year-old "fantasist" Seán Hodgson , who was convicted of the murder of his two-year-old son .
 Woodhouse married Liz Cullen in 1982 and they had three children. He lived in Oxfordshire . In his spare time he was an enthusiastic golfer and an active member of the University Club . He was also a member of the dining clubs of the Garrick , Travellers and City of London .
 Woodhouse died on 3 December 2009 in the Royal Gwent Hospital in Newport . He had suffered a suspected heart attack the night before and was taken to hospital in an ambulance . He was 59 years old.

The church of St Clement Danes is believed to date from the 9th century . The name may have come from Harold Harefoot , a Danis

-held town in Normandy that was held by the family of Robert de Sigille .
A church was originally dedicated to St Clement, the Pope who was martyred in the 3rd century. This dedication was replaced by that of St George, the patron saint of England, in the 11th century. During the reign of King Stephen (reigned 1135-54), the name was changed again to St Clement Danes.
The church was rebuilt in 1672-74 by Christopher Wren , and is the only Wren church in London that survived the Great Fire of 1666. The interior of the church was destroyed by fire in 1941, and was re-built in the 1960s.
One of the four sections of the old church's roof became the royal coat of arms for Queen Elizabeth II. The present church is the largest of the 56 churches in the City of London. At the heart of the church, in the Lady Chapel, is the monument to Samuel Pepys and his wife, Elizabeth.
A plaque on the south wall of the church reads: 'In memory of Sir John Vanbrugh (1664-1726) famous architect and builder of Castle Howard, Blenheim, Hampstead House, Queen Anne's Battery, Greenwich. He also built the Royal Naval Hospital at Greenwich and the Monument to the Great Fire of London. He was a friend and neighbour of Sir Christopher Wren. Buried in St Clement Danes.'

 331,000 students were in state secondary schools in 1945. By 1990 this figure had increased to 2.4 million.

  In 1945, 17 per cent of children went to university or specialised college. By 1975, this figure was 26 per cent and by 1977, 33 per cent. The number of young people attending university rose to 18 per cent in the 1980s.
  The number of state comprehensive schools rose from 200 in the 1950s to 1,600 in the mid-1960s and to 2,800 by 1977.
  About 50 per cent of students in comprehensive schools were from working-class backgrounds in 1977.
  By 1977, 60 per cent of pupils in state schools were receiving free school meals.
  In 1945, 9 per cent of pupils were taught by women. By 1990, this figure had risen to 23 per cent.

Hydrocarbon exploration is ongoing following the first major find at the Kinsale Head gas field off Cork in the mid @-@ 1970s .

In February 1975 the major British company Shell E&P Ireland (later renamed Shell E&P UK) began drilling the Rathlin gas field in the North Channel between Ireland and Scotland . The gas was successfully exploited and in the following years Shell drilled further gas fields off the Irish coast — at Bellanaboy, Knockmore, Corrib, and at the Clogherhead gas field. Gulf Oil and BP also drilled gas fields off Ireland's east coast and in the Celtic Sea .
BP drilled the first well in the North Sea in 1965, while the first well in the Atlantic was drilled by British Gas in 1971. In the following years, the North Sea became a major area of hydrocarbon exploration.
The Western area of the North Sea is the most prolific of the three major basins of the North Sea, with a total of 17,730 km 2 (6,843 sq mi) of acreage that is 100% owned by the industry . The Western area was the first area to be exploited and is the most developed area of the North Sea. The Western area is divided into the Central North Sea, the East North Sea, the Southern North Sea, and the Norwegian sector of the North Sea . The Central North Sea area comprises the Danish and Dutch sectors of the North Sea. The East North Sea area comprises the Norwegian and British sectors of the North Sea, while the Southern North Sea area comprises the Belgian and Dutch sectors of the North Sea . The main oil and gas fields of the North Sea are in the Central North Sea.
Shell E&P UK is the largest operator in the North Sea with a total of 1,996 km 2 (769.8 sq mi) of licensed acreage, and the company has interests in 123 gas fields. British Gas has 1,453 km 2 (560.9 sq mi) of licensed acreage, and the company has interests in 111 gas fields.
BP has 1,286 km 2 (496.6 sq mi) of licensed acreage, and the company has interests in 103 gas fields, while ExxonMobil has 1,244 km 2 (480.3 sq mi) of licensed acreage, and the company has interests in 111 gas fields.
The offshore oil and gas industry in the UK North Sea is in steady decline. The North Sea is the oldest offshore hydrocarbon province in the world and the industry has been plagued by high costs and a declining oil price.
The North Sea has produced over 45 billion barrels (7.2×10 9 m 3) of oil and 1.7 trillion cubic metres (56×10 9 cu ft) of gas.

Resuscitation begins with the assessment and stabilization of the person 's airway , breathing and circulation . If inhalation

anesthesia has already been given, this may make respiration more difficult. A person with a blockage in his airway may need artificial ventilation with a bag-valve-mask device or a supraglottic airway device such as a facemask, laryngeal mask, or endotracheal tube. If a person has a significant blockage in his upper airway such as that caused by an obstruction or a fracture, he may need surgical intervention. In some cases, a person may have a complete blockage of his airway and require a tracheostomy [surgical insertion of a tube into the trachea].
 Resuscitation of a person whose heart has stopped depends on restoring a normal heart rhythm. This may be achieved by defibrillation , which is the application of an electric current to the chest to stop the ventricles from quivering. Electrocardiogram monitoring is useful to confirm that the person's heart has normal sinus rhythm. If the heart rate is slow, it may be necessary to start an infusion of epinephrine, which causes the heart to beat faster.
 Cardiac drugs such as atropine , lidocaine , and epinephrine may be used to control abnormal heart rhythms.

 A person with a traumatic brain injury may be severely impaired. This may be due to loss of consciousness with severe head injury, or may be due to coma , which is a state of unconsciousness and inability to be awakened. In either case, a person may have serious neurological deficits such as poor movement and weakness, loss of sensation, and inability to speak. He may have behavioral problems and trouble thinking clearly.
 When a person is unconscious and unable to communicate, family members and friends may feel powerless and helpless. It may be difficult to know how to care for the person and when to seek professional help.
 A person with a traumatic brain injury may have a long-term disability that requires specialized ongoing care.
 Family members and friends may feel a great deal of stress when a person is in the hospital. It may be difficult to watch the person go through long-term therapy or be in a coma.

" Don 't You Wanna Stay " is a country pop song with a length of four minutes and sixteen seconds . It incorporates melancholic

orchestral accompaniment, such as the cello, violin, and double bass . The song was written by Chris DeStefano and Josh Kear , and produced by the latter. " Don 't You Wanna Stay " was recorded by American country music artists Jason Aldean and Kelly Clarkson . For her sixth studio album, Stronger (2011), Clarkson and Aldean co-wrote the song, which was initially intended for Aldean 's third album, My Kinda Party (2010). The song was released as the third and final single from Clarkson 's Stronger on November 22, 2011, in the United States.
" Don 't You Wanna Stay " subsequently became a commercial success in the United States, peaking at number two on the Billboard Hot 100 and number one on the Billboard Hot Country Songs chart, becoming Clarkson 's first number one on the latter chart. The song was also a sleeper hit in New Zealand, where it reached the top 10. " Don 't You Wanna Stay " was praised by music critics, who complimented the song's lyrical content and its production. The song was nominated for Best Country Duo/Group Performance at the 54th Grammy Awards . The song was certified 2× Platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), and Gold by the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA).
Jason Aldean's version of the song was released as the second single from his third album My Kinda Party on July 19, 2011. Aldean's version reached number 12 on the Hot Country Songs chart.

On 3 September , a tropical wave with a strong mid-level low pressure center moved into the Windward Passage. The low moved at a rapid rate, increasing the potential for development, and the National Hurricane Center issued the first advisory on Hurricane Gilbert at 1500Z on 11 September .
Hurricane Gilbert moved across the Greater Antilles and the Yucatan Peninsula and accelerated rapidly into the Gulf of Mexico. On 14 September, the hurricane intensified to category 3 strength and reached its peak intensity of 160 kt. The hurricane made landfall on the Gulf Coast of the United States at category 3 intensity with 115 kt winds, then moved across Florida and the southeastern United States before making a second landfall in the Carolinas. Hurricane Gilbert moved over eastern North Carolina on 16 September and made a third landfall along the coast of New England. The storm caused an estimated $6.7 billion in damage, and 160 people were killed.

## Biography

Busch was born in 1818 in Nörten-Hardenberg, near Göttingen, in the Kingdom of Hanover, where his father was a pastor in the Evangelical Lutheran Church . He studied art in Hanover, Berlin, Paris and in the Netherlands, and in 1844 finished his studies in Düsseldorf under the direction of Wilhelm Schadow and his father Adolph. In 1845 he was one of the founding members of the Düsseldorf Painters' Association ( Malkasten ).

Busch's paintings were popular in his lifetime. He was especially known for his portraits, but also painted genre scenes, and genre kitsch.
