 A week after the first meeting with Bennett, Payne, Reader, Passage and Rundle again met at Bennett's home, where a party of eight set out for the site the next day . On the way, they stopped at two other sites, both yielding small quantities of gold . They arrived at the site on the 11th of June and began an extensive prospecting operation . On the 14th, they returned to Bennett's home, and on the 15th, they left for the city of Moose Jaw.
On June 21st, the party returned to the site. They continued to work at the site until July 6th, when they left for Saskatoon, where they met with Bennett's father-in-law, B.M. Fisher . After discussing the work done at the site, they decided to leave the site for a few days. On July 10th, they returned to the site and resumed their work. The last day of the dig, they left the site, and on the 11th, Payne and Reader returned to Regina, while Passage and Rundle, accompanied by Payne's wife, returned to Moose Jaw. On the 20th, they again returned to the site, where they remained for 11 days, working at the site until the 31st of July.
After this, Payne, Reader, and the four men who had accompanied them on the dig, had a meeting with Bennett. At this meeting, they decided to set up a corporation to further the prospecting and mining operations at the site. In November, a meeting of the shareholders of the company was held. At this meeting, the directors and officers were elected, and the company was named the Golden Horseshoe Gold Mining Company . At this meeting, it was decided to further prospect at the site for a few days, to see if the gold could be found in larger quantities .
On November 16th, 1913, the company closed its first year of operation . From the information provided in the annual report, it is clear that the company was not profitable; however, it is unknown how much money was spent on prospecting and mining at the site.
 In November of 1914, the company issued a prospectus to the public, and issued shares for the sale . By this time, Bennett had been involved in other mines, and he was no longer associated with the company. Bennett was also a member of the board of directors . The company was again listed in the Canadian Mines Directory for 1915  , and although the company issued a prospectus in 1914, it does not appear to have been listed in the directory for that year .
The company continued to be listed in the directory for 1916  ; however, there is no record of it for 1917 .
In 1917, a prospector named R. M. Smith discovered a new gold bearing area on the site . He filed a claim on the area and began to prospect the site . As a result, the company became involved with Smith again .
 On May 5th, 1918, the company's annual meeting was held. At this meeting, it was decided to sell the company's holdings in the Golden Horseshoe Mine, and dissolve the company. Smith was called to the meeting, and was ordered to pay the company $10,000.
 On May 7th, 1918, the company was officially dissolved .

Maryland Route 194 ( MD 194 ) is a state highway in the U.S. state of Maryland . The state highway runs 23 @.@ 87 miles ( 38 @.

140 @.@) from the Delaware state line in St. Mary's County to U.S. Route 50 ( US 50 ) in Salisbury . MD 194 follows the entire length of the Southern Maryland coast, passing through or near the southern parts of Charles, St. Mary's, Calvert and Queen Anne's counties . This route was named for the Patuxent River , which it crosses at least 10 times. The highway was mostly paved by 1919 and numbered in the 1920s. In the late 1920s, MD 194 was extended south of Solomons to the Delaware border. The route was rerouted in 1930 when a new alignment was built in Calvert County . The path was realigned again around 1934 to bypass Lexington Park .
The roadway was widened in the 1950s and 1960s. The designation was extended west to US 50 in the 1990s. In 2006, MD 194 was extended east of MD 5 to MD 234 and U.S. Highway 50 ( US 50 ) in Solomons, replacing MD 4 .

The state highway crosses the Patuxent River , then turns west and north to follow the river through the Solomons Channel . The state highway heads north through the community of Morningside and crosses the Patuxent River for the first time. The highway continues north through the community of Marlton. Heidrich was 49 years old, a veteran of all the major campaigns of the war, who had been wounded three times in North Africa in 1941 and was awarded a Knight's Cross in the East. He had a reputation for leading by example, and had been given the nickname 'Dickie' by his men: 'Heidrich, Dickie, Dickie, Dickie, Dickie'.
The 1 . Parachute Division was one of the oldest and most experienced units in the division. It had been raised by the SS in 1936, but was not committed to action until 1940, when it took part in the invasion of France. From then on, it was involved in every major German operation. In 1942 it fought in North Africa, being involved in the defence of Tobruk, and in the advance to El Alemein. In the summer of 1943 it was transferred to Sicily, where it fought in the invasion of the island, and then took part in the ill-fated assault on Italy. The division was shipped to the Balkans in October 1943, where it played a major role in the occupation of Greece. In the spring of 1944 it was moved to the Ukraine, where it took part in the battle of the Korsun Pocket. In June it was involved in Operation _Bagration_ , when the 4th Army, which included the 1st Parachute Division, advanced into eastern Poland. The division was then withdrawn for rest and refitting.
The 1st Parachute Division was a fairly typical German formation. Like most of the parachute units, it was a mixture of volunteers and conscripts. The conscripts were drawn from the ranks of the Luftwaffe, the Wehrmacht and the SS, and the volunteers included foreigners and former prisoners of war. There were also two battalions of the SS-Waffe, a military police battalion and a tank battalion.
Although it was the oldest and most experienced parachute unit in the division, the 1st Parachute Division was still only a regimental formation, and had a regimental structure. Each of the divisions two regiments had four battalions, each of which contained three rifle companies, a machine-gun company and an anti-tank company.

Laborintus II is a recording of the 1965 composition of the same name by Luciano Berio , who wrote it for the 700th anniversary

of the University of Basel .
The piece is structured in four parts. The first begins with a cello solo, the second with a solo piano, the third with a soprano solo, the fourth with a solo accordion. In the fourth part, the soloist is accompanied by a mixed choir. The total duration is approximately 40 minutes.
In 1965, the piece was conducted by the composer himself and the soloists of the Basel Chamber Orchestra , the soloists of the Basel Symphony Orchestra and the soloists of the Basel Chamber Choir in the University Church of St. Peter . A recording from the broadcast was made of this performance, which was released on the album "Luciano Berio, Laborintus II" by Philips in 1966. This album also includes the short piece "Laborintus I" and the first movement of "Sinfonia".
The composition is based on the "Liederzyklus" by Arnold Schönberg . The music of the cello soloist is based on the "Meditation" from the "Liederzyklus". The piano part is based on the "Dreams" and "Transfigured night" , the soprano part on the "Five Songs" and the accordion part on the "Pierrot Lunaire" .
In the performance of the soloists, the musicians can choose whether to play their part with or without amplification.

Using Feulgen staining and electron microscopy (EM), it has been shown that the pSPECKLEs are associated with the mitochondrial cristae and this association is thought to be essential for the functional role of pSPECKLEs in apoptosis .
Paraspeckles are also subject to polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. In addition, there is a post-translational modification, an argi- nine-valine (RV)-like modification in the cytoplasm .
This modification, RV modification, is a type of non-methylation of arginine side chain, which is a reversible modification of proteins. At present, the role of this modification is not yet clear. However, there are some reports that RV modification is often a critical step in the interactome formation of the proteins . In addition, RV modification is related to various diseases such as cancer. It has been reported that RV modification of pSPECKLEs may be associated with cancer . However, the factors contributing to the occurrence of RV modification in pSPECKLEs, the mechanism of this modification, and its relationship with apoptosis are not yet clear.

Most gods were depicted in several ways . Hathor could be a cow , cobra , lioness , or a woman with bovine horns or ears . By d

int of her cobra form she was also associated with the goddess Serket , the mother of cobras . A myth told how she was brought to life by her father, the sky goddess Nut. The most famous of her cult centres was at Dendera , where a temple, complete with a shrine to Serket, was built in the Roman period.
Another important goddess was Mut , the wife of Amun . Although she was originally associated with the sun, and had a particular role with respect to the sun god Ra , she also had two other aspects. At Heliopolis she was known as the mother of the sun god, and in Thebes as the mother of Amun. Mut's temple at Karnak was one of the most important in ancient Egypt.
Another goddess associated with the sun was Sekhmet , who was described as the lioness wife of the sun god Ra. She had a human body and head of a lioness, and so was the most fearsome of the gods. A relief from the temple of Mut at Karnak shows her raising her paw as if to strike, and as a result she was depicted as having the same symbol as that of the sun god Ra.
Another important goddess was Isis , the wife of Osiris and the mother of Horus. She was described as the mother of all gods, and worshipped as a great healer. She was also associated with building, and so was given the title 'Mistress of the House'.

Within minutes of issuing the signal and turning his flagship HMS Queen Charlotte , Howe 's plan began to falter . Many of the

29 ships of the line he commanded had no anchors, and the few that had were too heavy to be deployed quickly. A row of ships including HMS Prince George , HMS Prince George 's 100-gun second-rate ship of the line, was driven onto the rocks at Woburn Bay . The next day, the wind shifted to the south, and the ships of the Channel Fleet were driven helplessly upstream against the tide.
With the wind not favourable for a sea battle, a land battle seemed the only option to rescue the situation. Howe's ships had to be anchored in shallow water near the enemy, and then the men on the shore had to advance and capture them. When a dawn attack was attempted on 6 June, a reconnaissance party was spotted and, with the fleet's guns silent, the attack was called off. The ships of the Channel Fleet were driven upstream again, and Howe ordered the fleet to anchor in the shallow waters of Harwich Bay, where the ships would be easy targets for the defenders. The fleet was anchored three miles (5 kilometres) from Harwich , and it was only the hard work of the crews that saved them from being captured.
The French fleet was ready to sail at any moment. As the Channel Fleet anchored off Harwich , adverse winds forced the French fleet to return to Le Havre , and it was not until the 10th that they were ready to sail again. At that moment, Howe's fleet was fully prepared to receive them.
With the advantage of the wind in the south, Howe's ships were able to position themselves so that they blocked the entrance to the River Thames. The French fleet sailed first, its flagship the Ville de Paris leading the way, and Howe's ships gave chase. A large fleet of fireships was set alight and sent to prevent the French ships from escaping. Although only one of them actually caught fire, the sight of the approaching fireships panicked the French ships, which turned and fled as quickly as they could. The British ships followed, but the French ships had the advantage of the wind in their favour. Many of the British ships lost their anchors as they tried to chase the French, and as the French ships sailed away, the British fleet was scattered.
With the French fleet gone, Howe decided to attack the Dutch fleet, which was anchored in the Medway . He was unable to contact the Dutch fleet through his flagship's ineffective flags to send a warning of his approach, and so the battle took the Dutch by surprise. The ships that tried to escape were caught by the British and forced to surrender. The British fleet had won a great victory, but only at the cost of 250 ships captured.
The battle of the Glorious First of June was a watershed in British naval history. It marked the end of the Dutch navy as a rival to the British, and it allowed the British to take control of the seas. For the first time, it was possible to control the trade between Europe and the Americas and the trade between Europe and India . The Royal Navy would go on to dominate the world's seas for over a century.

Some radioactive isotopes of xenon , for example , 133Xe and 135Xe , are produced by neutron irradiation of fissionable materia

l , and are used for inertial and gravitational measurements and for studying the physics of strong interaction s. Without neutrons, the 133Xe and 135Xe isotopes would decay by the emission of beta - particles. The rate of emission of beta particles from 133Xe and 135Xe is modified by the neutralization of the 133Xe and 135Xe protons by the 133Xe and 135Xe neutrons; with no neutrons present, the rate of beta emission from 133Xe and 135Xe would be the same as the rate of beta emission from 133Xe and 135Xe plus the rate of emission of alpha particles from the 133Xe and 135Xe protons by the 133Xe and 135Xe neutrons. The beta- and alpha-particle rates are independent of each other, but the alpha-particle rate is proportional to the square of the beta-particle rate. Thus, a small variation in the neutron density in the 133Xe and 135Xe will cause a nonlinear variation in the rate of beta emission.
Typically, the beta- and alpha-particle rates are determined by the method of the present invention by counting the beta particles emitted by a 133Xe or 135Xe sample and the alpha particles emitted by a 133Xe or 135Xe proton sample. However, the method of the present invention is not limited to counting the beta particle and alpha-particle rates, and the present invention also includes counting the beta particles emitted by a 133Xe or 135Xe sample and the protons emitted by a 133Xe or 135Xe neutron sample.
 The method of the present invention is not limited to measuring the rate of emission of beta particles and alpha particles from 133Xe and 135Xe. For example, the method of the present invention can be adapted to measure the rate of alpha emission from 133Xe and 135Xe, and to measure the beta emission from 133Xe and 135Xe, if it is desired to measure the absorption of neutrons by 133Xe and 135Xe. In this case, the method of the present invention includes counting the alpha particles emitted by a 133Xe or 135Xe proton sample.
 The method of the present invention is also not limited to measuring the rate of emission of beta particles. The method of the present invention can be used to measure the rate of beta decay of any radioactive isotope. However, the method of the present invention is particularly well suited for measuring the rate of emission of beta particles from 133Xe and 135Xe, because 133Xe and 135Xe are the only radioactive isotopes of xenon that experience beta decay.
 The method of the present invention is also not limited to measuring the rate of emission of alpha particles. The method of the present invention can be used to measure the rate of alpha decay of any radioactive isotope. However, the method of the present invention is particularly well suited for measuring the rate of emission of alpha particles from 133Xe and 135Xe, because 133Xe and 135Xe are the only radioactive isotopes of xenon that experience alpha decay.
 The method of the present invention is also not limited to measuring the rate of emission of beta particles, the rate of alpha emission from 133Xe and 135Xe, and the rate of alpha decay of 133Xe and 135Xe. The method of the present invention can be used to measure the rate of emission of protons from 133Xe and 135Xe, because 133Xe and 135Xe are the only radioactive isotopes of xenon that experience proton emission.

The prevalence of condom use varies greatly between countries . Most surveys of contraceptive use are among married women , or

15-49-year-olds regardless of marital status, but few are representative samples of the entire population. The prevalence of condom use in marriage is very low in developing countries , but it is not clear whether the use of condoms among unmarried people is also low.
This study examines trends in the prevalence of condom use and its determinants among unmarried people in Thailand.
The data for the study come from a nationally representative survey of Thai adults aged 15-49 conducted by the National Statistical Office of the Ministry of Interior. We used a six-year time frame from 1994 to 1999, the most recent year for which data were available. We examined only unmarried men and women, aged 15-49 years.
The questionnaire asked respondents about their use of condoms, and whether they had ever used a condom in the past year. If not, they were asked whether they wanted to use a condom in the future. In addition, we used information on pregnancy, abortion, and childbirth in the past year to identify women who were pregnant or had recently had a child.
The data were analysed using Stata version 6.0. We used a multinomial logistic regression analysis to model the determinants of condom use.
Of the 32,246 men and women aged 15-49 years who were included in the analysis, 49.7% had never used condoms. Among those who had ever used them, only 10.0% said they used condoms all the time. The remaining 80.0% said they used them some of the time.
Use of condoms all the time was associated with sexual minority status, older age, low education, and high income. Women who wanted to use condoms all the time were younger, less educated, and had lower income, compared with women who wanted to use them some of the time.
Although the prevalence of condom use all the time was higher among never-married people, the number of people who used condoms all the time was higher among people who were married.
The prevalence of women using a condom all the time was lower among those who were pregnant or had recently given birth. This is an important finding because increased use of condoms when pregnancy is likely could reduce the risk of unintended pregnancy, HIV and other STIs, or other sexually transmitted diseases.
The prevalence of unmarried people using condoms all the time could increase when the Thai government increases its policy and programme support for condom use.
Our findings suggest that the prevalence of condom use all the time among unmarried people in Thailand is low. The prevalence of condom use among married people was also low. To increase the prevalence of condom use among unmarried and married people in Thailand, the Thai government should increase its policy and programme support for using condoms.
Thailand has one of the lowest HIV prevalence rates among 15-49-year-olds and among pregnant women in the Asia/Pacific region.  However, although the prevalence of HIV is lower than in most countries in the region, the prevalence of HIV is higher among married people than among non-married people.  In the Battle of Transylvania 50,000 Romanian soldiers were killed.
On February 1, 1945, General Mihai Racoviţă was appointed commander of the 4th Army of the Romanian Army. On March 31, 1945, together with the 2nd Army of General Gheorghe Avramescu, he defeated the Soviet army in the Jassy-Kishinev Offensive.
 During the battle General Racoviţă was severely injured in the chest, and spent several months in a Bucharest hospital.
 For his accomplishments, General Mihai Racoviţă was decorated with the "Ordinul Steaua României" ( The Romanian Order of the Star) , and was promoted to general-lieutenant.
 Between 1946 and 1947 General Mihai Racoviţă was a prisoner of the communist regime in Romania.
 After being released from prison, General Mihai Racoviţă emigrated to the United States.
 In 1950, he was a candidate for the presidency of the US, but he lost to Dwight D. Eisenhower.
 General Mihai Racoviţă died on March 5, 1974, in Washington, DC.

In October 1941 , the newly installed mayor of Zagreb , Ivan Werner , issued a decree ordering the demolition of the Praška Str

ana district , which was inscribed in the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979 . The demolition, which took place in 1948–1957 , resulted in the destruction of 60% of the city centre. Thus, significant parts of the old town were lost forever.
The destruction of the old town was not the only negative consequence of World War II . After the war, Zagreb was left with heavy material damage, and many of its inhabitants were killed in the fighting. It was also a period marked by political turmoil, as the Communist Party began its takeover of the country.
In the 1950s and 1960s, Zagreb experienced a period of economic stagnation, which was partially alleviated by the country's accession to the European Union in 2013. With the onset of the new millennium, however, the city has begun to experience a period of growth and renewal, becoming an important centre of culture, science, education, and business in the region.
In 2018 , Zagreb was named the European Green Capital for its efforts to promote sustainability and environmental protection. The city has also been recognized for its efforts to improve public transportation and reduce traffic congestion.
Ethnic and Religious Diversity
Zagreb is a city with a diverse population, with people from different ethnic and religious backgrounds living side by side. The most common religions in the city are Roman Catholicism, Orthodox Christianity, and Islam.
The local cuisine is characterized by a mix of Central and Eastern European flavors, with dishes such as goulash , štrukli , and kulen being popular among locals and tourists alike. The city also has a vibrant nightlife scene, with many bars, clubs, and restaurants open late into the night.
Despite its tumultuous history, Zagreb remains a vibrant and dynamic city, with a rich cultural heritage and a strong sense of community. Whether you're a history buff, a foodie, or just looking for a great place to explore, Zagreb is sure to have something to offer.

Communications scholar Arthur Kroker argues that Innis 's study of the Canadian Pacific Railway was only the first in which he

"put into motion his major intellectual concern: the analysis of the 'technologizing' of space, and the contradictions  that are unleashed in the processes of its analysis."  Innis was also a scholar of technology.  However, the book on which his reputation now largely rests is _The Bias of Communication_ , which explores how media frames the message and what this does to our understanding of the world.  The theory of the bias of communication is the basis of Innis 's reputation as the father of media studies: "He is the founder of media studies as an academic discipline."  Innis 's bias of communication, in other words, is the foundation of what would become communication studies.
 Although scholars have written about Innis in terms of the frame, they are more likely to do so in terms of a series of biases that Innis identified, including the personal, social, cultural, and technical.  The biases, however, are not the subject of this chapter.  Rather, my interest is in the mechanism of the bias of communication.  The bias of communication is a mental process, and that is where this chapter begins.  Just as a fish doesn't see the water, a person does not notice how their brain interprets the world.  What is the nature of this mental process, and what does it tell us about the world?  How does a frame shape our perception?  Or, as Innis asks, "How does a bias of communication come into being?"
#  **2.1** _A Theory of Media_
The bias of communication is not a theory of media per se.  It is a theory of representation, and it is a theory of how our brain makes sense of the world.  The bias of communication is the bias of the brain, and the bias of communication is the bias of the mind.  It is a theory of how we understand the world, specifically how we understand media.  It is a theory of media in the broadest sense, a theory of how media makes sense of the world. Biblical descriptions indicate there were two major types of Qedarites : nomads ( Arabic : wabariya ) living in tents and seden

aries ( plural of sedenar ) - people living in sedentary villages.
* The Qedarites or Qedarites were the descendants of Qedar, the son of Ishmael ( Genesis 25:13 ), and were the descendants of his brother, Midian ( Genesis 25:4 ).
* The Qedarites ("Qedar is his name") were "a tribe, probably of Arabian origin [and] mentioned in the Old Testament in connection with Job ( Job 1:3 )" The Qedarites, as a result, were known as the Qedarites of the wilderness ( cf . Numbers 24:21 ).
* The Qedarites, as part of the Median confederacy, were mentioned by the prophet Jeremiah ( Jeremiah 49:28 ) in a list of nations and their territories, along with the nations of Ammon, Moab, Edom, Teman, and Ephraim.
* The Qedarites are also mentioned in Ezekiel 27 (in the context of a list of countries which traded with Tyre, in the 6th century BCE) and in the Book of Revelation.
* The Qedarites, with the Midianites, were also considered "the conspirators against Israel" in the Book of Judges ( Judges 8:10 ), when the Israelites were encamped at Mizpah, and Gideon and his 300 men were guarding the entrance of the camp, as Judges 8:10 says: "And the Midianites and Amalekites and the children of the east were gathered together against them in the valley of Jezreel."
* The Qedarites were also the people to whom Job's father belonged and who lived in the land of Uz ( Job 1:3 ), which was "beyond the wilderness" ( Job 1:3 ).
* The Qedarites were also one of the tribes of the Midianites ( Numbers 33:43 ), who were the descendants of Midian ( Genesis 25:6 ), the son of Abraham's brother, Ishmael.
* The Qedarites were mentioned in the Book of 1 Maccabees ( 1 Maccabees 10:28 ) as one of the enemies of the Jews, when they were in the Makedonian diaspora.
* In 150 AD, the church father Irenaeus, in Against Heresies, wrote: "And in the same place it is said, 'And the Lord said to Moses, Pharaoh's daughter called to Moses, and inquired of him concerning her child.' And when he was come to Egypt, and had married and had children, he called the name of the first-born son, Qedar, and of the second son, Midian, in commemoration of his travels in a strange land, and of his sojourning in a foreign land." The burial of people, their possessions and animals in communal sites was a central feature of the pagan culture of the early Iron Age and the Celtic societies of the early medieval period. The objects buried with the dead were intended to provide for the needs of the deceased in the afterlife, to provide examples of the wealth of the individual and his family and to provide material for the social and economic life of the settlement.
From the late 4th century AD, Christianity began to discourage the burial of grave goods. The reasons for this were most likely to be threefold. Firstly, it was perceived as a dishonour to God to bury treasures which had been created by God with the intention of using them for community benefit. Secondly, the Church regarded the wealth which had been buried in the past as being hoarded by the wealthy and the Church feared that its wealth would be used to gain favour with God. Finally, the Church feared that the wealth which was buried would be used to finance the worship of pagan gods and ghosts.
From this point onwards, the majority of metalwork examples that survive from the Christian period were made for the purpose of devotional use, decoration and bodily adornment.

Timothy Henry Hoʻolulu Pitman was born March 18 , 1845 , in Hilo , Hawaiʻi , the first son and second child of Benjamin Pitman

and his wife Caroline  (or Caroline Louisa) Pitman.
There were also six younger siblings.
The family had been in Hawaiʻi since the 1820s.
Benjamin had established a wholesale grocery business, and by the time of Timothy’s birth, he was a prosperous businessman who owned much land in Hilo.
Timothy’s mother, Caroline, was from Wainiha, Kauaʻi, and was a descendant of Kualii, a high chief. Benjamin Pitman was of English ancestry, and he was a descendant of William Pitt the Younger.
Educated at the Hilo Boarding School and at the Hilo Seminary, Timothy Pitman was the first in his family to speak Hawaiian.
As a young man, he was a teacher at the Hilo Boarding School, and then at the Hilo Seminary.
In 1870, at age 25, he was appointed as the first principal of the Punahou School, which had been founded in 1841 as the Oʻahu Collegiate Institute.
Punahou’s first principal was the Reverend John French. The school soon outgrew its first building, and, in 1850, it was relocated to Punahou Street, where it remained until 1881.
In 1870, the school had 90 students; by 1875, it had 130 students.
By 1880, the school had outgrown its location and the number of students. The school was moved once more to its present location on the crest of Diamond Head.
In 1881, Pitman returned to Hawaiʻi from a trip to the United States and was appointed the first principal of the new Punahou School.
The school was known as the “Punahou Seminary.” A few years later, it was chartered by the Territorial Legislature as Punahou College.
Punahou College, which is a private, co-educational college preparatory school, enrolls about 4,000 students in grades K-12.
In the early years of the school, Pitman was known for his strictness and for his physical punishment of students.
In addition, he required students to rise at 4:30 a.m. In 1884, he instituted a uniform for boys, and a school uniform for girls.
One of his innovations was the start of the “Huli Hoʻike” – an end-of-the-year performance, which was held in 1884.
Pitman was also instrumental in the development of the athletic program.
At the time, he was also a Justice of the Peace and was involved in local politics.
In 1882, he ran unsuccessfully for the House of Representatives, and in 1886, he ran unsuccessfully for a seat in the Territorial Legislature.
In 1888, he was appointed a member of the Oʻahu County Board of Education, and he served in that capacity until 1892.
During his term as principal, Pitman was married to Mary Paahana; they had five children.
In 1892, he resigned as principal of the school.
In 1895, he was appointed the first Hawaiian (or Native-Hawaiian) judge of the District Court of the Islands, and he served in that capacity until 1903.
In 1903, he was appointed a member of the first Board of Trustees of Kamehameha Schools.
He died on December 1, 1904, at age 60 and was buried at Kawaiahaʻo Cemetery.

When the first set of posted routes in New York were assigned in 1924 , the portion of what is now NY 38 from Freeville to Mora

ine was designated as part of US 20. The route was renumbered as part of NY 46 in 1927. The highway was realigned in the mid-1920s as US 20A, following the modern alignment from Moraine to the city of Ithaca. NY 46 was rerouted through the city of Ithaca along present-day NY 96B, where it met US 20A at its original alignment. In 1930, US 20A was rerouted onto present-day NY 79, and NY 46 was rerouted in line with the new routing. After the highway was renumbered as NY 13 in 1930, NY 46 was eliminated.

In 1938, the portion of NY 46 from Freeville to the Pennsylvania state line was added back to the state highway system as part of NY 14. NY 14 was realigned to bypass the village of Dryden shortly thereafter, using present-day NY 366. NY 14 was rerouted in Freeville in 1949, following the former alignment of NY 46 through the village. NY 14 was truncated to Dryden in 1960, and the former NY 46 alignment was deleted. The former NY 46 alignment through Freeville was designated as an extension of US 20.

The name "Haifa" is Hebrew, meaning "beauty" or "splendor". It derives from the Arabic word حیفا hayfa, meaning "beautiful", "delicate", "white", or "chaste". The name is cognate with the Syriac word ܚܝܦܐ kīpā, meaning "beautiful", which is used in the Syriac version of the Old Testament.
The name is also found in the Bible. In the New Testament the Jewish town of Caesarea Philippi is referred to as "Beth-Saida" or "House of Tyre" (Matthew 16:13). The name "Caesarea Philippi" comes from the Roman name for the city, "Caesarea" and the name of the Greek goddess "Philippos", whom the city was named after.
Other spellings include "Haipha", "Chiph" and "Chipa".

ropiated $20,000 for a lighthouse at the southwestern end of Norwalk Harbor.  The lighthouse was completed in 1901 , and was first lighted in 1902.
The lighthouse is situated on a foundation of stone quarried from Connecticut .
The light is 38 feet (12 m) above mean high water.
The light is a First Order Fresnel lens, which was created in France by Henri Lepaute at their Paris Works. The lens is 12 feet (3.7 m) in diameter, and is a 1000 mm lens.

The lighthouse is the second oldest lighthouse in Connecticut.
The lighthouse was placed on the National Register of Historic Places on September 27, 1989.
On June 27, 2008, the lighthouse was declared a Connecticut State Historic Site.

After numerous proposals the sand hills rear and north of the fort were removed in 1882 , improving the fort 's land defence an

d making it more suitable to artillery .  The new, improved fort was named Fort Clinton , and the new work was completed in 1883 .
A wooden " trust  " was erected over the moat  and connected to the fort 's north wall and also to the east wall via a drawbridge .  The trust , which was built by the United States Army Corps of Engineers  as part of the fortification of the harbour  provided a lookout point and defensive emplacement for men of the artillery .  It was located on the northern wall of the fort and could be accessed from the parapet walk via an interior stairway .  A metal-plated observation cupola was built atop the structure to allow the men to observe the harbour and surrounding area .
Fort Clinton was never used during the Spanish–American War , but was used during the later Philippine–American War .  When the Spanish–American War broke out, the fort was manned by the Sixth Company of the Maine National Guard .  During the war, Fort Clinton was used as a quarantine station, and received troops arriving in the US from the Philippines .  The Sixth Company was mustered out in September 1898 , and Fort Clinton was abandoned .
The structure was deactivated in 1915 , and later declared surplus by the U.S. Army .  The fort was subsequently sold to the City of Portland for $1 on August 19, 1916 .  The city demolished the wooden cupola , moat , and other structures,  but the walls and parapets remain to this day .  By the 1920s , Fort Williams was a popular destination for city residents , particularly families .  A 1920s postcard depicted old Fort Williams in ruins , with a beach in the foreground .  The ruins were removed that year, and a public park was established within the fort .
During World War II , Fort Williams was leased to the United States Army .  The 201st Coast Artillery Regiment established an anti-aircraft battery there in 1943 , and the 22nd Coast Artillery Regiment followed in 1944 .  The battery was equipped with five 90 mm guns , and emplaced in the parapet wall of Fort Williams .  A concrete observation post was built over the moat and connected via walkways to the parapet wall of Fort Williams .  The 22nd Coast Artillery Regiment was withdrawn soon after the end of the war in 1946 .
Fort Williams was replaced by the air-defence Fort Preble , which was built on nearby Harpswell Neck .  In 1968 , Fort Williams was leased to the State of Maine and the National Park Service for $1 per year .  Today, the fort is part of the Fort Williams Historic Site, which is managed by the City of South Portland .  On November 26, 2008 , the Fort Williams Historic Site was nominated to the National Register of Historic Places , and listed on the National Register on January 21, 2009 .
The fort was used as a filming location for several movies , including Birthday, The Guns of Fort Petticoat , Gus , and Sunshine Beach .  The fort was also used as a filming location for television shows , including the CBS television series The Defenders and PBS 's The Civil War .
Fort Williams has been the site of several events , including the 1925 Maine Junior Olympics ,  the 1971 Maine Marathon ,  the 1976 Maine Golf Open ,  and the 1978 Lipton International Players Championship .  In 1975 and 1976 , Fort Williams hosted the annual 100-mile (160 km) Portland to Portland race , which was considered to be the most difficult road race in the United States .

At national level in the UK , Mosley competed in over 40 races in 1966 and 1967 ; he won 12 and set several class lap records .

On 21 August 1966, Mosley set the lap record for the FIA Formula Two class at the Nürburgring, driving a Cooper T72 with a 2.2-litre BRM V8 engine . He took pole position for the British Grand Prix at Brands Hatch , but crashed in the race. Later in the year, he took another pole position for the Monaco Grand Prix , but retired on the first lap. He also competed in the International Trophy at Silverstone , finishing fifth.
In 1967, Mosley joined the Team Lotus junior driver team and competed in six Formula One races, finishing 7th in the British Grand Prix, with a Cooper T81. He also finished in the top ten in the US Grand Prix and the South African Grand Prix.
Mosley was the subject of the 1968 John Frankenheimer film Grand Prix . He was cast as himself in the movie, and several scenes were shot at the 1967 British Grand Prix.
Mosley's driving career was halted by a serious crash at the 1969 British Grand Prix, in which he was seriously injured. He was struck by his mechanic's axe during the race and suffered severe brain damage. Mosley was operated on by neurosurgeon Norman Dott . He recovered sufficiently to return to racing in 1973, after undergoing experimental surgery. This procedure involved the implantation of a titanium plate, and the procedure was repeated in 1986.
Mosley's son Alexander Mosley (b. 1972) was also a racing driver, but the two never raced together.
In 1970, Mosley was offered a seat in the Tyrrell Formula One team, but he declined. Instead, he was offered the position of a director of the British Racing and Sports Car Club (BRSCC), the governing body of British motor sport. Mosley became President of the British Racing Drivers' Club (BRDC) in 1971, and was elected as President of the British Automobile Racing Club (BARC) in 1974. He is the only person ever to have held both positions simultaneously, and his presidency of the BARC was the longest-ever.
Mosley became the first President of the FIA in 1991, succeeding Jean-Marie Balestre , following the FIA's decision to end the ban on British teams participating in Formula One. He was also a member of the World Motor Sports Council. He made the decision to allow the reintroduction of turbocharged engines to Formula One, and also allowed the introduction of the safety car to Formula One in 1993. He was re-elected by the FIA Congress in 2001 and again in 2005, and was succeeded in 2009 by Jean Todt .
In 1993, Mosley founded the Formula One Group (FOG), which owned the commercial rights to Formula One. In 1998, FOG was renamed Formula One Management (FOM), and Mosley became its chairman. In 2013, FOM was acquired by Liberty Media, and Mosley continued as chairman until 2016.
From 1996 to 1997, Mosley was a member of the International Olympic Committee . From 1997 to 2003, he was a member of the Court of Arbitration for Sport , and from 1997 to 2007 he was a member of the International Court of Arbitration.
Mosley was a member of the board of governors of the National Basketball Association (NBA) from 2000 to 2008, and was the first chairman of the NBA's International Committee.
In 2003, Mosley was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) by Queen Elizabeth II . In 2008, he was elected to the International Motorsports Hall of Fame .
In 2006, Mosley was appointed a Knight Bachelor by Queen Elizabeth II, to mark his contribution to motorsport. He was granted the title of 'Sir' on 14 February 2006.
In 2007, Mosley announced that he would be stepping down as President of the FIA at the end of his term in 2009. In January 2009, it was announced that he would be succeeded by Jean Todt .

The origins of Hurricane Abby were possibly from a tropical wave that moved in the vicinity of the Lesser Antilles in early Jul

1967. Abby began its life as a tropical wave that moved in the vicinity of the Lesser Antilles in early Jul 1967. On 13 Jul, a tropical wave emerged from the west coast of Africa and entered the Atlantic Ocean. On 19 Jul, the wave was centered over the north coast of South America, causing a low pressure system to form at 15N 50W. The system remained nearly stationary for the next two days.
On 21 Jul, the system was upgraded to a tropical depression. At 12:00 UTC 22 Jul, the depression was upgraded to a tropical storm and was named Abby. Abby moved northward at an average speed of ten miles per day. At 12:00 UTC 24 Jul, Abby was upgraded to a Category 1 hurricane. After reaching Category 1 hurricane status, Abby began to weaken. Abby was downgraded to a tropical storm on 25 Jul. On 27 Jul, Abby weakened to a tropical depression. After becoming a tropical depression, Abby was absorbed by a frontal system.

On September 24 , 1838 , William Pomkrotz and his wife , Milly , deeded a tract of land to a group of trustees , charged with c

emetery and burial ground maintenance and perpetual care . One of the trustees , James Walker , would soon go on to become a partner of the Pomkrotz family business , the firm Pomkrotz & Walker . The deed , a copy of which can be found at the New Jersey Historical Society in Newark , New Jersey , describes the land as an "unbroken parcel of land containing two acres , more or less , and being part of Lot No. 11 in Block No. 2 in the Town of Ridgefield , County of Bergen , State of New Jersey" .
There were no deeds filed with regard to the next piece of land purchased by the trustees . On March 2 , 1840 , the trustees sold 1 acre and 3 rods of land to Charles and Edwin Walker . Some of the land was sold again . This time , the property was sold to the Pomkrotz family . In 1849 , the family of William Pomkrotz purchased the remaining tracts from the trustees .
Charles and Edwin Walker , the first owners of the cemetery , were brothers . They were born to James Walker and his wife , Sarah , in New York City , New York . The brothers were raised by their grandparents , John and Elizabeth Walker . John and Elizabeth Walker were brothers and sisters to James Walker .
Charles Walker was born in 1805 . He married Elizabeth O'Shea in 1834 . Charles and Elizabeth had four children , William , Emily , James and Thomas . Charles died on January 27 , 1842 . He was buried in the Walker Burial Ground . Research at the Manhattan Marriage Bureau in New York City , New York revealed that Charles Walker was a "bondsman" at his sister's wedding on June 10 , 1828 .
Edwin Walker was born in 1803 . He married Sarah Ann McKee in 1832 . He and Sarah had four children , Charles , Henry , Mary and Sarah . Edwin also had a daughter , Mary , from his first marriage .
In 1834 , Charles and Edwin Walker were the first trustees of the Walker Burial Ground in Ridgefield , New Jersey . The brothers , along with James Walker , were the trustees of the Walker Burial Ground , which was set up as a perpetual care trust .

Estañol 's views represented those of the portion of the upper class which was willing to come to terms with at least a portion

of the revolutionary demands. In addition to his nationally recognized name, Estañol was the son of Vice President of the Republic Manuel Antonio Estañol, who was the brother of President Tomás Cipriano de Mosquera. Estañol was born in 1798 in the city of Bogotá. He joined the priesthood, was ordained in 1825, and was appointed bishop of the diocese of Popayán in 1842. In 1845, he was transferred to the See of Bogotá, where he died in 1861.
In the midst of the revolutionary crisis of 1840, the Constitutionalists of the Caribbean coast and those of the Andean region of the country were negotiating a common ground, and it was in this context that Estañol, supported by the doctrines of the conservative Andrés Bello, proposed the drafting of a new constitution in order to prevent the country from falling into civil war. In December 1840, the new constitution was promulgated, and the revolution ended without further complications.
In the years that followed the crisis, Estañol was one of the most influential figures in the opposition to the policies of President Mosquera. In 1841, Mosquera ordered the arrest of Estañol and his brother Manuel Antonio, who was also a representative in the congress of the Republic. His exile and isolation lasted until 1847, when he was appointed ambassador to Spain. In 1851, he was elected to the Colombian Senate, where he remained until his death in 1861.

In the letter, Estañol expressed his concerns about the situation in the country, as well as the political and economic problems of his time. ## Cast

The cast includes Tom Cruise as John Anderton, Colin Farrell as Danny Witwer, Samantha Morton as Agatha Lively, Max von Sydow as Dr. Iris Hineman (née Hineman), Patrick Kilpatrick as Lamar Burgess, Jessica Capshaw as Sarah Shannon, Kathryn Morris as Danny's girlfriend Theresa, Rick Gonzalez as Arthur Tack, and Steve Harris as Wally. The role of Anderton was originally offered to Harrison Ford . 

## Production

### Development

Steven Spielberg directed the film.

Pittsburgh's Southside Works business park was used as a double for the film's Chicago setting.

In 1998, Spielberg optioned the short story for a theatrical adaptation, in part because he was a fan of the short story. Initially, he wanted to adapt the short story into a television miniseries. In 1999, Spielberg and director of photography Janusz Kaminski began discussing the film's visuals, and the idea of a futuristic film set in a totalitarian state was brought up. The film's setting was changed from Washington, D.C. to Chicago, Illinois. No reason was given for the change; Chicago had been a major filming location for many other Spielberg films, including Jurassic Park and Indiana Jones and the Lost Crusade. A few Chicago buildings were used in exterior shots, including the Sears Tower and the Chicago Board of Trade Building.

In 2001, Spielberg approached writer Scott Frank to write the screenplay; Frank was considered a Spielberg favorite, having worked with him on A.I. Artificial Intelligence. Frank began adapting the story into a feature-length film, and the script was completed by October 2002, but it was not yet the final version that would be used in the film. Spielberg also had screenwriter Jon Cohen working on a different draft during that period. It was not until 2004 that Spielberg began pre-production and hired director of photography Janusz Kaminski to start shooting.

### Filming

Filming began in May 2004 in Chicago, and continued until July 2004. Filming took place in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in the summer of 2005. The film was shot in the South Side Works, a shopping and entertainment complex in Pittsburgh. The city's skyline was used elsewhere in the movie for scenes set in Chicago; for example, the Sears Tower was featured in shots of a sprawling skyline. The exterior of the Chicago Board of Trade Building was also used in the film.

## Release

### Promotion

The Basement Tapes are a collection of 50 song recordings made in 1967 by Bob Dylan and the Band in West Saugerties, New York, at Dylan's house (the "Big Pink" house).

The songs were recorded by Dylan and Band members Robbie Robertson, Rick Danko, Garth Hudson and Richard Manuel, using tape machines in the basement of the house.

## Story

### How the Basement Tapes came to be

In February 1967, Dylan, feeling overexposed and exhausted, retired from touring. He moved to West Saugerties, New York, to live in the house of his friend, Albert Grossman, the manager of Dylan, Peter, Paul and Mary, the Byrds and others. Grossman had recently secured a commitment from Columbia Records to release Dylan's next album, so in late March, Grossman, Dylan, Robertson, Hudson, Manuel and Danko (who had toured with Dylan) began making their own recordings in the basement of Grossman's house.

Dylan began writing songs again in August 1967. He had recovered some of his creative energy, so he and the Band continued to make recordings of their songs in the basement. Dylan wrote 25 new songs, and the Band completed 25 songs that it had already written. The recordings were not intended to be released as an album, but to give Dylan the opportunity to practise playing the harmonica and the guitar, and to refresh his songwriting skills.

### The Band's involvement

During the recording sessions, the Band members played many instruments, and sang harmonies.

Dylan's original plan was to record a few songs, and then return to his house in Woodstock, New York, to write more songs. However, the sessions continued for several months. Dylan's friend, the folk singer Happy Traum, has stated that, although Dylan was happy for the Band to record for their own enjoyment, he was unhappy that the songs were recorded for release as an album.

### Recording

The recordings were made in a second story bedroom, in a small basement room, and in the kitchen.

Dylan's harmonica playing was initially unpolished, but he improved during the sessions.

The Band was influenced by Dylan's work, and it worked with its own songs, but it also wrote many songs to Dylan's melodies.

The Band members would write songs in the morning, and bring them to the studio in the evening, to play for Dylan.

The songs that Dylan wrote were mainly humorous. racing its path from the eastern Caribbean to the southern United States coast, Janet killed 13 people and caused an estimated $1.5 billion in damage (1955 dollars). It was the second hurricane to make landfall in the United States in 1955, after Hurricane Connie .
Janet formed as a tropical storm on September 6 south of Hispaniola. The tropical storm intensified into a hurricane on September 8, and by September 10 had reached peak intensity with 135 mph (215 km/h) winds. Janet weakened after landfall in Puerto Rico on September 11, and later struck Florida on September 12, before moving across the Gulf of Mexico. In September 1847 Busch began studying mechanical engineering at Hanover Polytechnic . Busch 's biographers are not in agreemen

t as to whether he was studying or working at this time. In his thesis he stated that he was employed as a mechanical draftsman.
The following January Busch began a two-year apprenticeship at the Trier works of the Klein & Quenzer machine-tool company . At the beginning of 1849 Busch was employed in the workshop of the Klein & Quenzer factory in Trier as a draughtsman. In June of that year he went to France to work as a draftsman for a year, working for the Société Industrielle et des Métaux. He returned to Germany in 1850 and took over the post of foreman of the machine-tool department at the Klein & Quenzer factory.
In 1852 Busch was given responsibility for the management of the Trier factory. In 1856 he became a partner in the firm, and in 1858 he was given responsibility for the operation of the company's factory in Berlin. In 1860 Busch became sole owner of the Trier works.
Busch married Anna Maria Schrader on 25 February 1851. They had seven sons and two daughters. Two of Busch's sons, Alfred and Wilhelm, were also machine-tool makers.
In 1874 Busch formed a partnership with the engineers E. Zahn, H. von Closen-Ambras and R. von Carlowitz, to form the Gebr. Busch & Co machine-tool company, of which he became director and principal owner in 1883.
Busch's most important achievements include the invention of the self-adjusting lathe.
Busch's contribution to the founding of the German Machine Tool Builders' Association and the German Machine Tool Manufacturers' Association, and his position as the first president of the latter, were also important in the development of machine-tool making in Germany.

istle-shaped altars, and who have not first carefully tested the rocks beneath their feet.
A recent hark-back to the good old days of 'higher' and 'lower' classification is the 'species complex' ( _A. rubra_ ssp. _rubra_ , _s._ _pulchra_ , _s._ _baicalensis_ and _s._ _melanosticta_ ). Less than five decades ago, the genus _Aconitum_ was divided into seven subgenera, including _A. rubra_ in the subgenus _Aconitum_ , and this was the arrangement which was used by most botanists in the second half of the last century. Since the middle of the 20th century, a number of botanists have questioned this arrangement to various degrees, and there has been a gradual reduction in the number of subgenera.
In 1962, two Russian botanists, T. V. Shishkin and I. M. Gub.) published their scheme for the genus _Aconitum_ , which was based on the theory of 'phylogenetic taxonomy'. This was an attempt to unite the various subgenera into a single genus, using the evolutionary development of the plant as the basis. In 1963, _A. rubra_ was re-classified as _A. rubra_ ssp. _rubra_ , and in 1979 it was downgraded to _A. rubra_ ssp. _rubra_ var. _rubra_. In 1979, another Russian, I. P. Lazarev, published his own scheme, in which _A. rubra_ was again a subspecies, _A. rubra_ ssp. _rubra_ var. _rubra_. In 1980, L. L. Kudrjavzeva and G. K. Skvortsov published their 'species complex' scheme, in which _A. rubra_ was again a subspecies, _A. rubra_ ssp. _rubra_ var. _rubra_ , but with added subspecies _A. rubra_ ssp. _pulchra_ , _A. rubra_ ssp. _baicalensis_ and _A. rubra_ ssp. _melanosticta_. Most recent taxonomic works simply ignore these subspecies altogether, but they are still sometimes listed in the literature.
This is a species of Siberia, and of the Russian Far East. It has also spread to Western Europe, and is also known in cultivation in Australia and New Zealand.
In the last couple of years, the taxonomy of this species has been the subject of a great deal of discussion. In 1995, Skvortsov published a new species, _A. rubra_ ssp. _baicalensis_ , which he considered to be a distinct species, and he gave the name _A. baicalense_ to it. The plant is almost identical to _A. rubra_ , but the flowers are white, not violet. It is often treated as a variety of _A. rubra_ , but its flowers are different. This is the only species of _Aconitum_ which has white flowers.

From 1885 until his death in 1908 his work was dominated by prose and poems . The 1895 prose text Der Schmetterling contains au

­tographic elements and is also a reminiscence of his time in Grü­nenberg, while Der Kampf , written from 1902 to 1904, is a polemical work in which he develops his position as a writer of prose and as a poet.
 He was a frequenter of the café then known as the "Café des Westens" in Berlin, and the "Café Bauer" in Munich. The "Café des Westens" was a popular meeting place for artists and intellectuals, and also for those who wanted to show off their aesthetic knowledge. For the most part, however, the "Café des Westens" was not a social centre at all, but a place for conversation and dispute on philosophical, aesthetic, artistic and literary topics. He was also interested in the 19th century painter, Camille Pissarro, at whose death he wrote an obituary which he sent to the Berliner Tageblatt . The poet was a member of the "Münchner Lyrische Ring " [Lyrical Ring in Munich] from 1899 to 1900.
 For the most part he was a freelance writer, but also worked as a journalist. From 1890 he was a staff writer for the Berlinische Zeitung , in 1893 he was employed as an editor by the Berliner Tageblatt and in 1894 he became a member of its editorial staff.
 He was a founding member of the Münchner Lyrische Ring , but his work is not devoid of poetic elements. The prose text which is closest to his aesthetic ideas is: Der Schmetterling (1895).

English ornithologist John Latham described the noisy miner four times in his 1801 work Supplementum Indicis Ornithologici , si

xty years before the species was formally described. In 1810, German zoologist Heinrich Boie described the species as Sturnella torquata . The name torquata is from Latin torquatus, meaning "twisted", and refers to the noisy miner's twisted tail. Noisy miners are commonly called noisy miners in English, although other common names include yellow-throated miner, red-browed miner, white-eyed miner, yellow-throated miner, yellow-throated honeyeater, and red-browed honeyeater.

## Description

The noisy miner is a small honeyeater, measuring 14.5 cm (5.7 in) in length. The male's breast is black, and its belly is white. Its head and back are olive-brown, and its tail is black. Both the male and female have a white face, although the male has a white eye ring. The juvenile is similar to the adult female, but has a buffy-coloured breast. The noisy miner is similar in appearance to the large-billed miner (Manorina melanocephala), although the large-billed miner is larger and has a longer, more slender, and more downcurved bill.

## Distribution and habitat

Noisy miners are found in the coastal regions of northwest Queensland and the northern parts of Cape York Peninsula, Australia. They are found in woodlands and rainforests, where they feed on nectar and insects.

## Behaviour

The noisy miner is very social, with large flocks often roosting together at night in trees with a central hollow. Noisy miners are not shy when foraging, and they often join groups of other birds to feed. They have a loud, distinctive call which they use to communicate with each other. They also have a variety of specialized calls, including a chattering call used to scare away intruders.

### Breeding

The noisy miner's nest is constructed of sticks, grass and leaves, and is lined with soft plant material. It is built in a hollow in a tree, usually 3–5 m (9.8–16.4 ft) above the ground. Breeding occurs through most of the year, although there is a peak in October and November. The female lays two to four eggs in a clutch. The young leave the nest after ten to twelve days.

## In popular culture

Noisy miners feature prominently in the 2007 Australian children's television series Kangaroo Beach, in which they are depicted as antagonists.

"Stars and Stripes Forever"
"Stars and Stripes Forever" (1896), is a march written by John Philip Sousa featuring drums and a military style marching bass line. It was performed by Sousa's band, the United States Marine Band, and was published by Oliver Ditson of Boston in 1897. It became the official National March of the United States in 1987.
2 Composition and premiere
"Stars and Stripes Forever" has become the official National March of the United States.
The piece was inspired by the return of the 1896 United States presidential election campaign to the battle cry of "Hooray for the Speaker!" (Speaker Thomas B. Reed) in the 1890 election, which Sousa had heard in Washington, D.C.'s Hoffman Theater, where he had just seen a play. He had already written "The Thunderer" and "The Washington Post" that year.
On March 16, 1896, Sousa wrote the initial melody in a few minutes in his room at the Seminole Hotel in Saint Augustine, Florida, where he had gone to escape the winter weather in Washington, DC. He had also planned to give a concert, which was canceled by the weather but he performed at the hotel instead. The next day, he finished the song in 20 minutes. He then added the final drum cadence.
He wrote the lyrics later that year, after the Democrats dropped the "Hooray for the Speaker" slogan in favor of "Hooray for Grover". The lyrics were copyrighted on December 27, 1896, and published by Oliver Ditson & Company in Boston on January 1, 1897.
Composition and premiere[edit]
Sousa conducted the premiere of "Stars and Stripes Forever" on November 13, 1897, at the New York Naval Yard.
The lyrics are printed on the front cover of the sheet music, shown below. The original 1897 publication was titled "Stars and Stripes Forever" and included the lyrics in the same typeface as the music. This was to ensure that the lyrics would always be visible in the performance.
The song was originally written for concert band, but is now often performed by marching bands. The piece is 151 measures (264 bars) long and is in F major. Its opening theme is a 29-bar fanfare introduction, followed by its main melody, which is 120 bars of 2/4 time. The piece ends with a 10-bar coda. The drum pattern is written in cut time.
The melody is in the key of F major, and, like many other Sousa marches, the piece has a march bass underpinning the melody. Like many other Sousa marches, it includes a trio section or bridge, which is also in F major. The melody has been played by the U.S. Marine Band and other organizations since its premiere in 1897. Some marching bands omit the trio, while others use a different trio.
The trio's melody is played by the flutes, clarinets, bassoons and saxophones, and is 16 measures long. The rhythm is in eighth-note (quavers) with a triplet (sixteenth note) feel, while the basses play the same melody in whole notes.
In 1987, the United States National Archives and Records Administration made Sousa's 1897 arrangement of "Stars and Stripes Forever" the official national march of the United States. It is one of the most popular and well-known marches in the world.

Relay races emerged in the United States in the 1880s as a variation on charity races between firemen , who would hand a red pe

a-sized ball (called a "hose-nozzle" or "reel") from one team member to the next. There were few formal rules, so these races were sometimes decided by the first team to finish, but they were typically contested for distance (usually 250 yards) and time (usually three minutes). "Relay" is the name given to the handoff, and the person passing the baton is referred to as a "baton-bearer" or "baton-passer".
A local relay race was held on Wednesday, 26 May 1869 in New Bedford, Massachusetts. The race ran from New Bedford to Dartmouth via the New Bedford–Dartmouth Railroad. The distance was not standardized. The New York Times reported that the race was 26¾ miles, but the New London Telegraph reported it as 31.5 miles. Losing teams were awarded a gold medal, while the winning team was awarded a gold medal and a $100 prize.
The first North American relay race with a standardized length of 440 yards (400 m) was held on 29 October 1876 at the 1st Michigan State Fair in Detroit, Michigan. The race was won by the Detroit Athletic Club team of William D. Cusack, James W. Cunningham, and Frank K. Shipley in 1:31. The relay race was so successful that it was re-staged at the next Michigan State Fair (6 November 1877) and annual fairs thereafter.

Many Western Catholics and non @-@ Catholics have voiced disagreement on the Church 's support for natural family planning , an

expression of the Church 's 'pro-life ' agenda. But there has been a less publicized dispute over the Church 's emphasis on the sanctity of the family. In the 1960s, Cardinal Augustin Bea, a wise and well-respected theologian of the Church , spoke out against the Church 's insistence that the family is the most important institution in society. Conceding that the family is indeed important, Cardinal Bea nevertheless argued that 'the Church [is] on the wrong track' in making it an absolute priority.  But Cardinal Bea 's views were only one of several that could be heard in the 1960s. Other voices in the Church , especially among theologians and in the gay and lesbian communities, questioned the Church 's emphasis on the family.
The Catholic Church has been at the forefront of public debate over the family, and its stance on the family has been a source of both hope and disappointment for many people. But the debate over the Church 's position has shown signs of transformation. There are signs that the Church 's leadership, including the Pope, is increasingly willing to listen to dissenting voices. In the first years of the twenty-first century, the Church under the leadership of Pope John Paul II has begun to acknowledge the authority of dissenting voices in the Church .
The body of materials that follows is the result of my participation with Catholic theologians and theologians from other faith traditions in the public debate over the sanctity of the family. It is an effort to describe and analyze the nature of this debate, and to offer a new perspective on the issue of the family.
The debate over the sanctity of the family is a debate that is waged by a wide variety of actors, and it takes place in a variety of venues, from the pulpit to the courts. This book focuses primarily on the public debate over the sanctity of the family, but it does not ignore the debate that is waged within the Church . I will describe the arguments that can be heard in the Church , both from those in favor of the Church 's traditional stance on the family and from those who oppose it. I will also describe the ways that the Church 's traditionally negative view of homosexuality has influenced its understanding of the family.
The debate over the sanctity of the family has taken place in public venues, in the public square, over the past twenty years, and this book is an effort to describe and analyze that debate. The oribi is a small , slender antelope ; it reaches nearly 50 – 67 centimetres ( 20 – 26 in ) at the shoulder and weighs 12 –

16 kilograms ( 26 – 35 lb ). It has a long pointed snout and large, round ears. The tail is long and bushy. Its fur is a reddish-brown on the upper parts and white underneath.
The oribi has a number of different call sounds which it uses to communicate with other oribi. These call sounds include whistles, short barks, and whoops.
The oribi is found in the thorny scrub and savanna woodland areas in Angola , Benin , Burkina Faso , Cameroon , Central African Republic , Chad , Congo , the Democratic Republic of Congo , Côte d'Ivoire , Eritrea , Ethiopia , Gabon , Ghana , Guinea , Kenya , Liberia , Malawi , Mali , Mozambique , Namibia , Niger , Nigeria , Rwanda , Senegal , Sierra Leone , Somalia , South Africa , Sudan , Swaziland , Tanzania , Togo , Uganda , Zambia and Zimbabwe.
The oribi is a shy animal that prefers to feed alone. Like the duiker , it is active at night. The oribi feeds mainly on the leaves and fruits of small-leaved trees and shrubs. The oribi is a solitary animal .
The oribi is also known as the "African reedbuck" in English.
Agriculture, hunting and habitat loss are the main causes of the oribi's decline.
The oribi has the ability to run fast and jump high with its excellent eyesight and hearing . It is also a good swimmer.
The oribi has a gestation period of about 7 months , after which a single calf is born, which is then suckled for 6 months. The mother may continue to nurse the calf for another 6 months. The calf is weaned at about 18 months, but does not become sexually mature until 2 years old.
The oribi is hunted for its meat and for its horns.

Miller's employees became the pioneer group of white settlers in the area, which became known as Miller 's Landing.   In 1870 , the railroad's right-of-way through Nevada was sold to the Central Pacific and Southern Pacific railroads.
  In 1870 , Charles Crocker, president of the Central Pacific Railroad, and his party passed through the area on their way to the completion of the transcontinental railroad in Promontory, Utah. Crocker named the camp "Miller's Landing," after Miller, and the name stuck.
  In 1871 , the first post office was established at Miller's Landing.
  In 1906 , the Central Pacific Railroad and Southern Pacific Railroad merged into the Southern Pacific Company. The name "Miller's Landing" was abandoned and the town was known as "Reno Junction" until 1913, when the town was renamed "Sparks" in honor of John Sparks, governor of Nevada from 1909 to 1915.
  In 1908 , an 18-year-old high school dropout named John C. Fry settled in Sparks. In 1915, Fry was elected mayor of Sparks and, at age 24, he was the youngest mayor in the nation.
  In 1914 , Fry bought 18 acres (73,000 m²) of land, which included the town of Sparks, for $10,000.
  In 1916 , upon approval of the voters of Sparks, the city of Sparks was incorporated. Fry was elected the first mayor.
  In 1937 , Fry sold his land to the O'Brien family.

The musical bird, popular in Japan since the Meiji era, is a mechanical toy that plays music while moving its wings and body. It is based on Tatsumasa Yokoyama's 1879 invention, Kane-buburi ( literally "Clock Bird" ), which measured 15 cm (5 7/8 in) and played a 15-second tune while moving its wings. Setsuzo Honda, a musician who had been Yokoyama's assistant, refined the model and renamed it Kane-tori ( literally "Clock Bird" ). Honda's bird went on to be used as a mascot for the Tokyo 1964 Olympics and was featured on a postage stamp in 1981, among other things.
The modern musical bird is a 25-cm (9 7/8-in) model with a tall body, large wings, and small beak. It plays a 30-second tune while moving its wings and body, and it has a lever that can stop or start the tune. It sings in a soprano voice. The bird is made of plastic and is painted to resemble a blackbird. The tune is the same one that Yokoyama's original musical bird played, and it is approximately 0:35 seconds long.
The bird is sold in shops that sell toys and musical instruments, and it is often said to be a folk musical instrument.

1646 ordinance allowed excommunicants to appoint an advocate to speak on their behalf in any ecclesiastical trial, and the 1648 ordinance that created the Ecclesiastical Court allowed the defendant to choose someone to act as his counsel ( _Examinations_ , 292, 294, 295).
 In 1643 Parliament passed an ordinance ensuring that the judges of the ecclesiastical courts were to be appointed by Parliament and were to be paid by Parliament. The ordinance also provided that the judges should be chosen from among the bishops, archdeacons, and suffragans of the Church of England. In 1648 Parliament made the bishop of London a justice of the High Court of Ecclesiastical Court and required him to report directly to Parliament ( _Examinations_ , 362–63).
 In 1644 Parliament passed an ordinance permitting the Ecclesiastical Commission to appoint as many commissioners as it needed to fulfill its functions in the kingdoms of England and Ireland. The ordinance also allowed the commissioners to hold their hearings and execute their sentences in England, Ireland, or Scotland ( _Examinations_ , 362).
 On 16 September 1646 the Ecclesiastical Commission ordered the House of Lords to try the Scottish bishop of Edinburgh, Archibald Johnston, for denying the royal supremacy in the Church of England ( _Examinations_ , 367).
 As the Civil Wars continued, Parliament passed a number of resolutions and decrees establishing the Ecclesiastical Court and the processes for appointing the commissioners, judges, and proctors to be used in the ecclesiastical trials. The resolutions also established the procedures for prosecuting and executing verdicts against those found guilty of heresy and other religious offenses. This body of laws and procedures became known as the Ecclesiastical Laws ( _Examinations_ , 366).
 The laws that established the Ecclesiastical Court were passed by Parliament during the 1645–47 period. These laws required that the commissioners of the Ecclesiastical Court be appointed by Parliament from a list of candidates provided by the bishops of the Church of England. The laws also established the procedures for appointing the proctors for the defendants and the judges of the court. In 1646 Parliament passed an ordinance requiring that the judges of the ecclesiastical courts be chosen from among the bishops, archdeacons, and suffragans of the Church of England. Those who were not members of the Church of England were permitted to sit as judges of the ecclesiastical courts ( _Examinations_ , 362–63).
 In 1648 Parliament passed an ordinance establishing the Ecclesiastical Court. The ordinance appointed the bishop of London to be the chief justice and all bishops, archdeacons, and suffragans as judges of the court. The ordinance also required that the commissioners of the court be chosen by Parliament and that the judges be paid by Parliament ( _Examinations_ , 363). MD 194 begins at an intersection with MD 26 ( Liberty Road ) in Ceresville . The roadway continues south as MD 26 , which cross

es the Potomac River into Washington County , Maryland .

## History

MD 194 was defined in 1957 when MD 26 was split into two parts, with MD 194 being the northern part. MD 194 originally continued along present-day MD 355 to the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad at the eastern end of the Potomac River Swing Bridge, where it connected with MD 195. MD 195 was a spur route off MD 194 that went east to the B&O Railroad bridge. Both MD 194 and MD 195 were removed from the state highway system in 1971 when the bridge was replaced.

The portion of MD 194 north of the bridge was transferred to Washington County, Maryland and designated MD 26 in 1972.

## Junction list

The entire route is in Frederick County.

## Auxiliary routes

 MD 194A was the designation for the Frederick City section of MD 194 from 1957 to 1972.

Unlike their adversaries , the South Vietnamese military suffered heavily in their attempts to recapture the village of Bình Gi

ã in 1968.
Bình Giã, in the central Quảng Ngãi Province, was an example of the difficulties faced by the South Vietnamese in their efforts to break the Ho Chi Minh Trail. It was a staging area for the NLF before the Tet Offensive.
Because of its geography and its isolation; Bình Giã seemed in 1968 to be of little strategic importance. The village was strategically located at the junction of major routes, however, which made it a natural choke point. It was also surrounded by low hills that formed a natural, but deadly, firing position for NLF artillery and snipers.
As a result, Bình Giã was of great importance to the NLF. It was a staging area for the Ho Chi Minh Trail and for the NLF's 5th Northeastern Front. It was also a base for NLF intelligence operations in the A Shau Valley to the north and the coastal plain to the south.
The U.S. Army, under Lieutenant General William B. Rosson, did everything in its power to help the ARVN to recapture the village. The U.S. Army sent in supplies by helicopter. It also sent in the Southeast Asia Flying Column, a special forces unit of 200 men, which over the next few months would suffer 30 percent casualties.
The ARVN tried to recapture Bình Giã three times. After the second attempt, it lost 30 percent of its strength. The ARVN then decided to abandon the village.
This was a strategic decision. The NLF had done everything in its power to make the village untenable. By the time the U.S. Army withdrew, Bình Giã was a shambles. The ARVN did not want to lose men in such a useless endeavor.
The NLF had won a major victory. It had beaten back the ARVN and the U.S. Army. By 1968, the NLF was in a position to dictate to the South Vietnamese and to the Americans.
In 1968, the U.S. Army was still entrenched in the Vietnam War. As long as the U.S. was present, the NLF would find it difficult to take the initiative.
In the early months of 1968, however, the NLF had been able to demonstrate its strength on the battlefield. It had also demonstrated that it was able to dictate the pace of battle.
The Tet Offensive was the NLF's opportunity to make the most of its victories.

## Composition

For the song, its lyrical content draws from a relationship that has gone wrong. Houston sings the song's opening, which questions the listener whether she is "looking through a window into the heartbreak hotel". The lyrics state to the listener that the singer will be waiting for the person to come back to her. The song's composition is a mid-tempo hip-hop song, with its instrumentation based on a drum pattern and polyphonic synthesizer.

## Critical reception

"Heartbreak Hotel" garnered positive reviews from critics. Allmusic editor Andy Kellman deemed the song as "a jam perfect for the club and radio." He also stated that Houston "turns in a performance that's not only consistent with her powerful singing abilities, but also with the rhythm-heavy R&B style that has defined her music in recent years." Entertainment Weekly writer Chuck Arnold felt that the song is "a chilly, synth-driven hip-hop track that takes the classic clichés of hardcore breakup ballads and turns them into a wake-up call for the party set – and probably for those who've been in too many relationships and haven't learned from their mistakes." David Browne from Billboard magazine called it a "stomp-drumming hip-hop jam" and also stated that the song is "a song for the club, but it's got just enough pop-girl appeal to keep the heartbroken from running to the DJ."
