Personal interaction with the gods took many forms . People who wanted information or advice consulted oracles , run by temples

, priests, or magicians. These oracles were not always rational, but they were always effective. They answered questions on everything from the future to the here-and-now. The oracles were used for making predictions, and for finding out what to do in a difficult situation.
In the first oracles, the person consulting the gods had to ask their question, and wait for the answer. When the answer came, it might be a message written on a piece of wood or a stone, a dream, or a vision.
The oracle at Delphi was the most important oracle in Greece. It was in a cave, and the answer was given by a priestess . She sat on a tripod in the cave, and inhaled a vapour which came from the ground. She then gave her answer.
The oracle at Delphi had the reputation of being the most reliable. Priests at the oracle in Delphi were not allowed to be bribed. They had to interpret the oracle as given. The oracle at Delphi was used by kings and generals to make important decisions.
There were other oracles in Greece, which were less important. Oracles were also consulted in the East, and in Rome.
The earliest form of oracle was a dream. A person would look for a dream which would give them a hint about what to do. A famous Greek poet, Homer, dreamed about two paths. He decided to take the one which was more difficult, and his poem, the _Iliad_ , was the result.
 A person could also approach a magician to ask for an oracle. This method was used especially for business or practical problems, and sometimes for love affairs.
In the Bible, there are many references to oracles. The prophet Samuel was an oracle. He could talk to the gods. The prophet Isaiah was an oracle, as were the prophets Ezekiel and Daniel. The Bible also talks about the prophet Ahijah, who was an oracle.
In the Bible, oracles are usually thought of as coming from God, but this is not always the case. In the book of Judges, the prophet Deborah tells the people that God is sending an oracle. She tells them that the gods are sending a woman, who will lead the people to victory in battle. It is not clear if God is sending the oracle, or if the woman is a prophet.
 In the Bible, the word 'oracle' is also used to mean a place where people go to pray. The word 'temple' is used to mean a building in which people worship gods.
In the modern world, people sometimes go to psychics, fortune-tellers, and clairvoyants, to ask for oracles. They also read horoscopes, and use crystal balls. Some people even believe in the power of computers to predict the future.

During and after the debates over church government , the Assembly framed other documents which did not cause open rifts . The

1586 _Constitutions_ , written during the period of the Synod of Dort, was a church manual. The _Directory for Public Worship_ , drafted in 1645, was a manual for the conduct of public worship. The _Westminster Confession_ was an official confession of faith.
In all of these documents the Assemblymen, in accordance with their theological position, wrote under the influence of the _Institutes_ of the _Catechism_ of Calvin and Beza. The _Institutes_ and the _Catechism_ were published in 1559, but the _Catechism_ was not used in the assemblies of the Continental Churches until the 1640s. The 1647 _Confession_ is a revision of the 1643 _Confession_ , which was drawn from the _Catechism_. The 1645 _Directory_ , which is primarily a revision of the 1643 _Directory_ , has its source in the _Catechism_ and the _Confession_. The 1646 _Catechism_ also was a revision of the 1643 _Catechism_. The 1646 _Shorter Catechism_ , written by the Assembly's Scotch delegates, was a revision of the 1643 _Catechism_.
 The Assembly's writers, therefore, did not work in a vacuum. They were greatly influenced by what they had read and by what they had heard from others. This was not the case, however, with the 1658 Confession, which is in a class by itself and is unique in the Presbyterian history. It was prepared by the Scottish Presbyterians alone and was not written under the influence of the _Catechism_ or the _Confession_.
To a greater extent than the other documents, the _Confession_ reflects the thinking of the Scottish Presbyterians during the period of the Assembly and afterward. It was not merely a revision of the 1647 _Confession_ , but a new and original confession. It was composed by Scottish divines who came to the Assembly from Scotland in 1646 and who were not present at the 1643 Assembly. They were Alexander Henderson, Archibald Johnston, and Robert Bruce. Henderson was the senior minister at Leith. Johnston was the senior minister at Dundee. Bruce was a professor at St. Andrews. They were joined by other Scottish ministers and theologians who were present at the 1643 Assembly. They were Robert Baillie, James Guthrie, and Richard Cameron.
The Scottish ministers and theologians were not only present at the Assembly; they were also present in the theological movement that led to the Assembly and in the theological movement that marked the period after the Assembly. They were present at the founding of the Reformed Church of Scotland in 1560, at the founding of the Reformed Church in 1562, at the Westminster Assembly in 1643, and at the Synod of Dort in 1648.
The Scottish Presbyterian movement in the sixteenth century was a religious movement as well as a political movement. The Scottish divines were not only theists; they were theological theorists. They were not only Calvinists; they were Calvinistic theologians. They were not merely churchmen; they were Christian theologians.
This is not to suggest that the Scottish Presbyterians were theologians in the modern sense of the word. They were not theologians in the strict sense of the word. They were not systematic theologians. They were not objective theologians. They were not theologians who were concerned with abstract and universal theological issues. They were not theologians who were concerned with theology as a branch of philosophy. They were not theologians who were concerned with theology as a branch of history. They were not theologians who were concerned with theology as a branch of science. They were not theologians who were concerned with theology as a branch of culture.
They were theologians in another sense of the word. They were theologians as men who studied theology and whose sermons and writings were formulated by theological principles. They were theologians as men who preached and taught theology and as men who were affected by theology. They were theologians as men who were commissioned by theology to preach and to teach. Bodyline , also known as fast leg theory bowling , was a cricketing tactic devised by the English cricket team for their 1932 –

33 tour of Australia. It was a form of bowling that relied on the bowler to swing the ball in to the batsman so that it bounced awkwardly. The England captain Douglas Jardine decided to employ it because he thought the Australians were too good at playing conventional cricket; because he disliked the way the Australians played the game; and because he wanted to provoke the Australians into retaliating in kind, which he hoped would lead to the game being "played in the rough".  The tactic was a success, as Australia lost the series 4-1, but it also resulted in the most bitter and prolonged enmity in the history of cricket. The 1932 – 33 Ashes series was undeniably the most hostile ever played, with verbal and physical abuse being directed at the English players. There were threats of violence, and the English players' hotel was bombed by the Australians. The English players were widely vilified in Australia, and many of them were attacked by the crowd.
The opening Test of the series was played in Brisbane, and the English bowlers, led by the captain Douglas Jardine, bowled a succession of short, fast deliveries to the Australian batsmen. The English bowlers tried to bounce the ball into the body of the Australian batsmen, making it difficult for them to play the ball. The Australians, in turn, responded by trying to hit the English bowlers with the ball. The Test match was a closely fought contest, with Australia winning by 332 runs. The attitude of the Australians towards the English players was hostile from the start. The Australian captain, Bill Woodfull, felt that the English bowling was dangerous and unfair. The Australian press, also, were highly critical of the English tactics.
At the end of 1932, the Australians made some changes to the laws of cricket, outlawing the "short, fast delivery". However, the Australian authorities did not enforce the law, and, after some unpleasant exchanges between the players of the two teams, the Australians went out to bat again. The Australians, led by Woodfull, decided to take the law into their own hands and retaliated against the English bowlers. They defied the law and played their own brand of bodyline cricket, leading to a renewal of the rivalry between the two teams. The Australians won by 199 runs, but the English team had been subjected to a siege mentality and they were unpopular in Australia. In the following Test match in Melbourne, the Australians resorted to violence. They pelted the English players with snowballs, and abused them with language that was filthy even by the standards of the time. The English players were also subjected to a barrage of thrown objects, including golf balls, tennis balls and bottles of stout. At times, the crowd got in on the act and attacked the English players. The English players were also subjected to stone-throwing from the crowd at the Australian team hotel. The English team was also attacked by a mob of Australian supporters, who stoned their car and attempted to burn it. The English players were forced to return to England, where they gave up bodyline cricket. The controversy over bodyline ended in 1935, when the laws of cricket were once again amended.

The England captain Douglas Jardine decided to employ it because he thought the Australians were too good at playing conventional cricket; because he disliked the way the Australians played the game; and because he wanted to provoke the Australians into retaliating in kind, which he hoped would lead to the game being "played in the rough".  The tactic was a success, as Australia lost the series 4-1, but it also resulted in the most bitter and prolonged enmity in the history of cricket. The 1932 – 33 Ashes series was undeniably the most hostile ever played, with verbal and physical abuse being directed at the English players. There were threats of violence, and the English players' hotel was bombed by the Australians. The English players were widely vilified in Australia, and many of them were attacked by the crowd.

The Texas A & M Singing Cadets are a male choral group at Texas A & M University . Nicknamed " The Voice of Aggieland " , the S

.C.s can be typically identified by their green blazers and gold neckties.
Formed in 1945, The Texas A & M Singing Cadets are the only all-male choral group at Texas A & M University . The Singing Cadets were established by Dr. Leighton Roberts , who served as director from 1945-1960. Roberts was a well-known director, composer, and arranger in the Texas area prior to his tenure at Texas A & M. Roberts wrote several arrangements for the group as well as composing several works, including the Cadets' alma mater, "Conquest."
In 1962, Dr. George J. Barraclough became the group's second director. Barraclough served as director until his death in 1974. During his tenure, the group gained national recognition, having performed with the NBC Orchestra. The group also performed in the Kennedy Center, Royal Albert Hall, and Carnegie Hall.
The Singing Cadets have also performed with several other musical groups. In 1969, the group toured with the American Bandmaster's Association. In 1986, the group performed with the Moscow Chamber Choir. In 1997, the group performed with the Tanglewood Festival Chorus. In 2000, the group performed with the Dallas Symphony Orchestra and the National Symphony Orchestra.
The Singing Cadets are known for their Cadet Choral Series. Formed in 1997, the ensemble is designed to educate and train aspiring choral directors. The group has also hosted the Texas A & M Singing Cadets Choral Conducting Symposium, a weekend event in which students from across the country attend clinics, workshops, and masterclasses.
The Singing Cadets perform annually at the Texas A & M Homecoming Parade. The group has also performed at the Texas A & M Roundup and the Spoleto Festival USA. They have also performed at various conventions, such as the Texas Music Educators Association Convention and the Texas Choral Directors Association Convention.
The group has appeared on several television shows, including the Late Show with David Letterman, The Early Show, and the Today Show. They have also appeared on PBS and in the film Legally Blonde.
The Singing Cadets are recognized for their many awards. In 1991, they received the Ernst Bacon Memorial Award for Choral Excellence. In 2001, the group won the American Prize in Choral Performance. In 2007, they won the Texas Choral Directors Association Choral Performance Competition.
The Singing Cadets have released several albums, including Singing Cadets: 25 Years (1967), Singing Cadets: 50 Years (1995), and Singing Cadets: 65 Years (2010).

The first trading post on Corpus Christi Bay was established by Henry Kinney in 1838 in present @-@ day Corpus Christi . By the

mid-1850s, the bay had become a busy port en route to and from the rest of the world. The first railroad in Texas, a railroad that made Corpus Christi the second-busiest port on the Gulf of Mexico, was completed in 1882.
Shortly after the outbreak of World War I, Port Corpus Christi was designated the principal base of the United States Navy's Pacific fleet. From 1920 to 1952, the port was the primary port of debarkation for immigrants bound for the United States.
In 1971, the U.S. Navy decommissioned the Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. In 1979, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began channel dredging at the entrance to the bay.
The Port of Corpus Christi continues to be an important port of entry, with cruise ships, container ships, and oil tankers docking at the port.
The city of Corpus Christi is the county seat of Nueces County, which is located in southern Texas. The city is the 49th largest city in the United States and the 8th largest city in Texas. The city is 131 miles south of San Antonio, and 135 miles southeast of Austin.

Shaolin kung fu is a method of martial arts that applies principles of martial arts, such as forms, to a spiritual teaching of the Shaolin Monastery , located at Songshan in Henan province, China . The Shaolin Monastery is known for its association with the promotion of Buddhism in China.

The film is a parody of kung fu movies, and it features soccer as the primary mode of martial arts fighting. Shaolin ( 少林 ) is a 2011 Chinese action-adventure film directed by Benny Chan and starring Jet Li . This movie is the second martial arts film written and directed by Chan, after Fist of Legend .
The Shaolin Temple is a Buddhist temple in Dengfeng, Zhengzhou City, Henan Province, China. The temple was founded in 495, during the last years of the Liu Song Dynasty , by the eminent Buddhist master Boshan . It is one of the largest Buddhist temples in China, being the longest of its kind in the entire world, with an area of 74,000 m2 (800,000 sq ft).

The Adventures of Tintin are a series of comic albums created by Belgian cartoonist Georges Remi ( who used the pen name Hergé ). The series was one of the most popular European comics of the 20th century. By the time of the centenary of Hergé's birth in 2007, Tintin had been published in more than 70 languages with sales of more than 200 million copies. The books have been adapted for radio, television, and film. Tintin has also been featured in exhibitions and published in magazines.
The Adventures of Tintin are set mainly in Europe and around the world, and chronicle the adventures of Tintin, a young Belgian reporter, and his dog Snowy ( Milou in the original French-language versions). They are illustrated with Hergé's distinctive, ligne claire drawing style. The word "Tintin" has passed into the English language as a synonym for a freethinking, idealistic journalist.

Syādvāda is not only an extension of anekānta ontology , but a separate system of logic capable of standing on its own . As rea

lized by many scholars, Syādvāda is the quintessential philosophical and logical system of Indian Buddhism, and has been the object of study by Indian and Western philosophers, logicians, and linguists from at least the 19th century.
In this modern era, the rise of American pragmatism and analytic philosophy in the 20th century and their influence on 21st century theorists have led to a renewed interest in the philosophical and logical aspects of Syādvāda, and an increase in the number of Indian logicians and Western philosophers who are working on its logical aspects .
Thus, this paper is in the tradition of the great logicians of the 20th century, such as T.R.V. Murti , whose work clearly established the logical aspects of Syādvāda. In this paper, I will use the logical apparatus of modern logic in order to show the logical form of Syādvāda.
 The reader should be aware that in general, I will be using a translation of the Sanskrit terms according to the popular linguistic classification, and that this will not always reflect the terminology of the scholars of Syādvāda.

Until 2010 , despite a breeding range estimated at 12 @,@ 400 @,@ 000 km2 ( 4 @,@ 800 @,@ 000 sq mi ) , the corn crake was clas

- sified as 'near threatened' ( IUCN Red List 2009 ). It is now listed as 'vulnerable' ( IUCN Red List 2012 ).
 Most of the present-day breeding range was in the post-glacial Boreal Forest Zone of Russia and Scandinavia, with a smaller breeding range in the adjacent wooded tundra of Siberia. The European breeding range was in present-day France, Germany, Italy, and the Balkan Peninsula. The European population was thought to be much larger in the 1960s and 1970s, but declines in the 1980s and 1990s led to a reduction in the breeding range. This reduction of the breeding range seems to have been caused by a combination of habitat loss, the effects of climate change, and predation by introduced mammals. In addition to the declines in Europe, the population in the Russian breeding range was also reduced. Habitat loss in Russia was caused by conversion of hay meadows to agriculture. Predation by foxes in the Boreal Forest Zone was probably a key factor in the reduction in European and Russian numbers. The introduction of mammalian predators into the breeding range of the corn crake probably had a significant impact on the decline of this species. The most likely candidate is the American mink ( Mustela vison ). This mammal was introduced into Scandinavia around 1900 and into the Russian Boreal Forest Zone in 1924.
 In Britain, the corn crake was a common winter visitor and breeder from the 16th to the early 20th century. Its decline began in the 1930s and seems to have been caused by changes in agricultural practices. In recent years, the population has increased but this does not seem to be a result of changes in agricultural practices. The increased corn crake numbers are probably a result of the change in climate, which has caused a reduction in the numbers of the corn bunting ( Emberiza calandra ; see pp. 106–10). The corn crake and the corn bunting may be able to interbreed with each other. The two species were considered to be conspecific in the past, but are now treated as different species.
 The European breeding range of the corn crake is still declining and, although the species is still considered to be 'vulnerable', it may be downgraded to 'endangered'. The population in Scandinavia is apparently stable, but the population in Russia continues to decline.
 The name 'corn crake' is from the English 'crown' and 'crake', which in turn is derived from the Dutch 'kruuk'. This name was given to the species because the male corn crake calls from a small patch of earth at the edge of a corn field.
 The corn crake has been recorded in the Faroe Islands, but this record is probably based on misidentification of the Eurasian curlew ( Numenius arquata ).
 The corn crake is not closely related to the other two members of the genus _Crex_. These are the pheasant-creeper ( _Crex egregia_ ) of North America and the African cuckoo-roller ( _Crex egregia_ ) of eastern and central Africa.

Near the southern edge of Rockefeller State Park Preserve , NY 448 turns east and enters Kykuit , the estate of the Rockefeller

family. The driveway is lined with elm trees, many of which are more than 100 years old. In the distance are views of the Hudson River, the Catskill Mountains, and the Palisades.
After about a mile, the driveway curves to the right and begins a slow descent. It passes through a tunnel, and then, around the next bend, the driveway ends at an intersection with a road. To the right is the entrance to the house, and to the left the driveway continues. A sign directs visitors to park along this driveway, which proceeds for another mile to the visitor center and parking lot.
The driveway leads to a large parking lot, and a sign directing visitors to the visitor center and gardens. The visitor center and several gardens may be found at the south end of the parking lot, and the Rockefeller house and the rest of the gardens are to the north. A map of Kykuit is available in the visitor center.
The visitor center, which opened in 1963, is a spacious building that contains a bookstore and a cafeteria. The center also contains an exhibit room, and a room displaying the gardens of Kykuit.
At the north end of the visitor center, a door leads to the parking lot. To the left of the door is a path through a small wooded area, and to the right is a grassy path leading to the main entrance to the house. The path leads past a small fountain and to the main doors of the house.
The house itself dates from the 1700s and has been restored and redecorated to its original appearance. During the tour, a guide tells the history of the house and the family, and explains the details of the restoration.
The house has four floors. The basement is not included in the tour, but the space is used for storage. The first floor contains the main reception rooms and the dining room, which is used for special occasions.
The second floor contains the bedrooms, and is reached by a broad set of stairs. The third floor has a large room on the eastern side of the house. This room houses the library, which contains more than 20,000 volumes. The library includes books by and about the Rockefellers, rare first editions of classics, and other books of interest. The library is open to the public from June through September.
The third floor also contains the painting and sculpture galleries. The galleries include paintings and sculptures by artists such as Picasso, Matisse, and Rodin.
The fourth floor contains a room that houses the largest organ in the world. The organ was built by the Aeolian Company of New York and is 18 feet tall and 36 feet wide. The organ contains 7,500 pipes, and its keyboard is 25 feet long.
A path leads to the back of the house, and then to the gardens. The gardens include a sunken garden, a rose garden, a walled garden, and a Japanese garden. The Japanese garden contains a summerhouse and a teahouse.
A path leads from the garden to the Hudson River, and then along the river to the Kykuit Rock. The Kykuit Rock is a large outcropping of rock that juts out into the Hudson River. The Rock is visible from the house and from the gardens.
The path continues along the Hudson River, and then leads to the Rockefeller estate in Pocantico Hills.

In mid @-@ September , a weak tropical wave moved off the coast of Northwest Africa . It moved westward and entered the eastern

tropical Atlantic on September 19 . On September 24 , the disturbance crossed the equator as a tropical depression , and over the next two days it moved west-northwestward across the central tropical Atlantic . It was named “Sixteen-E ” on September 25 . On September 26 , the tropical depression strengthened into Tropical Storm “Ophelia ” .

## History

During the morning of September 27 , Ophelia was located at latitude 14.2°N and longitude 21.3°W, or about 630 mi (1,020 km) east of the Lesser Antilles and about 720 mi (1,160 km) southeast of Bermuda . Ophelia had winds of 50 mph (85 km/h), and it was moving west-northwestward at 16 mph (26 km/h), with a minimum central pressure of 1006 mbar (hPa; 29.7 inHg). This was its peak intensity .

The tropical cyclone was forecast to move west-northwestward and become a hurricane within 36 to 48 hours . On September 28 , Ophelia was upgraded to Category 1 hurricane status, and at the same time its convection became asymmetrical and the storm became elongated . Its winds were estimated at 80 mph (130 km/h) and its path was forecast to take it to the vicinity of Bermuda . On September 29 , Ophelia was forecast to pass north of Bermuda .

At 0000 UTC on October 1 , Ophelia was located at latitude 30.2°N and longitude 53.6°W, or about 800 mi (1,290 km) southeast of Cape Race , Newfoundland . It had winds of 80 mph (130 km/h), and was moving northwestward at 13 mph (20 km/h), with a minimum central pressure of 989 mbar (hPa; 29.2 inHg). This was its peak intensity .

Hurricane Ophelia continued to move northwestward, and shortly after 0600 UTC, it was upgraded to a Category 2 hurricane. At 1200 UTC, Ophelia was located at 31.0°N and 54.8°W, about 575 mi (925 km) southeast of Cape Race . It had winds of 105 mph (165 km/h), and was moving northwestward at 12 mph (19 km/h), with a minimum central pressure of 984 mbar (hPa; 29.1 inHg). On October 2 at 0000 UTC, Ophelia made a turn to the north-northwest and its motion slowed. It continued to strengthen further, and at 0600 UTC it reached its peak intensity of 110 mph (175 km/h) with a minimum central pressure of 966 mbar (hPa; 28.5 inHg).

Wilhelm's pitching success earned him a promotion to the major leagues in 1955 , where he spent the rest of his career.
Wilhelm was a switch-pitcher who played from 1955 to 1980 , and holds the major league record for the most career wins with a switch-pitcher with 224. He was the last player to win 20 games in both leagues in a career and he was the first pitcher to win 20 games in each league in the same season. He played for the St. Louis Cardinals , San Francisco Giants , New York Mets , Oakland Athletics , and Chicago White Sox . He was named to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 1985 .
After retiring from baseball, Wilhelm became a pitching coach for the Mets and White Sox . He was the pitching coach for the 1986 World Series champion Mets, where he helped coach Dwight Gooden to his 24–4 record and 1.53 ERA in 1985. He was also the pitching coach for the White Sox when they won the World Series in 2005.

The Soviet Union was a communist state in Eurasia that existed from 1922 to 1991. A union of multiple subnational Soviet republics, its government and economy were based on the Marxist–Leninist ideology of communism. One of the world's first socialist states, the Soviet Union was a one-party state under the authority of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.
The Soviet Union was founded in December 1922 when a Soviet Socialist Republic was established in the Russian SFSR by the Russian SFSR's Second Congress of Soviets. Until 1953, the Soviet Union was ruled by Joseph Stalin. During Stalin's rule, the state adopted a centralized administrative economy, and encouraged a rapid industrialization. The Soviet Union became a nuclear power and the third country to achieve a spaceflight. The Soviet Union also had a large military, and was a leading member of the Warsaw Pact, a collective defense treaty.
In the 1950s, the Soviet Union had the second-largest economy in the world. It was an active participant in the Korean War and many other major conflicts of the Cold War. In the 1970s, a Soviet Union-wide reform known as Perestroika was instituted. This led to the end of the Soviet Union, and the rise of the Russian Federation.

The " zombie apocalypse " genre was born in the United States in the 1960s with the publication of James Howard's 1964 novel _The Savage Dead_ and _The Serpent Eaters_ (1965). In the late 1970s, the genre gained momentum with the publication of George A. Romero's _Night of the Living Dead_ (1968). These works introduced the concept of a zombie apocalypse as a possible possibility and established the zombie as the central figure in the genre.
The genre received its name after the 1985 publication of _The Zombie Survival Guide_ , a work by American author Max Brooks that details strategies and tactics for human survival in the event of a zombie attack. Brooks's novel was the first of its kind to offer a comprehensive analysis of the psychology and nature of the zombie and the implications of a zombie apocalypse.
The growing popularity of the genre in the 1990s led to the publication of numerous zombie survival guides, including _Zombie Survival Guide_ (2003), _The Zombie Survival Guide: Recorded Attacks_ (2007), _World War Z_ (2006), and _A Zombie Apocalypse: The History and Future of the Zombie_ (2011). In 2010, a zombie survival kit was released, complete with a bug-out bag and a tactical knife. The kit was designed to provide consumers with everything they need to survive a zombie apocalypse. In 2012, a zombie survival course was offered at the University of Central Florida.
The genre has also been used to explore a wide range of themes, including race, gender, class, and sexuality. For example, _The Walking Dead_ (2010–present) features an all-black cast and explores themes of race, class, and gender. In the novel _World War Z_ (2006), a zombie apocalypse is triggered by a pandemic that begins in China and spreads to the rest of the world. The novel explores themes of globalization, immigration, and xenophobia.
The zombie apocalypse genre has been adapted into numerous forms of media, including television shows, movies, video games, and comic books. The genre has also been the subject of numerous scholarly studies, including _Zombies in the Academy: Living Death and the Academy in the Postmodern Era_ (2010) and _Zombiphobia: A Critical Reader on the Living Dead in Popular Culture_ (2012).
In recent years, the genre has been criticized for its depictions of violence and the treatment of women. Critics have argued that the genre reinforces gendered and racialized stereotypes and promotes an unhealthy obsession with death and violence. Nevertheless, the genre continues to be popular and has spawned numerous works of art, including the popular video game series _Left 4 Dead_ (2008–2014) and the television show _The Walking Dead_ (2010–present).
In conclusion, the zombie apocalypse genre is a popular and influential part of popular culture that has explored a wide range of themes and has been adapted into numerous forms of media. # THE MISSING PROTAGONIST
# 1
In 1977, the French philosopher Jean-François Lyotard published a little-known and poorly circulated essay entitled “La condition postmoderne: réinventer le sujet” [The Postmodern Condition: Inventing the Subject] in the French newspaper Libération. The author—inspired by the work of the sociologist Jean Baudrillard—claims to be offering a diagnosis of the contemporary situation: it is a diagnosis that is both positive and negative. On the one hand, he claims that the modern notion of subject is becoming archaic and that, hence, we can no longer speak of the subject in the same way as we did in the nineteenth century—that is, as the Cartesian ego. On the other hand, he claims that, in the face of this disappearance, we must invent a new subject. The essay is an attempt to define the new postmodern subject.
Lyotard's essay is still very much in vogue today, and it has been widely debated and discussed. His thesis has been repeated and echoed by many other authors, some of whom argue that the disappearance of the subject is a simple consequence of globalization, the market, and the technological revolution.
In this essay, however, I do not intend to discuss Lyotard's thesis. Rather, I intend to show that the disappearance of the subject in narrative fiction—and the corresponding search for a new subject—is a much more complex process than has been theorized. I shall do so by examining the literary genre of the novel, and in particular narrative and character development in contemporary fiction. This examination reveals that the disappearance of the subject in the novel is not a consequence of a single historical event, but rather the result of a complex series of recent developments that have been incrementally transforming the novel for the past three centuries.
The first of these developments is the increasingly significant separation of content and form in the novel. This development is related to the gradual disappearance of plot, and, simultaneously, an increasingly significant role for character development. The next stage in the evolution of the novel is the increasingly significant role of the so-called authorial voice in the narrative. The third and last stage is the impersonal narrator.

The crisis was resolved , but the war of words continued . In his address to Congress on January 25 , 1962 , Kennedy declared that the United States would not hesitate to use force to maintain the peace .

In the fall of 1962 , the Soviet Union sent missiles to Cuba . Kennedy imposed a quarantine on Cuba and threatened to use force if the missiles were not removed . The Soviet Union agreed to withdraw the missiles .
The Cuban missile crisis and the conflict in the Congo demonstrated that Kennedy's foreign policy was dominated by the Cold War . He was committed to the containment of Communism , and he was willing to use military force to maintain the peace .

Xenon difluoride is the compound of xenon with the formula XeF 2. Due to its high reactivity, it has been used as a reagent in organic synthesis.
Although the compound is a liquid at room temperature, it is not stable. The compound decomposes into xenon monofluoride and xenon trifluoride.
Xenon difluoride is prepared by the reaction of xenon trioxide with hydrogen fluoride (HF). This reaction requires relatively high temperatures (>200 ° C) to proceed.
Xenon difluoride is a clear liquid with a strong odor .
Xenon difluoride is a strong fluorinating agent and reacts with many compounds, including alkenes and aromatic hydrocarbons. The fluorination reaction is a nucleophilic substitution reaction.
Xenon trifluoride and xenon difluoride have been used to synthesize 2,6-difluorobenzoic acid.
The oxidation of xenon difluoride with water yields xenon dioxide and xenon difluoride as a by-product.
Xenon difluoride is used as a fluorinating agent in the synthesis of substituted xenon derivatives.

## History

### Early years

In the 1880s, the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railroad extended its line from Dodge City to the Arkansas River, and the company built a depot on the north side of the river. The depot was in the territory of Osage County, and the town and the depot were named Young Station. Later the name was shortened to Young.

In 1892, a post office was established in Young Station. An agricultural and livestock fair was started in 1892, and the town was incorporated as a city in 1893.

### 20th century

The first railroad bridge across the Arkansas River was located in Young. In 1912 the bridge was replaced by a steel bridge.

The city was the site of the Young State School for "feeble-minded" children. The school was established in 1913. In 1949 the state legislature changed its name to Young State Training School. The school was closed in 1972.

The high school in Young was closed in 1964 and the students were sent to La Harpe. The building was then used as a community center.

### 21st century

In 2002 a tornado touched down in Young, destroying 10 homes and damaging several others.

There are a number of methods to determine the TBSA , including the Wallace rule of nines , Lund and Browder chart , and estima

tion of TBSA based on the percentage of the body affected. The Wallace rule of nines is one of the most common methods used to estimate the TBSA.
It is based on the assumption that the body surface area is 185 cm2 and is obtained by dividing the body into nine parts (skin, upper extremities, lower extremities, head and neck, chest, abdomen, back, upper back, and buttocks). The body surface area is then calculated by adding the surface areas of all the nine parts. For example, if the TBSA is 20%, it would be equal to 0.2 x 185 = 37 cm2.
The Lund and Browder chart is another method used to estimate the TBSA. It is based on the assumption that the body surface area is 1750 cm2 and is obtained by dividing the body into seven parts (upper extremities, lower extremities, head and neck, chest, abdomen, back, and buttocks). The TBSA is then calculated by subtracting the surface areas of the lower and upper extremities from the total surface area. For example, if the TBSA is 20%, it would be equal to 0.2 x 1750 = 350 cm2.
Another method used to estimate the TBSA is by calculating the percentage of the body that is affected. This method is more accurate than the Wallace rule of nines and Lund and Browder chart as it takes into account the location of the burns on the body. For example, if the TBSA is 20%, it would be equal to 20% of the total surface area of the body.

During World War II he worked at the Radiation Laboratory at Harvard University on the development of radar detectors. After the war he continued his studies at Columbia , receiving his Ph.D. in 1948.
 Reines studied under Isidor Isaac Rabi , who encouraged him to study nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). He went to work with Rabi and Owen Chamberlain at the University of California at Berkeley , where he began an experimental study of NMR. He detected the first evidence of the NMR of the nucleus of the hydrogen atom in 1947.
 In 1950 Reines moved to the California Institute of Technology as a research associate and began to study cosmic rays. He and his colleagues were able to detect the primordial radiation he believed to be a residue of the big bang . This discovery earned him the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physics.
 In 1963 Reines left Caltech to become a professor at Washington University in St. Louis , Missouri . He remained there until 1981, when he became a professor of physics at the University of California at Irvine . His research focused on particle physics and the study of the cosmos. He received many honors and awards for his work, including the National Medal of Science in 1979.
 Frederick Lawrence Reines died of cancer in 1998.

The Crown Fountain is 50 feet (15 m) high, 8 feet (2.4 m) wide and is composed of two glass blocks, each 50 feet (15 m) in height. The Crown Fountain is constructed as two 50-foot-wide glass blocks: one is a solid, opaque block; the other, with its backside exposed, is filled with 108 water channels, each fitted with a nozzle that shoots water up to a height of 50 feet (15 m). Above each block is a video piece of the artist's own design: one block shows a reversed image of a Chicagoan's face, while the other shows a live image of a Chicagoan's face projected onto the solid block. The average visitor to the Crown Fountain will see their reflected image projected onto the smaller, opaque block. THE WICCA OR THE WICCAN RELIGION, IN ITS ANCIENT FORM, WAS NOT A RELIGION BUT A SYSTEM OF WITCHCRAFT.
Its aim was to help mankind to gain knowledge of Nature and the laws of Nature by means of magical experimentation, and to enable those who endeavored to learn to do so in safety.
It was a tradition, a body of knowledge, handed down from teacher to student; and the most important part of it was a solemn oath, taken by all who wished to be initiated, that they would preserve the tradition inviolate, and would hand it down to their successors.
The oath was a compact between the individual and the Craft, and was as binding and as sacred as the most solemn religious vow.
Of course, as time passed the tradition became cloudy and rather confused, and many of the secrets were lost, and those who had the knowledge and knew how to use it were often careless about training their pupils properly, and thus the tradition suffered.
But it was believed that the time would come when all the secrets would be recovered and the tradition perfect again.
The important part of the tradition was the Book of Shadows, which is a book of spells and knowledge of magical experimentation, and secrets of the Craft.
The Book of Shadows was kept by a high priestess (or high priest) and was not allowed to be read by any but the initiated.
The Book of Shadows is a record of all the names and natures of herbs, flowers and trees, their properties and uses, the methods of preparing them, the magic and charm-formulas which can be made from them, and the magical experimentation which can be done with them.
The Book of Shadows is the Bible of the Wica, and it is the Bible of Witchcraft.
The first mention of the Book of Shadows in any literature is in a book by John Dee (1527 – 1609), the celebrated magician and astrologer of the Elizabethan Age.
Dee published a work in three parts in 1582, under the title "Monas Hieroglyphica", in which he said: "Magical operations also have their Monas, which is the book of Art, and contains all the forms of operations, the names of the things to be used, and the properties of them".
Magical operations are the same as magic and magical experimentation, and they are the main object of the Wica.

In 1765 , when he visited the ruins at the site , he found the people of the village collecting large ancient bricks exposed at

the surface and bringing them to the centre of the village to make a new church. What he saw was 'a great many of these bricks, some of them as large as a man's head'.
There was a village church at Petworth from at least the eleventh century, but it was destroyed by Cromwell's army in 1642. The village was then renamed Petworth, after the way it was pronounced in the surrounding area.
The present church was built in 1786-88, and in 1822 a stained glass window was placed in the church as a memorial to the poet William Cowper.
William Cowper (1731-1800) was a member of the religious group known as the Holy Club, which was founded by John Wesley. He attended Oxford University, where he was a friend of Oliver Goldsmith, and he completed his degree in 1749. He was ordained as a clergyman in 1768, and became curate at the church in St. Nicholas, Olney. It was there that he met and became friends with fellow clergyman John Newton.
Newton was a former slave trader who, after a spell at sea, had been converted to Methodism. He was an authority on hymns, and wrote the words to 'Amazing Grace', 'Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken', and 'How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds'. 'Amazing Grace' became so well known that, in the twentieth century, it was adopted as the music for the Negro spiritual 'Sweet Chariot'.
Cowper's poetry was written in a simple style, which made it popular with ordinary people. Many of his poems were written about Christian subjects, and he was a member of the church's official 'standing committee' at Olney. He also wrote a book called _The Task_ in which he described the activities of a country squire, and wrote two plays, _The Woodlanders_ and _The Castle of Fidelity_.
It was during his time at Olney that Cowper met Mary Unwin, who became his housekeeper and companion, and who nursed him through a breakdown. They lived together in the nearby village of Easton, where they were married in 1796.
After Cowper's death, his housekeeper Mary died. In 1822 a stained glass window was placed in the church at Petworth in her memory.

It was during this time that he wrote his famous hymn, 'From Greenland's Icy Mountains', which was inspired by the account of the arrival of a Greenland missionary in Hodnet in 1821.
Reginald Heber was born in Malta in 1783, the son of a chaplain in the Royal Navy. He was educated at Westminster School, and then at Balliol College, Oxford, where he gained first prize in Greek and second in Hebrew. He was ordained in 1805 and appointed to the city of Bristol as curate.

Heber's _Hymns and Other Poems_ was published in 1821, and includes 'From Greenland's Icy Mountains'. In the early twentieth century , archaeological and historical research was conducted regarding a potential connection between

the Trojan War and the Mycenaean Age. The most important result of this research was the discovery of the ancient city of Troy, the authenticity of which was confirmed by Heinrich Schliemann. On the occasion of the excavations, Schliemann's wife,  Agnes Sophie Schliemann, published the novel _Troy_ (1898), in which she described how Agamemnon, during the siege of the city, found his wife Clytemnestra with her lover Aegisthus in a tomb. The story, which the author of the novel told in a more or less realistic way, was the basis for the subsequent tragedies of Euripides _Iphigeneia at Aulis_ (413/2 BCE) and _Iphigeneia in Tauris_ (412/1 BCE), which also tell of the murder of Agamemnon.
 The connection between the death of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra's adultery was first mentioned in the Greek myths, and from the time of the Homeric epics onward, the story of the murder of Agamemnon was widely known. In addition to the tragedies of Euripides, the story was also recounted in the Hellenistic novel _Cassandra_ by Xenophon of Ephesus, in the _Ehoai_ of Lucian of Samosata, and in the _Megalogan_ of Valerius Flaccus. In the novel of the same name by the French writer  Gustave Flaubert, which was published posthumously in 1857, and in the novel by the English writer  Robert Louis Stevenson, _The Silverado Squatters_ , from 1883, the murder of Agamemnon became the central subject.
 Two of the most famous dramatizations of the story of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra are the opera _Agamemnon_ , written by the German composer  Richard Wagner in 1875, and the opera _Agamemnon_ , written by the Albanian composer  Ermanno Wolf-Ferrari in 1908.
 The work of the German philologist and archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann (1822–1890) is of fundamental importance to the history of the ancient world. In 1869, Schliemann conducted the first archaeological excavations at  Mycenae. The results of the excavations, which were also published in his book _Mykenische Funde_ (1878), confirmed the existence of the Mycenaean Age. In 1871, Schliemann conducted the excavations of Priam's citadel at Troy. The archaeological finds, which included the famous "golden" mask, were the evidence that confirmed the authenticity of the city. The results of the excavations were published in the two volumes of the book _Ilios_ (1880–1881) and in the book _Die Alt-Griechische Hygiene_ (1882). The work was continued by Schliemann's wife, Agnes Sophie Schliemann, who participated in the excavations of Hissarlik, the site of Troy, and published the novel _Troy_ (1898).

) began construction of a bridge to carry Route 116 ( Woonsocket Avenue ) over the Pawtuxet River in Cumberland. The bridge was to be located at the northern limit of the project.
By the late 1950s, RIDPW had completed a number of important state highways. The arterial system had been identified in the 1941 Public Works Plan as a major project for the state to undertake with federal aid. The arterial system consisted of a network of spine and collector roads designed to carry traffic from suburban centers to the state's major highways and to each other. By 1960, RIDPW had completed Route 146 , Route 102 , Route 113 , Route 114 , and Route 37 .
Part of the arterial system was Route 116 , a spine highway which connected the communities of Woonsocket , North Smithfield , and Cumberland . The route was approximately 10 miles in length and consisted of portions of Main Street , Mendon Road , and Woonsocket Avenue .
Because of the importance of the route, RIDPW had determined that it was necessary to construct a bridge to carry Route 116 over the Pawtuxet River between Main and Mendon roads. This bridge would effectively complete Route 116 to the north and would also facilitate the future construction of a bypass of Route 116 through the communities of Woonsocket and North Smithfield.
At the time the bridge was proposed, the Pawtuxet River was a free-flowing river with a wide, sandy bed. The proposed bridge would be located in a narrow valley at the northern end of the river.
When RIDPW set out to construct the bridge in 1958, it was faced with several significant problems. The site was located in a narrow valley between steep, wooded hills. The river had a wide, sandy bed and was shallow and wide at the proposed bridge site. The topography of the bridge site was such that the construction of the roadway and bridge would have to be carried out from the river bottom. As a result, the project presented a considerable challenge to the RIDPW engineers.
The bridge was to consist of two spans of 350 feet each. The bridge would be constructed on three piers, one in the center of the river channel and the other two on the river banks. The bridge was to be located just above a point where the river narrowed to a width slightly less than 100 feet.
Problems arose as soon as construction began. The site required special engineering to overcome the difficulty of the location and the topography of the area.

In the club 's early days Athletic struggled to attract crowds of over 150 , but by the time the club reached the Conference ,

Wrexham supporters were coming and taking over the ground .

The club were invited to join the English Football League in 1978 after being promoted from the Alliance Premier League , but they turned down the offer fearing they would not be able to compete at that level.

Having initially refused the offer of League membership , the club changed their stance and in 1992 , they were accepted into the Football League's third tier , the Football Conference .

The club's first season in the Conference saw them move from their original home at the Racecourse to the town's Central Park .

The club's first season in the Conference saw them finish 11th , but in the 1993–94 season , they reached the Conference play-offs , where they were beaten 2–0 by Kidderminster Harriers in the semi-finals .

The club also won their first major piece of silverware , the Welsh Cup in the 1995–96 season , beating Chester City 2–0 in the final.

### Early 2000s

The club reached the Conference play-off final again in 1998 , but they were beaten 3–0 by Bristol Rovers .

The club have continued to be successful on the domestic front , winning the Conference title in 2002–03 , finishing 18 points ahead of second placed Yeovil Town .

The club also won their second Welsh Cup , beating Rhyl 3–0 in the final .

In 2004 , the club became the first Welsh club to reach the League Cup quarter-finals , beating Wolverhampton Wanderers , Preston North End and Nottingham Forest on the way .

The club reached the League Cup semi-finals the next season , but were knocked out by Blackburn Rovers .

In 2006 , the club reached the League Cup final for the third time in their history , but they were beaten 2–1 by Cardiff City .

### 2007–2010

In 2007 , the club signed former England international Robbie Fowler on a three-month deal .

On 19 November 2007 , Wrexham made history by becoming the first Welsh club to reach the FA Cup quarter-finals .

Wrexham secured the Conference title once again in 2008–09 , beating Luton Town 2–0 in their final match of the season , and securing promotion to League Two .

Wrexham beat Yeovil Town 2–1 in the League Two play-off final , and returned to the Football League after a 13-year absence .

In their return to the Football League , Wrexham finished 10th in League Two in their first season , and finished 16th in the following season .

### 2010–2012

In January 2011 , the club announced their intention to leave the Racecourse Ground , and relocate to the new ground by 2013 .

On 19 May 2011 , the club were fined £10,000 and deducted three points for entering into a contract with Wrexham AFC Supporters' Trust (WAST) in September 2009, which was in breach of Football League rules.

On 21 June 2011 , the club were relegated to the Conference Premier , ending their Football League status after just one season.

On 13 March 2012 , the club were relegated to the Conference North , after losing 3–2 at home to Rushden & Diamonds.

### 2012–2013

In December 2012 , the club announced that they would not meet their financial commitments to the Football League , and would face points deductions.

In February 2013 , the club requested a 12-point deduction for the 2012–13 season, which was subsequently granted.

In April 2013 , the club were relegated to the Conference North after finishing 22nd in the Conference Premier, on the same number of points as York City , but with a worse goal difference.

The fieldfare has an extensive range , estimated at 10 million square kilometres ( 3 @.@ 8 million square miles ) , and a large

breeding population estimated at 26 million to 100 million individuals. The population trend has been classified as being stable .
The fieldfare is an uncommon winter visitor to the United Kingdom, but regular in Ireland and the Isle of Man. It is a rare breeding bird in Ireland but regular in Scotland. Its range in Iceland and Greenland is limited to the southwest. It is found in most of Scandinavia, the Baltic region, and the rest of Europe except the Balkans. It is also found in North Africa and western Asia.
It is resident in Siberia, Japan, and the Aleutian Islands .
The fieldfare breeds in northern Europe and Asia. It is migratory in the rest of its range. It is a winter visitor to western Europe, North Africa, and western Asia. Fieldfares arrive in the United Kingdom in late August or early September, but peak numbers do not occur until October. Fieldfares can be found in the United Kingdom until April or May.
The fieldfare is a short-distance migrant, but its exact migratory route is not quite clear. Fieldfares do not travel as far south as the common Redwing, but it is most likely that this species visits the Mediterranean, southern Iberia, North Africa, and the western part of the Middle East. This species might be more mobile than previously thought, as it is known to reach the eastern and central part of Asia during the cold months.
The fieldfare feeds on fruits and berries, and also on insects, worms, and spiders. It roams about in flocks, searching for food. In winter, it may feed on waste grain. It is a frugivore, and a bully, and will chase other species from feeding areas.
A frugivore is an animal that eats fruit.

ries the binding can be monovalent, bivalent, or multi-valent. The forms of binding can be competitive, noncompetitive, uncompetitive, and allosteric, depending on the type of binding.
The amino acids that are involved in protein-protein binding are often called helix, sheet, and strand. The functions of binding are often as enzymes or as scaffolding molecules.
Proteins can also bind to cells, to DNA, to RNA, to membranes, to small molecule substrates, and to many other components of living cells.
The binding of proteins to cells, membranes, and small molecules is almost always noncovalent.
A molecule that can bind to cell membranes and that also can bind to cell proteins is called a receptor. A receptor can be a protein, a lipid, or a carbohydrate.
Proteins that bind to cells can be either enzymes or effectors.
Proteins that bind to DNA or to RNA are called transcription factors. Proteins that bind to DNA or to RNA can also be called effectors.
There are many kinds of proteins in living organisms. Some proteins bind to other proteins. Some proteins bind to cells, membranes, DNA, and RNA. Some proteins bind to small molecule substrates. Some proteins bind to other proteins in ways that are competitive, noncompetitive, uncompetitive, and allosteric.

In the three years since the publication of this book, I have been repeatedly asked if I have any regrets about it. I have to say that my conscience is clear. I did not write the book to offend any of the individuals mentioned in it, nor did I set out to impugn their personal or professional integrity. I do not believe that I have done so. I have never claimed that they are all corrupt.
Certain events and statements in the book are incontrovertible: the president's speech on 15 May 2008 was made; his whistle-stop tour of Kinshasa, Brazzaville and Bujumbura really did take place; the meeting between the foreign ministers of the three countries was held. There is no doubt about these facts, and the circumstances which led to them are also clear.
I have taken care to stick strictly to my sources, and to base my conclusions on what they say. I have tried to speak to the individuals concerned, but, as I have explained, I was simply informed that I had no right to speak to them. In the case of Jean-Marie Mabila, I was told that he was not available because he was not in Kinshasa.
The only person who has questioned the book's accuracy is Jean-Édouard Thouvenel, whose evidence is not confirmed by the other sources. Thouvenel has never denied the events described in the book, and I believe that I have demonstrated beyond any doubt that they did take place. I am confident that no court would find that I have in any way abused his right to a private life.
But it is true that I could have included more information. I could have included a list of all the people who had been involved in the deal, and I could have explained why the deal was cancelled. All these questions are answered in the book. They have not explained what happened to the money, or how it was returned to the three countries. They have not explained why the anticorruption unit in the Ministry of the Economy was not effective in fighting corruption.

The Met Office was the first to issue advisories on the storm , with BoM issuing advisories from two days later .
The United States National Hurricane Centre ( NHC ) issued advisories on the storm , using the advisory format used for tropical cyclones in the North-West Pacific basin . The United Kingdom ' s Met Office issued advisories on the storm , using the advisory format used for tropical cyclones in the North-West Indian Ocean basin .
Domoina was upgraded to Tropical Cyclone status by the Australian Bureau of Meteorology ( BoM ) on February 18 , 2002 , at 0600 UTC .

Somalia 's military, the Somali National Army ( SNA ), was one of the biggest recipients of international aid, with $150 million pledged in 1994 alone.  The military was also one of the most corrupt institutions in the country.  According to a 1995 report, the military was rife with racketeering and extortion, and its officers portrayed the SNA as a government institution when in fact they had little to do with the actual government.
By 1997, the SNA had become a power unto itself, and had become heavily involved in extortion, protection rackets, drug trafficking, and robbery.  The SNA had become so powerful and independent that they were able to finance their operations through extortion, protection rackets, and blackmail.  According to the International Crisis Group, the SNA was responsible for 40% of all extortion in the country.
Under the Barre regime, Somalia 's economy was ranked 20th in the world in terms of GDP in 1980.  By 1990, however, the country ranked 159th in the world in terms of GDP per capita.  By 1992, the value of the Somali shilling had dropped to the point where one shilling was equal to about 25 U.S. cents.  As a result, prices of goods and services soared.  Furthermore, the country was suffering from recurring crop failures and an influx of refugees from the civil wars in Ethiopia and Eritrea .
The country was suffering from a widespread famine in 1992, and the number of Somalis living in refugee camps in Kenya and Ethiopia was growing.  In 1993, famine struck again, this time affecting 1.4 million Somalis.
The 1992 famine was blamed on the government's inability to carry out agricultural policies and its failure to create effective famine relief relief efforts.  However, as the government was disintegrating and Barre was out of power, the famine relief effort was slow and ineffective.  The result was a death toll of more than 200,000 Somalis.
Somalia 's economy was further crippled by the civil war in 1993.  The economy of Mogadishu , which had been the commercial center of the country, was almost completely destroyed.  An estimated 80% of the population was unemployed, and the average income per person was less than $1 per day.
Somalia 's currency, the shilling, had so little value that it was almost impossible to buy basic necessities such as sugar, salt, or detergent.  Somalis who wanted to purchase these items had to barter with merchants.  The economy was further ravaged by the heavy taxation of the central government, which led to a black market that was controlled by the warlords.  The black market was used by the warlords to finance their operations.
An additional factor in the decline of the economy was the lack of revenue generated by the government.  In 1992, the central government was forced to lay off 80% of its workers, and the reduced government revenue had a negative effect on the economy as a whole.
The loss of revenue resulted in a decrease in public services, and the healthcare system became completely neglected.  The government was unable to provide essential medicines, and the number of hospitals and clinics declined from 200 to only 70.  The healthcare system also suffered from the lack of basic sanitary facilities and lack of clean water, and the country was plagued with a widespread cholera outbreak.
The country's economy was also suffering from the lack of basic infrastructure.  The road system was almost completely destroyed, and the country was cut in half by the civil war.  The lack of basic infrastructure led to a lack of tourism, which was once an important part of the country's economy.
The lack of economic activity and the lack of basic infrastructure also had a negative impact on the country's education system.  The majority of schools were destroyed during the civil war, and many of the remaining schools were in poor condition.  Furthermore, the lack of basic infrastructure prevented students from getting to school.

The governor was to be from the Church of England, though other denominations were allowed to worship freely, and anyone who wanted to settle in the colony was to be allowed to do so. The design of what became the O 'Brien class was the result of discussions between the General Board of the United States Navy

(GB) and members of the Chief of Naval Operations  (CNO) staff. The Board submitted to the CNO on April 11, 1944, a recommendation that the Navy commence detailed design of an 8-inch (203-mm) gun-armed cruiser. The Board believed that such a class of ships was essential to ensure that the United States would retain naval superiority over Japan once the Pacific war had been won. The O 'Brien class was to serve as a ship for convoy escort, commerce protection, anti-aircraft duty, and bombardment of shore installations. The first two ships were to be completed as soon as practicable, and the remainder were to follow in order of priority as authorized by the CNO.
The designers were faced with a number of problems that included the handling characteristics of a ship of this size and the adequacy of her defenses against air attack. The Board and CNO staff agreed that too much emphasis had been placed on the speed of the light cruisers and that what had been lacking was adequate protection. The O 'Brien class was to have twice the armor of the light cruisers and to be armed with a powerful gun battery that would provide protection against any air attack that could be launched against it.
The O 'Brien class was to be 190 feet (58 meters) long, displacing about 12,000 tons, and capable of developing 33 knots (38 miles per hour/61 kilometers per hour) on her two boilers. The designers were able to achieve a sufficient reduction in weight from the light cruiser to allow the hull to be kept down to a 20-foot (6-meter) draft. The crew was to consist of 1,400 officers and men. The ship would be protected by 2.5 inches (64 millimeters) of armor on her main belt and 1 inch (25 millimeters) on her deck.
The O 'Brien-class cruisers were equipped with eight 8-inch (203-mm) guns in four turrets and sixteen 5-inch (127-mm) guns mounted in twin turrets at the corners of the ship. They were also armed with twenty-four 40-mm and twelve 20-mm gun mounts. The cruisers were originally equipped with two 5-inch (127-mm) high-angle gun turrets mounted over the forward superstructure but these guns were removed before the ships were delivered to the fleet.
The O 'Brien class was equipped with a large flight deck aft, capable of handling a single floatplane, and was equipped with an ASW helicopter hangar. The hangar was located on the port side amidships.
The design of the O 'Brien class was further modified by a decision of the General Board in October 1944. The Board recommended that the length of the hull be increased by 8 feet (2.4 meters) and the mast height increased by 9 feet (2.7 meters). The designers were able to achieve this by increasing the height of the forecastle and deck house and by the addition of a forecastle house. The modifications increased the weight of the ships to about 12,400 tons.
The entire design was the subject of a protest by the New York Yacht Club. The protest centered on the lack of a raked bow, which the NYC believed was a serious naval design disadvantage. The protest was unsuccessful.
 The O'Brien-class cruisers were built by Bethlehem Hingham Shipyard, Hingham, Massachusetts, and Bethlehem Steel Company, Fore River Shipyard, Quincy, Massachusetts, and were completed in 1945 and 1946.

In DEA, the primary purpose is to calculate the efficiency of a decision-making unit (DMU), defined as its ability to improve the efficiency of another DMU (the basic idea is that one DMU can transfer its superiority to another one). Efficiency is expressed as the maximal ratio of the weights of inputs and outputs between the two DMUs. In many applications, the weights of the inputs and outputs are given, but the weights of the inputs of the output are not known. DEA may be used to determine the optimal output from each DMU, given the inputs.

The miners' action was as shocking to the British public—which had never seen such organization of working-class power—as it was to the government. In the late nineteenth century, British public opinion was so firmly behind the state that a slogan that summed up the attitude of many was "Whoever said the people were sovereign meant the government." The government was seen as omniscient, omnipotent, and benevolent. It was certainly not held responsible for the misery of the British working people. The government, in turn, believed that it alone was responsible for the nation's welfare. It saw the working people as a collection of children in need of guidance; even when it tried to "help" the working class, it commonly did so by providing only a pittance or some clothing. The government also believed that the working class, like a child, needed to be disciplined, and that the state was responsible for that discipline. The miners' strike was an attack on that view of the state, a strike against the state itself, and it was quickly put down, with 65 miners killed.
A few weeks after the strike, the British government passed the Criminal Law Amendment Act, a law that, among other provisions, made it illegal to persuade workers not to join a union. The British government had a huge fear of revolution, as did most of the other advanced capitalist countries in the nineteenth century. The British government believed that the reason these other countries had not had revolutions was that their governments had organized them, and they wanted to be sure that they could do the same. The British government also had a fear of the general strike, which it knew was a tactic that would be used to organize working-class revolt. But it was not only the working class that was to be organized; the British government wanted to organize all of society, including the middle class.
The British government was not the only one to be afraid of the general strike, for it was a tactic that other advanced capitalist countries used as well. The general strike was seen as the ultimate form of working-class organization, and the working class was threatening to use it. The British government was determined to make sure it could not.
The Criminal Law Amendment Act was one of many laws that the British government passed to limit the power of workers to organize. But the British government feared that workers would not accept this limitation. It was more than a little frustrated when it discovered that workers did accept it. In 1889, for example, the British government passed the Trade Union Act, which allowed workers to form unions, but which also gave the government power to dissolve unions, and, as it was to do a few years later, to ban strikes. But the workers accepted the law.
Why did the British working class accept such limitations on its power? The answer is that workers in the advanced capitalist countries filled their lives with many other forms of organization. They worked in trade unions, which were so numerous that it was not possible for a single union to take on the entire state. They organized themselves in the armed forces and the police, which had been set up to suppress their revolutionary tendencies but which they used instead to organize their working lives. They formed sports clubs, which were a powerful form of organization. They even formed religious groups, which were so numerous that they were a major force in British society. They organized themselves in their communities and in their neighborhoods, and they organized themselves in their families.
The British working class was able to organize itself in so many ways because it had a strong tradition of organization. The British working class had long been one of the most organized working classes in the world. The tradition of organization went back to the 1830s and the Chartists, a working-class movement that had organized itself to demand universal suffrage. The tradition was further developed in the 1860s by the First International, one of the first international labor organizations. It was further developed by the trade unions, which were the first modern organizations to organize workers by occupation, and by the Fabians, a group of intellectuals who were the first to develop a theory of how working-class power could be organized.

Mozambique is a low-lying country with a 2,470-km (1,535-mi) coastline on the Indian Ocean. It is bordered by Tanzania to the north, Malawi, Zambia, and Zimbabwe to the northwest, South Africa and Swaziland to the southwest, and the Republic of South Africa to the south and southeast. Mozambique, a former Portuguese colony, became independent in 1975 after a protracted struggle for liberation from Portuguese colonial rule.
The country's population is predominantly of Bantu origin, with a small proportion of Indo-Mozambicans. The official language, Portuguese, is spoken by a majority of the population as a second language.
Geographically, Mozambique is one of the world's most diverse countries. The country's landscape ranges from wide plateaus to tropical coastal plains, mountainous areas, and lowlands.

Tautiška giesmė ( The National Hymn ) is the national anthem of Lithuania , also known by its opening words " Lietuva , Tėvyne

".

Tautiška giesmė

The anthem was written by Vincas Kudirka in 1898, and the lyrics were written in 1899 by Vincas Mykolaitis-Putinas. The music was composed by Kudirka.

The words are sometimes translated as "Lithuania, [the land of] our fathers", although the translation used by the Lithuanian government is "Lithuania, our beloved land."

The melody is in the key of C major.

Although "Tautiška giesmė" was adopted as the national anthem of Lithuania in 1918, it was banned by the Soviet Union when Lithuania was occupied in 1940. It was reinstated after Lithuania regained independence in 1990. The music was slightly modified in 2004 to reflect the new spelling of the Lithuanian language.

## History

### Vincas Kudirka

Vincas Kudirka was born in 1858 in Lithuania. His father, a farmer, was a member of the Lithuanian National Revival Movement, which was a pro-independence movement. Vincas Kudirka was educated in religious schools, where he and his brother Jonas experienced religious persecution. He spent four years in military service, and volunteered for the Polish-Lithuanian army in the war against the Russian Empire.

In 1894, Kudirka settled in Chicago. He worked as a baker and as a journalist, writing for various Lithuanian-language newspapers. He was a member of the Lithuanian National Drama Society, and a founder and editor of several Lithuanian-language newspapers.

### Vincas Mykolaitis-Putinas

Vincas Mykolaitis-Putinas was born in 1869 in Lithuania. He was educated in a Catholic high school, and he taught there after his graduation. He also graduated from seminary, but did not become a priest. From 1903 to 1904, he was a professor of history at a Lithuanian high school in Chicago.

He wrote the lyrics to "Tautiška giesmė" in 1899. The lyrics were first published in 1904 in the Chicago Lithuanian-language newspaper Ausra.

### Selection as national anthem

A competition to select a national anthem was announced in 1917. A panel of judges chose "Tautiška giesmė" as the winner. It was first performed on 18 November 1917, and it was officially adopted as the national anthem of Lithuania on 18 March 1918, when Lithuania declared independence from Russia.

### Soviet occupation

Main article: Soviet occupation of Lithuania

In 1940, Lithuania was occupied by the Soviet Union. The Soviet government banned the use of the anthem. The Soviet Union also made changes to the spelling of the Lithuanian language, and the anthem was later adapted to reflect these changes.

### Post-Soviet independence

In 1988, the Soviet Union granted Lithuania the right to secede. Lithuania declared independence on 11 March 1990. The anthem was reinstated. In 1992, the Lithuanian government adopted the spelling of the Lithuanian language that was used in the second printing of the anthem in 1991. The words "Tėvyne" (lit. "Our fatherland") were officially changed to "Tėvyne į aukų" ("To our ancestors") in 2004.

### Protests

Lithuania's president, Dalia Grybauskaitė, attended the 2010 UEFA European Football Championship in Poland and Ukraine. During the championship, she was booed and heckled by some Lithuanian fans when the national anthem was played. The president responded by saying she would not attend another such event. She also said that the booing was "unacceptable".

It has been argued that the play 's themes of duplicity and ambivalence are inextricably bound up with Wilde 's homosexuality ,

but others have pointed out that the play can be interpreted as a warning about the dangers of false values and blind obedience to authority.
For example, the audience is encouraged to sympathise with Lord Illingworth, the protagonist of A Woman of No Importance, a man who has publicly announced that he has left his wife, and has since kept a mistress in London.
You are making a mistake, my dear fellow.
You don 't know me.
The audience is also invited to admire Mrs Arbuthnot, John Gerald 's aunt, who has refused to marry a man she does not love, but who has also spent time in prison for her principles.
The play's best-known character is Lord Illingworth, who, as he tells Hester, is a "man of the world".
He is a man who knows, and admires, "all the charming things of life" and is not particularly interested in work or politics.
He has married, at least in name, but has never seen his wife and has spent time with a succession of mistresses in London.
He is a man who likes roses, music and art, and who has a "bouquet of flowers" in his pocket.
He is a thoroughly modern character, whose only interest is himself and his own enjoyment.
He is, in fact, a personification of the "aesthetic" movement of the times.
The play's name, in fact, is a pun.
The play is set at a small country house in London in 1893, the year in which Wilde went to prison.
The play takes place in a room furnished in "Alhambra red" and "lavender", the colours of the aesthetic movement.
Hester is implied to be a member of the movement, which is in many ways a rebellion against the values of the Victorian era.
She likes to keep a "sylvan" house, and is condemned by the aunt for being a "free-thinker".
But Lord Illingworth, a man of the world, has no time for such ideals.
He is a man who is ultimately concerned only with his own pleasures.
This is a common theme in Wilde's plays.
In Lady Windermere's Fan, for example, Lord Darlington is similarly concerned only with his own pleasures, and the play is ultimately a criticism of such a man.
The play also explores the theme of duplicity and ambivalence.
Lord Illingworth, for example, is constantly changing his opinions, and is, in fact, two people in one.
He is a man who is both a "man of the world" and a "man of the people".
He is also a man who is, in one sense, conservative, but who is, in another sense, modern.
He may be a "man of the people" in some ways, but he is also a man who is constantly changing his opinions and his beliefs.
Lord Illingworth is also a man of great wealth, and he is, in a sense, a "man of means".
He lives in a large house in London and has a large staff.
He is also a man who is, in fact, a "man of the law".
He is a lawyer who is also a member of Parliament.
The play is, in fact, a critique of the values of Victorian society, and the playwright argues that the Victorian age was a time of great change, and that this change was ultimately good.
The play, in other words, is an argument against the idea that the Victorian Age was a period of great uniformity.
The play also explores themes of social justice.
The aunt, for example, is a woman who works for a living, and she is condemned by the other characters for being a "workhouse woman".
The play also critiques the idea, in the Victorian era, that all women were expected to be housewives.
The play is also a critique on the idea in the Victorian Age, that women were supposed to be servants to men.
The play is a criticism of what is often called "the cult of the female" in the Victorian period, and Wilde is, in fact, an advocate of the idea that women should be allowed to work in a variety of occupations, such as nursing and teaching.
The play also has a strong focus on love, which is, in many ways, a central theme in the play.
The characters are all deeply concerned with their love lives, and they spend much of the play discussing love, and how to pursue it
